1965-03-16.label: Mike Ducy Early Personal Log
1965-03-16.attribution: Mike Ducy Early Personal Log — Ducy Family Archives
1965-03-16.text:
MIKE DUCY — EARLY PERSONAL LOG
Handwritten, 3 pages, blue ink
Covers March 16, 1965 through September 27, 1967

Mike's chronological record of his Navy career milestones from enlistment
through reporting aboard USS Jouett.

========================================================================================
PAGE 1
========================================================================================

16 MAR 1965
  Enlisted in the Naval Reserve as [rate obscured] for six years as a 2x6 en.

JUN. 1965
  Attended RTC at Great Lakes for 2 weeks.

JUN. 1965
  Advanced to E2 (Seaman) upon return from boot camp.

11 JUN 1966
  Attended Ashore/Afloat school at Great Lakes for two weeks.
  Spent one week aboard USS Havre (PCE).

25 JUN 1966
  Advanced to E3 (Seaman) upon return from Ashore/Afloat school.


========================================================================================
PAGE 2
========================================================================================

4 DEC. 1966
  Attended Class "A" FT School at Great Lakes for 18 weeks.

21 APRIL 1967
  Graduated from Class "A" FT School as a FTGSN and returned home.

21 JULY 1967
  Took FTG3 advancement test at USNRTC Decatur, Ill.

16 AUG. 1967
  Reported to Treasure Is., SF, Calif. for assignment to duty station
  for 2 years active duty.

12 SEP. '67
  Trans. to S. Diego, Calif. to await USS Jouett (DLG-29)


========================================================================================
PAGE 3
========================================================================================

26 SEPT '67
  Trans. from S.D. Calif. to Bremerton, Washington to report
  aboard USS Jouett.

27 SEPT. '67
  Reported aboard USS Jouett at 1407 date.


========================================================================================
TIMELINE SUMMARY
========================================================================================

  Mar 16, 1965  Enlisted Naval Reserve, Decatur, IL (6-year obligation, 2x6)
  Jun 1965      RTC (Recruit Training Command) boot camp, Great Lakes, 2 weeks
  Jun 1965      Advanced to E-2 (Seaman Apprentice)
  Jun 11, 1966  Ashore/Afloat school, Great Lakes, 2 weeks (1 week on USS Havre)
  Jun 25, 1966  Advanced to E-3 (Seaman)
  Dec 4, 1966   Class "A" FT School begins, Great Lakes (18 weeks)
  Apr 21, 1967  Graduated FT "A" School as FTGSN (Fire Control Technician Gun SN)
  Jul 21, 1967  FTG3 advancement test, USNRTC Decatur
  Aug 16, 1967  Reported to Treasure Island, San Francisco (active duty assignment)
  Sep 12, 1967  Transferred to San Diego to await Jouett
  Sep 26, 1967  Transferred to Bremerton, WA to report aboard Jouett
  Sep 27, 1967  Reported aboard USS Jouett (DLG-29) at 1407

1965-06-01.label: Company A-44 Boot Camp Graduation Photo
1965-06-01.attribution: Company A-44 Boot Camp Graduation Photo — Ducy Family Archives
1965-06-01.text:
COMPANY A-44 BOOT CAMP GRADUATION PHOTO — U.S. NAVAL TRAINING CENTER, GREAT LAKES, ILL. (~June 1965)

[Color photograph: Formal group portrait of approximately 60 recruits of Company A-44, U.S. Naval Training Center, Great Lakes, Illinois. The company is arranged in eight rows on indoor steps/risers beneath red lettering reading "U.S. NAVAL TRAINING CENTER / GREAT LAKES, ILL." on the wall behind them.

All recruits wear undress whites (white working uniform) with white dixie cup hats. In the front row center stands the Company Commander, an African American petty officer (appears to be a First Class Petty Officer based on visible rating badge) wearing dress whites with black neckerchief — the only member in formal dress uniform. To his left, a recruit kneels holding the company guidon, a blue pennant bearing "A 44" in white lettering on a staff.

The young recruits appear to be in their late teens to early twenties. Several wear glasses. Mike Ducy (future FTG3, USS Jouett DLG-29) is among the approximately 60 men pictured, though his specific position in the group has not been identified.

This photograph was taken upon graduation from Recruit Training Command (boot camp), approximately May-June 1965. Mike enlisted and reported to Great Lakes around March 1965 (his early personal log begins March 16, 1965). Boot camp was approximately 9 weeks, placing graduation in approximately May-June 1965.]

1966-09-09.label: MC CREARY to Mike - FT School Selection
1966-09-09.attribution: MC CREARY to Mike - FT School Selection — Ducy Family Archives
1966-09-09.text:
MASTER CHIEF CREARY TO MIKE — FT SCHOOL SELECTION NOTIFICATION
September 9, 1966
1 page, handwritten letter

========================================================================================
TRANSCRIPTION
========================================================================================

                                                          9 Sept 1966

Mr. Michael F. Ducy
1525 N. Ellen St.
Decatur, Illinois


Dear Mike:

Just got the word!  You have been selected to attend FT "A" school
in Great Lakes, Illinois.  Your class convenes 5 December 1966.
You will be leaving here late November.

Just one catch!  You will have to be given a SECRET clearance.
Please fill out the enclosed forms and return them to me for typing.


                              Sincerely,
                              MC CREARY

[Handwritten notes/numbers visible in margins]


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

MC CREARY = Master Chief CREARY (MCPO, E-9), the senior enlisted
leader at NRTC Decatur, Illinois (Naval Reserve Training Center,
Lake Shore Drive). This letter notifies Mike of his selection for
Fire Control Technician "A" School at Great Lakes.

Key details:
- Class convening date: 5 December 1966 (confirmed by FT A School
  Class 2163-66 Roster and Active Duty Orders of Oct 26, 1966)
- Departure: late November 1966
- Requirement: SECRET security clearance
- Enclosed forms: security clearance paperwork for Mike to complete

This letter predates the formal Active Duty Orders (Oct 26, 1966)
by about six weeks, suggesting MC CREARY passed the news informally
before official orders were cut. The tone is enthusiastic and
personal — "Just got the word!" — indicating a close working
relationship between Mike and his reserve unit staff.

1966-12-01.text:
TRAINEE INDOCTRINATION AND INSTRUCTIONS — SERVICE SCHOOL COMMAND, USNTC GREAT LAKES (~December 1966)

Source: 5 scans (cover + introduction/pg 1 + pg 2-3 + pg 4-5 + pg 6)
Document: 9ND P 3838 (Rev. 5-66)
Reviewed and Approved: 13 May 1966
Signed by: W. A. ROBIE, Captain, U.S. Navy, Commanding Officer

---

[COVER]

[Handwritten notes by Mike Ducy, in blue ink:]
[Upper left corner, circled:] 2B
[Below title, scattered notes:]
603 B.C.
300 Awaitee Havre check in
P.H. 214    Throat Culture

Trainee Indoctrination
and Instructions

[Emblem: Shield with crossed wrenches, banner reading "TRAINING PRECEDES VICTORY", text inside shield: "SERVICE SCHOOL COMMAND / U.S.N.T.C. / GREAT LAKES / ILL."]

SERVICE SCHOOL COMMAND
U. S. NAVAL TRAINING CENTER
Great Lakes, Illinois

---

[INTRODUCTION AND PAGE 1]

Introduction

The purpose of this information pamphlet is to familiarize you with the organization and regulations of the Service School Command.

An organization chart posted in each school will explain the chain of command. Requests MUST go through the chain of command. The easiest way to solve personal problems is via the chain of command. Never hesitate to bring your problems to the attention of your section counselor or instructor. He will advise or direct you to the proper person or office that will help you resolve your problem.

This pamphlet prescribes the regulations and standards of conduct you must observe while attached to the Service School Command. Familiarity with these regulations will prevent you from committing an offense unknowingly. Learn these regulations and abide by them, they are for the common good of all.

Remember always that the mission of the Service School Command is to prepare you for a useful future in the service of our country and to assist you in attaining a successful and profitable career.

The Commanding Officer extends an invitation to your family to attend your graduation exercise. He also will welcome correspondence from them at any time.

REVIEWED AND APPROVED 13 MAY 1966

[Signature: W. A. Robie]
W. A. ROBIE
CAPTAIN, U.S. NAVY
COMMANDING OFFICER

9ND P 3838 (Rev. 5-66)

---

MISSION

The mission of Service School Command is: "To administer those schools assigned to the Service School Command by the Chief of Naval Personnel which train selected officer and enlisted personnel, including the Naval Reserve, in order to prepare them for early usefulness afloat in their designated specialty and to supplement training afloat by providing advanced and/or specialized training when such training can be given more advantageously ashore.

REGULATIONS

Regulations are necessary for the safe and efficient operation of any organization. In an organization as large and complex as the Navy, it is necessary to have rules to insure uniform performance throughout all components. Each individual command must have additional regulations to cover situations peculiar to it's locality and mission. Prior to reading the pertinent Service School Command instructions, read the following excerpts from your enlistment contract. These quotes will remind you of your obligations to the Navy and the United States of America.

"For and in consideration of the pay of wages due to the ratings which may from time to time be assigned me during continuance of my service, I agree to and with (name of enlisting officer) of the United States Navy, as follows: First: To enter the service of the Navy of the United States and to report to such station or vessel of the Navy as I may be ordered to join, and to the utmost of my power and ability discharge my naval service or duties and be in everything conformable and obedient to the several requirements and lawful commands of the officers who may be placed over me ."

"OATH OF ALLEGIANCE: I, ........................ do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the United States of America: that I will serve them honestly and faithfully against all their enemies whomsoever; and that I will obey the orders of the officers appointed over me, according to the regulations and the Uniform Code of Military Justice."

SIGNED BY ALL PERSONS ENLISTED IN THE NAVY

-1-

---

[PAGES 2-3]

1. UNIFORMS and PERSONAL GROOMING
   a. The uniform of the day as prescribed in the Plan of the Day shall be worn:
      (1) In classrooms.
      (2) To the messhall, exchange, cafeteria, club and movies.
      (3) At the 1800 muster.
   b. A full seabag is required.
      (1) Uniforms must be cleaned, pressed, and in good repair.
      (2) Shoes must be shined.
   c. A clean shave and neatly trimmed hair is required at all times.
      (No haircutting is allowed in the barracks at any time. Wearing mustaches and/or beards must be authorized by the Commanding Officer or Executive Officer.)
   d. Identification tags will be worn. However, every effort should be made to prevent chains holding tags, medals, keys, etc., from hanging outside your clothing. (This is a safety hazard when working on or around electrical devices and equipment.)

2. INSPECTIONS (SSC INSTR. 1010.1 series)
   a. Daily — by class advisor.
   b. Weekly — by assigned chief.
   c. Monthly — by Officer-in-Charge or his designated representative.
   d. Locker inspection — when called. (No advance notice)

3. LEAVE
   a. Annual leave for student personnel: Annual leave will normally not be granted to student personnel under or awaiting instruction except during holiday periods as authorized by the Chief of Naval Personnel. Special notices will be published concerning procedures to be followed in granting leave to student personnel during holiday periods.
   b. Emergency leave: Leave is granted when the existing situation warrants. The emergency must be verified by the American Red Cross.

-2-

4. LIBERTY

Student liberty will be granted in accordance with SSC Instruction 1050.2 series. Seventy-two hour passes will be granted by special request only. All hands must be aboard on inspection Saturdays until after inspection. Special requests will be filled out in duplicate on the proper form, submitted to your instructor and then to the general office for approval.

5. OUT OF BOUNDS

Request for out of bounds passes will be filled out on the proper form and submitted to your instructor or class counselor. Approved request may be picked up from the Duty Petty Officer before departing on liberty. An out of bounds pass must be obtained to travel beyond the 100 mile limit while on liberty. The limits on out of bounds distances are: 250 miles for privately owned vehicles, and 300 miles on commercial transportation when a ticket is held. An out of bounds pass does not authorize leave or liberty.

6. CIVILIAN CLOTHING

Non-rated trainees are not allowed to keep civilian clothing aboard the station. (SSC INSTR. 1020.3 series)

7. AUTOMOBILES

Trainees are not permitted to have automobiles aboard the station. Exceptions are specifically authorized in SSC INSTR. 5450.1 series.

8. HITCH-HIKING

Is strictly forbidden (SSC INSTR. 5450.1 series) and is against Illinois State law.

9. DRINKING
   a. No person under 21 years of age is permitted to consume alcoholic beverages of any type within geographical limits of the Ninth Naval District, unless authorized by the applicable state laws (9ND INST 5800.4A). Illinois does not permit possession or consumption of alcoholic beverages by persons under 21 years of age.
   b. No person is permitted to keep or consume any alcoholic beverage in any barracks (SSC INST 5450.1C)

-3-

---

[PAGES 4-5]

10. PROFANITY
    NOT TOLERATED!!

11. MARRIAGE

You must submit notification of marriage intentions to the Commanding Officer via the chain of command. Forms may be obtained from your instructor. (SSC INSTR. 1752.1 series).

12. SMOKING

There will be no smoking in any formation, when walking on the streets, in barracks berthing areas, or in any classrooms.

13. GAMBLING

Gambling in ANY form is strictly prohibited.

14. MILITARY COURTESY

All persons shall observe and exercise appropriate courtesies on all occasions when and where applicable.

15. DUTY

All duty section personnel shall remain in the barracks except when on watch, at meals, or when permission is granted by proper authority to be away from the barracks.

16. WATCHES

All trainees should expect to be assigned watches when his Section has the duty. Persons assigned the watch will:
   a. Sign the watch bill posted at MAA Office.
   b. Place an appropriate call with the Barrack's sentry if his watch occurs between 2200 and 0600.
   c. Wear the prescribed uniform of the day.
   d. Become familiar with the instructions for the watch and observe all orders/instructions applicable to the post.
   e. Be prompt in assuming the watch and relieving others for meals.

17. MESSING FORMATION

All hands are required to proceed to the messhall for the noon meal in a military formation in accordance with the messing schedule for their school/barracks.

-4-

18. CANDY AND SOFT DRINKS

No candy, soft drinks, coffee or food of any type are to be consumed in classrooms. Food should be consumed in designated areas before entering classrooms.

19. PAY DAY

Service School students are paid by check every other Tuesday. Check cashing service is available in Building 211 on Tuesdays and Thursdays of each week. The hours for this service are: 1000-1400
                                                    1600-1800
Other check cashing services on the base are located in Building 111 Main Exchange and the bank located in Building 3.

20. LITERATURE

Only printed material authorized by the Officer-in-Charge will be brought into school buildings. Non-technical books, newspapers, magazines, or pocket books are NOT allowed in school buildings.

21. RADIOS

No radios of any type are allowed in school buildings except in spaces authorized by the Officers-in-Charge.

22. BARRACKS REGULATIONS

Rules and regulations for your barracks will be posted on the barracks bulletin board.

23. SCHOLASTIC PARTICIPATION
    a. A maximum effort for scholastic participation is required of all trainees. You must ask questions and contribute to class discussions.
    b. No effort toward participation indicates a lack of interest and in-attention to duty which can result in disciplinary action.

24. CONDUCT IN CLASS

Sleeping in class, failure to do assigned homework, and lack of full effort are violations of Article 92, UCMJ, and may subject you to Captain's Mast. It can result in a Drop D. If you receive a Drop D, you forfeit your chance to attend another school during your current enlistment.

-5-

---

[PAGE 6]

25. EXTRA SUPERVISED STUDY

Training Division Officers are authorized to require trainee's attendance at Compulsory Additional Study on week day evenings and Saturday mornings when the marks of such trainees do not meet the minimum designated standards, regardless of the trainee's liberty status on the day in question.

Additional voluntary study outside of the regular classroom period is required to complete homework assignments. Those who desire may take advantage of facilities provided in voluntary night study rooms. Staff instructors are assigned to assist with study problems.

26. CLASSROOM BOOKS AND EQUIPMENT

Students are responsible for the care and return of any books that are issued to them. Each piece of equipment in the school is accounted for. Do not remove any equipment from the classroom. Report any lost or damaged equipment to the instructor. Class room equipment and training aids are not to be used except under the supervision of the instructor.

27. CHEATING

In the Service School Command, as in any other school organization, cheating is strictly prohibited. By definition, "to cheat" means to defeat the purpose of. Any one acting so as to defeat the purpose of an examination, test or quiz is guilty of cheating. During an examination, test or quiz, students are forbidden to communicate with each other, to copy answers of any other examinee, or have in their possession any notes, cribs or unauthorized books or devices that might conceivably be used to assist them in answering the questions of such examination, test or quiz. Copies of the examination, test or quiz, or notes concerning them will not be taken or removed from the classroom without the instructor's permission.

28. RECREATIONAL FACILITIES

There are many recreational facilities located on the Naval Training Center. Consult the Great Lakes Bulletin, published weekly, for particular areas and hours of recreation.

-6-

Grade tracking sheet for FT (Fire Control Technician) "A" School Class 2163-66
at Service School Command, Naval Training Center, Great Lakes, Illinois. The class
convened December 5, 1966 and graduated April 21, 1967 — an 18-week course.

23 students are listed. Mike Ducy (DUCY, M.F.) sat in Row 2, Seat 7, rated SN
(Seaman) with the annotation USNR-R (U.S. Naval Reserve — Regular). He graduated
as FTGSN (Fire Control Technician Gun, Seaman).

GIVEN, W.F. (Row 3, Seat 4) is the same W.F. Given who later served with Mike
aboard USS Jouett (DLG-29) as an FTG-3. Given wrote Mike a letter dated June 20,
1968 (already in the collection). This roster confirms they were classmates at
FT School before being assigned to the same ship — a connection that began at
Great Lakes and continued into the Tonkin Gulf.

The grade columns are blank, suggesting this was the master roster template rather
than a filled-in weekly grade sheet. The form tracked daily quizzes (20 pts) and
weekly exams (80 pts) for a 100-point final mark.

The mix of SN (Seaman) and SA (Seaman Apprentice) rates reflects different
enlistment paths — some students entered with higher rates from prior service
or reserve training. Several have reserve designators (USNR-R, NR-R), indicating
they were reservists called to active duty or transitioning to regular Navy,
like Mike.

1966-12-16.text:
DEPARTMENT OF THE NAVY
SERVICE SCHOOL COMMAND
U. S. NAVAL TRAINING CENTER
GREAT LAKES, ILLINOIS 60088

                                                    IN REPLY REFER TO:

                                                    ARE/pmw
                                                    16 December 1966

Mrs. Dan Ducy
1525 N. Ellen
Decatur, Illinois 62521

Dear Mr. Ducy,

    It is my pleasure to inform you that your son is enrolled in the latest class of the Fire Control Technician's "A" School here at Great Lakes.

    As you may or may not already know, Fire Control is the technique of controlling the fire power of the many complex weapon systems used on our Navy vessels today. This means not only the operation of these weapon systems, but the preventive and corrective maintenance necessary to keep them operating at top efficiency.

    Prior to the year 1800, battles were fought at point blank range and Fire Control was mainly a problem of navigation. One of our first major developments was the invention of the gunsight. We have leap-frogged from that point to modern missile batteries with massive radar and digital computer systems. Now! Our greatest need is for highly trained technicians to service these systems. (Your son has shown a desire to become one of these technicians.)

    Many educational opportunities are open in our program for young men who desire to become Fire Control Technicians. He is already in the first phase of one these programs. In this eighteen week phase he will receive a thorough grounding in the fundamentals of Fire Control, Electricity, Electronics, Data Transmission, and Gyroscopes. He will also receive counseling from our Special Programs Group on the many programs available to further his education while he is part of the team engaged in the defense of our country. If he decides not to take advantage of any of these programs he will continue down the regular path of the one enlistment man. That is, he will finish this eighteen week phase one of Fire Control Technicians "A" School and then be assigned to one of the many Naval vessels in our world-wide fleets.

    Our most popular program is what we call the Surface Missile System path. Briefly, it works like this. Following graduation from phase one of FT "A" School, your son will immediately enter phase two of FT "A" School. Here he will receive fourteen more weeks of advanced training in Special Circuits, Test Equipment, Analog and Digital Computers, and Radar Components and Systems. From phase two he will enter another twenty to thirty-one weeks of FT "C" School on a specific section of a Gun or Missile Weapon System. This is usually a school of his own choice, and can be located here at Great Lakes, at Dam Neck, Virginia, or at Mare Island, California.

    In exchange for this additional education, he will be asked to extend his present enlistment to a total of six years. In an exchange like this, the Navy will have trained and utilized a highly skilled technician in a time of critical need to our country. By this time your son should be a second or first class petty officer. The young man will have served his country, and if he desires to leave the Navy at the end of his enlistment, he takes with him education and experience that is in great demand in every corner of this great country of ours. His acquired skills will be an important contribution to the protection of our country and will be of everlasting value to him. You have reason to feel proud of your son as he works toward this goal.

                                        Sincerely yours,

                                        /s/ A. R. Ertl

                                        A. R. ERTL
                                        Lieutenant, U. S. Navy
                                        Officer in Charge
                                        Fire Control Technician Schools

Every Friday approximately 400 Navy men graduate from the various schools here

After graduation, your son will be transferred to a new command and further

Your son has received the finest training available. The Navy instructors

fine performance as a student have prepared him to assume the leadership
responsibilities of a future petty officer. The Navy has a very real interest
in and continuing need for intelligent, responsible young men.

You can be very proud of his ability and foresight to seek new challenges. His

1967-08-22.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-08-22.text:
Aug. 22, 1967
Tuesday

Dear Mother + Dad,

It's Tuesday evening and about 5:15 p.m. here. I thought I'd drop you a few lines and let you know how things have been going.

The plane trip out here was all right but it did seem like a long trip anyway.

As I told you on the phone Sunday, most of the day Thursday was spent in classification. I picked Long Beach and San Diego for home ports and Hawaii for overseas. Thursday night I went into San Francisco for a while. Practically all-day Friday I was at the medical building for a physical and shots. I got 4 shots but will get more later on when I get ready to leave here.

That night I had duty, so I stayed here.

I got up about 10 AM Saturday and went into town to the ball game. After the game we went back downtown and went to China Town and Fisherman's Wharf. I rode the cable car back downtown and later came back here.

Sunday morning I had mess cooking and had to get up about 4:30 AM. I was over there till about 11:30 AM then came back to the barracks and called you. I had duty Sunday, so of course I had to stay here. I went to the movie here that afternoon. The rest of the day I slept and just took it easy.

Yesterday I didn't do much of anything. I just loafed around the barracks and went to the library later on. That evening I went into San Francisco and went to a show. By the time it was over it was rather late so I came back here.

Today was much the same as yesterday. I usually go over to the Exchange three or four times a day for a cup of coffee to occupy some of my time.

Well, Bill is probably on his way to St. Louis now. I hope he sold his car and got what he wanted for it.

There's not much to do around here during the day. Some of the guys get put on working parties but that usually doesn't amount to much. So far I've been able to avoid any of this manual labor!

I'm in the duty section today so that means I have to stay here tonight. I'm going to wash my clothes tonight and go to the show at 8 PM.

I'd like for you to send me some of my civilian clothes if you will. I'd like that brown pair of pants that I wear (Levi's permanent press) with the black wide belt. Send the light-colored permanent press shirt along with the paisley one.

Send my shoes along with a pair of my green socks and a pair of the dark brown ones. I'd appreciate it also if you would send my little radio. Don't get any batteries because I can get them cheaper here. Of course if my ring is back, send it also. Thanks.

The temperature is usually around the 60's here. We wear our blues all the time which came as a surprise to me.

You might check with the reserve center — later on, no hurry, and see if I made third class. Tell them not to notify me here but to wait till I get on board ship, or they can use their own judgement and do what they think is best.

Its not too bad here. This place is nothing like Great Lakes though. It's a lot smaller and its not as strict. I don't know when I get paid while I'm here. I have heard that after you are here 10 days you get your first pay.

Tell everyone I said, Hi. I'll probably write next week or sometime later. There isn't really much to write about because there is not much happening here.

I hope everyone is fine and am sure David is anxious to go back to school. Write if you have the chance.

Your son,
Mike
1967-08-22.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1967-08-30.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-08-30.text:
Aug. 30, 1967
4:30 PM
Wed.

Dear Mother + Dad,

How is everyone at home? I am getting along fine but anxious to find out when I'll be leaving here.

I got your letter of last Friday yesterday. I received the package this afternoon. Thanks a lot.

I was very glad and surprized to hear that I passed the test for third class. I'll be looking for some kind of notice from them in the next few days.

Do you remember my writing the last time that I usually didn't have to do any work on working parties or anything like that? Well the past three days that I've had duty (Sat., Mon, today) I have had mess cooking. I usually put in about 10 hours each day when I get stuck with that. It's not really bad, just a long time on your feet. We just fix the food and get it ready to be served. We don't have to do dishes or wipe off tables, fortunately. Usually they try to break it up so that you don't have mess duty every day you have duty, but there isn't many men in our barracks so that means you have to do it more often. Actually, I'd rather do that than cleaning up the barracks. It does make the day go faster for me.

Last Wednesday when I came back to the barracks about 3 PM, I found a note laying on my rack. It was from this guy who I palled around at Great Lakes last winter. He had seen my name on a list at his barracks and decided to look me up. He had just got here that day. We were really surprized that we both would be here about the same time. So, we have been going into 'Frisco when we have the chance.

Sunday we went there and spent most of the day. We went to Fisherman's Wharf then went to the Haight/Ashbury section and paid a visit to the "hippies." There are a few of them downtown but if you want to see a lot of them you have to go there. I wish I had a camera with me that day. They lay in the grass in the parks and sleep (among other things), hold public speeches in the parks, paint pictures on the sidewalk! Some of them walk around with a little kitten tied to a string and crawling across their shoulders. There are a lot of tourists that go out there and this makes it easier for the hippies to get publicity and attention.

I haven't heard anything from Bill yet, have you? He probably wishes that he had thought things over a little better before he signed the papers and raised his right hand, but he'll get over it soon, no doubt about that.

I am glad to have my ring back. That new set looks real good. I'll try to take better care of it now that I know the set breaks so easily.

I hope the weather was good for your trip to Effingham. Did David have as much fun this time as he did last time?

I think I am going to buy me a movie camera or do you think a still camera would be best. Just in case I do get one, what size projector do we have 8mm or 16mm? I'd like to take a lot of pictures to remember the places I've been and the things I've seen and will be seeing.

These two weeks have went by fast for me, although it seems that I've been here longer. I should be finding out in the next week or so where I'm going and when.

That's about all I have to say for now. I'll try to write next week. Bye,

Your son,
Mike

P.S.
I noticed you didn't send my radio. That's alright because a lot of the other guys have radios, so I really don't need mine so don't send it in case you remembered you forgot it.
1967-08-30.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1967-09-06.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-09-06.text:
Wed. 6 Sept. 1967
3 PM.

Dear Mother & Dad,

I got your letter yesterday morning along with one from Bill. I have enclosed his address just in case you haven't heard from him by now. He only wrote one page and explained that he didn't have much to time to write.

Today is the David's birthday, or is it tomorrow, haha. He should have got a card from me, I mailed it Saturday morning.

I got paid for the first time yesterday and cleared $92.00 for the twenty days I was here.

I have been here exactly three weeks today. This morning I was put on assingment. I got the USS JOUETT (DLG-29) out of San Diego. DLG stands for guided missle frigate. I went to the library and found out a little about it;

they finished building it on Dec 3, 1966
cruises at 34 knots
has a crew of 400
547' long, 54' wide and
sets 19.5' out of the water
has [redacted] anti-submarine rockets and torpedoes
1 - 5" gun mount
2 - 3" gun mounts

So, it sounds like a good ship, especially since its not even a year old yet. The living conditions will probably be pretty good. I don't know when I am to report to it, but expect to be out of here in another week.

I think I may buy an instamatic camera. I saw some at the Exchange for $14.50, but I may be able to get a cheaper one in San Francisco.

Yes, I did find the radio when I took the socks out of my shoes to shine them.

Saturday, this buddy of mine from G.L. and I went across the bay and saw the carrier Enterprise. It has been back from Viet Nam for about four weeks and is going back out when it gets some more planes. Its neuclear powered and the biggest ship in the Navy. Let me tell you it is really big. It doesn't seem like your on a ship when you walk around on it.

This Friday night or Sunday, I'm going to the ball game and watch the Cubs play the Giants, providing I'm still here.

When my Reserve check comes, just put it in my checking account and write it down in the account book which is in the dresser drawer.

I haven't heard anything yet about being advanced to third-class. I checked my service record today and there was nothing there in regards to it. The way they run things at the reserve center, it probably won't be official and I'll have to take the test again in the fleet. I wouldn't be suprized at what happens.

I had mess-cooking last night from 4 PM to 12 midnight, but they let us go at about 9:30.

I'll enclose my new address when that I have once I get on the ship. I'll try to let you know some way when I know that I'll be leaving here.

MICHAEL F. DUCY FTGSN 796 16 12
USS JOUETT (DLG-29)
F.P.O.
SAN FRANCISCO, CALIF.
ZIP--?

Its going on 4 o'clock and about time for muster. I'll go over and eat supper after that then probably go into Frisco.

I suggest that you don't write anymore because by the time you get this letter, then get a return letter from you, I'll most likely be gone, and I doubt if they forward any mail. Just wait till you hear from me.

I'll let you know when I leave, bye for now.

your son
Mike

1967-09-17.label: San Diego Union - Vietnam War Headlines pg A-2
1967-09-17.attribution: San Diego Union - Vietnam War Headlines pg A-2 — Ducy Family Archives
1967-09-17.text:
THE SAN DIEGO UNION — Sunday, September 17, 1967 — Page A-2

BUDDHISTS PLAN BID TO TOPPLE THIEU REGIME

SAIGON (UPI)—South Vietnam's militant Buddhists yesterday said they would march in the streets and use "all forms of non-violent struggle" to overthrow the government of President-elect Nguyen Van Thieu.

The warning by a spokesman for militant leader Thich Tri Quang came as Thieu, as he promised in his campaign, began a purge of corrupt military officers from the army, including at least five generals.

There were these other developments:

1. The Information Ministry warned Saigon's 29 newspapers it had noticed "exaggerated news reports" recently and it could result in them being shut down. Censorship, although forbidden by the constitution, was only lifted recently under pressure from the American mission.

NO 'EMERGENCY'

2. The government denied reports that a state of emergency had been declared in the northern city of Da Nang because of increasing anti-government activity by Buddhists.

3. Col. Pham Van Lieu, former national police director accused of illegally campaigning for civilian presidential candidate Phan Khac Suu, was transferred to a new minor post.

Plans for new Buddhist demonstrations were announced at a news conference called by Thich (venerable) Lieu Minh, one of Tri Quang's closest associates.

"The election (Sept. 3) was only a further step in the process of legitimizing the Thieu-Ky clique," said. "As far as we are concerned, there has been no election at all.

"We are going to use all forms of non-violent struggle, including mass demonstrations, to topple the present military dictatorship."

OTHER FACTION

The militant Buddhists are particularly unhappy with Thieu because he recently signed a decree recognizing the more moderate faction led by Thich Tam Chau as the only representatives of South Vietnam's more than 13 million Buddhists or associated splinter groups.

How far the military purge would go, meanwhile, was not known. Thieu had said during the campaign about 50 officers would be drummed out of the army because they used their offices to line their own pockets.

"The first four generals to be 'forcibly retired'" were Maj. Gen. Ton That Xuang, former commandant of the Dalat National Military Academy; Brig. Gen. Pham Dang Lan, former Saigon port director; Maj. Gen. Bui Huu Nhon, commander of the Thu Duc military training center, and Brig. Gen. Nguyen Thanh Sang, formerly in charge of military training.

Also fired was Lt. Col. Tran Dinh Vong, chief of Binh Dinh Province, the most heavily populated in South Vietnam, who was accused of taking bribes in land reform deals.

---

RUSSIA TELLS OF CANTON GUN DUELS

MOSCOW (AP) — Supporters and opponents of Mao Tse-tung are fighting heavy battles in the south China city of Canton, with pillboxes being built and artillery dueling, the Soviet news agency Tass said yesterday.

The Tass dispatch carried a Moscow dateline but said information it contained came from the Red Chinese press and radio and foreign correspondents.

At the same time, Radio Moscow claimed the struggle against Mao, the aging Communist party chairman, was intensifying throughout the Chinese mainland.

The broadcast cited as one instance an anti-Mao outburst between late August and early September in the northeastern city of Harbin. There it said the Red Chinese army garrison supported the anti-Maoists with tanks. The radio quoted no source for its information.

Travelers reaching Hong Kong from Red China said fighting had broken out between the opposing factions in Kwangsi Province and that the flow of supplies to North Vietnam had been disrupted. This province borders on North Vietnam.

"Military units of the 40th and 47th Corps have been moved up to the city," Tass said. "Open battles between the Maoists and their opponents are being waged with the use of automatic weapons, grenades and even artillery pieces."

"Warships patrol the river that flows through Canton. The city is actually split into two hostile camps."

Tass said the battle was between the pro-Maoist Red Banner group, about 100,000 strong, and the Red Workers detachments [text continues below fold]

---

RED BLOC FLIERS TO AID HANOI, THANT REPORTS
(Continued from Page a-1)

[...] reciprocal action toward peace as the United States has asked. "If Hanoi is asked to do something, take some reciprocal actions as a price for the cessation of bombing, Hanoi will not pay that price," Thant said.

Recognizing pressures in Washington to put the Vietnam issue before the United Nations for settlement, Thant said he is "hopeful that new peace initiatives will be considered very seriously by all members of the United Nations."

In Washington, a State Department source yesterday said volunteer technicians from countries sympathetic to North Vietnam already are there and that this has been known for some time.

The source said North Korean pilots and Chinese engineers are in North Vietnam and that an increase in the numbers of such volunteers "would not exactly be precedent-setting."

He was skeptical of the reports that Soviet and Chinese military missions are meeting in China to discuss greater aid to North Vietnam.

U THANT
... talks to newsmen

[Photo: Small portrait photo of U Thant]

---

BRITISH STAGE MILITARY RITES AT CHINA BORDER

HONG KONG (UPI)—British troops staged colorful military rites for the first time along the Communist Chinese border yesterday.

Nepalese gurkhas clad in jungle green uniforms marched to the sound of pipes and drums in the traditional "beating retreat" ceremony.

A military spokesman said the exercise was meant to "show the flag—part of our hearts and minds program" to maintain the loyalty of the colony's 4 million inhabitants despite a Communist campaign to oust the British.

For 30 minutes the 2nd Battalion, 7th Duke of Edinburgh's Own Gurkha Rifles marched and countermarched through the streets of Shataukok, a village which straddles the border.

Villagers from both sides of the border came out to watch the parade. The Communist Chinese are allowed to cross freely. The border is marked only by a concrete post in the middle of the main street.

Shataukok is where, on July 8, Communist Chinese troops opened up with machine gun fire and killed five border police.

---

Long Dock Delays [headline visible at bottom, text cut off]

---

SHOP MONDAY 'TIL 9 P.M.

1967-09-17.text:
THE SAN DIEGO UNION — Sunday, September 17, 1967 — Section B

World's Largest Warship Arrives

[Photo: Large aerial photograph of the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Enterprise (CVN-65) moored at North Island, San Diego. The carrier's hull number "65" is clearly visible on the island superstructure. Crew members line the rails in dress whites. Staff Photo by Joseph Florini.]

The nuclear-powered carrier Enterprise makes her first appearance in San Diego harbor after a trip down the California coast from her home port of Alameda. The "Big E," largest warship in the world, carries a 3,000-man crew, many of whom line the rails in greeting to San Diego. Moored at North Island, Enterprise will operate off Southern California for refresher course. (Story, a-1)

1967-10-05.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-10-05.text:
Thursday Oct. 5, 1967
Bremerton, Washington

Dear Mother And Dad,

It's about 10/30 pm now so I'll try to type out a quick letter. I would write tomorrow or over the weekend but we are suppose to go out to sea till Sunday evening.

I like it real well here on the ship. We have some real great guys in our division and the work is not too hard. I do have trouble finding things to do in the evening though. I usually pass some of my time writing letters one night a week. They do show a movie here on the ship every night but they aren't the greatest. Tomorrow morning I am going to put in for some electronics correspondence courses to give me something to do in my spare time. I really don't want to go on liberty every night because there isn't that much to do around here. And anyway I'd rather save as much money as I can and the best way to do it is to stay on board the ship.

I have enclosed $80.00 to have you put in my checking account. I still have one check for $20.00 that I am going to keep just in case something comes up. I also have about $35.00 in cash so that ought to last till the next pay day. We got paid today and the next one is on the 19th. of this month. I'll send home some more then.

We had a Capitian's inspection Tuesday. I got a very good rating but the division got a good bucause some of the guys were not up to par.

My last letter I wrote I think I said that I was in Seattle. Actually, we are about an hour away from Seattle by ferry. That's one bad thing, if you wan to go over there it takes so long and it costs $170 for a round trip.

The weather has been rather bad for about the past week. We have had a lot of rain and it is rather cool.

I watched part of Wedensday's World Series Game on TV and listened to most of it on the radio today. I think the Cardinals will winx it. At least that's the way Harry Kary figures it will end up so I can't be too wrong.

We went out to sea Friday and came back Saturday evening, earlier than we expected. We were suppose to come back Sunday evening but they had something happen to one of the boilers so we had to return here. We'll be going out again this weekend.

I got the letter you wrote Monday, the 25th. of Sept. Monday of this week.

I think that your job isn't the kind which it is really necessary to put in that after hours time in at meetings and whatever. I agree that what you do on your own time is your own business.

More than likely, next summer I will be returning from the Wes Pac cruise and have 30 days leave coming. Bill will probably have his leave come up about the same time. We could spend part of it here on the coast if you want to come out then we could go home for the rest of it. That's a long way off but I am sure we will be able to figure something out.

Sunday I didn't do much either. I stayed on board and watched the baseball game and the football game on TV. It rained all day then just like the rest of the week.

I got a letter from grandma and she said that she sent Bill a piece out of the paper and she was afraid that he would get in trouble for having it. I'm sure that he would got rid of it real quick if he knew that some trouble might result in it. They say that the Marines build men, but they have a strange way of doing it.

If I were you I'd try not to discuss anything about Bill and the trouble he has had with her. He isn't causing anyone any hardship now and the past should be forgotten, as far as that's concerned.

I sent Edna a postcard like the one I sent with your birthday card, which I hope you got in time. I wasn't quite sure of the date and wanted to make sure you got it in time.

Well, I'm getting pretty tired. I'll write a few more lines next week. So long.

Your son,

Mike

1967-10-05.label: Familygram — Capt. Robert S. Hayes, CO
1967-10-05.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1967-10-05.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FPO SAN FRANCISCO 96601

                                                Bremerton, Washington
                                                5 October 1967

Dear Family and Friends of JOUETT,

Now is an appropriate time to report to you on JOUETT's activities during the past six months and to share with you our plans for the future.

Since joining the Pacific Fleet on the 23rd of February, this newly constructed guided missile frigate, with a crew of 406 officers and men, has led a vigorous and exciting life. Early in our schedule a series of tests and training exercises took the ship to inland waters we had never heard of before: Hood Canal, Bangor, Dabob Bay and Carr Inlet; all in the state of Washington. Other bodies of water which soon became familiar sights in the binoculars of JOUETT lookouts were Puget Sound, Admiralty Inlet, and the Straits of Juan de Fuca. Our geography lesson was not complete until we had also transitted the Strait of Georgia and the San Juan Islands for operations near Nanoose, Canada; and visited Vancouver, the bustling metropolitan seaport and business center of British Columbia. Everywhere our ship sailed we saw evidence of the great lumber industry of the Pacific Northwest as the tiny tug boats slowly pulled large log rafts and as JOUETT dodged stray logs floating in these waters. The weather was surprisingly mild, but it did rain a lot.

A 700 mile voyage south took JOUETT to San Francisco Bay where we loaded missiles at the Naval Weapons Station at Mare Island. Our entry took place around midnight so we didn't get the same view of the impressive Golden Gate Bridge as we did at noon time on our departure.

San Diego was the next stop, and it was a happy homecoming for over a third of our crew who have dependents residing in the "home port".

In May we commenced a special seven week training phase called Shakedown. Shakedown is to a ship what Boot Camp is to a new recruit. The training starts with basics and gradually increases in breadth, complexity and intensity. We fired our guns and launched torpedoes, Terrier missiles and ASROCS. For the first time we really proved to ourselves that JOUETT was one of the most versatile, powerful, and complex combatant ships yet built. While performing dozens of seamanship, engineering and navigation drills we developed a high level of team work and ship spirit. Sometimes we made mistakes, but seldom the same one twice. This was a period of much work and little play. Day and night we trained and drilled. Over one third of our crew were serving in their first ship. Another third were rusty after a year or more of duty or school ashore. The results were dramatic in terms of increased ship proficiency and added individual self confidence. Not a man was injured and our scores were among the highest possible. We graduated from Shakedown a tired but happy and proud crew. We had steamed over 8000 miles, spent 28 days at sea and burned over 650,000 gallons of fuel.

For all new ships it is routine to return to the shipyard after shakedown to receive a major "tune up" - just as a new car returns to the garage for its first thousand mile check. JOUETT is also receiving a substantial increase in communications equipment and some of the latest electronics hardware to assist us in doing any task assigned. Our ship has received a number of habitability improvements that will make living aboard more comfortable. These include increased capacity of air conditioning, additional bunks, a clothing store, a soft ice cream machine and an additional candy vending machine. Our athletic gear locker has been stocked with golf clubs, tennis rackets, boxing gloves, fishing tackle and softball equipment. In addition we have outfitted our helo hangar with a punching bag, wrestling mats, weight lifting equipment and a ping pong table.

JOUETT's stay in Bremerton has given us a golden opportunity to travel through the Pacific Northwest. Vancouver and Victoria, British Columbia, are just four hours away. Then there are Seattle, Tacoma, and Portland, Oregon. The scenery is spectacular, especially in the cloudless warm summer days. For the camper, hiker or just tourist, the Olympic National Park and Mount Rainier National Park, and the Cascade Mountains are within three hours travel. Fishing of all kinds, especially salmon, is always available. Our more athletic crew members have organized sports teams in softball, tennis, bowling, and golf.

As the summer draws to a close we are all anxious to complete the shipyard period and get back to sea. We hope to arrive in San Diego in mid October and for most of us this will be a joyful reunion with our families and friends.

The remainder of October and November will be a busy period of training with other ships and aircraft of the Pacific Fleet. From early December until mid-January JOUETT will be in-port making final preparations for deployment on 16 January.

During the past six months 3 officers, 34 petty officers, and 30 non-rated men have received promotions. About 40 percent of the crew have taken examinations this summer for advancement to the next higher rating.

As you probably know, the officers and men who were attached to JOUETT on 3 December 1966, the day of Commissioning, are termed "Plankowners". They have received elaborate certificates and miniature plankowner plaques testifying to this distinction. About 10 percent of our Plankowners have been detached for shore duty, service in other ships, or return to civilian life. Replacements have been received and the entire crew is now stabilized for deployment.

It was my pleasure in July to present JOUETT's Outstanding Service Award, consisting of a letter of Commendation and an appropriately engraved plaque, to the following senior petty officers:

    Master Chief Steam Propulsionman Edward B. Gray
    Senior Chief Fire Control Technician James C. Cook
    Senior Chief Storekeeper Joseph S. Harris Jr.
    Chief Shipfitter (now Warrant Officer) Terrance A. Vickers
    Hospital Corpsman First Class William H. Ford

It is my plan to continue letters such as this during the coming months and during deployment. If you have questions that I might be able to answer, please don't hesitate to write to me. I know that you are our most loyal supporters and thus very important to JOUETT.

Sincerely,

Robert S. Hayes
Captain, U.S. Navy
Commanding Officer

1967-10-12.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-10-12.text:
October 12, 1967
Bremerton, Washington

Dear Mother and Dad,

It has been about a week since I last wrote so I thought that I'd let you know how things have been going since then. I got your letter of Oct. 2 last Friday. Thanks for sending the clipping from the paper. It gave me some idea of what was happening back there. I meant to send it along to Bill when I wrote to him the other day but I forgot to. The next time I write to him I'll be sure to send it to him.

You said that you spoke to Brant's mother when they called about the records. Have they came by and got them yet. That guy is really in such a mess that he gives me every indication that he is a little crazy.

Tomorrow we pull out of this place and head for sunny San Diego. We will stop at Seal Beach, which is near Long Beach, and load ammunition all day Mon. We will go out the rest of the week and run some tests then get in San Diego Friday sometime. Unfortunately, I have duty that weekend and won't be able to see Bill if he gets liberty. I got a letter from him yesterday and he said that Sunday the 22th (thats the way he spelled it) he gets liberty on the base and that I could come out there and see him. If I can get someone to take my duty that day, I'll go out there. He said that he would have base liberty while he was up at Camp Pendelton so, it looks like we will be able to see each other while I'm down there.

I saw the final game of the world series on TV today. I am glad the Cardinals won it.

I've been on the ship for two weeks now. It seems like only a few days ago when I left on August 16th. I don't think that things could be much better than what they are here on the ship. The guys in the division are really good to work with and they think that I will have no trouble in getting acquainted with the operation of some of the equipment that we use. There are eight FT's and eight gunner's mates in the division. Of course, I work with the FT's.

I haven't had any opportunity to take many pictures with my camera up here. I will try to take some in San Diego and send them home.

I hope you didn't have any trouble putting that money in the bank that I sent home. Would it be just as easy for you to send some of those bank by mail envelopes and deposit slips to me and let me take care of it? If you do send it, send a book of checks also. Do whatever you think is best. As long as it is alright for you to put the money in the bank for me I don't see why I should have to bother with taking care of it from here. Just make sure that you keep the deposits recorded in the book, that's all hard-earned money. Speaking of money. Bill sent me $5.00 of the money that he owed me. That came as a surprise to me. He also said that he sent $10.00 home. Weather he sent it to Connie or you he didn't say.

It sounds like David is going to have plenty of hard work ahead of him in school this year. He better try to do the best he can if he doesn't want to take the year over. I am sure he will do better after he gets use to the idea that summer vacation is over with and its time to concentrate fully on his school work.

We had one of the generators go out yesterday and for a while every one thought that we would be staying up here for at least another week till it was repaired. They found out that the ship could get by without it and a new one will be put in at San Diego. I think every one will be glad to get away from here, especially me.

I wrote a letter to Georgia Mae last week and let her know that I would be back in San Diego this month and that I would like to come up and see them some weekend if it was okay. Actually, it was Sunday when I wrote to her and I haven't got an answer as of yet.

I have been doing a little looking into that 3rd class advancement. My leading petty officer went up to the ships office today and they called Treasure Island. They didn't have a thing about it, so the ships office is going to write a letter to the Reserve Center and see about it. I was talking to the chief the other day about it and I told him that after seeing what some of our duties would be that I felt if I had made 3rd class I may not be able to show that I knew what it was about. He said that he felt if a man passed the test that was all the proof he needed to know if a guy deserved the rating. He said that if it did go through and I didn't feel confident enough to take it that I could have it put off for a month or two until I had a chance to get acquainted with some of the dutys of the 3rd class. He said that he would reccomend me for the test in February if this deal didn't go through by then.

Well that's about it. There hasn't been too much to talk about this week. Perhaps the next time you hear from me will be if I call from San Diego next week. It's time to go eat supper so I had better go for now. Bye.

Your son,
Mike.

P.S.
You can start sending the Review now. Thanks.

1967-10-19.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-10-19.text:
October, 19 1967
San Diego, Calif.

Dear Mother and Dad,

At last, I'm back in San Diego. When I left here the first time I thought I was glad to get away from here but nothing could be any worse than up there in Washington. We got in about 4 o'clock this afternoon. We were not suppose to get in till tomorrow afternoon but things went off so well at sea that we got in a day early.

We didn't get any mail all week while we were at sea but they had mail call about 6 o'clock this evening. I was glad to get the card, your letter, the clippings and the Heath catalog. I really appreciated the card, it made me feel proud to be in here and glad to know that people on the out side are thinking about us.

I have enclosed a money order for $50.00. Please put it in the bank. Since you are not having any difficulty with the money, you can continue to handle my finances. Don't bother about sending the check book. I really intend to save a lot of money because there are a lot of things that I plan to do with it when this two years is over with.

It really stunned me to hear about what happened to David. I am glad he wasn't hurt seriously. Your editorial hit the nail on the head and I bet that woman had some trouble sleeping for a few nights if she read it.

I guess that deal with Allied will never come to an end. They haven't got a foot to stand on. Wasn't that stuff insured. Why don't they just forgetit then? I imagine grandpa is still hot on the idea of getting one of the county radios but he will have to forget about it now.

You asked me in one of your letters how I liked it when we went out to sea. I hoped you'd never ask. The first two weekends out I got seasick and the same thing happened last Saturday after we went out. But, I can assure you that I wasn't the only one who did. About 50% of the crew gets sick when we go out. The sea is really rough up there and that is the reason for it. I think I have overcame it and am used to it now. The sea was really nice when we started to get off the coast of California. We cruised at a condition III watch, (wartime crusing). This is really rough on a guy. The watches are four hours on and either four or eight off plus the regular daily work routine. I stood my watches in the gun director and believe me it is really cramped in there. There are three of us in there and it is like the inside of an Army tank. I lived through it and it wasn't all that bad come to think of it. We will cruise like this for the rest of the time before we head out on Jan. 16th.

That letter you got about the ship, you will get one each month. I put your name in and Bill's too to make him think how great our ship is.

I won't be able to get out to see Bill Sunday because it is almost impossible to get a standby this weekend. He will have liberty Monday and so will I so it looks like we can see each other after all. I told him how to call the ship if he wants to get hold of me and how to get out here if he wants to see me.

Tell Duce that I have some hats to send to him when I have the chance. They are a little frayed but should be okay for him. It sounds like he has been a busy boy with all the days off of school and his outside activities. I bet he really likes it when he goes over to Champaign. I would like to see him join the boy scouts, but if he is having a little difficulty with his school work perhaps it would not be such a good idea after all. I bet he is using my radio, just tell him to keep fresh batterys in it. ha ha.

After I write this letter I will only have two of the envelopes left. Send more if you wish to. I would like dad to send me about a dollars worth of mint commorative stamps similar to the ones on the envelopes. The postal clerk said that he noticed them on my letters and wanted to know if I had any with me. I expalined that my dad was a stamp collector and that he put them on the envelopes for me to send home. He is really a nice guy, he is rather old and has been in for over 16 years and I would like to do this as a favor to him. Send what you think is worth a dollar and he will pay me for them then I'll send you the money for them. I'll try to get him interested in a little more if I can.

Yes, it has been over two months since I left. Its hard to believe all the miles I'v traveled and all of the country that I've seen and I didn't have to pay a cent for it. Big deal! The time has really went fast and I have been on the ship for over three weeks.

I think I remember hearing about that guy that collects stamps and that is a little wierd, They ought to put their foot down and ban him from the stamp club meetings.

It was really something to see when we got in this afternoon. There were a lot of wives and realtives on the pier waiting for the ship to get in. The ship has been away from here for over three months and there were a lot of happy people when we got in. I can imagine what it will be like when we get back from the Wes Pac cruise.

Well it's about 9:30 now and I have to iron my dungarees before taps so I had better go. Write again.

Your son,
Mike

1967-10-24.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-10-24.text:
24 Oct. 1967
Tues.

Dear Mother + Dad,

I hope you get this before you send the clothes. Here is what I want, Levis permanent press pants both pairs (brown + blue), light colored permanent press shirt, pasley shirt, black belt (wide one), socks (green pair) and shoes.

I forgot to mention it, but I would appreciate it if you would send the '68 Allied and Lafayette catalogs. Also send any mail + have that you think I may be interested in.

Use this money for the postage.

I'm glad we had the chance to talk on the phone this evening. I'll write more later on in about a week. Bye.

Love, Mike
1967-10-24.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1967-10-31.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-10-31.text:
Oct 31, 1967
8:30 PM

Dear Mother and Dad,

I got your letter of the 23rd yesterday after we got back in port. It's really nice to have mail waiting for you after you've been out for a few days.

I hope you got my short note with the money before you sent the clothes. I got three of the newspapers today. It sure is nice to be able to read whats going on.

I sent the pictures to Bill and told him to send them back home when he finished with them.

Here is the first roll of film I took with my camera. You might wonder how Grant got that bad eye. I don't think I told you this, but I gave it to him. It took two stiches to close it up. I'll tell you some other time about it.

I guess the world is full of surprizes after what you told me about Jeanne. I wondered why they moved the wedding up from August to July, now its pretty apparent why. But from what you've told me it looks like they didn't move the date up quite enough.

I guess the one big thing on my mind now is weather to come home for Christmas or not. I'll have to talk to Bill and see what he is going to do then maybe make up my mind. I'm afraid that things may be just as boring as when I left and I don't want that.

I got the new envelopes and the stamps. I haven't had a chance to see the postal clerk but will probable sell them for face value.

It seems like just about every time you write, David is out of school. I bet he looks forward to the next day off so he can do what he wants to. Be sure to take a picture of him in his new suit. Tell him I said for him to keep those new shoes shined up.

So he out Halloweening tonight?

Out of the clear blue sky today I got a check for $17. This was to cover my eating and living expenses for the trip from San Diego to Seattle. Needless to say I again made money on that deal.

Do you remember that big box I left laying in the closet floor in the back bedroom? If you look in there you will find a question and answer book titled "Military Requirements PO 3 and 2". Send that out here as soon as you can. If it isn't there look every where you can. I think that Swinger camera and some other Navy papers were in there too. I need this because that damned reserve center did not enter it in my record that I completed the course. I have to do this over again real quick in case I have to take the test in Feb.

I will most likely go up to see Georgia Mae this weekend. I can leave here at 4 PM Friday and don't have to be back till Monday morning. I am going to try to get in touch with Bill and see if he can make it too.

I hope you will like your new job at Roosevelt. I imagine working the extra two hours won't be too hard to get use to.

Well I hope I didn't forget anything to say. I have one more letter to write then will get ready for bed. I'll write again. Bye

Your son,

Mike
1967-10-31.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1967-11-12.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-11-12.text:
Nov. 12, 1967
San Diego, Cal.

Dear Mother and Dad,

I got your letter along with the correspondence course last Thursday. I got the clothes the same day. It has been a while since I last wrote so I had better try to write a few lines now.

Last weekend, as you know I went up to Georgia Mae's. I got there about 7:30 Friday night. We had given up hope on Bill and were eating supper when he called. I was really glad to see him and I could tell he was glad to get away from there even though it was a short weekend since he didn't get there till about 6:00 Saturday evening. They were sorry that there was not enough time for them to take us anywhere but it was fine just to be able to relax and take it easy. We had plenty to talk about and it was a good weekend as far as I was concerned. Since I have duty on Thanksgiving day I will probably go back up there on the weekend after. I don't know just what Bill's liberty will be then. Sunday evening they took Bill back to Camp Pendelton then brought me on down to San Diego. I took them on the ship and showed them around after we got here.

We left port Monday morning and were suppose to be gone till Friday but we got back a day early on Thursday. This was good and it was planned to give us all day Friday off to commerate Veteran's Day. This didn't strike me to much because I had duty Friday. Well, before we even got in Thursday we were told that the plans had been changed and that we would most likely be going out again on Friday morning for some special operation. Then the news came out about the President coming out here and we were to be one of the ships in the task force with the Enterprise along with about five other ships. Saturday we got back in about 11:00.

Bill was waiting on the pier when we got in. I brought him on the ship and we ate dinner then went into San Diego and spent the rest of the weekend there. He left this afternoon about 2:30 for Pendelton because he had to be back at 5:00. We went out to the zoo and Balboa Park yesterday afternoon. It is really nice out there and quite a change from the downtown district.

I have got a locker for my civilian clothes and Bill is going to put his in with mine when he gets some. I havent wore mine yet but will when I get my next weekend liberty which is the weekend after Thanksgiving.

I hoped you watched the papers closely in regard to the President being here. It would be nice if our ship got mentioned but they probably gave all the publicity to the Enterprize.

I have some more pictures to send home that I took here on the ship and at Georgia Mae's. They should be ready about Thursday. Thank's for sending the picture of David. I haven't forgot what any of you look like but it does help me to remember the ones back home.

The other day as I was looking at one of the newspapers, I just happened to notice the rates for the subscriptions. From what I could tell it is $24 for the year. I think that is rather expensive. If you would, I would rather have you change it to Sunday only. Do what you want to but I wanted you to know what I thought about it. I do enjoy reading all the news even though it may be old news.

If I do make it home on leave, I'll go down to the reserve center and see what I can do about that advancement. If not, I'll just let things take there course and see what happens.

Something else I noticed in the paper. The police department is getting a new radio communications system. I wonder if this will effect our still being able to pick them up on the radios.

As you might notice, some of these stamps are in rather poor shape. When the package came one of the second-class petty officers in the division decided he would be a wise guy and peel them off for me. I let him know that the next time he pulled a stunt like that with any of my mail he would be sorry he did. I kept the ones that wern't too bad. I hope you can still use them. I doubt if it will happen again because I think he got the idea that I meant what I said.

I wonder what you are sending in the package you mentioned in the note. I imagine I'll be suprized and happy to get it.

I have got a course on fire control to help get me ready for the test in case I have to take it again in February. As soon as they get some applications, I am going to take out the courses on electronics. These count as much as three hours credit at junior college level. It costs $5 for the first one and the rest are free. You get to keep the textbooks that they furnish so this is a good deal.

We will be in port for 18 straight days before we go out again. We go out that time then will be here till the middle of January when we leave for West Pac. Bill said that it will be the monsoon season over there then so I imagine we will have some bad weather at sea for a while.

Bill got his liberty Friday at 3:00 so he spent Friday night here in town by himself. He got pulled off of the sidewalk by one of those photographers who take pictures then tell you to come back the next night and see the proofs. Last night we went back to look at them. I think the guy was a little dissapointed to see that Bill brought his older brother back with him. Get this, they wanted $5.25 for a 5x7 black and white. We didn't stay there long. I warned him to stay away from those joints because they are all out to take your money. They don't bother me but they can tell a guy who just got out of boot camp and figure they can take his money.

Tell David to keep up the work in school and before he knows it Christmas vacation will be here. It sounds like he has figured out some good ways to try to get sent home early.

Well, it's about time for the movie on the base to start so I had better close here. Let me here from you again when you have time to write. So long for now.

Your son,
Mike

1967-11-20.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-11-20.text:
Nov. 20, 1967
Monday

Dear Mother + Dad,

It's been about a week since I last wrote. I have got two letters from you since then, one of them came today.

I hope this letter brings you good news. If you noticed the return address, I am now third class. I found out last Wed. and sewed the "crow" on today. I figure I have about $123 in back pay coming. I'll get this next pay day. Now I'll get $84 a pay day instead of the usual $65. So, I should end up with about $200 pay next time.

It really feels great. Its like getting your report card and finding out you passed to the next grade. Now, I've got a chance to make second before I get out.

I have decided to come home for Christmas. I will be home for about 14 days starting on Dec. 19th. Of course, the way they run things here, there might be something to change that somewhat. But at any rate, it's a pretty sure thing.

I'm glad to hear that Bill's car is back. It should help boost his morale, if he makes it home.

This weekend I'll probably go up to Georgia Mae's again. She said she would like to have us up there for the Thanksgiving holidays, but I have duty Thanksgiving day and won't be able to make it till Friday evening.

I would have liked to talked to grandma that day when she called but of course I was asleep. I think it did more good for Bill to talk to her than it would have me.

We had our first rain here yesterday in over seven weeks. The weather is so nice I can't believe it. I will have to be ready for the cold weather when I come home, so had better get my p-coat cleaned.

I really can't think of what I would like for Christmas. There isn't anything I need and I wouldn't have any room to keep anything I could use. I'll give it a lot of hard thought and try to come up with something by the next time I write.

I hope you like these pictures. Bill sent the ones you took to Georgia Mae and she sent them on to me to send back with the ones I took.

I still haven't got that package you wrote the note about. Perhaps it will get here tomorrow or the day after.

I am glad to hear that one of the radios got there. I would rather have you let that man in Springfield put them together than wait for me to do it at Christmas. I intend to use that time for rest + relaxation and would rather not be occupied by that.

Danny Wiggins predicted to Bill and me last summer that someday he would be a family man. I guess he is getting off to a start. He ought to stay in the Army for another six years, they could really use his kind. ha ha

We have one more operation to go out on. This one starts next Monday and lasts for about 5 days. We'll be here in port till the 16 of January when we go on the operation that really counts.

It sounds like Daddy is keeping pretty busy around the house and with the stamp auctions. I suppose the new stove ought to make the food taste better, but come to think of it, it always was pretty good. Tell David not to get too lazy over the holidays and to keep at his school work. He can start to slack-off after the year is a little over half way through, but its the time now that counts. I'm sure he will get through this year in pretty good shape.

I'm glad to hear he is taking an interest in the glee club at school.

You might be wondering why I haven't sent any money home for a while. I have lent quite a bit to Bill and am saving most of it to come home on. I'll probably put some in the bank when I get home.

Its almost 7:30 here and I have to iron my dungarees for tomorrow then will go over to the show on the base. I'll be waiting to hear from you & again and will write in about a week.

Bye

Your son,

Mike

P.S. If you "happen" to see Bill before I do, give him these "portraits" of himself.
