1. Exercise BLUE LOTUS.
   a. Yesterday. Friday was a busy but profitable day with activity in
many areas. A JOUETT first occurred when a helicopter carrying RADM DAVIS
set down on the helo deck and secured for the entire morning. In the months
ahead this will become routine for JOUETT but yesterday it was a novelty.
The SAMEX went extremely well for JOUETT in the face of various material
casualties that threatened to put our missile battery out of commission.
Three missiles were fired and two hits were scored. Quick reaction and a
high state of training were required and displayed. Contributing in large


========================================================================================
PAGE 2
========================================================================================

measure to the success of the exercise was JOUETT's CIC Team which detected
and tracked the targets and aided Commodore EMERSON in coordinating the entire
evolution. In the afternoon the engineers were called upon on short notice
to conduct a full power trial and responded almost effortlessly. The last
major evolution of the day was a night refueling from CALIENTE.

   b. Today. Late last night JOUETT assumed Search and Rescue station
and commenced performance of duties exactly like those which we will perform
during our deployment. This assignment will continue throughout today and
tomorrow and though the pace may appear slow throughout the ship be assured
that CIC is alive with activity.

2. Caution. Be careful about keeping money and other valuables locked up if not
actually on your person. Do not place temptation in the path of someone who
might yield in a weak moment.

3. Change of Command. ADM John J. HYLAND, USN, relieved ADM Ray L. JOHNSON, USN,
as Commander in Chief, U. S. Pacific Fleet on 30 November. Upon his retirement
ADM JOHNSON sent the following message to the Pacific Fleet:

   As my term of service as Commander in Chief comes to a close, I can look
back upon a multitude of rich experiences. When the tempo of conflict increased
in the Vietnam area, we moved up together to meet the enemy and took a stand to
insure that freedom and democratic opportunity will endure for future generations.
In carrying out the many demanding tasks that provide this insurance, all of you,
from Seaman Apprentice to Admiral, have upheld the highest naval traditions of
skill, sacrifice, and professionalism.

   Together we have helped to maintain the balance of national power in this
vast Pacific area. In no other part of the world has the need for seapower
been more obvious, nor has its application been more artfully tailored to meet
a delicate situation. The trust that the American people have placed in us
serving now, and those who have served, in the fleet, has made the job of
Commander in Chief one of awesome responsibility for me. But in attempting
to satisfy this trust through the support and dedication of the finest Navy
professionals who ever went to sea, I have found my life's greatest satisfaction.

   The dictates of time say that I must leave my present assignment. But never
really will I leave you for the spirit of the mission, which never ends, will
keep my thoughts of all of you, and my prayers for your successes, always
close at hand.

                                        ADMIRAL ROY L. JOHNSON, USN

4. Return to Port. JOUETT will return to port on Monday, 4 December at the
conclusion of exercise BLUE LOTUS rather than on 5 December as previously announced.

5. Security. Serving on a nuclear-capable ship places the burden of security
on all hands. If you see a stranger wandering about the ship without a badge of
any sort, you should immediately conduct him to the OOD on the quarterdeck. Like-
wise, a visitor with a red "E" badge without an escort, should be conducted to
the quarterdeck. Only visitors wearing the green "J" badge are authorized to move
about the ship without an escort. But this green badge in no way constitutes
clearance to enter any restricted area of the ship.

                                        J. H. ADDAMS
                                        CDR       USN
                                        EXECUTIVE OFFICER


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

Exercise BLUE LOTUS was Jouett's pre-deployment workup exercise off San Diego.
Key events on Dec 1-2, 1967:
- RADM Davis helicopter visit (first helo landing on Jouett's deck)
- SAMEX (Surface-to-Air Missile Exercise): 3 missiles fired, 2 hits scored
- Full power trial
- Night refueling from USS Caliente (AO-53)
- Assumed SAR station duties (first time performing deployment mission)

Change of Command: ADM Roy L. Johnson relieved as CINCPACFLT by ADM John J. Hyland
on November 30, 1967. Full text of Johnson's farewell message included.

Commodore Emerson = CAPT Arthur T. Emerson, Jr. (COMDESRON ONE), who would later
give remarks at the Oct 11, 1968 Awards Ceremony.

Signed by CDR J.H. Addams, Executive Officer (same XO throughout the deployment).

1967-12-05.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-12-05.text:
Dec. 5, 1967
Tuesday

Dear Mother + Dad,

Another week at sea and now we are back in port. I got the letter Dad wrote today. We got back here about 1500 today. We got as far north as 90 miles out of San Francisco. The next time we go to sea it will be for good.

It's really great having got this new rate. I got $207 payday of which $143 was back pay. Yes there are a few fringe benefits that I've waited a long time for. But they could never give me enough benefits to make me stay in here any longer than I have to.

Bill will probably be on his way back here tomorrow. I hope we can see one another before I come home.

I was surprized that you called me at Georgia Mae's that Friday. I figured you might call me there that weekend but wasn't sure.

That picture of Bill really makes him look happy. He looks like a real "Devil Dog."

You might know, the first day we get back, I have got duty. I have a four hour watch that starts at 2000 (8 PM).

I got reservations on American Airlines. Enclosed you will find my flight schedule. I think I'll call when I get in Chicago and let you know I'm on my way. I'll call after 4 PM from O'Hare airport.

It really seems strange that it's cold and snowing back home. The weather is really great out here.

Since you mentioned buying my return ticket that will be fine for Christmas. Actually that is what I had in mind if I were able to make it home.

I'm sorry this is so short but there hasn't been much happen during a week at sea. I'll let you hear from me once more before the 19th. Bye.

Your son,

Mike
1967-12-05.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1967-12-06.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1967-12-06.text:
Dec. 6, 1967
Wed. 9:15 PM

[Written on USO "A Home Away from Home" stationery]

Dear Mother & Dad,

I got the letter that mother wrote on the 28th, today. I kind of rushed the letter I wrote last night so will try to say a little more here.

I got early liberty today at noon. I went out to the airport about 3:30 to pick up my tickets. While I was on the way there I decided that I'd wait around for Bill and see if he came in. Sure enough, his plane got in at 4:20 and I met him there. He just caught the 9:00 bus back to Camp Pendleton a few minutes ago. From what you wrote and from what he told me, I guess he really had a high time. He is lucky he didn't get into serious trouble over that car wreck. He should be keeping out of trouble for a while now that he's back in the care of the USMC.

I didn't mention the money he owes me yet, but will if I see him this weekend. In case you're wondering how much it is it's $45. I have to give him a lot of credit though for going out and working those three days.

I'm starting to get things done and taken care of that have to be done before I go on leave. It seems as if there is always something you need to do or buy and have to run over to the exchange to take care of it. By this time next week, I should have just about everything ready to come home.

Bill has put his civilian clothes in the locker here with mine. He had to pay $2.50 for the rent and .15¢ for the key. We got out of our uniforms as soon as we got back from the airport and put on our civvies.

I bought him a wallet for his birthday and gave it to him today. He had been using an old one of mine that I let him have when I saw how ragged and beat-up his was. I figured this would be something he could use and would like.

Tell David that I'll try to gather up enough energy to take him hunting at least once. Maybe we can have some better luck.

Oh yes, I got your cookies and candy about 10 days ago. It was pretty shook up and crumbly. One of the guys in my division said that if you had put more popcorn in it it wouldn't have got so shook up. A couple of days later I got the candy from the Marine League. I shared both yours and theirs with the rest of the guys in the division. They thought it was pretty good and so did I.

Thats about all there is left to say for now. Its about time for this place to close so I had better get going. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike

1967-12-10.label: Familygram — Capt. Robert S. Hayes, CO
1967-12-10.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1967-12-10.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FPO SAN FRANCISCO 96601

                                                SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA
                                                10 DECEMBER 1967

Dear Family and Friends of JOUETT,

The two months since my last letter to you have passed quickly and I would like to take this opportunity to bring you up to date on our past achievements and our future schedule.

October was an activity filled month. Even after thirteen weeks in the shipyard a last minute rush was required to make JOUETT ready for sea. Crew members returned from leave and school to finish last minute details prior to our departure from Puget Sound Naval Shipyard. Bremerton friends of DLG29 watched from the shore as we cast off our lines for our final voyage from USS JOUETT's birthplace. With a last farewell sounding from the ships whistle, JOUETT entered Rich Passage, the first leg of our trip to homeport San Diego. We sped through the familiar waters of Puget Sound and the Straits of Juan de Fuca, into the Pacific. Constant drills, exercises, gunshoots and maneuvers lubricated the rusty battle hinges of JOUETT. The dust was blown off the operational drill books and we acclimated to our familiar role of sailors at sea rather than land-locked shipyard workers.

After a short stay in San Diego, where we stocked up on "beans, black oil, and bullets" JOUETT was ready to join the fleet again. October 25th found us on our way to sea, participating in the fast-action carrier strike exercise, "Bell Buster", which duplicated as realistically as possible, an environment JOUETT is likely to encounter in WESTPAC deployment. We flexed our muscles, firing guns, torpedoes and surface-to-air missiles. Upon completion of "Bell Buster" JOUETT, tired but confident, returned to port. The Admiral in charge of the exercise said this of our performance: "Every phase of operations, AAW, SAW, Surface Ops, Tactical and Administrative Communications were conducted in an outstanding manner. Such performance by JOUETT, who has newly joined the fleet, is particularly noteworthy." Five days later JOUETT participated in another Naval exercise where she demonstrated her skills in Anti-submarine Warfare and Surface Gunnery. JOUETT had been selected to escort the super-carrier ENTERPRISE during President JOHNSON's visit to the West Coast. A rare privilege indeed to man the rail as the Commander-in-Chief reviewed some of his finest Naval Forces. We returned to San Diego and visited with our families for two weeks. These inport days rushed past as we prepared for exercise "BLUE LOTUS".

JOUETT set sail on 28 November for "BLUE LOTUS", the largest fleet exercise in the past three years, with 44 other Naval ships, composed of U.S. Pacific Fleet Forces from the Hawaiian Islands, San Francisco and Long Beach along with units of the Royal Canadian Navy. New and old salts alike found that "BLUE LOTUS" demanded much from JOUETT, but that she was both willing and able to fulfill all tasks assigned to her. This exercise gave us the opportunity to really "sharpen-up" for our upcoming WESTPAC deployment. We returned to homeport on the fifth of December just in time to join our families in preparation for the holidays.

While at sea on 3 December 1967 JOUETT celebrated her first birthday. A year ago, it was a green and awkward crew that stood in the rain to observe the commissioning pennant being raised on their first ship. A year later finds JOUETT in the forefront of the action, a well trained and finely honed machine able to perform any task. JOUETT's crew will celebrate her birthday with an all hands party on 11 December.

JOUETT will remain pierside in San Diego until she deploys to WESTPAC in January. We will be rearming at Seal Beach Naval Weapons Station early in January and JOUETT will host her families and friends with a one day "Dependents Cruise" on 19 December. All dependents are urged to come out. A fine program is planned in the calm waters off San Diego.

Those dependents who reside in the San Diego area, please mark your calendars for a special event. At 1:00 P.M. on Wednesday 13 December 1967 there will be a very important Pre-Deployment Briefing at the Naval Station Theatre for all married crew members of JOUETT, HALSEY, PREBLE and HULL and their dependents. Captain Arthur T. EMERSON, Jr., Commander Destroyer Squadron ONE will be in charge of the program. He has lined up a number of well qualified speakers who will give advice to wives on how to best "weather" the WESTPAC cruise. Topics covered will include mail service, emergency leave, legal assistance, wills, power of attorney, contracts, civic affairs, home safety, Navy Relief, Medicare and community resources.

All married men in JOUETT are being encouraged to attend. They will be granted early liberty, return home, and bring their wives to the presentation. Free baby sitting is being provided at the Commissary Nursery. With refreshments provided and lots of friends around, it can be an enjoyable as well as instructive outing for married personnel.

It is with pleasure, that I note that 53 officers and men have received promotions within the last two months, and that I have awarded JOUETT's OUTSTANDING SERVICE AWARD, consisting of a letter of commendation and engraved ship's plaque to the following Petty Officers:

    G. L. BUSCH, ST1             A. W. IRWIN, EMCS
    F. M. WALKER, CS1            V. H. LODGE, RM2
    M. L. DAUGHTERY, SM1         J. H. WEST, MMC
    B. J. GEE, BM1               B. E. FOX, ST1
    T. COLLINS, BMCS

I will continue to keep JOUETT's family and fans informed with letters during the coming months of our deployment, however, since I probably will not be able to write to you again prior to the holidays, I would like to take this opportunity to extend to you my sincerest best wishes for a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year.

Sincerely,

ROBERT S. HAYES
CAPTAIN, U.S. NAVY
COMMANDING OFFICER

personal libraries of paperback books and magazines or materials that would be
enjoyed by others. Any publications donated can be left at the MDCS Office
for placement in the library.

4. Travel Information. BUPERS Instruction 4650.16 of 21 November 1967
promulgated information concerning the travel of military personnel while in
a leave status. Copies of this information are available at your department
office, and it is suggested that all personnel going on Christmas leave obtain
a copy. This information should be used only as a guide.


========================================================================================
PAGE 3: CHIEF OF NAVAL OPERATIONS — 1967 CHRISTMAS MESSAGE
========================================================================================

5.

                   [CNO seal/emblem]

              CHIEF OF NAVAL OPERATIONS

                         1967
              Christmas - New Years Message

   With the advent of the Christmas Season, it is time for
each of us to reflect on the teachings of our individual faiths
and on the blessings of our great country. In this reflection,
we continue to pray that the true spirit of Christmas will reach
the hearts of men throughout the world and that peace and
freedom may come to all mankind in our time.

   The American Navyman and his family are the first to
know the realities of the un-peaceful years. You are first on
the front line and then must remain until a balance of peace
is achieved. In the past year your duties have again called on
you to meet the challenges of men who do not know or do not
wish to know true peace. As in the past, your response has
been superb.

   To all Americans, your accomplishments and those of
your shipmates in 1967 have been a source of the greatest
confidence and pride. Those of you who serve in Vietnam
combat operations deserve a special measure of their thanks
and prayers during Christmas.

   I salute each of you, and consider it an honor to represent
you and the earned integrity of the Navy-Marine Corps Team.
I go about my duties, as do all Americans, in the wake of your
accomplishments. God bless you all.

                                   Thomas H. Moorer
                                   THOMAS H. MOORER
                                   Admiral, U.S. Navy


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

In port San Diego, one week before Christmas. Jouett would deploy to WestPac
on January 16, 1968.

CDO is LT Loveless — Jerry M. Loveless, who would receive a Bronze Star Medal
for the deployment (one of only two Bronze Stars awarded, alongside CAPT Hayes).

Duty division OC/OI — Operations divisions (not Mike's division).

FTCS Cox again standing OOD watch (0000-0400), same as on Dec 16 POD.

Dependent's Cruise scheduled for December 19, 1967: families invited aboard
for a day cruise to Coronado Roads. Lunch on the helo deck. Ladies advised
to wear flat heels and slacks. Guests must be 12+ years old. This was likely
one of the last family events before the January 16 deployment.

The CNO Christmas message from ADM Thomas H. Moorer is significant — Moorer
was Chief of Naval Operations from August 1967 to July 1970, and later became
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (1970-1974). His message acknowledges
"those of you who serve in Vietnam combat operations" — Jouett would join them
in five weeks.

Ship's Library note suggests crew should donate paperback books before
deployment — building up reading material for months at sea.

BUPERS travel instruction for Christmas leave — last leave period before
WestPac deployment.

1968-01-04.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-01-04.text:
Jan. 4, 1968
Thurs., 8 PM

Dear Mother & Dad,

As you know, I made it back out here okay, its really nice weather here but I still feel a little lazy after the two weeks leave. I guess I'll be back in the routine by the weekend.

Bill is going up to Georgia Mae's Friday night and I will get up there Sat. afternoon.

Its really going to be different when we leave here on the 16th. The liberty won't be often or as good but the time will go by pretty fast and before you know it we'll be back in the states.

We are having a lot of inspections this week and next. Next week we go up to Seal Beach and load ammo on Thursday and get back Friday. I wish I didn't have duty the last weekend here, but thats the way it goes.

Do you remember me telling you about that other 3rd class wanting me to take his duty? Well as I figured, he wanted me to take it for him Wed. I turned him down though, because I didn't feel like standing duty the day after I got back.

Tell David that we will get the boots next week and send them home when we have a chance.

I got the watch for Dad and got a band too. I hope he likes it. I also got grandpa a lighter. I'll try to mail them home this weekend from Georgia Mae's.

Heres my W-2 from the Navy for my active-duty. Put this check in the bank. We get paid again next week and I'll send home some more money.

Bill seems to be doing real fine. He too is getting a little itchy about leaving the states, just as I am.

I took the test for the Navy drivers license yesterday and passed it. I made a few mistakes but nothing bad. When my state license comes just send it on out here to me.

I am glad I did come home during the holidays. I think it helped my morale a lot and I'll be able to face the months overseas a little better.

I suppose David was really anxious to get back to school. Tell him to be good and work hard on his home-work.

Well, I have to go now and thats about all there is for now. I'll write again, soon.

Your son,

Mike
1968-01-04.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-01-14.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-01-14.text:
Jan. 14, 1968
Sunday

Dear Mother & Dad,

Even though I am going to call tomorrow night I thought I'd go ahead and write. I owe you a letter anyway.

Today is Sunday and things are pretty quiet around here. Its 73° outside now and a real nice day. I wish I didn't have duty this weekend but thats the way it goes.

I served mass this morning for the chaplian. He said I did real good.

I drove one of the guys into town to pick up the mail this morning.

I was suppose to meet Bill here Friday evening, but he never made it for some reason. Maybe he is on his way over now.

Georgia Mae called me here on the ship yesterday and wondered if I'd heard from him. She thought she would be up there this weekend if he could make it.

I played the tape recording for them. They liked it but those kids couldn't sit still or be quiet during the whole thing.

I'll send those Christmas pictures back but I have some I'm waiting for to send with them.

I saw the movie "Valley of the Dolls" the other day. Its really a good movie, see it if you have a chance.

Things have been pretty busy on the ship in the past week. We have had a lot of inspections and they have been loading stores about every day.

Tell David that the boots are on their way. We mailed them from Oceanside, Tuesday evening. (Jan. 9)

I have got my civilian clothes ready to go. I may take them up to Georgia Maes Monday if we get liberty early.

I hope you can get things straightened out at work. I am sure it will work out okay if you can get back to only four hours.

I don't like this job either but all I can do is bear with it. Thats one thing about Navy vs civilian life, if you don't like it you can do something about it but not in this outfit.

My electronics correspondence course was waiting for me when I got back from leave. I have done 2 of the 25 lessons. It is a good one and is easy.

I hope you get the package with the watch okay. Georgia Mae was suppose to mail it for me last week.

Well thats about it for now. So long, I'll write again.

Your son,

Mike

After a welcome holiday respite from fleet exercises, shipyard availabilities, and
formal training ashore, which men of the JOUETT spent with their families and loved
ones, preparation for deployment commenced in earnest. Stores and supplies were
loaded aboard, all equipment was brought up to top condition, and the men, well-
rested and eager, returned from their Christmas leave.

[Photo: USS Jouett (DLG-29) at pier, hull number 29 visible, families and wives standing on the pier watching, bus visible in background]

On the morning of January 16, 1968, JOUETT cast off all lines, put both engines
astern, and backed away from the pier, leaving wives and children, sweethearts and
friends behind. The long months of training and preparation had borne fruit. For the
first time, DLG-29 proceeded to conflict, ready to serve.

1968-01-16.text:
FATHER, SON REQUEST DUTY TOGETHER ON USS JOUETT

Clayton O. Childs, PC1, and his son David O. Childs, SN, both serve aboard the San
Diego-based guided missile frigate USS Jouett (DLG 29).

The elder member of the family is a Jouett Plankowner, having been aboard Jouett since
her commissioning Dec. 3, 1966. David, who was stationed aboard the USS Caddo Parish
(LST 555), applied for a transfer to his dad's ship.

The senior Childs is Jouett's Postmaster and, at 58 years old, is the oldest member of
Jouett's crew. David is presently assigned to the Deck Division in the Weapons Department
and hopes to follow his father's footsteps and become a Postal Clerk. David, at 21, is one
of the youngest members of the crew.

[Photo: Jenkins' whaleboat finished third.]


USS JENKINS' CREW THIRD IN REGATTA

The Pearl Harbor-based destroyer, USS Jenkins (DD 447) participated this year in the annual
Whaling Spree in Lahaina, Maui.

Although many activities were planned, the highlight was a whaleboat race in which the
Jenkins' crew participated. After only one hour of practice, the Jenkins' whaleboat was at
the starting line with the other entrants. At the sound of "Go", backs began to strain and the
small boat was on her way to the finish line.

As the race progressed, a plug worked loose in the bottom of the boat and water began to rush in.
Quick action on the part of RD3 Suddeth saved the day. He plugged the hole with his big toe, and
the race continued.

In spite of the lack of training and experience on the part of the Jenkins crew, the small boat was
third to cross the finish line.


FIRST OLYMPIAD HELD

USS England (DLG 22) edged out the destroyer USS Walke (DD 723) by four points with a total score
of 134 to capture first place in "Olympiad '68" held recently at the Long Beach Naval Station.

A late finishing, hard fought battle in the medicine ball volleyball contest in which England placed
first, gave her 25 points, enough to capture overall honors among the 32 ships and staffs
participating.

Independent Businessmen's Association (IBMA) president, Chet Baldwin, presented the first place
traveling trophy to Cdr. S.D. Landersman, Executive Officer of England. Cdr. R. Ennis, Commanding
Officer of Walke, accepted second place trophy from IBMA executive committee member Bill Brewer.

Third place award, presented by Joe Waddington, IBMA executive secretary, was presented to PFC
John L. Rico of the USS Galveston (CLG 3). Rico earned points for Galveston by placing second in
the marathon run.

"Olympiad '68" was the first of the planned annual Olympiad events to be held for cruiser and
destroyermen of Long Beach. The program was initiated by Rear Admiral Thomas J. Rudden, Jr.,
Commander Cruiser-Destroyer Group in an effort to promote esprit de corps and good fellowship
among units in Long Beach.

[Photo: PULL-USS England sailors trying their best in the tug-of-war. They came back strong in
other Olympiad events, capturing enough points to win the overall award.]

[Photo: CHESS-SN Ang of the USS Duncan plays chess against Lt. Hughes of ComDesRon 23 staff.]

USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FPO SAN FRANCISCO 96601

PLAN OF THE DAY
WEDNESDAY, 17 JANUARY 1968

THE PLAN OF THE DAY CONTAINS OFFICIAL INFORMATION. ALL HANDS ARE CHARGED
WITH THE RESPONSIBILITY OF HAVING KNOWLEDGE OF ITS CONTENTS. THE POD IS NOT
TO BE REMOVED FROM THE SHIP OR SHIP'S OFFICES.

                       5 JAN 68 to 9 JAN 68.                E-3

                       10 JAN 68 to 11 JAN 68. Viol.        Recommendation for

                       Movement.

SN KORTLANG            Viol. Art. 86, UCMJ, UA from         30 Days Restriction
                       14 JAN 68 to 16 JAN 68.              20 Hours Extra Duty

2. Ship's Schedule. During our transit to Pearl Harbor, a full round of
communications and CIC exercises is scheduled. Because of the relatively high
speed of advance required, however, there will be a minimum of exercises that
involve ship maneuvers. On Thursday, Friday, and Saturday mornings JOUETT will
exercise at General Quarters and test fire gun mounts. A period has been set
aside each morning for the ships to practice making approaches on each other.
Friday afternoon JOUETT is scheduled for a 15 knot economy trial. JOUETT and
PREBLE will arrive in the Pearl Harbor op area on Sunday morning and conduct
AA gunnery, shore bombardment, and air control exercises. Arrival Pearl Harbor
is scheduled for 0800, Monday, 22 January.

3. Time Change. At 1900 all clocks will be set back one hour to conform to
Time zone VICTOR (+9).


========================================================================================
PAGE 3
========================================================================================

4. Uniform. The following uniform regulations are effective immediately:

   a. Uniform of the day for officers and chief petty officers is tropical
khaki long. Long sleeve khaki shirts are optional, but must be worn with a
tie.

   b. Enlisted men standing watch in the pilot house, radio messengers,
missile house sentries, roving patrol, and men routinely working in office
spaces shall wear the uniform of the day - undress blues.

   c. Enlisted men will not be required to shift to the uniform of the day
for evening meals. Clean presentable dungarees may be worn. A schedule will
be devised to press dungarees.

   d. The blue ball cap may be worn except by messingers, sentries, patrols,
and pilot house watch.

   e. All sentries, patrols, and messengers shall wear a clean, white guard
belt.

   f. The uniform of the day will be changed to undress whites at 0800,
Saturday, 20 January. Liberty uniform in Pearl Harbor will be undress white
with neckerchief or tropical white long. A laundry and pressing schedule for
whites will be announced.

5. Security of Movements. JOUETT is now, and will be, operating under a
classified movement schedule. This schedule has not been widely disseminated
nor will it be, except in the cases of unclassified movements or port visits
which have been cleared and declassified. The details of our operational
assignments are similarly classified - e.g. assignment to a particular station
or task such as SAR or PIRAZ. The actual facts of our movements and assignments
will be quite widely known aboard JOUETT, however. Therefore all hands must be
constantly aware of security requirements. Do not talk about ship's operations
while ashore, especially to civilians or to persons unknown.

6. Check-ins. The following men will report to Ship's Office at 0830.

RD3 MCILWEE              RD3 SMITH               RDSN WYLLIS         RD3 MANGERI
RD3 BRONCACCIO           RDSN WOOD               SD3 REYES           TN LUZANO
RD2 RETTZO               RD2 DEAVER              RDSN VIORAL

7. Water Consumption. Fresh water aboard ship is not an unlimited commodity.
This ship is equipped with two distilling plant units which distill from sea
water the potable water which we use for cooking, drinking, laundering, and our
personal use; and feed water which is used for feeding our boilers. These dis-
tilling units make about 24,000 gallons per day necessitating very judicious use
of all water. The crew is allowed to use about 25 gallons per man per day. In
order to do this each must conserve water by taking only Navy type showers, using
water sparingly, and reporting any leaks to D. C. Central. Do your part. Do not
waste water!

                                        J. F. ADDAMS
                                        CDR       USN
                                        EXECUTIVE OFFICER


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

First full day underway for the 1968 WestPac deployment. Jouett departed
San Diego January 16, 1968 — the same day Captain's Mast was held.

Seven sailors received non-judicial punishment for unauthorized absence (UA)
in the days and weeks leading up to deployment. Most were AWOL for short
periods during the Christmas/New Year's leave period or in the final days
before sailing. MM3 Edwards was the most serious case — he both went UA
and missed the ship's movement entirely (Article 87, UCMJ). SN Kortlang
went UA from January 14 to 16 — literally missing departure day.

Transit plan: San Diego to Pearl Harbor with exercises en route. GQ drills
with live gun mount firing, CIC exercises, economy trial. Jouett traveling
with USS Preble (DLG-15). Arrival Pearl Harbor: Monday, January 22, 1968.

Duty Division M — Mike's Missile division. The uniform change to tropical
khaki and the time zone change signal the ship heading west into the Pacific.

Security of Movements note is significant — from this point forward, the
ship's schedule, station assignments (SAR, PIRAZ), and movements were
classified. Crew warned not to discuss operations ashore.

Signed by CDR J.F. Addams, Executive Officer.

1968-01-19.label: Familygram — Capt. Robert S. Hayes, CO
1968-01-19.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-01-19.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FPO SAN FRANCISCO 96601

                                                        At sea
                                                        19 January 1968

Dear Family and Friends of JOUETT,

It has been over a month since my last letter to you and I would now like to review what JOUETT men have been doing and what lies ahead in our cruise.

First let us go back to early December. The beginning of the month found JOUETT hard at work at sea in a major fleet training exercise titled "BLUE LOTUS". Under Commander First Fleet, Vice Admiral Bernard Roeder, the JOUETT and some fifty ships, hundreds of aircraft, and several thousand Marines conducted realistic wartime training in the ocean areas off Southern California. During this seven day exercise, JOUETT had the opportunity to demonstrate proficiency in her many capabilities. Anti-submarine operations, air defense, shore bombardment, search and rescue, aircraft carrier plane guard, were some of the tasks assigned. Also the ship provided command and communication facilities for Commander Destroyer Squadron ONE and his embarked staff.

When the exercise ended for us on 5 December, we returned to San Diego. However, being in port did not ease our tasks. Ahead were a number of difficult inspections by teams of experts to determine any flaws in our equipments or procedures before we sailed for duty in the Western Pacific. Almost every facet of the ship was checked - electronics, ordnance, security, engineering, communications, navigation, supply, dental and medical. All inspectors had fine things to say about the preparations made by JOUETT men. We uniformly received grades of Excellent and quite a few areas were rated OUTSTANDING. All of us agreed that the hard work was well worth it, knowing we were ready for the tasks ahead.

In addition to preparing the ship for deployment, we were busy preparing ourselves as individuals for the six month's absence from home port. We registered allotments, made arrangements for savings, found locations for our cars, executed wills, and brought on board athletic/sporting equipment for some of the planned at-sea extra curricular activities. We continued to receive innoculations against typhus, diptheria, small pox, typhoid, cholera, and polio. You would be surprised to see how quickly our crew can line up for shots if we also place the paymaster at the end of the innoculation line.

Our dependents were also prepared for the cruise. Those in San Diego were able to attend a two hour briefing by a team consisting of representatives of the local police department, the Navy Legal Office, the Navy Dependents Medical Clinic, Red Cross, Navy Relief Society, local church organizations. I believe everyone who attended came away with much useful information and a confidence that a number of San Diego agencies cared about dependents of deployed Navy men and would readily lend special assistance when summoned.

On the 11th of December we celebrated the first birthday of JOUETT with an all hands dinner-dance at the Naval Training Station Petty Officers Club. The party featured two dance bands in separate ballrooms, a roast beef dinner, and ample liquid refreshments. In addition to about 300 officers and crew members there were over a hundred invited guests (nurses, waves, lady marines, college students, and airline hostesses). While the cost of the party depleted our Welfare Fund by $2,000 everyone agreed that it was a great success.

On the 16th of December, the children of JOUETT officers and men were guests of Santa Claus at our Annual Christmas Party sponsored by the Wives Club. Each youngster received a gift appropriate to his or her age. JOUETT cooks baked over a thousand cookies for the party which was held at the Fleet Recreation Park. On 19 December JOUETT crew members hosted over a hundred wives and teenage children to a very special "at home" at sea. This operations known as a Dependent's Cruise is permitted about once a year to enable the family and friends of the crew to see what life aboard ship is really like at sea. Informality was the keynote as the guests roamed the ship watching the crew carry out their normal functions. Most everyone was situated topside during the ninety minute transit of San Diego harbor but after that they scattered to the engineroom, fireroom, focsle and fantail. Commander Addams, the Executive Officer, gave a running commentary of the ship's internal activities as well as sights along the shoreline as we threaded our way out of the harbor. After a short run out to sea, we returned to anchor in Coronado Roads. Here we shared a buffet lunch - barbecue pit style on the helo deck or cafeteria style in the crew's dining area. Returning to port about 3 P.M. a host of happy wives, parents, friends, and children departed the ship claiming they had felt no "mal de mer", and were experienced sailors like "ole Dad".

For the remainder of December and until 4 January, a sizeable portion of the crew was on leave, many traveling to the other three corners of the U.S. and even to Hawaii. During this period our work was lighter and we were able to enjoy early liberty most working days. Of course, the Duty Section of about 75 men was always on board caring for the ship and maintaining security.

It is customary for U. S. Navy ships inport over the holidays to erect some kind of decoration to celebrate the season. Under the direction of Lieutenant Commander Malone, our Engineering Officer, a tree of lights sixty feet tall was constructed on JOUETT's foremast. On top of this a large white star was situated. Additional lights outlined the main deck lifelines and another tree was erected on the fantail. All in all, our electrical gang did a great job and made us very proud of JOUETT each time we saw the lights from ashore.

After the 4th of January we snapped back to work in earnest to prepare for our pre-deployment inspection by Commander Destroyer Squadron ONE. Once again the hard work paid off, because the Commodore, in speaking to all hands stated that he was quite pleased with the results.

Right up to our departure on 16 January, we were busy topping-off with supplies for our cruise of six months away from the continental United States. We stock over 50,000 separate items in our 22 storerooms maintained by the Supply Officer, Lieutenant Commander Lantsberger. During the last few days we took on 11,500 pounds of beef, 800 gallons of milk, 1600 dozen eggs, and last but not least, 800 pounds of popcorn for our nightly movies. Some of our men had sore muscles after all the loading because even in our modern computerized Navy we still load stores by hand.

Since the last Familygram, promotions have taken place for a number of officers and men. I had the pleasure of presenting the JOUETT Outstanding Service Award to the following petty officers: Chief Quartermaster William E. JOHNSEN, Chief Electronics Technician Charles N. BOWERS, Chief Storekeeper Jack R. MEAD, and First Class Fire Control Technician Paul J. STANGE.

Tuesday, January 16th, was a warm, clear day in San Diego, but a number of eyes were moist as the long blast on JOUETT's whistle signified that she was backing away from pier No. 2, U. S. Naval Station, to commence the voyage to the Western Pacific. Prior to JOUETT's departure, wives, children, parents, and friends were on board for coffee and pastries and a last look at the ship. The CRUDESPAC band, embarked for the voyage, played music on the helo deck which helped remove some of the sadness from the occasion. As JOUETT nosed her way out the channel, the pier thronged with families, the city of San Diego, and finally Point Loma disappeared in the mist as we proceeded west to new adventures and service to our country.

Out at sea we are busy with training and briefings. We have an important job to do and all hands seem eager to get on with the challenges ahead. In these last months a motto has sprung up, as these things do, which seems to fit the image we have of ourselves - "JOUETT CAN-DO-IT". I am so proud of our crew - never has a more highly trained or more motivated crew set out to do the job ahead.

I plan to continue these familygrams during the cruise in the hope they may fill the information gap and above all gain your support. Your letters from home are the best way of telling us that you care.

Sincerely,

ROBERT S. HAYES
CAPTAIN, U.S. NAVY
COMMANDING OFFICER

1968-01-21.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-01-21.text:
21 Jan., 1968
Sunday

Dear Mother & Dad,

Things have been going just fine since we left San Diego at 10:00 Tuesday. We are close to Pearl Harbor now and should get there about 4 PM today. We have some gun shoots to go through today then head for port. They have scheduled today as a payday so that liberty in Hawaii will be a little more enjoyable.

I got back to the ship about 5 PM last Tuesday. Bill called us at Georgia Mae's about 10 Monday evening. We had tried for about 30 minutes earlier in the evening to get a hold of him but didn't have any luck. We were glad that he called. I stopped at Oceanside on the way back to San Diego and saw him for an hour or so. That was a long night but since it was the last time I'd see anyone I knew, it was worth it.

The ship has been riding pretty well. The first day was hard to get use to after being in port for such a long time. I am use to it now and it doesn't bother me a bit. The first night a lot of us had trouble sleeping because of the rocking. I am eating pretty good so I guess thats a good indication I am in good health.

The days have been sunny and fair. You can notice it getting warmer the farther west we go.

We will be in Pearl Harbor for three days. It should be quite an experience the time we are there. Our next stop is Guam then on to the Phillipines.

One other ship left with us and we have been running side by side all the time. It gives you something to look at and at least we know we aren't the only ones out here.

I hope the weather isn't getting any worse back home, or could it get any worse? I'm sure David is having plenty of fun in the snow.

We have a calendar back here in the gun control room that we are keeping track of the days on. We figure the longest the cruise could last is 190 days (July 30). That seems like a long time but some day we will be able to look back on all the days as a lot of new experiences for most of us.

In my spare time, I've been keeping busy working on my electronics course. I have done three of the lessons since we left Tuesday. I stand my watches here on the radar console.

Thats about all there is for now. I'll write again when I know the mail will be going out. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike

1968-01-26.attribution: USS Jouett Evening News — Ducy Family Archives
1968-01-26.text:
USS JOUETT
EVENING NEWS
26 JAN 68

(AP) TWO MOVES WERE MADE THURSDAY BY THE UNITED STATES IN CONNECTION WITH THE NORTH KOREAN CRISIS. NEARLY FIFTEEN THOUSAND RESERVE AIRMEN HAVE BEEN CALLED UP. AND THIS HAS BEEN FOLLOWED BY AN APPEAL FOR AN URGENT MEETING OF THE UNITED NATIONS SECURITY COUNCIL. BOTH MOVES WERE MADE AT THE INSTIGATION OF PRESIDENT JOHNSON. THE U-N APPEAL CAME AFTER MR. JOHNSON HAD CONFERRED WITH ARTHUR GOLDBERG, AMERICA'S AMBASSADOR TO THE WORLD PEACE ORGANIZATION. GOLDBERG FLEW BACK TO NEW YORK ALMOST IMMEDIATELY. ONE POSSIBLE SNAG IS THAT NORTH KOREA DOES NOT BELONG TO THE U-N AND IN THE PAST HAS GENERALLY IGNORED IT. U-N DIPLOMATS EXPECT THE SECURITY COUNCIL WILL MEET FRIDAY TO TAKE UP THE CRISIS TRIGGERED BY NORTH KOREA'S SEIZURE OF THE U.S.S. [text cut off]

(AP) THE OFFICIAL SOVIET NEWS AGENCY, TASS, DESCRIBED AS A "THREATENING ACT" THE UNITED STATES CALL-UP OF NEARLY FIFTEEN-THOUSAND RESERVE AIRMEN. AND THE SOVIET GOVERNMENT NEWSPAPER, IZVESTIA, SAID WHAT IT CALLED NERVOUS ANXIETY IN WASHINGTON OVER THE PUEBLO INCIDENT SUSPICIOUSLY RESEMBLES THE ATMOSPHERE DURING THE GULF OF TONKIN INCIDENO IN NINETEEN-SIXTY-FOUR.
    (UPI) KENTUCKY SENATOR THRUSTON (THROOS'-THUN) MORTON IS CALLING FOR A WASHINGTON-MOSCOW SUMMIT MEETING AS A MEANS OF EASING COLD WAR TENSIONS. IN REMARKS PREPARED FOR DELIVERY IN NEW YORK THURSDAY NIGHT, THE REPUBLICAN LAW-MAKER SAID THAT A SUMMIT MEETING MIGHT UNLOCK THE DOOR TO SETTLEMENT IN VIETNAM, THE MIDEAST AND OTHER GLOBAL HOT-SPOTS.

(AP) TEL AVIV REPORTS AN EXCHANGE OF GUNFIRE BETWEEN ISRAELI AND EGYPTIAN KORCES AFTER THE ARABS LAUNCHED A SMALL BOAT ON THE SUEZ CANAL AT PORT SUEZ. THE FIRST BRIEF CLASH ON THE CANAL IN SEVERAL MONTHS CAME WITHIN HOURS AFTER ISRAEL AGREED TO LET THE EGYPTIANS START CLEARING PEACEFULLY.

(AP) RADIO MOSCOW SAYS COMMUNIST NORTH KOREA ACTED RIGHTFULLY IN DETAINING THE SOVIET UNION HAS COME TO THE PUEBLO. THE COMMENT IS THE CLOSEST APPROVAL OF NORTH KOREA'S ACTION REGISTERING OFFICIAL.

---

(AP) SECRETARY OF STATE RUSK HAD SOME SHARP ANSWERS FOR NEWSMEN WHO ASKED ABOUT POSSIBLE NORTH KOREAN CHARGES AGAINST THE PUEBLO CREWMEN. HE CALLED THE SEIZURE AN "OUT-RAGEOUS ACT," AND SAID HEATEDLY: "THESE MEN HAVE COMMITTED NO CRIME." HE ADDED THAT THE U-S HAS NO FIXED DEADLINE FOR THEIR RELEASE, BUT ADDED: "TODAY WOULD BE A GOOD TIME..."

(AP) PRESIDENT JOHNSON CONFERRED AGAIN FRIDAY WITH HIS TOP ADVISERS. BUT HE IS HOLDING BACK ANY NEW ANNOUNCE-MENTS PENDING THE U-N CONSIDERATION OF THE QUESTION. AT THE PRESENT TIME, THE PRESIDENT IS NOT CONSIDERING ADDRES-SING THE UNITED NATIONS.

(AP) THE F-B-I HAS CHARGED SEVEN MEN WITH PLANNING TO ROB FOUR BANKS AFTER BLOWING UP A POLICE STATION AND A POWER PLANT IN TWO SUBURBS OF SEATTLE, (-7 8,859). THE FEDERAL MEN SAY THAT SEVERAL OF THOSE ARRESTED WERE MEM-BERS OF AN ULTRA-PATRIOTIC GROUP CALLED THE "MINUTEMEN." THE F-B-I SAID AN ARSENAL INCLUDING MOLOTOV COCKTAILS, GUNS AND KYHUMITE ALSO WAS SEIZED.

(UPI) DOW JONES CLOSING AVERAGES...INDUSTRIALS EIGHT HUNDRED SIXTY FIVE POINT OH SIX, UP ZERO POINT EIGHTY ONE RAILS TWO HUNDRED THIRTY ONE POINT SEVENTY FIVE, UP MNE POINT NINETEEN, UTILITIES ONE HUNDRED THIRTY POINT TWENTY FOUR, BOWF YERO POINT TEN, STOCKS THREE HUNDRED SIX POINT SEVENTY, UP ZERO POINT SIXTY TWO.

(AP) IN SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA, THE WIFE OF THE SKIPPER OF THE PUEBLO HAS BEEN SHOWN A PHOTOGRAPH RELEASED BY THE NORTH KOREANS PURPORTING TO SHOW HIM SIGNING AN ALLEGED CONFESSION. MRS. ROSE BUCHER SAID IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO BE SURE WHETHER THE PHOTOGRAPH IS OF HER HUSBAND, COMMANDER LLOYD BUCHER.

(AP) REPUBLICAN REPRESENTATIVE MELVIN LAIRD OF WINCON-SIN HAS CHARGED THAT THE U-S GOVERNMENT HAD BEEN FORE-WARNED BY NORTH KOREA NS THEY INTENDED TO MOVE AGAINST THE PUEBLO. LAIRD SAID THE COMMUNISTS MADE KNOWN THEIR INTENTIONS IN A RADIO BROADCAST EARLY THIS MONTH PROTEST-ING THE ELECTRONIC SURVEILLANCE SHIP.

(AP) SENATE DEMOCRATIC LEADER MIKE MANSFIELD HAS CAU-TIONED AGAINST ANY "RASH ACT" THAT COULD LEAD TO ANOTHER ASIAN WAR BECAUSE OF THE SEIZURE OF THE PUEBLO. MANSFIELD SAID HE HOPES THE U-N SECURITY COUNCIL CAN SOLVE THE CRISIS PEACEFULLY.

---

SPORTS

(UPI) THERE IS A FOUR-WAY TIE FOR THE LEADERSHIP AFTER THE OPENING ROUND OF THE ONE HUNDRED-THOUSAND DOLLAR LOS ANGELES OPEN GOLF TOURNAMENT. AT SIXTY-SEVEN...FOUR UNDER-PAR...ARE GENE LITTLER, DAVE EICHEL-BERGER, JIMMY CLARK AND AL GEIBERGER. SIX MORE PROS ARE TIED AT SIXTY-EIGHT. THEY ARE GEORGE ARCHER, DON BIES, DAVE MARR, GEORGE KNUDSON, RAY FLOYD AND DOUG SANDERS. ARNOLD PALMER FIRED A SIXTY-NINE. HE IS THE DEFENDING CHAMPION AND IS DEADLOCKED WITH CHARLIE SIFFORD, TERRY WILCOX AND DALE DOUGLASS. FOURTEEN MEN ARE IN WITH SCORES OF SEVENTY. INCLUDED IN THE GROUP IS BILLY CASPER, THIRD LEADING MONEY WINNER ON THE TOUR LAST YEAR. PROBABLY THE TWO-BIGGEST SURPRISES OF THE FIRST ROUND ARE EICHELBERGER AND CLARK. EICHELBERGER TURNED PRO IN NINETEEN SIXTY-SIX AND THEN TOOK OFF SIX MONTHS TO SERVE IN THE MARINE CORPS. CLARK WON THE AZALEA AND FORT WAYNE TOURNAMENTS IN NINETEEN FIFTY-TWO AND IS MAKING A COMEBACK ON THE P-G-A TOUR. PAR TOOK A BEATING WITH TWENTY-EIGHT GOLFERS BETTERING IT AND ELEVEN EQUAL-LING THE REGULATION FIGURE. FIRST PLACE IS WORTH TWENTY THOUSAND DOLLARS.

(UPI) BOB SEAGREN OF THE UNIVERSITY OF SOUTHERN CALI-FORNIA ESTABLISHED A WORLD INDOOR POLE VAULT RECORD WHEN HE CLEARED THE BAR AT A HEIGHT OF SEVENTEEN-FEET... FOUR AND ONE-QUARTER-INCHES. HE ACCOMPLISHED THE FETE AT THE MILLROSE GAMES AT NEW YORK'S OLD MADISON SQUARE GARDEN. MEET RECORDS WERE SET BY BYRON DYCE OF NEW YORK UNIVERSITY IN THE ONE-THOUSAND YARD-RUN. HIS TIME WAS TWO-MINUTES...TEN AND ONE-TENTH SECONDS. LARRY JAMES OF VILLANOVA RAN THE FIVE HUNDRED-YARD EVENT IN A NEW TIME OF FIFTY-SIX AND ONE-TENTH SECONDS. MARTIN MCGRAY'S MEET RECORD WAS IN THE SIX HUNDRED YARD RACE. THE ATHLETE FROM SANTA CLARA YOUTH VILLAGE WAS CLOCKED AT ONE MINUTE TEN POINT-ONE SECONDS. AND GEORGE YOUNG OF COSA GRANDE, ARIZONA, WENT INTO THE BOOKS FOR HIS THREE MILE-RUN. HIGH JUMPER JOHN THOMAS OF BOSTON BECAME A MILLROSE WINNER FOR THE SIXTH TIME BY WINNING HIS SPEC-IALTY WITH A LEAP OF SIX-FEET...TEN-INCHES. OTHER OUT-STANDING PERFORMANCES WERE TURNED IN BY LENNOX MILLER OF SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA AND LEON COLEMAN OF THE SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA STRIDERS. MILLER WON THE SIXTY-YARD DASH IN SIX AND TWO-TENTHS SECONDS. COLEMAN TOOK THE SIXTY-YARD HIGH HURDLES WITH A TIME SEVEN-POINT-TWO. AUSTRALIAN RALPH DOUBELL CAPTURED THE HALF-MILE RUN WITH A CLOCKING OF ONE-MINUTE-FIFTY-THREE-POINT-FIVE-TWO-NINE SECONDS.

---

(UPI) THE BIGGEST GAME ON THE COLLEGE BASKETBALL SCENE THURSDAY NIGHT WAS FIFTH-RANKED ST. BONAVENTURE'S SEVENTY-FOUR-FIFTY-EIGHT WIN OVER ST. FRANCIS OF PENN-SYLVANIA. BOB LANIER PUMPED IN THIRTY-THREE POINTS AND GRABBED TWENTY-THREE REBOUNDS IN LEADING THE UNDEFEATED BONNIES TO THEIR FIFTEENTH STRAIGHT WIN. IN OTHER GAMES BRADLEY ROUTED MEMPHIS STATE NINETY-TWO-SIXTY-NINE... OKLAHOMA CITY NIPPED ARKANSAS NINETY-TWO-NINETY IN OVER-TIME...AND PITTSBURGH DUMPED BOL WIN-WALLACE EIGHTY-THREE-SEVENTY-SIX. PROVIDENCE TOOK MASSACHUSETTS EIGHTY-THREE-SEVENTY-SEVEN...FORDHAM KNOCKED OFF RUTGERS SIXTY-SEVEN-FIFTY...WHILE KENT STATE WALKED OVER TULANE NINETY-THREE-SEVENTY-THREE. IOWA STATE WITHSTOOD OKLA-HOMA EIGHTY-SEVENTY...AND BAYLOR TROUNCED TARLETON STATE ONE-OH-ONE-SIXTY-SEVEN.

(UPI) IN THE NATIONAL BASKETBALL ASSOCIATION THURSDAY LOS ANGELES RALLIED TO DEFEAT CINCINNATI ONE-EIGHTEEN-

ONE-SIXTEEN...ST. LOUIS DROPPED BOSTON ONE-OH-FIVE-NINETY-THREE...PHILADELPHIA WHIPPED DETROIT ONE TWENTY-THREE-ONE OH-EIGHT...BALTIMORE BEAT SAN DIEGO ONE TWENTY-SEVEN-ONE-THIRTEEN...AND NEW YORK OVERCAME CHICAGO ONE TWENTY-SIX-ONE-EIGHTEEN. FRIDAY BOSTONQ CINCINNATI IS AT PHILADELPHIA...NEW YORK TRAVELS TO ST. LOUIS...AND SAN FRANCISCO PLAYS AT HOME AGAINST BALTI-MORE.

(UPI) THURSDAY'S AMERICAN BASKETBALL ASSOCIATION GAMES ENDED WITH MINNESOTA ROUTING NEW JERSEY ONE THIRTY-SEVEN-ONE-OH-FOUR... OAKLAND LOSING TO ANAHEIM ONE TWENTY-FOUR-ONE-SIXTEEN...AND DALLAS EDGING NEW ORLEANS ONE-OH-TWO-ONE-OH-ONE. THE FRIDAY NIGHT CARD READS KENTUCKY AT ANAHEIM...HOUSTON VISITING DALLAS... NEW ORLEANS ENTERTAINING DENVER...AND PITTSBURGH PLAYING MINNESOTA AT HOME.

1968-02-01.label: All Hands - USS Wainwright Has Lots of PIRAZ
1968-02-01.attribution: All Hands - USS Wainwright Has Lots of PIRAZ — Ducy Family Archives
1968-02-01.text:
USS WAINWRIGHT HAS LOTS OF PIRAZ
All Hands magazine, February 1968, pp. 16-17
2 scans from Mike Ducy's collection
Handwritten note on page 16: "I guess this is something like your ship"

========================================================================================
PAGE 16 (page 1 of article)
========================================================================================

[Photo top left: Logistics helicopter departing guided missile frigate at sea.
Caption: "LOGISTICS HELICOPTER leaves Wainwright for other ships."]

[Photo top right: Silhouette of watchstander wearing headset.
Caption: "Rt: Long day of watching continues through the night."]

[Handwritten note in margin of top photo: "I guess this is something like
your ship" with arrow pointing to ship photo]


                    USS WAINWRIGHT HAS

PIRAZ, officially known as Positive Identification Radar Advisory
Zone, is an area covering much of the Tonkin Gulf. It is also the sta-
tion name of the ship which controls this zone.

USS Wainwright (DLG 28), a guided missile frigate, is one such
ship. She provides Navy and Air Force pilots with continuous air navi-
gation, quick advice on the nearest tanker service, and sorts out the good
guys from the bad guys.

Wainwright frequently cruises some 100 miles north of Yankee Sta-
tion where Navy carrier-based pilots begin and end their combat flights.
The distance to Hanoi and Haiphong is much less to the north and west.

On a typical day on Piraz, activity in CIC (Combat Information Center)
begins to pick up around daybreak.

[Caption across middle: "ON PIRAZ STATION—Reveille is sounded and the morning watch
is set as USS Wainwright (DLG 28) maintains a radar fix for pilots flying in Vietnam."]

[Photo bottom: USS Wainwright (DLG 28) at sea, port quarter view, with helicopter
nearby. Hull number 28 visible.]

Shortly thereafter, planes of the three attack carriers of Task Force 77 are
overhead on their way to targets in North Vietnam.

This routine is repeated day after day and often hour after hour by the
men and ships who man the Piraz station. For Wainwright, this is her
second line period.

One piece of gear which makes her particularly useful at this sort of
job is her Naval Tactical Data System, which is a high-speed, com-
puterized system of collecting, displaying and evaluating combat infor-
mation. Wainwright needs all the help she can get, for at times the air
space in her area is as crowded, if not more so, as the world's busiest
airports during peak flying hours.

For 24 hours a day, Wainwright air intercept controllers identify and
track all aircraft over the Tonkin Gulf. During the almost-daily strikes,
they have their hands full.

First come the defensive F4B Phantom jet fighters, then the sup-
porting tankers and radar aircraft. Finally, the attack aircraft — the
Phantoms, Thunderchiefs, Intruders, Skyraiders, Skyhawks and Crusaders
—check through Piraz on their way to the north.

All the aircraft in the armada are identified, assigned a computer iden-
tification code and tracked to the target and back out.

At the same time, Wainwright's


========================================================================================
PAGE 17 (page 2 of article)
========================================================================================

[Photo top left: Watchstander viewing radar scope or chart.
Caption: "CONTROLLERS track all aircraft over the Tonkin Gulf."]

[Photo top right: Flight deck crewmen refueling helicopter.
Caption: "Below: Flight deck crewmen help refuel SAR helicopter."]


                    LOTS OF PIRAZ

helicopter takes off. In company with the other sea-air-rescue helos,
"Big Mother" will hover just off the coast of North Vietnam near the
coast-out (or attack exit point) throughout the mission. They wait
to give a helping hand to returning pilots who may be in trouble and
have to ditch.

Back in CIC the air intercept controller identifies and tracks all
friendly aircraft. By doing so, he will be able to know promptly of any
enemy air activity and to divert the defensive Phantoms to the intercept.

Should the enemy break through the defensive fighters, or if the enemy
were to make an attempt on the fleet in the Tonkin Gulf, Wainwright
would shift to her main battery, the Terrier surface-to-air missile system.

More than once, Terriers have been readied when unidentified and
unaware friendlies forgot to check into the Piraz area.

Although Wainwright's Terriers have never been fired in anger, her
missilemen check and double check the system daily to ensure it will be
ready if needed.

In addition to her primary mission of keeping track of all aircraft over
the Gulf, Wainwright also passes such information as weather, courses
to home base and locations of other aircraft in the Gulf to pilots when
they need it.

Throughout the day, the cycle continues. Attack aircraft coast-out
with empty bomb racks, take a fix on Wainwright and head for home.

No matter whether they are going in or coming out, work does not slow
down aboard Wainwright. During the lull between strikes, data on the
next attack is fed into the computers and marked on the plotting board.

Men and machines work together to form a team where a score of 99
out of 100 is not good enough.

                              —Text and photos by
                              Willard B. Bass, Jr., JO1


[Caption: "MISSILE CHECK—Member of Wainwright's weapons division relays informa-
tion via phone as the ship's Terrier surface-to-air missile system is checked."]

[Photo bottom right: Crewman standing near Terrier missile launcher on deck]

FEBRUARY 1968                                                              17


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

This article describes exactly the mission USS Jouett (DLG-29) would perform
during her 1968 WestPac deployment. Wainwright (DLG-28) was Jouett's near-sister
ship — both were Belknap-class guided missile frigates with NTDS (Naval Tactical
Data System) and Terrier missile systems.

The handwritten note "I guess this is something like your ship" was likely written
by a family member (Dan or Dorothea Ducy) who clipped this article from All Hands
magazine and sent it to Mike, or kept it at home. The note suggests they were
trying to understand what Mike's ship would be doing — the article was published
in February 1968, just as Jouett arrived in WestPac.

Key parallels to Jouett's deployment:
- PIRAZ station duty (Jouett served on PIRAZ)
- CIC air intercept control (Mike's Fire Control division supported this)
- SAR helicopter operations ("Big Mother" SH-3A helos — Jouett hosted HC-7 dets)
- NTDS (Jouett "pioneered tactical development of NTDS configured DLG in limited war")
- Terrier missile system (Jouett fired missiles in SAMEX during BLUE LOTUS)
- F4B Phantom CAP control (Jouett-controlled CAP got 1 MIG kill + 1 probable)
- 24-hour operations tracking all aircraft over Tonkin Gulf

Article by JO1 Willard B. Bass, Jr. (Journalist First Class).

1968-02-01.label: Jouett Visits the Philippines
1968-02-01.attribution: Jouett Visits the Philippines — Ducy Family Archives
1968-02-01.text:
JOUETT VISITS THE PHILIPPINES — PORT GUIDE (~February 1968)

--- COVER ---

[Hand-drawn cover art in green ink: A circle containing two palm trees with mountains in the background, signed "Mac". Below the circle in stylized block lettering:]

JOUETT
VISITS THE

PHILIPPINES

--- PAGE 1 ---

[Blank — back of cover, bleed-through only]

--- PAGE 2 (printed as unnumbered) ---

HISTORICAL - GEOGRAPHICAL

Subic Bay is located on the west coast of the island of Luzon approximately 35 miles north of the entrance to Manila Bay.

Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese navigator in the service of Spain, landed in the Philippines on 16 March 1521. When the Spanish came, contrary to popular belief, a comparatively advanced culture already existed in the Philippines. The majority of the people lived in independent settlements or "Barangays" which were united to form a federation. The laws under which they lived were largely traditional but as early as 1433, or 88 years previous to the arrival of Magellan, there existed a penal code.

Colonization was not begun by the Spanish until 1565 when Miguel Lopez de Legaspi took possession of the islands. He was the first civil governor of the Philippines, named in honor of Philip II of Spain. The Spanish occupation greatly changed the spiritual life of the Philippines. Under Spanish rule, the Catholic Church converted a relatively large portion of the population to Christianity, although many old superstitions and much native culture continued to exist under a thin veneer of western civilization.

War and uprisings, in which the perennial struggle for power between the church and the state was often involved, characterized the history of the islands from the beginning of Spanish rule to the American occupation. A revolution had broken out just prior to Admiral Dewey's capture of Manila. In the treaty of Paris, Spain ceded the islands to the United States. The revolutionary Philippine government, headed by Emilio Aguinaldo, protested that Spain had no right to cede the islands because their control had passed from her hands to the insurgents. Then war began between the United States and the insurgents. Resistance ended with the capture of Aguinaldo.

On 15 November 1935 the Commonwealth Government was established with Manuel L. Quezon and Sergio Osmena as president and vice-president. The capture of Manila by the Japanese on 2 January 1942 forced the government into exile in America where Quezon died of tuberculosis. Three years later, with the liberation of Manila by the Allied Forces under General Douglas MacArthur aided by thousands of Filipino guerrillas, the Commonwealth Government was restored on 27 February 1945. Although Manila had been declared an open city by United States Forces, its liberation was bitterly contested by the Japanese and the resultant damage was extremely severe. During the Japanese occupation, thousands of Filipino non-combatants were murdered; agriculture and other industries were devastated; and public and private buildings were wantonly destroyed.

On 4 July 1946, in accordance with the provisions of an agreement made with the United States, the Philippines proclaimed their independence.

Manuel Roxas and Elpidio Quirino were inaugurated as president and vice-president. In the years since 1946, the Philippine Republic has struggled against an organization of dissidents commonly known as the "Huks" or the "HMB". The organization was started in March 1942 under the name of "Hukbalahaps" (The People's Army to Fight Japan). During the war, the Huks were active against the Japanese and to a lesser extent, against other Filipino guerrilla units. Following the liberation of the Philippines, the Huks did not completely disband or turn in their arms. At the end of 1949, the name of the Huks was changed, to the "Hukbong Mapagpalayang Bayan" (People's Liberation Army) from which comes the common abbreviation HMB. Since that time, the Huks, in tune with world communism, have advocated the overthrow of the Philippine Government and the assumption of power by popular elements. However, during the recent years an understanding government has undertaken the rehabilitation of many ex-dissidents who have indicated their desire to return to peaceful and useful lives. The Huk situation is definitely under control, but danger of harassing action still exists in the outlying areas in Central Luzon.

AIRFIELDS AND AIRCRAFT FACILITIES

NAS, Cubi Point, is located about three miles by road from the Naval Station and Naval Supply Depot, Subic Bay, and about one mile by water. Scheduled flights are made to Clark AFB and NS, Sangley Point, on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. A carrier pier is located immediately adjacent to the air strip. The main runway is 8000 ft. long and 200 ft. wide and will accomodate jet aircraft. The Philippine Air Lines flies between NAS, Cubi Point and the International Airport at Manila on Friday and Sunday.

TRANSPORTATION

Air and land transportation are the primary methods of moving personnel and material to and from the Naval Base, Subic Bay. No rail transportation is available.

The Public Works Center operates regularly scheduled shuttle buses which provides service from all waterfront areas, except Leyte Wharf at NAS Cubi Point, to all areas of the Base. Special and Liberty Bus Service from Leyte Wharf is available through the PWC Transportation Department (Telephone 44-2401/3260) or the PWC Duty Officer (Telephone 44-3111).

Jeepney service (05¢) is available in the Naval Station and Naval Supply Depot areas.

The Navy Exchange operates a commercial base-taxi service to any point of the U. S. Naval Base. These taxis are not allowed to carry passengers off the Naval Base. The rates charged are 20¢ for the first mile, 5¢ for each additional half-mile thereafter, and 5¢ for each 5 minutes waiting time. Call 44-3231 for service.

In Olongapo jeepney service is available and costs 10 centavos to any part of the town. Personnel are advised to ride in jeepneys with other Americans when traveling late at night in Olongapo and to stay on the main street.

--- PAGE 3 ---

Taxi service is also available in Olongapo, but fares are based on time rather than distance, as follows:

    First minute - 15 centavos
    Each additional minute - 5 centavos

Commercial bus service to Manila is available in Olongapo for personnel holding written permission to leave the military reservation.

No government or Special Services vehicles are permitted to leave the Naval Base unless driven by a licensed Filipino civilian driver.

Regularly scheduled bus runs are as follows:

TO CLARK AB

From Administration Building, Naval Base, Subic at 0715, and Naval Station Receiving Barracks at 0730, daily. From MATS Terminal (Navy ATCO) Clark at 1300 daily.

TO MANILA (Limited passenger capacity)

From Administration Building, Naval Base, Subic at 0500, Tuesday and Thursday. From American Embassy, Manila at 1300, Tuesday and Thursday.

COMMUNICATIONS

Commercial telegraph and cable service is available through RCA at an office just inside the Main Gate.

Overseas telephone calls can be made from the PWC Telephone Office in the PWC Administration Building; Clark Air Base; Baguio and Manila.

U.S. MAIL

Two post offices exist on the Naval Station. The TNPO (Bldg. CA-21) located at the west end of WATERFRONT Road handles all U. S. mail less finance for the Subic Bay area and is the serving facility for fleet units. Only duly accredited Navy Postal Clerks, Assistant Navy Postal Clerks, or Mail Orderlies bearing properly executed official identification (DD Form 285) may pick up and deliver U. S. mail to the TNPO. The Terminal is open 24 hours daily for fleet mail. The Naval Station Post Office (Bldg. 244) located on WATERFRONT Road near ALAVA Wharf provides postal services including finance for Naval Station personnel and fleet units without postal facilities aboard.

Hours of operation of the Naval Station Finance Section are as follows, except all operations secure from 1130 to 1230 daily:

    Stamps/parcel post  - Monday-Friday - - - - 1000-1600
    Money orders        - Monday-Friday - - - - 1000-1400
    Registry cage       - Monday-Friday - - - - 1000-1400

--- PAGE 4 ---

CURRENCY

CINCPACREPPHIL/COMNAVPHIL Instruction 7200.9 provides Financial Regulations for all financial transactions which may occur on U. S. military bases in the Philippines. As indicated therein, U. S. currency and dollar instruments are the medium of exchange on all U. S. military bases in the Philippines, with few exceptions. The use of U. S. currency and dollar instruments for financial transactions with Philippine citizens, or, institutions is not desired. The Peso is the medium of exchange in the Philippines, and should be used whenever possible.

For the convenience of all hands, the following facilities are available for conversion of U. S. currency to Philippine Pesos:

(1) Disbursing Office, Naval Supply Depot - Hours of operation:

(2) Navy Exchange Cashiers' Booths, located at the Main Navy Exchange

    Monday through Friday      - 0930-2100
    Saturday, Sunday and holidays - 0800-2100

Pesos may be converted to U. S. dollars only at the Navy Exchange Cashier's Booth, located at the Main Navy Exchange, during the hours of operation.

    1 U. S. dollar = 3.85 Pesos

RECREATIONAL FACILITIES

LIBERTY

Regular liberty is limited to the Naval Base and contiguous areas within a radius of ten miles from the Main Gate, U. S. Naval Base. A curfew for all personnel is established within the 10 mile regular liberty area from 0100 to 0500. Except for personnel authorized overnight liberty under the strict criteria set forth in SOPA Subic instructions, personnel must be back on base through the Main Gate by 0100 or be reported for violation of the curfew.

Regular off-base liberty expires at the Main Gate, U. S. Naval Base, Subic not later than 2330 for pay grades E-3 and below, and 0030 for pay grades E-4 through E-9. As noted above officers on shore leave are required to be back through the Main Gate not later than 0100 when the curfew takes effect.

--- PAGE 5 ---

Liberty beyond a radius of 10 miles from the Naval Base Main Gate will require a special request, showing liberty address, together with the signature of the cognizant commanding officer or executive officer.

The Main Gate of the Naval Base is the only gate authorized for liberty parties.

Loitering within the limits of the Naval Base after the expiration of liberty or after closing of various clubs, movies, and other authorized entertainment is prohibited.

RESTAURANTS, FOODS AND BEVERAGES

Numerous restaurants and clubs are operated on the Naval Base, and personnel are strongly advised to patronize these activities rather than those in Olongapo. The Spanish Gate Cafeteria is open from 0600-0100 daily. Uniform of the Day is required after 1600 hours. Snack Bars operated by Navy Exchange are located at the Bowling Alley, Binictican Valley Golf Club and Retail Store Shopping Plaza. All are air-conditioned and are open as indicated below:

TOURS AND POINTS OF INTEREST

Tourist Bureau. The Tourist Bureau is located in the Special Services Office (telephone 44-3798). This bureau can arrange with commercial companies for tours of the Philippines, Hong Kong, or Japan. The bureau will make hotel reservations where desired. Cable charges are to be paid by persons requesting reservations. Flight reservations may be made to Manila (P13.00 round trip)

--- PAGE 8 ---

and to Clark Air Base (P5.00 round trip). A Manila Tour is offered on a regular basis for nominal charges. Contact the Tourist Bureau for details. Trips can also be arranged for the group and individual to Baguio, Corregidor, Hundred Islands, Tagaytay, Pagsanjan, and other points of interest.

ENLISTED CLUBS

Sampaguita Club. The Enlisted Men's Recreation Club is known as the "Sampaguita Club" and is a membership club for members of the Armed Forces, active or retired, pay grades E-1 through E-6, their dependents and guests. Facilities include the Calesa Bar, the dining room, the dance floor and the game room (pool, ping pong, slot machines). The club is open to all personnel at noon. CPO CLUB. The Chief Petty Officers' Mess (Open) located in the EM Barracks area, is operated by the chief petty officers of all the commands of the Naval Air Station. It is open to all personnel of pay grades E-7, E-8, and E-9 and their guests.

The club better known as the TOP O' THE MARK serves beer and mixed drinks. Food is served at the snack bar and in the dining room. Bingo is played on Thursday beginning at 1900, and is followed by a dance until 0100.

Dinner is served in the dining room. Short sleeve shirts are appropriate civilian attire. A happy hour is scheduled each Friday night from 1600 - 1800. Call 55-9411.

    Monday - Thrusday                   0900 - 2330
    Friday, Saturday and Holidays       0900 - 0100
    Sunday                              0900 - 2300
    Day preceding holidays              0900 - 0100

Baguio (John Hay Air Base). This is a rehabilitation center for the U. S. Air Force. Privileges at John Hay Air Base have been extended to the U. S. Navy, Civil Service, technical personnel and their dependents. Request for accommodations may be made through Special Services Department. Enlisted personnel are berthed in barrack-type quarters and officers are billeted at BOQ at a cost of one dollar per night. Meals may be purchased at four non-appropriated fund restaurants. Reservations may be made through Special Services Department, U. S. Naval Station, Subic Bay.

BEACHES

Grande Island. A recreation area is located on Grande Island. Special Services and Navy Exchange activities are available.

Organized parties can be arranged by calling 44-3775

Transportation to and from Grande Island may be either by ship's boat or by ferry from Fleet Landing as follows:

--- PAGE 10 ---

NAS Cubi Point. A beach recreation area is located near the approach end of runway 07. Tow boats for water skiing are available. Open 0800 until sundown daily. Special parties may be arranged. Softball and volleyball equipment is available.

GENERAL INFORMATION

There are four movie houses in Olongapo but none are air conditioned. Movies are shown on the Naval Base, at the Naval Air Station, Hospital, and Marine Barracks.

The most popular items of Philippine merchandise are rattan furniture, carved wood, linen and embroidery, and special fabrics such as pineapple and coconut fiber cloth. Monkey pod and red narra woods are especially recommended. The barong-tagalog formal shirt is available and worn throughout the Philippines at formal occasions. The Navy Exchange, Subic Bay, is the best source for such items. Carved Philippine carabao horns cannot be taken to the United States.

OUT OF BOUNDS AREA

The area of Santa Rita on the north end of Olongapo north and west of the Santa Rita River is out of bounds.

Personnel are not authorized to leave the highway between Maquinaya Beach and the Naval Base main gate, or to wander off the highways and populated areas in any part of the naval base.

During hours of darkness, servicemen on liberty in Olongapo are authorized to be in jeepneys only on Magsaysay Drive and Manila Avenue from the naval station main gate (gate No. 2) to the Grandilla Night Club and on those streets bordering the Public Market.

POLICE STATION

Civilian police are located at the Olongapo Police Headquarters on Rizal Avenue (Phone Olongapo 2220).

The Armed Forces Police Station is located at the Main Gate of the Naval Base (Phone 44-3567).

1968-02-02.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-02-02.text:
Friday 2, Feb.
1968

Dear Mother & Dad,

How is everything back home? Its been over two weeks since we left San Diego and the days have really gone fast. Actually its hard to tell one day from the other out here. I hate to say this knowing how it is back there, but it gets quite warm during the day. They let us go around in T-shirts and that sun is really hot, just like summer.

I had a good time in Hawaii and hope we stop again on our way back. I have three rolls of film being processed now and will send them to you as soon as I get them.

Tomorrow morning we arrive in Guam. We will only be there for about 8 hours then are on our way to Subic Bay, Phillipines. That will take about 6 days. After that we go to Da Nang for a couple of days then off the coast of N. Viet Nam for about 40 days.

Have you heard anything about Bill? I suppose he is over there or on his way by now.

We have only got mail once since we left the states and that was in Pearl Harbor. There should be some tomorrow. After we get into the combat zone they will fly it to us about twice a week. That will be better than none at all like it has been.

Tuesday morning I began working topside where we have two of our directors. As you know I had been in the gun control room as a working space. They decided to switch me and this other guy around for a while. I like working out side in the sun and I find things pretty easy up there. I still stand my four hour watches on the radar console as before. I'm still keeping busy on my correspondence course and find it keeps some of the time occupied. Believe me there is plenty of that (time) out here.

The way things are shaping up over there, I hope we don't get extended while we are here. It would just be my luck that things would get real serious and they would extend the reserves about the time I get out.

By all means keep up the prayers for Bill and me, because there is no safe place when you are in the combat zone. We figure to draw combat pay 5 months of the 6 so you know we will see some action.

I hope David is making good use of the boots. I'm sure he is quite proud of them. How is he doing in school. Good, I hope.

Is there anything like cameras, radios, silverware etc., that I could get anyone while I'm over here? I have a few things that I am going to get.

I'm sorry but there isn't really too much to tell about. When you're out here not too much happens. But I do know for sure that there will be a lot to talk about the next time you see me.

I have to close here and will write again when I know the mail will go out. So long for now.

Your son,

Mike
