1968-02-04.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-02-04.text:
Sunday 4, Feb.,
1968

Dear Mother & Dad,

We left Guam yesterday at 1800. I was glad to get your letter and hear about the news back home.

We should arrive in Subic Bay around 1700 Wednesday, the 7th. I figured I'd go ahead and write now because mail will be going out there.

We had six hours liberty while we were in Guam. You remember my telling you about that buddy of mine from "A" school. Well, his ship is home-ported in Guam. His ship was in yesterday so I went over and saw him. He was glad I made it over and was pretty surprized. He said his wife had a baby girl on Dec. 7. He showed me some pictures and is pretty proud and would really like to get a couple of weeks leave but no chance of it. We had plenty to talk about and later on went over to the E.M. Club for a couple of beers. He was suppose to mail a letter, some postcards and pictures for me, you should have got them by now.

I was glad to get my pictures and the one of Bill. The one Uncle John took is at least something I can look at occasionally and think of you back home.

I'm glad David has been doing so good in his schoolwork. I bet he'd wear those boots to bed if you would let him.

Last week the captian was talking to the crew. One of the first things he said was, "No one is going to take the Jouett into port." We will be operating off of N. Viet Nam but from what this buddy told me there isn't really that much action at sea. He said it gets to the point where you don't even know there is a war.

I got a letter from Bill yesterday and he said he was to leave for Nam at 0930 on the 30th of Jan. I wonder if we will be fortunate to see one another over there. Only time will tell.

Since this is Sunday afternoon they have planned a jam session at 1430 for the entertainment of the crew. It will be a sort of talent show and will help take the edge off of the usual routine of the cruise.

I hope you liked the pictures. I have one more roll yet to get. I should get it in Subic Bay. If Dad can get some of those large envelopes (that I send the pictures in) at work, I would like some more. I only have one left and it may be hard to get some more.

Well thats all from this part of the world. Take care and keep me up on how things are going back home. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike

P.S.

Can you figure out how far from home I'll be when we get in the Phillipines, Wednesday. By my figuring its about 8000 miles. Am I right? Let me know just for curiosity.

1968-02-08.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-02-08.text:
MIKE DUCY TO HOME — MANILA POSTCARD
February 8, 1968, from Subic Bay, Philippines
Postcard: "An Aerial View of Manila, PHILIPPINES"
2 scans (front and back)

========================================================================================
FRONT
========================================================================================

[Color aerial photograph of Manila, Philippines, showing the Pasig River
winding through the city center, the Intramuros walled district, Jones Bridge,
and surrounding urban area. Large neoclassical government building (Manila
Central Post Office) visible at river bend.]

Caption: "An Aerial View of Manila, PHILIPPINES"

Published by Kruger (#17501)
"Exclusively Distributed by National Book Store, Manila"


========================================================================================
BACK (Mike's handwriting, blue ink)
========================================================================================

8 FEB. 1968.

I GOT THE PACKAGE YESTERDAY, WHEN WE GOT HERE IN SUBIC BAY. I'M NOT SURE
HOW LONG WE WILL BE HERE BUT YOU CAN BE SURE IT WON'T BE FOR LONG. I HAVE
HEARD FROM BILL A COUPLE OF TIMES BUT NO ADDRESS. NO DOUBT ABOUT IT, HE IS
IN 'NAM BY NOW. I AM WAITING FOR MORE PICTURES AND WILL WRITE WHEN THEY COME.

                                        MIKE

Addressed to:
   MR. & MRS. DAN DUCY
   1525 N. ELLEN
   DECATUR, ILL. 62526
   U.S.A.

Stamp: 8-cent U.S. Air Mail (red, Capitol Building design)
Postmark: FEB 10 [year partially obscured]
Handwritten: "AIR MAIL" in blue ink with underlines


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

First Subic Bay port call of the deployment, approximately February 7-8,
1968 (per logbook). Mike received a package from home upon arrival.

The most significant detail is Mike's mention of Bill: "I HAVE HEARD FROM
BILL A COUPLE OF TIMES BUT NO ADDRESS. NO DOUBT ABOUT IT, HE IS IN 'NAM
BY NOW." Bill (Pfc. William P. Ducy, USMC, 7th Communications Battalion)
arrived in Vietnam in February 1968 but had not yet sent Mike his mailing
address. Mike knows his brother is in the war zone but cannot write to him.

The brothers would eventually meet face-to-face in Da Nang Harbor on
June 13, 1968 — four months after this postcard was written.

The postcard was purchased at the National Book Store in Manila, a major
Philippine bookstore chain. Subic Bay Naval Station was located on the
western coast of Luzon, about 60 miles northwest of Manila.

This is the second postcard in the collection. The first (July 9, 1968,
from Guam) was sent on the homeward voyage.

1968-02-09.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-02-09.text:
9 Feb., 1968
Subic Bay, Phillipines

Dear Mother & Dad,

I know I just wrote to you a couple of days ago but, in the meantime I have received the package, your note with the W-2's, and a letter today, so I figure I have some writing to do.

When the tax refund comes, just put it in the bank. Take these money orders and do the same. I figure after the tax refund I'll have about $500. Am I right?

No one really knows for sure what ships we will join when we leave here. One thing is for sure, we'll be in the combat zone at last.

This is a pretty nice base here. There is a lot to do without going into the town. They try to discourage that because its not the best place to go on liberty. In case you wonder just where we are, its about 50 miles west of Manila.

This afternoon I took some of the guys from the division to pick up some machine-gun ammunition in the pick up truck. As is usual we didn't get it because of a lack of proper authorization on the part of the ship. At any rate it helped waste the afternoon. Tomorrow is Saturday and a full working day. They just don't let up, but I can say that I don't really exert myself too much.

Thanks for taking the time to have those extra pictures made. She will be glad to get them. The picture here was taken by one of the guys one afternoon while I was on watch.

The package arrived in good shape and got here on the 7th, the day we got in here. I was really glad you sent it. Thanks a lot.

Bill has wrote a couple of times but hasn't sent a new address. He wrote when he left the states and sent a card from Hawaii.

I am expecting some pictures back any day, and will send them when they come.

You and David might be counting the days till school is out, but you can be sure that I'm counting the days till we get back in the states. We are over three weeks out of the states and really a long way from home.

I have been doing pretty good on the course. I think I will put in for the test and take it before I finish the course, you can do this if you feel you know the material.

I think I'll have you cancel the newspaper subscription as soon as it runs out. I enjoy getting it but when you don't get mail every day the papers are pretty old by the time you get them. They print up papers off of the teletype when we are at sea, so you can see we aren't really shut off from civilization in that respect.

I'll probably go over to the E.M. club tonight and have a few beers then come on back to the ship.

That's about it for now. The next time you hear from me we should be off of 'Nam. Take care of everyone and write again.

Your son,

Mike

1968-02-16.text:
Office of the Chaplain
7th Communication Battalion
FPO San Francisco 96602

                                                    19/AHW/jep
                                                    1732
                                                    16 February 1968

Mr. & Mrs. Dan F. Ducy
1525 N. Ellen Street
Decantur, Ill. 62526

Dear Mr. & Mrs. Ducy:

The purpose of this letter is to offer my assistance as your son's Battalion Chaplain.

I sincerely trust the information written in this paragraph will not have to be used, however, it could be invaluable if needed. If a death or serious illness occurs in your immediate family, contact the local American Red Cross office and that office will contact your son. Should your son be involved in any similar circumstances, you will be properly notified through Marine Corps channels. Please do not believe in rumor or hearsay. If you are in doubt about your son's welfare, please write directly to me and I will promptly investigate.

Mail is of utmost importance to your son. Write to him as often as possible. Your letters should include words of encouragement, love, and cheer. Depressing letters are not easy to accept and can be most difficult with which to cope. Please try to avoid letters of sadness and despondency.

Divine Services are available here as they are at home. Your son does have frequent opportunity to worship in the manner of his preference. Please urge him to avail himself to Divine Services.

Again, if I can be of assistance in regard to the welfare of your son please write me. Address your correspondance to: Office of the Chaplain, 7th Communication Battalion, FPO San Francisco 96602. Do not address to the signee of this letter. This Chaplain may not be the Battalion Chaplain when correspondance is necessary. May God Bless you.

                                        Sincerely,

                                        /s/ Aubret H. White

                                        Aubret H. White
                                        LCDR, CHC, USNR

1968-02-17.label: Vigilance — Page 30
1968-02-17.attribution: Vigilance, Cruiser-Destroyer Group publication, August 1968 — Ducy Family Archives
1968-02-17.text:
DD, SUB UNREP EXECUTED IN TONKIN GULF

Underway replenishments are a common sight on board CruDesPac ships, but the USS John A. Bole
(DD 755) accomplished an unusual "unrep" recently. She supplied the submarine USS Sterlet with
more than a ton of food and mail sacks while at sea in the Tonkin Gulf.

Ordinarily, subs must put into port for replenishment, thus losing valuable at-sea time when they
could be on patrol.

The Bole improvised the unrep with a manila highline attached to the sub's conning tower and
hand-pulled by the destroyer's crew. The Bole is a 23-year-old destroyer and the Sterlet is the
oldest operational submarine in the Pacific Fleet.

Lifeguard for the two ships during the unrep was one of the Navy's newest ships, the nuclear-
powered guided missile frigate USS Truxton (DLGN 35).

[Photo: SUBREP-Supplies are transferred from the USS John A. Bole (left) to the USS Sterlet in an
unusual underway replenishment in the Tonkin Gulf. The USS Truxton is in the background.]


FIRST DAY EXCITING FOR JOUETT, BUCKLEY

On their very first day on station the USS Jouett (DLG 29) and the Dennis J. Buckley (DD 808) found
themselves involved in Search and Rescue Operations (SAR) in the Tonkin Gulf.

Shortly before eight o'clock the first warning was received by Captain Arthur T. Emerson, ComDesRon 1.
An Air Force helicopter had suffered a serious engine casualty and had made an emergency landing less
than 20 miles from the enemy coastline. Buckley was immediately dispatched to assist the craft.
Carrier-based jets were called in to patrol overhead and a salvage ship was soon there.

The downed helo was in danger of capsizing in the turbulent seas, and danger of hostile attack remained
a possibility. While a repair party from Da Nang was on the way, USS Hollister (DD 788) had begun
manufacturing the needed part. Only five hours had elapsed when the giant helicopter rose from the water
under its own power.

Jouett received the next alert when the word came that one of our fighters had been hit and the pilot
was bailing out. Search and Rescue operations were underway as the San Diego-based Jouett turned into
the wind to launch the rescue helicopter. A second jet aircraft remained in the area to maintain a
vigilant protection and the stricken fighter splashed into the water fifteen miles from the hostile
coastline.

When the first rescue helo reached the scene, the pilot was floating on his back, with the inflated
orange lifejacket clearly marking his location. A crewman from the helicopter leaped into the churning
water to fasten the long hoist wire to the jet pilot and himself. A second crewmember pulled the two
men into the helo even as the rescue aircraft was clearing the area.

The pilot was obviously injured and this information was radioed back to the Jouett. He was tenderly
lifted from the helicopter and taken to sick bay where emergency treatment was given.

The injured man was taken to his aircraft carrier where complete hospital facilities were available.


COCHRANE HURLS AMMO AT SHORE

After providing gunfire support for friendly forces in Vietnam, USS Cochrane (DDG 21) has departed the
area, credited with a job well done.

Hurling more than 4,200 rounds of 5-inch ammunition during an eleven day period, the Pearl Harbor-based
Cochrane was credited with destroying or damaging more than 65 enemy gun emplacements and bunkers.

A 24-hour working day was nothing rare during this period, but the crew of Cochrane rose to the
occasion time after time. They were commended by the Tactical Commander for providing valuable
assistance to our forces ashore.

A Mardi Gras night was observed on the ship, with many gourmet dishes carrying out the New Orleans
theme. The sounds of the guns firing lent noise to the festivities, but the time for relaxation was
short.

1968-02-18.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-02-18.text:
18 Feb., 1968
Tonkin Gulf,
Viet Nam

Dear Mother & Dad,

Today is Sunday and things are going pretty smooth. This afternoon we got mail for the first time since we left Subic Bay when the helicopter brought it aboard. I was hoping to hear from you and sure enough there was your card with the letter and pictures.

We left Subic on Tuesday, the 13th and in 48 hours were in Da Nang. We anchored in the harbor there Thursday and left Friday afternoon to go on station up here. Its been real cloudy and cool with a little rain ever since we got over here Tuesday. While we were anchored there I had an M-1 rifle and a clip of cartridges by my side during the day while I was topside working. When they say there are about 500 air strikes a day you better believe it. With all the air traffic a person might think he was at O'Hare or some other large airport. We could hear some shooting in the hills but we were in a safe place (I think).

I was hoping to get a letter from Bill today but nothing yet. I don't suppose he will have much time for writing.

I was glad to see the pictures. As I looked at them it made me feel like I was in a small way there with the rest of you. Even the snow outside looked good believe it or not!

I'm really glad you got rid of the car. All I can say is I have pity on the poor guy who bought it.

I'm happy to hear that David will be taking the drum lessons. He won't be sorry he did. By the time he gets in high school he should be pretty good and may get into a band. Then he could make a few dollars on the side and have a great time doing it.

The table in the picture was a nifty idea. It keeps the toys off the floor and all the better to sweep under, of course.

About my buying souveniers over here. On all the bases they sell the same things in the exchange that they sell in the city. The prices are cheaper and you know the merchandise is good. I would like to buy a stereo tape recorder if I can find the one I'm looking for. I'll bring something home for everyone as souveniers.

I have been keeping a day to day log of the days on the cruise. By the time we get back to the states I'll have a good summary of what and where we went.

By looking at the calendar I figure that there is only 18 more months left till August '69. I can't get over how fast these six months have gone. At times the days seem so boring and drag along. But when you look back on it, it wasn't so bad after all.

We will be here on station till around March 25 then go back to Subic Bay for a few days then up to Japan. The sea is real calm over here but we all realize that the waters are hostile as far as we are concerned. It is no longer just another operation off of California, this is what we have been waiting for. Everyone looks at this from a serious view and thats the way it should be. I often wonder about Bill, knowing he is close around here somewhere. I know he is going to have some hard times in the year he is over here and I also pray that he can make it okay. As for myself I can think of no better way and safer way to get in the combat duty and extra $65 a month than to be right here where I'm at.

Here are some more pictures to put in my album. I hope you have got the ones I mailed from Guam, the same day I mailed the letter, Feb. 4.

In one of your previous letters you asked if I have heard from Father Bauer yet. So, far I haven't but will let you know when I do.

Now that we have a helicopter on board we should get mail about every three days. So, keep writing because I'll get the letters someday. I hope this has brought you up to date on how things have been so far. No doubt, there will be more to tell the next time I write. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike
1968-02-18.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-02-18.label: Familygram — Capt. Robert S. Hayes, CO
1968-02-18.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-02-18.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FPO SAN FRANCISCO 96601

                                                        18 FEBRUARY 1968

Dear family and friends of JOUETT,

Last evening we arrived on our station in Tonkin Gulf and have begun our patrols as a search and rescue unit of task force 77. So far we haven't much to say about our duties here, but we can tell you about our voyage from San Diego to Viet Nam.

Since that morning when we cast off all lines and slowly moved away from Pier Two in San Diego, we have cruised almost 8,000 miles. With the exception of three days in Pearl Harbor and a ten-hour fueling stop in Guam, it took 21 days before we arrived in Subic Bay, Philippine Islands. All of this time was spent in steaming steadily westward on a great circle route. We have been greatly impressed with the immensity of the Pacific Ocean. A jet transport can fly across this expanse of blue water in one day, but for even the fastest of ships it is a voyage of several weeks. On many of the days, our radarmen or lookouts did not pick up even one other ship, and when we did sight another ship, it was a special occasion to steer close enough to exchange signals by flashing light or flags. Of course with our modern communications we were constantly in touch with the outside world. Several of our men received messages from home announcing the birth of a son or daughter.

The Pacific transit, in company with the guided missile frigate PREBLE and destroyer HULL, was punctuated by two stops which not only rested the machinery of our ships, but also refreshed the crew. On January 21, the green mountains of the island of Oahu welcomed us into Pearl Harbor. A visit to this Naval Base is a visit into history. As our line of ships swung into the channel, there ahead was the pass between the mountains where one arm of Japanese planes emerged on a Sunday morning in December, 1941. We moved past the great, rust-stained concrete mooring quays of Battleship Row, deserted now. On the bank of the channel lay side by side the sixteen inch gun barrels of another war and another fleet, half covered with weeds. Directly across from our berth stood the impressive Arizona Memorial, built on the sunken battleship, that is still a tomb to a thousand men, and still bleeds oil occasionally into the placid harbor. Those are reminders of the past, but today Pearl Harbor is a bustling port and headquarters for the Commander-in-Chief of the Pacific Fleet. First thing Monday morning, huge piles of stores appeared beside the ship, and then disappeared into our holds; an oil barge arrived: and off went our crewmembers in all directions to gather parts and to attend special briefings.

We accomplished plenty of important work in Pearl, but we also had time to see why Hawaii is world-famous as a resort area. The Welfare and Recreation committee hired buses and treated the crew to a tour of the island. They came back chewing on sugar cane, bearing green coconuts and stories of how they climbed palm trees to pick them. The "Surf was Up,"and the more adventurous of our crewmembers tackled the waves around the island's beaches.

Three days out from Pearl Harbor, our formation rendezvoused with a Navy oiler, and took a deep drink of oil. The Navy's nuclear-powered ships do not have to worry about this business of refueling, but ships that run on "Fossile Fuel" have to find a place, every few days of steaming, where we can "top off" on black oil. The operation of refueling at sea from another ship is as great a proof as you will find of the U.S. Navy's expertise in seamanship. The oiler sets a course and speed and holds it throughout the evolution; it is up to the ship recieving the fuel--in this case the JOUETT-- to do the fancy maneuvering involved. We make an approach from astern of the oiler, and drop speed just as we come alongside her, so that two ships end up on the same course and speed, 60-120 feet apart, with no relative motion between them. The ships are so close that there is little time to react if any thing goes wrong. A slip by the conning officer or the helmsman could spell collision. The men in after steering must be ready to take control instantly if there is a steering failure on the bridge. The engineers down in the Firerooms and Enginerooms must tend their throttles carefully and constantly so that the ship makes the desired speed through the water. Meanwhile, the First Lieutenant and his Deck Force are passing the lines and fuel hoses between the two ships. Engineers with sounding rods monitor the flow of oil into JOUETT'S tank and signal the tanker when to "stop pumping."

At sea, the emphasis has been on training, training, and more training. Not because the ship is unready, but because it wants to be perfectly ready to handle any situation and meet any committment. Our Squadron Commodore, Captain Emerson, has devised some training games that make our preparations fun as well as effective. One game, called "Hot Potato" is designed to familiarize us with the volumes of publications we will be using in the coming months. One ship shoots a question at another ship by flashing light or radio and then measures the time it takes for the recipient to report back the correct answer. Competition is keen, and some of the questions are pretty obscure. In another "game", called Leap Frog, our ships make practice approaches on one another. The ships line up in a column, and the rearmost ship moves up the line, going alongside each of the two ships ahead of it. When it reaches the head of the column, the new rearmost ship moves up the line, and so on.

We stopped off at Guam on 3 February, just long enough for fuel and an hour on the beach. Again, we remember history and how this little island changed hands more than once in the battles of the Pacific. In many ways Navy bases are the same the world over, and it's nice to know that in this one, as in all of them, you will find a supply depot for needed parts or provisions, repair facilities for technical assistance, and even Navy exchanges and service clubs in which the visitor can shop or relax.

We made a 24 hour transit of San Bernardino Strait, right through the middle of the Philippine Islands, with volcanoes and jungle on either side of the narrow strait, and arrived in Subic Bay on 7 February. Here we received our long awaited mail from home and it was amazing to see morale soar after Mail Call. I can only say, "keep those letters coming."

The four days in Subic Bay flew by quickly as our crew was busily engaged in preparing the ship for the next lap of our voyage. Much touch-up maintenance was performed and provisions, stores, and oil were loaded aboard. The U.S. Naval Base at Subic Bay provides excellent support to those Seventh Fleet ships with facilities comparable to those naval stations in the United States. Our crew enjoyed shopping for foreign merchandise in the Navy Exchange, relaxing at the various clubs, or taking advantage of the athletic facilities.

Two days out of Subic Bay and we were in the highly publicized port of Da Nang, South Viet Nam. The stop here was only for one day while a few key officers went ashore to be briefed on our forthcoming assignment. Passing through Tonkin Gulf a day later, we passed by the famous Yankee Team Station where we saw our attack aircraft carriers launching aircraft and where we rendezvoused with an oiler for more fuel.

Now we are busy adjusting to our new routine as a Search and Rescue Unit of the Carrier Task Force. A lot of effort goes into keeping ourselves ready and alert. I believe it is evident that spirits are high and the crew of JOUETT are now working more harmoniously than ever. We think we are capable of anything, because our motto says,"JOUETT can DO-IT."

The letters you receive say how much you are missed by us. Our satisfaction is that what we are doing out here is necessary and important.

Sincerely,

ROBERT S. HAYES
Captain, U. S. Navy
Commanding Officer

[Hand-drawn map showing JOUETT's route from San Diego to the Western Pacific, with stops marked at Pearl Harbor, Guam, Philippines, and the final destination, connected by a dashed line across the Pacific Ocean.]

1968-02-21.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-02-21.text:
21 Feb. 1968
At sea, Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother & Dad,

Here's a few lines to let you know I got the envelopes and your letter of Feb 12 yesterday. I also got a letter from Bill. Of course he was very descriptive in his observations of the situation there.

No, as you probably have figured out by now Bill and I were unable to see each other in Da Nang. For obvious reasons that is not a liberty port and the only way I could see him would be for him to come out to the ship when he knew we were there.

I'm glad you gave me some indication of the mileage breakdown. I figure that Bill and I are about 10,000 miles from home now that we are here. It doesn't seem possible. Look on the map and find the Tonkin Gulf. We are in the southern part off of N. Viet Nam.

You mentioned baking bread. Thats a coincidence because they bake all the bread when we are at sea. Just like home!

I'm glad you have mailed the magazine to me. If it is Popular Electronics, they were suppose to have changed the address so it is mailed to me. Oh well just as long as I get it, I'll at least have something to read.

Tomorrow is payday. I will get $167. Thats tax-free base pay for two weeks and combat pay for 22 days. These are only a few of the benefits of being over here. Big deal, the pay is the main thing.

We should be getting mail brought out to us just about every day now. There is not much to look forward to out here but the mail makes up for some of the monotony.

Yes, I too was a little curious about the situation at the Greve's. I guess Larry is in for four years. Bill and I will have our time in and the rest of the guys we know will still have a long way to go. Have you heard anything about Mike Siebert. I read the article about the Bates kid in one of the papers I got in Subic. I kind of had him figured for that type. I guess he is afraid to let go of the apron strings.

Since I just wrote a couple of days ago there isn't much more news. I'll be awaiting to answer your letters. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike
1968-02-21.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-02-26.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-02-26.text:
26 Feb., 1968
at sea, Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother and Dad,

I got your letter of the 19th today. Although I just wrote a few days ago I am sure you are always eager to hear from me so I'll see if I can bring a few lines together. Any letters I get I usually like to answer the same day. The helicopter has been making a mail run every other day but starting today its suppose to be every day now.

I'm sorry to hear that everyone is down with the cold and flu. The weather is pretty nasty up here but I'm managing to stay in good health thanks to the great medical care of the Navy.

Good luck in getting into the nursing program. It may be the break you're waiting for.

I thought the clipping about the Cubs was interesting and found a little humor in it, considering the source. I'm sure going to miss sitting in front of the T.V. on weekends taking in the games, but someday I'll be able to enjoy the privileges of civilian life again.

Because of the weather being so bad up here there has been a limited number of air strikes in the north. As a result, we have just been cruising around waiting for something to happen. Over the weekend two planes did go down somewhere away from our station. They rescued the pilot from one with a helo from one of the carriers. The other ones they gave up for lost. There are three carriers operating in our vicinity. They are the Enterprise, Bon Homme Richard, and Ticonderoga. Watch for them in the news, of course they get all the publicity. The only time someone pays any attention to the other ships is when they get captured (the Pueblo).

This drawing is of a cabinet I would like to build for the stereo equipment I intend on buying over here. Maybe you might have some better ideas and I may think up a different style. But I like this one the best. Anyway, try to be on the lookout for some wood and hardware. Let me know what you think of the design.

Here are some more pictures. I probably won't have any more till after we get back from Japan.

They are trying to make plans to have a priest fly in on Sundays to hear confessions and say Mass. It will make things seem a little more like Sunday if it works out.

We observed Washington's birthday and had holiday routine. They had a bingo game, for the first time, and showed a movie in the afternoon besides the usual evening one. It was a good day and gave us a chance to relax a little.

Well, thats all the good (?) news from here. I'll be waiting for your letters and anxious to answer. So long for now.

Your son,

Mike

USS JOUETT (DLG-29) 1968 CRUISE BOOK — PAGES 78-79

[Photo: UH-2A helicopter silhouetted against dramatic sunset clouds over the Tonkin Gulf, lowering a crew member on a cable]

During our first period "on the line" in the Tonkin
Gulf, JOUETT became familiar with the procedures re-
quired for a search and rescue (SAR) unit. To enhance
our ability to rescue downed aviators, the ship oper-
ated as one-half of a SAR team. The other member of
this team was a UH-2A helicopter, which flew aboard
the day the ship steamed out of Subic Bay, and operated
off our flight deck throughout the remainder of deploy-
ment. The helicopter itself, in its protective coloration
of black and olive drab, presents a sleek and stream-
lined appearance, whether resting on JOUETT's deck
or in flight. It is capable of proceeding to the locale of
a downed aircraft at high speeds, hovering over the
scene, locating survivors, lowering crew members to
the ground or into the sea, and effecting a rescue that
would have been otherwise impossible.

1968-02-29.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG-29) 1968 CRUISE BOOK — PAGES 80-81

Equally adept at hovering or flying at
speeds well in excess of 100 knots, the UH-
2A helicopter is uniquely fitted to its role in
the search and rescue effort.

[Photo: UH-2A helicopter in flight low over the ocean, seen from above/side angle, showing black and olive drab coloration]

[Photo: HC-7 helicopter detachment crew posed in front of UH-2A on Jouett's flight deck, approximately 8 men in flight suits and uniforms, flight helmets visible on deck]

The UH-2A helicopter carries a pilot, co-pilot, and crew of two, all of whom are
expert swimmers and marksmen, skilled in rescue techniques and first-aid
procedures. Other Helo detachment members function as a ground crew, responsible
for maintaining the aircraft in a condition ready for instantaneous response.

1968-03-01.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-03-01.text:
Mar. 1, 1968
at sea, Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother & Dad,

Its Friday and just about 10 PM here. I am on watch now and thought I'd answer your letter of the 24th which I got this afternoon.

We refueled from an oiler tonight about 2000. It was pretty cold and windy up there but things went off okay. They sent some mail over to us and I got a paper from 11 Feb..

Yesterday a plane went down near us. In the afternoon we moved into the area but they only found the wreckage, no pilot. We have the remains of the plane and the helmet of the pilot on board. I took some pictures of it.

Twice this week we went to general quarters when they picked up MIG's on the radar, the closest they got was about 60 miles but we were manned and ready just in case. I suppose it was just an harassment because they stayed well out of our range.

You mentioned that Bill had said somthing about finishing up school. If he can't do it while he is in here, he can make use of the G.I. bill and get $130 a month to go to school on. I have been thinking a lot about this myself. I think I will go to a two-year technical school or a junior college and make use of the money. With what I have planned to save up, it should be no problem financially.

When you send the box I'd like some magazines to read. Newsweek, Look, Readers Digest, or Sports Illustrated is okay. They don't have to be new issues because I just want something to read and help pass some of the time. I could use a couple of jars of Fostex soap. They don't have any here on the ship and it works real good for me. Also how about a calender. I would like one about the size of a small wall calendar.

I would like to see Bill while I'm over here. It would probably boost our morale a little. Maybe the next time we are in Da Nang he might make it out to the ship somehow. I know we won't get liberty there, so its got to be up to him if he can make it.

Its been 19 continuous days at sea for us now. The 25th of March seems so far away when we go back to Subic Bay. There is very little to look forward to and when the mail comes it makes the day seem a little brighter. We haven't went on water hours yet which is a surprize to me. The food isn't too bad either but how can you compare it to anything else when thats all there is?

This seems to be David's best year in school so far. Maybe he is learning a little from the experience of his older brothers. Its good to hear that he is interested in his schoolwork and eager to get his homework done in school.

I suppose this is about all the news for now. I'll write again, bye for now.

Your son,

Mike

1968-03-12.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-03-12.text:
12 March, 1968
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother + Dad,

I got your note with the crossword puzzles today and your letter of last Monday yesterday.

Everything is still the same over here. The weather hasn't changed a bit and the days continue to go by. We only have 11 more days on station then are to arrive in Japan on the 29th of this month.

Last Friday a chaplain came aboard and said Mass for the first time since we left the states. They are going to arrange it so he comes once every two weeks.

Yesterday an Air Force plane went down inland about 65 miles southwest of us. They made some attempts to find the pilots but gave them up for lost in a couple of hours.

I am having a years subscription of "All Hands" sent home to you. You might say its the Navy's answer to "The Leatherneck". It will give you some idea of what goes on in some of the operations and you just might read about the Jouett.

If I can find a tape recorder that plays cartridges, I'll buy one in Japan. Those type aren't in use too much yet and the only ones we have here on the ship are the ones like mine. It shouldn't cost much and it will be good to send messages back and forth. I'll be sure to keep an eye out for one.

I know I mentioned this before but would you let me know how much I have in the checking account. Also include the tax refund. I have been trying to keep track of it but would like to know the exact figures.

I read the newspaper clipping you sent me. That guy has a brother that is in the reserves also. At first I thought it was him but remembered he had an older brother.

Yes, if you can find some paper back books, I'd like for you to send them. Mysteries, science fiction or short stories are okay. I can do without any of the off-color type if you know what I mean. We usually trade back and forth with the guys and it helps to occupy your time if you have something to read while on watch or waiting in line.

I haven't heard from Bill lately but expect to any day. I suppose he finds it hard to write and may not have the time. I could write letters everyday but there would be nothing to write about. But as soon as I get one of your letters I am anxious to sit down and answer it.

I have sent the application in for the correspondence course test. I don't know when it will get here but in the meantime am going to cram up on things I need to know a little better.

We have had a couple of intelligence briefings since we have been out here on station. They point out on the map what operations have been taking place and how it involves us. Actually its a lot of the news that comes out in the "Stars & Stripes" but the explanation makes it more interesting. They say that at Khe Sahn there is most likely to be one of the most decisive battles take place soon. Of course the way news travels over here it may have been over by the time you get this letter. If you keep one eye on the map and another on the paper you will be pretty well informed about just what the score is over here.

What kind of bike is David planning on buying? How did he get the money, rob a bank? I think you ought to make him wait till school is out that way he has to be good till then. Only kidding of course. Tell him to be good in school and keep struggling along with the drum lessons no matter how hard they may seem at times. I noticed the little note he wrote on the letter and could picture him sitting down writing it.

I have held off long enough telling you, but I have grown a mustache. I started it on Jan. 28 and will probably shave it off in Japan. I don't really care for it but it is something a little different. I remember Bill telling me that he was going to grow a beard and the whole works when he got over here. They wouldn't let us grow beards so the guys had to settle on mustaches instead.

Well, thats all the "exciting" news for now. I'll be looking forward to hearing from you again and will keep everyone back there in my thoughts. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike
1968-03-12.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-03-16.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-03-16.text:
Mar. 16, 1968
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother + Dad,

Its a little after 7:30 PM Saturday evening. I got your letter of Mar. 1 and the calendar yesterday. Today I got a letter from Grandma that was postmarked Mar. 5 but I wrote to her yesterday so she should get it soon. The mail is very unpredictable at times. I guess its just like the weather.

I also recieved a letter from Bill yesterday which he wrote Feb. 28th. Figure that out if you can, they must send mail over here by carrier pidgeon.

You mentioned that Bouchey had malaria. That is something they worry about over here. Every Monday evening at supper they pass out these malaria pills for us to take. They make you feel a little sick the next day but thats better than being laid up in some hospital for a couple of months. I suppose those Marines welcome that because at least they can get away from here without having to take a bullet to do it.

Our next stop in Subic will be for such a short time I am sure I won't be able to look up that guy. We will probably anchor out in the morning and get underway early in the evening. Our only reason for going back there is to unload the helo and its crew and pick up some supplies and mail.

Only one more week left up here and in two weeks we will be in Japan. Everyone is looking forward to getting there and it should be good liberty providing the ship doesn't make us stay on board over the weekend like they did in Subic Bay.

If you can, would you send me some more information about that tape recorder you bought. The instruction book would be fine. I'd like to have some idea what its like. In case I have a chance to buy myself one I want it to match up with yours.

Today the ship had its 100th helicopter landing. Right now we have two on board. Ours is being repaired and in the hangar and a bigger one is on the flight deck.

About 1330 we had a fire break out in one of the radar power rooms. They got it put out quick and there was very little damage. It was an electrical fire caused by some overheated wiring. So today has been one of our more eventful days out here.

I think after I finish off this roll of film, I am going to start taking slides. No doubt I can buy a slide projector over here and they have certain advantages over prints.

I'm glad to hear David finally got to get his new bike. If he takes good care of it, it should last long enough so his next set of "wheels" will be a car (hint). With Easter vacation coming up I suppose he is getting eager and has a lot of things he wants to do then. I bet he talks Daddy into taking him to work at least one day. Its always good to hear that he is doing better in school, just keep at it and he will get along fine.

Its been 34 days at sea since we left Subic Bay. Everyone is in good spirits but I am sure we all could use a few beers right now. By the time we get in Japan I'm sure we all will be glad to set foot on land again.

That about sums it up for now. I'll try to write one more "free" letter while we are here, but if I don't you will hear from me in Japan. Keep the letters coming and I'll be looking forward to getting the package and magazines. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike

P.S. Good luck on the diet!

1968-03-18.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-03-18.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FAMILY GRAM

18 March 1968

Dear Family and Friends of JOUETT,

In the month that has passed since my last letter to you, the days have been full of activity and have passed swiftly. I would like to tell you now of our duties of the past month.

On February 17, JOUETT arrived in the Tonkin Gulf and commenced operating as a Search and Rescue (SAR) unit of Task Force 77. In order to enhance our efforts, JOUETT is operating as one-half of a SAR team. The other member of this team is a UH-2A helicopter, which flew aboard the day we steamed out of Subic Bay, and has been operating off our deck since then. This helicopter carries a pilot, co-pilot, and crew of two, all of whom are expert swimmers and marksmen, skilled in rescue techniques and first-aid procedures. The helicopter itself, in its protective coloration of black and olive drab, presents a sleek and streamlined appearance, whether resting on JOUETT's deck or in flight. It is capable of proceeding to the locale of a downed aircraft at high speeds, hovering over the scene, locating survivors, lowering crew members to the ground or into the sea, and effecting a rescue that would have been otherwise impossible.

To further complement this DLG-UH-2A SAR team, JOUETT's Combat Information Center maintains close radio and radar contact with all aircraft flying into North Vietnam from the huge Seventh Fleet aircraft carriers to seaward. Should one of these planes encounter difficulty, the word is passed from CIC "SAR Alert--SAR Alert"; the CIC watch section is bolstered by the presence of additional officers and enlisted men who man JOUETT's highly sophisticated electronic search equipment. At the same time, our helicopter, affectionately known as "Clem II", is readied for immediate launch. As the Officer of the Deck turns the ship into the wind, pilots and flight crew dash to their places in Clem II; the ship's Helo Detail--deck handlers and firefighters--man their stations. Within minutes, Clem II is cleared for take-off and rises into the air, slowly at first, but then rapidly accelerating toward the SAR location.

Not all days, however, are filled with the drama of a SAR incident. A typical day on station would begin at 0600 as the Boatswain's Mate pipes "Reveille", and the crew turn out of their bunks to commence another day's routine. After breakfast--our Supply Department serves over 1200 hot meals each day--all hands fall in at their divisional quarters for "muster, inspection, and instruction." The Executive Officer informs Department Heads of special evolutions planned for the day's activity for each man in their division.

If the day happens to be a payday, the pay-line forms in the Crew's Mess immediately after quarters. JOUETT Sailors are paid every other week, on alternate Thursdays. The ship's Disbursing Officer distributes in check or cash, some $50,000 every payday. While the crew is being paid, officers assemble in the Wardroom with Commodore EMERSON and his staff, for the daily Intelligence Briefing. Here various topics concerning JOUETT's role in the Vietnam conflict are discussed--such topics range from weather forecasts to forthcoming flight plans.

When payday is completed, the Ship's Store and Post Office are opened for the convenience of the crew. Both store and post office conduct a booming trade: over $18,000 worth of money orders are purchased each payday to be mailed home; the Ship's Store, with a selection of merchandise extending from soap and razor blades to cameras and tape recorders, takes in $7,500 each pay period.

At 1000, "Flight Quarters" is sounded, and Clem II conducts a daily test flight; during this flight, mail and freight are carried from JOUETT to our "Shotgun", USS SOUTHERLAND (DD-743) who is steaming in company with us. After Clem II is recovered on board, another safe landing is entered in the log. At the present time, JOUETT has completed well over 100 accident-free helicopter landings, safety record which is a source of pride to all concerned.

Lunch is served at 1130, and all hands return to their tasks at 1230. During the afternoon, various training lectures or films may be presented to several divisions. At 1500 "Flight Quarters" is sounded again, and Clem II is launched rapidly. The lookouts watch a speck on the distant horizon grow until they report "Log Helo is in sight." Each day a logistics helicopter comes to JOUETT from one of the aircraft carriers on "Yankee Station". The Log Helo's arrival is eagerly anticipated by all, as it carries freight, which may consists of repair parts for an inoperative pump or radar set, visiting passengers from other units in the Tonkin Gulf, and, finally, first class mail. The last item is carefully taken to the Post Office, quickly sorted and distributed to all those fortunate enough to receive letters from home. Having observed the effect mail from home has on our men's morale, I can only urge you all to write frequently. Your letters are the best indication of your support of our endeavors.

At 1530, some recreational activity is in order. A movie may be shown on the Mess Decks, or a bingo game may be held. Many members of our crew visit the ship's library, while others utilize the punching bags and weight-lifting equipment in the hangar.

After supper is completed and Eight O'Clock Reports have been made to the Executive Officer, a movie is shown for those who were unable to attend the afternoon presentation. In the quiet hours before Taps, most men take time to write to their loved ones back in the States. Many men pursue some hobby in the evening; sketching, painting and leatherwork are popular; many musical instruments are carried on board, and it is by no means unusual to find several people gathered around a guitar or an accordion, singing some popular song or favorite ballad.

At length, "Taps" is sounded, lights are extinguished, and men rest to gather strength for their efforts the next day.

Although each day our tasks become more and more a matter of routine, morale remains high aboard JOUETT. It is extremely gratifying to note the interest and dedication displayed by our men. Our satisfaction lies in doing our assigned tasks to the best of our ability and in your continued support and understanding.

Sincerely,

ROBERT S. HAYES
Captain, U.S. Navy
Commanding Officer

1968-03-26.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-03-26.text:
March 26, 1968

Dear Mother + Dad,

By the time you get this letter I will be in Japan. We are on our way there now after stopping in Subic Bay for five hours Sunday. I got your card and the letter with the pictures then. As always I was glad to hear from you and its always nice to see pictures of those back home. David still looks the same and I can imagine the coaxing you had to go through to get him to pose for them. I am sending them to Bill and he will send them back to you.

The ship should arrive in Yokosuka about 1400 Thursday. You can't imagine how glad I'll be to get off this ship for liberty. After the 2½ months of this cruise I am well convinced this isn't the life for me. Some of the nonsense and fools you have to put up really get under your skin during these days at sea.

Since I have last wrote we have had two fires here on the ship. One was in a radar power room and yesterday a transformer burnt up. They were put out quickly and no one was hurt. Things like that can sink a ship just as well as anything else. But we have had everything go fine so far and no doubt it should continue to.

We left the Gulf of Tonkin Friday evening after 34 days up there. The chaplian came aboard and said mass that evening and we refueled from an oiler later in the night. That was one of the more active days up there.

I shaved off the mustache a week ago. I got tired of it and it was somewhat of a nuisance.

I had it figured right in regards to the amount I had in the bank. I hope to have at least twice that in there by the time I get back to the states.

Sunday I also got the package and the magazines. Thanks a lot. By reading the magazines I was reminded of some of the things that are going on in the world. There is only one thing we are concerned about over here and thats how the war is going so of course thats all you hear.

Thats all there is for now. I'll write from Japan. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike

1968-03-30.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-03-30.text:
Mar. 30, 1968
Yokosuka, Japan

Dear Mother + Dad,

I got a letter from you on Thursday the day we arrived and another one today. The package with the books and candy also came today. So it looks like mail is getting here real quick. I got one paper today dated Mar. 22, so you had better see if they have been cancelled.

Its Saturday evening here and I have duty today. It has rained most of the day and is rather cool outside. I had liberty the first two nights here and enjoyed a good steak dinner both times. Its a lot of fun to go out buying souveniers and jew down those peddlers.

I have sent some brochures on the stereo equipment I have bought. Save them for me. I have not got a turntable yet and may get one from Allied for a good price when I get back home. I can buy a cartridge recorder like yours for $34.00 and I'll get over to buy it next week. If you want to you can answer this with a tape and I'll send one back.

From what I have been able to pull out of the papers it looks like Decatur got beat out in the state tournament. Did they lose to Springfield? I have also noticed a lot of the guys Bill and I both knew have been either getting drafted or enlisting in the service. In a way it's nice to see someone else getting their share of time in this outfit. I would like for you to clip out the "Service News" sections of the review (Tuesday?) and send them to me.

Thanks for remembering to send the specifications on your tape recorder. I was almost sure what it was like but wanted to make sure before I got one.

The Easter bunny in the box was really a surprize. We hung it up in our working space. I wonder how long it will be there before some one makes us take it down?

I have signed up for an all day tour of Tokoyo tomorrow. Providing there is enough seats on the bus I'm all set to go. In case you're wondering Tokoyo is about 40 miles North of here.

As for as a slide projector goes, I plan on buying one here. I think one of those slide viewers would be better for Bill and they should sell for around $2.50. I am going to get one here and I will be all set for slides. I also bought a pair of 16 x 50 binoculars here for $17.50. I have made all of my purchases here on the base at the exchange. You are guaranteed of good merchandise at the best of prices.

There is some rumor that we may make a final stop here before we head back to the states. If there is anything you need or want let me know ahead of time and I'll bring it back. I really don't think we will be here again but who knows. Its 2200 miles from Subic Bay and 4 days, one way so any extra miles of travel by then may be discouraged.

This month is coming to an end pretty fast. We will be approaching the half way point in the cruise in a couple of weeks. After those 45 days since our last liberty it was good to get off the ship Thursday and get some of that good American beer for 15¢.

I hope you have good luck in the L.P.N. test. How's the cafeteria union panning out?

Well I have to go for now and write a couple more letters. I'll be looking forward to a tape from you. So long.

Your son,

Mike

1968-03-31.attribution: Tokyo Day Tour Itinerary — Ducy Family Archives
1968-03-31.text:
TOKYO DAY TOUR / NIGHT TOUR — ITINERARY
Yokosuka Port Call, March 31 – April 7, 1968
Mike went on the Tokyo Day Tour on March 31, 1968 (per logbook)
2 pages, typed on blue mimeograph paper

========================================================================================
PAGE 1
========================================================================================

TOKYO DAY TOUR

$6.50 per person - 25 minimum            $8.50 per person - less than 25
Leaves ship's pier at 0830               Returns at 1830

TOUR EXPENSES COVERED:

1.  English speaking guide.
2.  Transportation from your ship's pier, tour of the Tokyo area and return
    to your ship's pier.
3.  Tokyo Tower. The world's tallest tower (nearly 60 feet taller than the
    Eiffel Tower) and the pride of Tokyo. The tower serves six television stations
    and 56 radio stations, contains a science museum, shops, snack bars and two
    observation platforms. On a clear day the view of Tokyo from the top is
    magnificent.
4.  Olympic Stadium. Built for the 1964 Olympics in Tokyo, the stadium was
    used for the swimming and diving events. It is now open to the public for
    swimming and ice skating. The stadium is a gigantic modern concrete structure,
    seating 11,000 people under a soaring concrete roof.
5.  Yasukuni Shinto Shrine. This is a shrine dedicated to those who have given
    their lives for their country. Before World War II the ashes of all war dead
    were buried here; today only those who request it are enshrined at Yasukuni.
    Until 1946 the shrine grounds were filled with battle trophies—guns, statues,
    etc. In April and October huge festivals are held at the shrine in memory of
    the war dead.
6.  Lunch at Suehiro's Restaurant. Suehiro's was originally a Kyoto-based
    restaurant that was so successful it branched out into other cities of Japan.
    Your choice for lunch is between Kobe beefsteak or sukiyaki, either served
    by kimono-clad waitresses.
7.  Kokusai or Nichigeki Music Hall. Both of these theaters feature girl
    dancing troupes, modeled somewhat like the Rockettes, with glittering (and
    minimal) costumes, lavish arrangements, and hundreds of girls. The show
    is usually a combination of western style M show dancing and traditional
    Japanese dances.
8.  Tour expenses not covered: Drinks and souvenirs.


TOKYO NIGHT TOUR

$10.00 per person - 25 minimum

TOUR EXPENSES COVERED:

1.  English speaking guide.
2.  Transportation from your ship's pier at 1200, tour of Tokyo area, and
    return to your ship's pier at 2330.
3.  Lunch at Suehiro's Restaurant. This is the same restaurant as on the Tokyo
    Day Tour. Once again, your choice for lunch is between Kobe beefsteak (from
    deep-fed, hand-massaged cows), and sukiyaki, a Japanese dish that contains thin
    slices of beef and various vegetables, cooked in a soy-sauce flavored broth.
4.  Kokusai or Nichigeki Music Hall. Also covered on the Tokyo Day Tour. The
    theater varies, depending on the time of the month and the availability of tickets.
    If Kokusai tickets are available, you will see an all-girl troupe at Nichigeki
    there are both men and women dancers. Sometimes the tours are sent to the
    Nichigeki Fifth Floor Music Hall, which shows an elaborate, all-girl strip show.


========================================================================================
PAGE 2 (partially legible — bleed-through from reverse printing)
========================================================================================

5.  Restaurant-Theater Hayasubaya. This is a dinner and show combined in one
    restaurant. While you are eating, feudal Tokyo is re-created for you through
    the dances of the Oiran, a professional performer in old Tokyo. The dancers
    wear authentic costumes; elaborate hairdos, chalk-white faces, and kimono with
    sleeves so heavy they are carried by two assistants. After the Oiran finish their
    dancing, the professional jesters of old Tokyo perform folk dances.
6.  Cabaret Hollywood. One of the largest cabarets in Tokyo, boasting over
    four hundred hostesses, a live band, and floor show. The tour stops here
    after dinner, for approximately two hours, for drinks, dancing, and the show.
    Included in the tour are two drinks, the company of a hostess, and the floor
    show. Note: Anything over two drinks must be paid for by the individual.

Tour expenses not covered: Drinks, other than specified above, and souvenirs.

de la technique japonaise la plus moderne. Y sont installées également des maquettes explicatives
de certains produits dans le but de montrer en détail leur construction. C'est ainsi que la Sanyo
Denki a présenté des électrophones stéréophoniques et que la Matsushita a exposé un ensemble de
téléphone télévisionique et des appareilles électriques de ménage, tandis que la Hitachi a
présenté des frigidaires, des pompes et autres articles. Il faut ajouter que la compagnie Fuji
Télévision a l'un de ses studios au 4e étage, d'ou un programme populaire "Variétés de la Tour"
est diffusé chaque jour à 14h., sauf les samedis et dimanches. Vous êtes invités à voir cette
présentation.


We have the pleasure of inviting you to our Modern Science Museum where you would find many
interesting exhibits:

* Broadcasting Transmission Hall (5th floor)
Located here are the broadcasting and transmission facilities of various TV broadcasting companies
in Japan.

* Hall of Telecommunication and Broadcasting (4th floor).
Telecommunication and broadcasting companies join in showing most up-to-date technics and products
of electronics. Nippon Electric Company exhibits models of a broadcasting system; Tokyo Electric
Power Company displays a sample of power station facilities. Toshiba presents a miniature of
"Future City" and electrical products which adds more enjoyment for your visit to this Museum.

* Industrial Hall of Electric Machinery (3rd floor)
Exhibited are home electrical appliances, industrial electric machinery, up-to-date products and
manufacturing technics of various items closely connected with our daily life. Not only the
finished products are exhibited, but also models in horizontal section are being displayed so that
you may be able to nourish the so-called "scientific mind".

At the Sanyo Exhibition Room, a stereo concert hall is installed and experimental stereo music
performances are being held, while, Matsushita Electric Showroom displays TV telephone facilities
and home electrical appliances. In the Hitachi Showroom, the directions on how to use electrical
appliances are shown.

On the fourth floor, there is the Tower Studio of Fuji TV Co., from where the popular program
"Tower Variety" is being broadcasted everyday, except Sturday and Sunday, from 2:00 pm. The public
is invited to watch this TV show on the spot.

[Photo: Sanyo Showroom showing electronic equipment display]

Sanyo Showroom


                        Functions of Tokyo Tower

[Diagram: Cross-section of Tokyo Tower showing antenna components and labels from top to bottom:
Lightning Rod, Signal Lamp for Air Traffic, NHK TV, NHK Education TV, Earthquake pick-up, NET TV,
Fuji TV, Tokyo Ch 12 TV, NHK FM, Tokyo Ch 12 pick-up Relay, FM4 Field pick-up Relay, Fuji Field
pick-up Relay, NHK Micro Relay, The Postal Factory, HF Testing, Clock, VHF Travelling Radio,
Reader for Sight-seeing, TV Studio Relay, Strong Earthquake Indicator, Elevator Hall for Special
Observatory, Grand Observatory (150 m), The Police Agency, Maritime Broadcasting, Special
Observatory, Wind Velocity Indicator, Wind Direction Indicator, Lightning Current Indicator,
Altitude Classified Thermometer, FM Broadcasting, Public Safety TV Relay, Tokyo Elph Field pick-up
Relay, NHK Field pick-up Relay, Fuji Field pick-up Relay, TV Transmitter, Fuji TV Link]

Tokyo Tower has been designated for integrating the whole transmission of TV broadcasting in Tokyo
area. Its height of 333 meters makes it possible for the electric waves to cover the every spot in
Kanto Plain.

This tower acts not only as TV transmissions but also as the relays for sports, games and drama etc.
For example, an electric wave is sent from a stadium to Tokyo Tower and is relayed at the tower to
the broadcasting stations. The stations then return the wave, after adjustment, to the tower to be
extended finally to homes.

Besides the TV broadcasting antennae, the antennae for FM are installed since plans of FM
broadcasting are now under way. It will be in the very near future that the FM broadcasting would
start from the Tower.

Tokyo Tower has also antennae for an experimental broadcasting transmission of the Ministry of Posts
and for the Police Agency, which is used for giving instructions to their patrol cars. Along with
the growth of utilization, electric waves would be extended from every part of the tower.

In addition to the above mentioned, the tower's rolling caused by the wind is furnishing useful data
for building new iron towers.

The tower also plays an important role in investigation of the discrimination of air which is now
causing public interest.

This high iron tower attracts many lightnings. There are various indicators on the tower so that we
know how many lightnings strike and the capacity of strong electric currency.

The data found from the indicators are useful for the studies of meteorology and industry.


Ce que fait la Tour de Tokio

La construction de la Tour de Tokio a permis d'assurer la transmission de toutes les émissions de
radio et de télévision dans le district de Tokio. Haute de 333 metres, elle est capable de
retransmettre les programmes sur diverses ondes dans tous les coins de la plaine du Kwanto.

Outre celles destinées à la télévision, elle comporte les antennes de la station de M.F., du
ministère des P.T.T. et de la police. Les oscillations provoquées par le vent fournissent des
renseignements utiles pour la construction d'autres tours métalliques. La tour joue un rôle
important pour l'analyse de l'air. Comme elle attire souvent la foudre, elle permet de savoir avec
quelle fréquence elle est atteinte et de calculer la force des courants électriques. Les résultats
ainsi obtenus sont d'une grande utilité pour les études météorologiques et industrielles.


========================================================================================
PAGE 3 — Q & A about Tokyo Tower / Guide for Tokyo Tower
========================================================================================

[Panoramic header photo continued: "In the direction of Ginza", "In the direction of Tokyo Harbor"]

Q. How many electric waves does Tokyo Tower transmit?
A. It transmits six waves for TV broadcastings (NHK, NHK Education, TBS, Fuji and NET, Japan
Science Foundation Telecasting Bureau 12ch), some 15 waves for relaying of TV stations, 4 waves of
communications for the Government Agencies, 10 waves for FM experimental broadcasting and some
waves for radars and amateur transmitters.

Q. How strong are the wires of the elevators up to the observatory?
A. The weight of the box of each elevator is 3.4 tons. As the full charged of weight is limited to
2 tons, the whole weight of each elevator becomes 5.4 tons at most. The strength of the wire which
supports an elevator is 15 times more than the strength actually required. And the wire is to be
replaced with a new one when its strength is reduced to 10 times.

Q. Why is the tower painted in orange and white?
A. The stripes of orange and white are used in U.S.A. as a signal color for air traffics. They can
be easily seen even in a bad weather.

Q. What grade of rolling has the tower during typhoon?
A. During Isewan Typhoon, the top of the tower rolled at the width of 82 cm at most by the wind
pressure of 52m per sec. Although, we had expected 1m rolling in the original plan. By the same
calculation, the tower would have a rolling of 3.5 m width by 90 m per sec. It is estimated that
the tower would not be affected even with a pressure of 90 m per sec.

Q. Please tell me the materials used for Tokyo Tower.
A. The steel used for it is all produced at factories of Yawata, Fuji and Nihon Kokan, and it is
called S S-41. The SHT-52 type of steel, known as the strongest kind, is used at the upper part of
tower supporting the antennae. While 7,000 tons of steel is used for the Eiffel Tower, only 4,000
tons is used to construct Tokyo Tower. This fact shows the advanced quality of steel in Japan.

Q. How about the foundation of the tower?
A. At each corner of the basement 8 supporters are sunk so deeply into the earth that their lowest
part reaches the water level of the Tokio Bay. The supporters of each corner hold 4,000 tons body
and the four corners are linked to each other with 20 steel of 50 mm in diameter, so that even an
earthquake with a severity of Kanto Earthquake would not give any influence to the tower.

Q. When was the construction of Tokyo Tower started and when was it completed?
A. The construction of Tokyo Tower began on June 29, 1957 and was accomplished on Dec. 23, 1958.
Special (upper) Observatory with a height of 250m. was opened on July 28, 1967.

[Box:] Q and A about Tokyo Tower

The strength of the wire which supports an elevator is 15 times more than the strength actually required.


Q.: Combien d'ondes électriques transmet la Tour de Tokyo?
R.: Elle transmet six ondes pour la télévision (N.H.K., Programme d'éducation de la même station,
T.B.S., Fuji, N.E.T., Fondation des Sciences), une quinzaine d'ondes pour le relais des stations
de la télévision, 4 ondes pour des administrations gouvernementales, 10 ondes pour les émissions
expérimentales de M.F. et quelques ondes pour les radars et les sans-filistes amateurs.

Q.: Quelle est la puissance des câbles qui actionnent les ascenseurs desservant la plate-forme
d'observation?
R.: Le poids de chaque ascenseur est de 3,4 tonnes. La charge maximum en est limitée à 2 tonnes.
Cela represente donc 5,4 tonnes au maximum. Les câbles qui actionnent l'ascenseur sont capables de
supporter un poids 15 fois plus important. De plus, les câbles sont remplacés que leur force de
résistance a diminué d'un tiers.

Q.: Pourquoi la tour est-elle peinte en orange et en blanc?
R.: Les couleurs orange et blanc sont employées aux Etats-Unis d'Amérique comme couleurs de signal
dans le trafic aérien. Elles sont visibles même par mauvais temps.

Q.: Quel est le degré des oscillations de la tour; quand elle est exposée à un typhon?
R.: Lors du typhon dit d'Isewall, au plus sous la pression d'un vent qui faisait 52m. à la
seconde. Nous nous étions attendus à une oscillation d'un mètre. D'après ce calcul, la tour
devrait osciller de 3,5 mètres par un vent de 90 mètres à la seconde et résister à un vent de
cette puissance.

Q.: Voulez-vous parler des matières qui ont servi à la construction de la tour?
R.: L'acier dont on s'est servi a été produit dans les usines de Yawata, de Fuji et de Nihon
Kokan; il est appelé SS-41. L'acier que nous dénommons SHT-52, comme le plus résistant, a été
employé dans la construction de la partie plus élevée, qui supporte les antennes. On a utilisé
7,000 tonnes d'acier dans la construction de la Tour d'Eiffel, tandis que n'en avons eu besoin que
de 4,000 tonnes.

Q.: Comment ont été faits les fondements de la tour?
R.: A chaque coin huit colonnes ont été plantées jusqu'au niveau aussi bas que celui de l'eau de la
baie de Tokio. Les colonnes de chaque coin supportent le poids de 4,000 tonnes et les quatre coins
sont liés l'un à l'autre à l'aide des 20 câbles dont le diamètre est de 50 mm, ce qui doit
permettre à la tour de résister à un tremblement de terre, tel que celui qui a détruit le district
de Tokio, 1923.

Q.: Quand a-t-on commencé la construction et quand est elle achevée?
R.: La construction de la tour a été commencée le 29 juin, 1957, et achevée le 23 décembre, 1958.
Et la plate-forme d'observation spéciale, 250 mètres de hauteur, a été dévoilée pour publique le
28 juillet, 1967.
