1968-04-08.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FAMILY GRAM

8 April 1968

Dear Family and Friends of JOUETT:

Three weeks have passed since I last wrote to you, and a great deal has occurred in that time. I would like to tell you now some of the highlights of JOUETT's many activities.

On March 22, JOUETT was relieved on South SAR station by the USS HALSEY (DLG-23), a ship which many of you have crossed when visiting JOUETT last fall in San Diego. We proceeded then to YANKEE STATION, refueled from one of the SEVENTH Fleet Oilers there, and received stores from the USS POLLUX (AKS-4), another of the many support ships necessary to maintain ourselves and other "ships of the line" in top fighting trim.

The next morning, JOUETT set out for Subic Bay, P.I., at high speed. The cruise was uneventful, but as we steamed away from the mainland of Southeast Asia, many hearts were lightened to see the sun break through the clouds once again. Vietnam, as you may know, was under the influence of the northeast monsoon during JOUETT's first period on station; rain, fog, and low visibility were standard during the five weeks we spent in Tonkin Gulf. In the late afternoon of Sunday, March 24, JOUETT moored at the U.S. Naval Station, Subic Bay. During the few hours of our stay there, the ship's helicopter detachment and Clem II were off-loaded, to return to the Naval Air Station at Cubi Point. Some of our crew members of Filipino extraction departed the ship to enjoy leave in their homeland. A few stores, repair parts, and a great deal of mail was received; "Mail Call" was held at least four times that evening, and it was gratifying to observe the men's reaction to letters from home.

Later the same evening, all lines were cast off, and JOUETT turned her bow northward, toward Japan and a well-earned period of rest and recreation. We made this journey alone and we steamed as rapidly as possible. All hands turned to in an effort to show the ship at its best: some compartments were freshly painted; brass and brightwork were polished; scrubbing and cleaning were the order of the day. As we drew nearer to Japan, we were passing the scenes of many fierce struggles of World War II, where the U.S. Navy played so prominent a role. Although we did not come within sight of land, our radar scopes showed many shores whose memory will long live in American hearts: Leyte--Luzon--Okinawa--Iwo Jima. Reflecting on the violence of only a quarter-century ago, it is little short of incredible to view Japan today. The U.S. Occupation wrought sweeping changes. Good will and energetic effort on the part of both the Japanese and the American peoples have transformed Japan into a symbol of hope for the future. A friend and an ally, Japan is now a working democracy, able to successfully compete, economically and socially, with the United States.

During the early morning of 28 March, JOUETT began to thread her way through the fleets of small fishing junks and sampans which are so common in this part of the world. Shortly after noon, we commenced our approach into Yokosuka (Yo-kous'-ka), and moored there at the U.S. Naval Station in mid-afternoon. Yokosuka, like several other naval, air and army bases in Japan are U.S. Military reservations leased from the Japanese government in accordance with the peace treaty of 1952, which states in part that such bases may be leased to be utilized for "maintenance of international peace and security in the Far East".

Of the 436 men and officers who make up JOUETT's crew, it is likely that we now carry away 436 different memories of Japan. I will, however, attempt to touch briefly on a few of the experiences and impressions which are common to most of us. We were most fortunate in that our visit to Japan coincided with the first weeks of spring; the cherry blossoms, long a symbol of this island nation, were in full bloom while JOUETT was in port. These beautiful trees are identical to those which are so admired in Washington, D.C., where they are carefully tended around the Tidal Basin and the Jefferson Memorial. The trees bear no fruit, but are grown solely for their blossoms, which lend a delicate pink tint to the land for only a week or ten days each spring. A clue to the character of the Japanese people may be found in their willingness to carefully tend these trees year-round in order to enjoy the blossoms for only a few days each spring.

One of the first places visited in Yokosuka, and one of the most popular, was the Navy Exchange. Here foreign merchandise from all over the Orient is gathered together under one roof, and offered for sale at prices considerably lower than in the United States. Some of the best bargains found here are in Japanese-made electronics equipment; tape recorders, stereo phonographs, amplifiers, speakers and television sets were among the more popular items purchased by JOUETT sailors. High quality optical instruments, too, are manufactured in Japan, and many cameras, camera accessories, binoculars, and telescopes are now stowed in our storerooms. The Japanese textile industry is world-famed, and many of our men invested in the colorful silks, elaborate brocades and delicate laces offered for sale in Yokosuka. Table china, crystal, pottery and silverware were also popular purchases, as were the many and clever varieties of toys; many of the latter were small enough to be mailed home, and your children may be enjoying them already.

Many organized tours were made available to the JOUETT during our stay in Japan. LT R. N. JAMES, the ship's Tour Officer, reports that over two hundred of the crew participated in such tours, at an average cost of slightly less than $10.00 per man. One of the most popular tours was that which went to the nearby town of Kamakura. A combination holiday resort and museum town, Kamakura was the capital of Japan for 150 years during the middle ages. Since Buddhism came to Japan from China during this period, Kamakura has many historic sites, shrines and temples. Most famed of Kamakura's landmarks is the colossal statue of Buddha known as the Dai Butsu, which is familiar even to many persons who have never visited Japan. Buddha is here portrayed in a sitting position; the statue is cast of bronze, towers 42 feet above the ground, and is well over 700 years old. The nearby Hachiman Shrine, with its ancient ginko tree is also a popular spot for tourists.

Another well-patronized tour took JOUETT sailors to Hakone National Park, a beautiful highland area in central Honshu, which is dominated by the lofty slopes of Mount Fujiyama, respectfully known throughout Japan as "Fuji-san". Lake Hakone (often seen in pictures or paintings with Mt. Fuji reflected in its placid waters) is a popular resort area, and the entire area is dotted with natural hot springs. The many small villages in the Fuji-Hakone area typify the rural life of Japan, closely tied to the soil, conservative, and bound up in centuries-old tradition.

Our welcome to Japan, in fact, was so warm, and our stay so enjoyable, that many wished to be able to do something in return. As a part of the Navy's "People To People" program, a group of thirty-two men, under the direction of the Chaplain of Destroyer Squadron ONE, LT A. R. TREIBEL, and JOUETT's Master Chief Petty Officer, J. V. PATTISON, volunteered two days of their liberty time to assist the Japanese people in some way. Specifically, they contributed their labor to two small churches in villages near Yokosuka, completely painting one church and the pastor's home, and touching-up the paint and carrying out other repairs on a second church. These churches, incidentally, belong to the Kyodan, or "United Church of Japan", an ecumenical group of the major Christian denominations. Those who participated in this most commendable project have helped to forge still stronger the bonds which unite our two countries, and they all carry with them warm memories of their experience.

Although other interesting sights were seen, other customs and traditions observed, and other experiences remembered, I cannot begin to recount them all at this time. Your sons or husbands will, I am sure, give you a glowing account of this rugged and beautiful land and its charming, gentle people.

At present, we are steaming south to Subic Bay, where we will embark our helicopter detachment, and return to the Tonkin Gulf, to carry out our yet-unfinished tasks. Although our days will be busy, a part of us will always be with you, at home.

Sincerely,

ROBERT S. HAYES
CAPTAIN, U.S. NAVY
COMMANDING OFFICER

1968-04-14.label: Tape 1 — Mike Ducy
1968-04-14.attribution: Audio cassette recording, Tape 1 — Mike Ducy. Transcribed by OpenAI Whisper. Ducy Family Archives

segments.text: Hello, Mother, Dad, and David, and anyone else who might be listening.
Right now, it's Saturday evening, April 13th.
We are at sea heading back to Subic Bay.
This morning, we got underway about 7.30 from Subic,
and have been out most of the day for missile shoots and gunnery exercises.
Two days ago, I got your first tape that you taped on April the 3rd.
Needless to say, I was very surprised to hear about David's broken arm.
I'm sure this is no new experience for him since, as you mentioned, it did happen once
before about a year and a half ago.
I was really happy to hear all of your voices and it seemed like you were right beside me
and you all sounded the same, although it was kind of hard to get used to to really
know that I was actually hearing your voices.
I did find it very enjoyable to listen and will look forward to receiving another tape
from you.
We should be in the harbor in just about another hour, and I might sign off here before I get
this whole tape finished, but in case if I do, I'll finish it up tomorrow morning.
As you know, tomorrow will be Easter, and we are scheduled to get underway tomorrow
after church services, I assume, and we will proceed to Da Nang.
It will take us two days to get there.
I received two boxes of slides from Bill and a tape along with them.
It was very interesting what he had to say and I forwarded the tape and the slides on to Georgia May
and have instructed her to send them on home to you when she gets done.
I got two boxes of slides back that I took back in Tokyo while I was there
and the first chance I get I will make a tape to go along with them and send them on home to you.
this tape and any other tapes that i might send in the next day or so will probably
be mailed from denang when we get there because the tape will be able to be mailed free
and it's just a matter of one or two days time so i figure i'll go ahead and wait till then
instead of having to hurry around and take care of it now yes bill ideas of his situation where
he's at right now it sounds like it's a real resort area more than anything else yes he told
me about going swimming in the china sea but if he would happen to be out here on the ship someday
and see some of these sea snakes come swimming by i'm sure that he'd change his mind pretty quick
about swimming out here in this ocean so many sea snakes are about eight feet long and about as round
as a guy's arm and they're real hard to see or a brownish color so as a result we don't have
swim call out here on the ship over here in the Pacific especially up there in the
Gulf of Tonkin because of the sea snakes and other creatures that might be
wandering around in the water but I'm sure right there where Bill's at I'm
sure it's just exactly what he likes and I got these slides from him like I said
he seemed to be in pretty good spirits from his pictures and looks to me like
he's put on a little bit of weight around the waist I've also sent some
pictures on to you actually I sent them through Bill when he gets done looking
at him he'll send them on home to you there are a few pictures of me in there
and it might look like I put on some weight I actually feel like I have I
haven't had a chance to weigh myself since I've been home the last time and I
would really like to see how much weight I put on I can really feel like I have
and I always want to go on our diet so to say the next day like everyone else
does and says.
Can't ever get around to it.
But I suppose that
someday I will probably
bring my waistline back down to where it should be.
Just like last night.
I got ready to go on Liberty.
Put on a set of my white pants.
Started to put them on.
And I popped two buttons off of them
trying to get them buttoned around my waist.
So you can figure right there
just what the situation is.
The weather over here is real nice here in the Philippines.
This morning it was 84 degrees about 8 o'clock.
It's been sunny all day and really hot.
Right now it's dark outside.
And I can see some of the land over there. I can see a few ships off the coast over there.
It's real peaceful and calm out here. The moon is real bright.
And the air is rather still and quite humid and heavy.
heavy. Tell Dad thanks a lot for the small sports summary on the Cubs game there. I'm
sure like he said that we'll probably be able to pick up baseball games over here on the
Far East Network. This is a radio network which serves most of the area over here and
we're usually able to pick it up on the short wave and put it on the entertainment system
for the crew. Also while we are up in the Gulf of Tonkin on station we always get the
Stars and Stripes, which I'm sure was a very popular newspaper back in World War II.
They bring it out to us every day with the mail helo.
And it's only about two or three days old in printing,
but of course the news would possibly be about a week old.
But it's still just like getting a hometown newspaper,
and there's some very good articles in there from sports to the Ann Landers column.
So this kind of lets us know what's happening back home,
plus also the radio newscast over here.
I suppose you're all wondering,
since President Johnson has called a halt to the bombing
in the major parts of North Vietnam,
just exactly what we'll be doing over here our next time on station.
And we should be there in just about five days.
Well, we don't know yet.
All we know is our next stop after we leave here
will be in Da Nang on the 16th,
which I believe is next Tuesday or Wednesday.
We'll pick up our orders right there, just what we're supposed to do
and where we go out on station over there.
But, like I said before, if the bombing has been halted,
it will be another slow time up there on station for the 30 days we're there.
You also mentioned about you would recommend that the bombing be stepped up a little bit more.
well the reason why they don't do this from what i understand over here they have
major points there in north vietnam outside of haiphong and hanoi which they can only hit
they are instructed not to bomb any civilian installations housing areas or anything like
that only factories and transportation lines so they don't want to involve the north vietnamese
civilians in this war. So you see it's kind of a touchy situation when you go in there dropping
bombs and you really can't do much damage. And they say that after they have destroyed something
within 48 hours or so, it's built right back up again. So it's just a mad circle over here,
which I'm sure you can testify to by reading the newspapers.
And it's really going to take something and some good politicians to get it settled.
we got here in Subic Bay last Thursday I had Liberty that night and last night I had duty
yesterday morning a submarine pulled in beside us to tie up alongside and last night I went
aboard it it's a nuclear-powered submarine it was the fourth nuclear-powered submarine of its class
to be built and I kind of thought being out here on the Jewett was kind of bad duty for a lot of
reasons but I tell you I couldn't see living on one of those submarines because they have a crew
of about 100 on there and believe me it's really crowded and after I finished a little tour over
there on the submarine I came back aboard the ship here really felt kind of funny being able
to walk down a passageway without having to step sideways or anything like that and being
able to walk on a ship which was actually a lot more roomier even though to some people
a ship is not a very roomy place I found that ours is better than some. Like I mentioned
before we're due back in the harbor about 9.30. We're not going to tie up at the pier
this time we're on the anchor out and they're supposed to have liberty as soon as we get in
well liberty will expire for me at one o'clock in the morning so it's going to be a pretty
short liberty i believe i'm going to go over to the em club with a buddy of mine we're going to
have a couple of beers and catch the liberty boat back to the ship about 12 o'clock
Well, they just passed the word there.
We're going to be entering port in about 10 minutes.
So I believe I'm going to sign off here pretty soon,
go down and get into my uniform.
Like I said before, I'll probably go over to the club
and come back about 12 o'clock
and be all ready to go tomorrow
because we'll be getting underway possibly by 10 o'clock.
And we also have some ammunition to load in the morning.
So I'll sign off right here and pick this tape up again tomorrow
and finish up for you.
Well, here I am back again.
It's Sunday morning now, about 11 o'clock.
Last night's liberty was not exactly what I had expected it to be.
Most of the guys didn't get off the ship until about quarter after 11,
so I decided that it was too late to leave the ship then
and have to be back within such a short time,
so it actually wouldn't be worth it.
So I stayed on board and got a pretty good night's rest.
Right now we're waiting to load ammunition.
They've run into some difficulty in getting it over here.
So we're just kind of waiting around now.
As soon as we get it all loaded,
we're supposed to get underway this afternoon about 2 o'clock.
Among some of the things that I did buy back in Yokosuka while we were there,
I bought a slide projector. It cost me $39.50. I'm pretty proud of it. I think it's really nice and
seems to do a pretty good job. I had one drawback with the show the other day. The
white bulb burned out in it, so now I'm faced with trying to find a new one some way. I'll
probably have to wait till the next time we get back in port, which will be in Hong Kong,
and no doubt I can probably pick up one there. But in the meantime, I'll just have to use my
little slide viewer that I have.
And in case you're wondering what I plan to do with my high-flyer
equipment that I bought over here, we have a place here on the ship where we are
stowing most of this stuff, and I'll just keep it here on the ship when I get back
in San Diego and take it up to Georgia Maze House
and take it from there in case anyone would happen to be coming out here for a
vacation in the near future. I suppose some of it could
go back with them but if not i can always send it on home from there but i'll probably keep most of
it up there until i i'm actually ready to have it sent home so there's no trouble about keeping it
here on the ship the only thing is that we can't really have it up and out it's set up so we can
listen to it so i've got it all stowed away real real secure and everything and
it'll probably stay there
until we get back into state.
Of course, this is Easter Sunday,
April 14th, over here.
And it's another hot day.
I'd say the temperature's right around the 90s.
Real sunny and a real clear sky.
Of course, last summer,
excuse me, I mean last year,
I believe I spent Easter up at Great Lakes,
if I can recall.
I hope this background noise isn't very bad like I said before there's always noise here on the
ship somewhere and just happens to be one right here where I'm making a tape recording at
the tape that I made last night the earlier part of this tape probably you could notice an awful
lot of noise in the background there well I was causing the noise from outside from the ship
but now I've got the hatch closed down and there's only this little winding sign in the background
and I don't really think that it should bother the reproduction on the tape recorder too much.
We also mentioned about a voice switch on a microphone,
which is only actuated when a voice is being transmitted through the microphone.
I've seen these before in some magazines that I have back home.
They show plans on how to build these,
and you can also buy tape recorders with this feature built in.
I believe that sound right there is a jet going overhead outside.
As I was saying, these little switches that you can build, it's a transistorized relay
circuit.
You can build this into a tape recorder or build it into an external box on the outside
of your tape recorder to use only when there's being voice transmitted through it.
I haven't seen any of these sold separately.
The only ones I've seen are the ones already built into a tape recorder
or the ones that you can build yourself.
This would be a pretty handy little gadget
if you actually did a lot of this type of tape recording
where you only wanted the recorder to run
while there was a voice being recorded into it.
In Bill's last letter that he wrote me,
which I received about three or four days ago,
he said he felt there would be a fairly good chance,
So I'm almost 100% sure that he would be able to see me in Da Nang when we arrive there this Tuesday, the 16th.
All hands stand clear of the forward back while rating 48 radar.
And a little interruption right there. I suppose you heard it all.
So he feels that he'll have a pretty good chance to see me when we get in there.
But of course it all depends just on how long we're going to be there.
I understand we're not going to be staying overnight, just there during the day and the afternoon.
so we'll see by then just exactly what does happen.
I hope David got his little envelope of souvenirs that I sent him.
He ought to be pretty well happy about the coins.
He can take them to school and show them to his classmates
and I'm sure he'd be quite proud of them.
Some little souvenir that I figured he would like to have there.
As for the patches, if you want to, you can sew them on the back of his khaki jacket
that we got him for Christmas.
I've got some of those just like that on a jacket that I bought over here,
and I've got quite a few patches on them.
I've been keeping it for a souvenir.
Most likely I'll be buying another tape recorder over here.
This time I think I'll buy a rather inexpensive and small recorder,
which takes a two, three-inch reel.
I can get one pretty cheap, and I feel this is an easy way
to send tape recordings to those back home and Bill
who have the conventional type recorder with the take-up reels on it.
I imagine this will be a well of a way to keep everyone happy and satisfied,
and this will be a rather inexpensive investment for me.
I can imagine what it's like back home right now
with the spring weather starting to come around.
It's really nice to hear everyone say that the weather finally turned for the good back
there after the winter that you had.
But like you said, I'm sure that after summer does get here, you'll all be hoping for a
few days when it does cool off and you do have some rain.
Over here, like I said before, it's always hot, warm, sticky.
just about everything you can associate with the summer back home.
On the 11th, I received two letters from you back home.
I received one also there from David.
One of the two was from him about the thank you note for the chopsticks
and, of course, the bad news about the broken arm.
And as I read his letter, I kind of figured it wasn't his right arm that was broken
because he wouldn't have been able to write the letter,
so I came to a quicker conclusion
that it must have been his left arm.
If you're listening, take good care of that arm
and before long,
you'll be feeling just normal again
after they take that cast off.
And try to keep that cast clean, you know.
You can't go around having a dirty cast on your arm
all the time.
Always carry a pen in your pocket
so your friends can write their names
and autographs on it, okay?
Well, since this Tuesday is the 16th of April, it seems to be a pretty important milestone
for me in more ways than one.
Of course, it'll be three months since we left San Diego and only three more months
to go until the 16th of July when we are due back.
Also, March 8th month since I've been on active duty and only 16 more to go.
So that puts me just about a third of the way through my short career, so to say, in this outfit.
And the 16th of last month, March, marked my third year since I enlisted in the reserves while I was still in high school.
Of course, I went up another bracket of pay, which increased to about $12 a month, which is really a big deal.
but as long as they're willing to give me more money i guess i shouldn't really complain about it
of course there were a lot of unhappy guys on the ship last night because as i mentioned earlier in
the tape we were expected to be anchored about 9 30 and liberty call would go soon after that
well they horsed around as usual and they got anchored about 10 o'clock
and they didn't have the liberty boats launched or anything
and guys started filing off of the ship between 11 o'clock and 11.15 finally
and we decided that it just actually wasn't worth it to go over on the base
and have to be back so soon.
So like I said, I decided to stay aboard
and I guess I have to wait for the next liberty boat in Hong Kong
as we get off the line up there in the Gulf of Tonkin.
But I must admit that our Liberty in Yokosuka
was one of the finest Liberty ports we've had over here
and the longest Liberty that we ever will have.
But it was a pretty good experience up there,
and, of course, as my pictures will testify when you see them,
I did quite a lot of sightseeing up there,
and of course I do have an awful lot to say about the place.
A day or so before I sent my last tape to you,
which was about two weeks ago,
I had quite a scare, even though I didn't amount to very much.
One of my buddies that worked down at the ship's office
had told me the night before that one of the officers
had went to the ship's office and took out my service record
for some reason.
I didn't really think too much of it because it's something that they do quite often when they want to check up on a guy.
So the next morning, I was up here at my working space,
and one of the other fellas came around and told me that this officer wanted to see me immediately.
So I proceeded to where he was,
and he informed me to put on my undressed blues because we were going over to the base for a moment.
Okay, of course, I started to wonder what it was about,
but I didn't dare ask him because you just don't do these type of things unless you're actually told.
So I went down and got dressed and went off the ship and got in the car with him.
He told the driver to take us to the officer of naval intelligence
over by the radio communications building here on the base.
Well, perhaps I thought that there might be some bad news from home
or you can just imagine some of the thoughts that went through my mind
when I didn't actually know what was going on.
And he didn't have the courtesy to tell me just exactly where we were going or why.
Well, after we got there, I soon found out that I was being taken there for questioning
concerning the theft of some money from a guy's locker.
Well, this is my side of the story in brief.
I have been given the combinations of this guy's locker to obtain some...
...to obtain some papers of mine which he had put in his locker.
So I got the papers out of his locker and I did not even see the money or I had no knowledge of it being there.
so as a result the next morning he finds that his money has gone from his locker
and has pointed an accusing finger at me so i was
very willing to cooperate with the questioning that i went through over there because anything
to help prove that i didn't have anything to do with it i was really glad to go along with
so i went over there over there that morning here with the officer and he left me there with this
investigator and I answered all kinds of questions and accounted for most of my activities
for the preceding three or four days and where I had spent my money and what on
this guy was a pretty nice guy he didn't give me any trouble and I went right along with him
they took my fingerprint because they were going to check the fingerprints on the wallet which had
the money stolen out of it to see if mine were on there and he also typed up a statement for me
in my own words and I signed it saying that I had nothing to do with it and accounting for my side
of the story he then asked for permission to come back to the ship with me and look through my
locker to see if they could find any evidence which would point an accusing finger at me
if I didn't have anything to do with it. Of course, I agreed to this and signed a permission
paper for him to do so. And he came back to the ship and checked the locker and found
nothing that should have been there. And he told the officer who took me over there that
He felt that I had nothing to do with it because I had told him everything I knew,
and I was very cooperative with him.
And the officer also told me that he thought that I was off the hook
and I had nothing to worry about.
So there's been a theory disclosed to me by this investigator
that perhaps the money wasn't actually taken from the guy's locker.
He just tried to make up a story so he could get sympathy from his friends
in order to borrow some more money because they had intended on making some rather large purchases over here.
So I asked the legal officer here on board the ship who sent me over there to the investigator
if I could have a statement, a copy of that statement that I made,
which my service record needs as well.
They've only got one copy, and it's here on board the ship.
But he says that I am off the hook and I have nothing to worry about.
so I guess it does make a pretty good story a detective story and
I know I didn't have anything to do with it so that's somebody else's job to find out just
exactly what the story is but I think they've let it all kind of fade away right now because
perhaps they didn't find any evidence to really point anyone out as being the one who did it
so I feel a little bit better about it now that I've been questioned about it
and I've been told that there is really nothing to say that I had anything to do
with it but you can just imagine some of the thoughts that went through my mind
as we were going over there and such secrecy so to say I had no idea exactly
what what it could have been about even though I knew that this money had been
ticket from the guy's locker. I thought that perhaps they had already solved the crime
and it was all forgotten about. But like I said, it's all over with now. And I'm kind
of glad that they did question me so thoroughly. And I have got myself off the hook. So there's
No need to worry about anything back there.
If anything else happens to come up about it, I'll be sure to let you know.
But the way it looks right now, it's going to be all forgot about.
And I haven't heard anything else about it.
I have cornered that officer a couple of times and asked him just what it was.
And he says, well, we feel that it's all over with now and you don't have anything to worry about.
So it does actually make me feel a lot better about it.
One of the chiefs just walked in to get a chair to take outside on the deck.
This is a pretty nice place up here for sunbathing when it's nice and sunny and clear outside.
A lot of guys come up here during the noon hour and soak up a little bit of sunshine.
Things here on the ship haven't changed too much since I last spoke to you.
Of course, every day you run into a few rather disgusting things,
which seems like it could only happen here on the Jewett.
But I am strongly thinking about putting in for a transfer to another ship
when we get back in the States,
because they do have an awful lot of nonsense on this ship,
mostly because it's rather new and unorganized.
And I understand that we will possibly be back in the States
for at least another year before coming back over here again.
And I'd like to make another cruise over here before I do get out.
But I'm going to think an awful lot about it
in the next few months before we do get back to the States
and really decide whether I would want to get off of this ship
and come back over here on another ship.
Of course, it could always be worse in some ways.
Chief Collins, 740. Chief Collins.
It could always be worse in some ways and better in others.
But as far as the living conditions...
Now, Samson, FPM 3, dial 201. Samson.
As far as living conditions here on the ship are, they're really fine.
But in the long run, you still have to put up with some of the nonsense
that you wouldn't find on a lot of other ships here in the Navy.
Don't get me wrong that I'm the only one that's complaining about this
because just about everyone here has a certain gripe about the ship,
everyone from the officers on down to the lowest enlisted men aboard.
And from what I've heard the guys say who have been on other ships,
they say that this one is really a bad one in most of the respect
in which they treat the enlisted men aboard.
I actually wouldn't know because this is the only one that I have been on,
but if there's anything better, I'd certainly like to see it.
But the old saying about the grass always being greener on the other side of the fence
can certainly hold true for anything that might have concerned the way they run things here.
You can probably hear some aircraft noise in the background.
We're anchored just about 500 yards from an airfield here in Subic Bay.
as Airfield has flights come in quite regularly,
similar to a busy airport back in the States.
And all the flights bring the mail in.
They all stop here and then plane from the carriers
out on Yankee Station in the Gulf of Tonkin,
come in and pick up the mail, take it back to the carriers,
and the helicopters take the mail from the carriers
and bring it out to us on the ship.
So this is a pretty busy place over here,
in Subic Bay, one of the more important naval installations here in the western Pacific.
Well, it looks as if my tape is about to run out here, so I'll have to sign off here and
tell everyone back home I said hi, and I'm getting along just fine,
and I'll be eager to receive a return tape from you. I guess I'll say goodbye for now, and
everyone take care.

1968-04-14.text: Hello, Mother, Dad, and David, and anyone else who might be listening. Right now, it's Saturday evening, April 13th. We are at sea heading back to Subic Bay. This morning, we got underway about 7.30 from Subic, and have been out most of the day for missile shoots and gunnery exercises. Two days ago, I got your first tape that you taped on April the 3rd. Needless to say, I was very surprised to hear about David's broken arm. I'm sure this is no new experience for him since, as you mentioned, it did happen once before about a year and a half ago. I was really happy to hear all of your voices and it seemed like you were right beside me and you all sounded the same, although it was kind of hard to get used to to really know that I was actually hearing your voices. I did find it very enjoyable to listen and will look forward to receiving another tape from you. We should be in the harbor in just about another hour, and I might sign off here before I get this whole tape finished, but in case if I do, I'll finish it up tomorrow morning. As you know, tomorrow will be Easter, and we are scheduled to get underway tomorrow after church services, I assume, and we will proceed to Da Nang. It will take us two days to get there. I received two boxes of slides from Bill and a tape along with them. It was very interesting what he had to say and I forwarded the tape and the slides on to Georgia May and have instructed her to send them on home to you when she gets done. I got two boxes of slides back that I took back in Tokyo while I was there and the first chance I get I will make a tape to go along with them and send them on home to you. this tape and any other tapes that i might send in the next day or so will probably be mailed from denang when we get there because the tape will be able to be mailed free and it's just a matter of one or two days time so i figure i'll go ahead and wait till then instead of having to hurry around and take care of it now yes bill ideas of his situation where he's at right now it sounds like it's a real resort area more than anything else yes he told me about going swimming in the china sea but if he would happen to be out here on the ship someday and see some of these sea snakes come swimming by i'm sure that he'd change his mind pretty quick about swimming out here in this ocean so many sea snakes are about eight feet long and about as round as a guy's arm and they're real hard to see or a brownish color so as a result we don't have swim call out here on the ship over here in the Pacific especially up there in the Gulf of Tonkin because of the sea snakes and other creatures that might be wandering around in the water but I'm sure right there where Bill's at I'm sure it's just exactly what he likes and I got these slides from him like I said he seemed to be in pretty good spirits from his pictures and looks to me like he's put on a little bit of weight around the waist I've also sent some pictures on to you actually I sent them through Bill when he gets done looking at him he'll send them on home to you there are a few pictures of me in there and it might look like I put on some weight I actually feel like I have I haven't had a chance to weigh myself since I've been home the last time and I would really like to see how much weight I put on I can really feel like I have and I always want to go on our diet so to say the next day like everyone else does and says. Can't ever get around to it. But I suppose that someday I will probably bring my waistline back down to where it should be. Just like last night. I got ready to go on Liberty. Put on a set of my white pants. Started to put them on. And I popped two buttons off of them trying to get them buttoned around my waist. So you can figure right there just what the situation is. The weather over here is real nice here in the Philippines. This morning it was 84 degrees about 8 o'clock. It's been sunny all day and really hot. Right now it's dark outside. And I can see some of the land over there. I can see a few ships off the coast over there. It's real peaceful and calm out here. The moon is real bright. And the air is rather still and quite humid and heavy. heavy. Tell Dad thanks a lot for the small sports summary on the Cubs game there. I'm sure like he said that we'll probably be able to pick up baseball games over here on the Far East Network. This is a radio network which serves most of the area over here and we're usually able to pick it up on the short wave and put it on the entertainment system for the crew. Also while we are up in the Gulf of Tonkin on station we always get the Stars and Stripes, which I'm sure was a very popular newspaper back in World War II. They bring it out to us every day with the mail helo. And it's only about two or three days old in printing, but of course the news would possibly be about a week old. But it's still just like getting a hometown newspaper, and there's some very good articles in there from sports to the Ann Landers column. So this kind of lets us know what's happening back home, plus also the radio newscast over here. I suppose you're all wondering, since President Johnson has called a halt to the bombing in the major parts of North Vietnam, just exactly what we'll be doing over here our next time on station. And we should be there in just about five days. Well, we don't know yet. All we know is our next stop after we leave here will be in Da Nang on the 16th, which I believe is next Tuesday or Wednesday. We'll pick up our orders right there, just what we're supposed to do and where we go out on station over there. But, like I said before, if the bombing has been halted, it will be another slow time up there on station for the 30 days we're there. You also mentioned about you would recommend that the bombing be stepped up a little bit more. well the reason why they don't do this from what i understand over here they have major points there in north vietnam outside of haiphong and hanoi which they can only hit they are instructed not to bomb any civilian installations housing areas or anything like that only factories and transportation lines so they don't want to involve the north vietnamese civilians in this war. So you see it's kind of a touchy situation when you go in there dropping bombs and you really can't do much damage. And they say that after they have destroyed something within 48 hours or so, it's built right back up again. So it's just a mad circle over here, which I'm sure you can testify to by reading the newspapers. And it's really going to take something and some good politicians to get it settled. we got here in Subic Bay last Thursday I had Liberty that night and last night I had duty yesterday morning a submarine pulled in beside us to tie up alongside and last night I went aboard it it's a nuclear-powered submarine it was the fourth nuclear-powered submarine of its class to be built and I kind of thought being out here on the Jewett was kind of bad duty for a lot of reasons but I tell you I couldn't see living on one of those submarines because they have a crew of about 100 on there and believe me it's really crowded and after I finished a little tour over there on the submarine I came back aboard the ship here really felt kind of funny being able to walk down a passageway without having to step sideways or anything like that and being able to walk on a ship which was actually a lot more roomier even though to some people a ship is not a very roomy place I found that ours is better than some. Like I mentioned before we're due back in the harbor about 9.30. We're not going to tie up at the pier this time we're on the anchor out and they're supposed to have liberty as soon as we get in well liberty will expire for me at one o'clock in the morning so it's going to be a pretty short liberty i believe i'm going to go over to the em club with a buddy of mine we're going to have a couple of beers and catch the liberty boat back to the ship about 12 o'clock Well, they just passed the word there. We're going to be entering port in about 10 minutes. So I believe I'm going to sign off here pretty soon, go down and get into my uniform. Like I said before, I'll probably go over to the club and come back about 12 o'clock and be all ready to go tomorrow because we'll be getting underway possibly by 10 o'clock. And we also have some ammunition to load in the morning. So I'll sign off right here and pick this tape up again tomorrow and finish up for you. Well, here I am back again. It's Sunday morning now, about 11 o'clock. Last night's liberty was not exactly what I had expected it to be. Most of the guys didn't get off the ship until about quarter after 11, so I decided that it was too late to leave the ship then and have to be back within such a short time, so it actually wouldn't be worth it. So I stayed on board and got a pretty good night's rest. Right now we're waiting to load ammunition. They've run into some difficulty in getting it over here. So we're just kind of waiting around now. As soon as we get it all loaded, we're supposed to get underway this afternoon about 2 o'clock. Among some of the things that I did buy back in Yokosuka while we were there, I bought a slide projector. It cost me $39.50. I'm pretty proud of it. I think it's really nice and seems to do a pretty good job. I had one drawback with the show the other day. The white bulb burned out in it, so now I'm faced with trying to find a new one some way. I'll probably have to wait till the next time we get back in port, which will be in Hong Kong, and no doubt I can probably pick up one there. But in the meantime, I'll just have to use my little slide viewer that I have. And in case you're wondering what I plan to do with my high-flyer equipment that I bought over here, we have a place here on the ship where we are stowing most of this stuff, and I'll just keep it here on the ship when I get back in San Diego and take it up to Georgia Maze House and take it from there in case anyone would happen to be coming out here for a vacation in the near future. I suppose some of it could go back with them but if not i can always send it on home from there but i'll probably keep most of it up there until i i'm actually ready to have it sent home so there's no trouble about keeping it here on the ship the only thing is that we can't really have it up and out it's set up so we can listen to it so i've got it all stowed away real real secure and everything and it'll probably stay there until we get back into state. Of course, this is Easter Sunday, April 14th, over here. And it's another hot day. I'd say the temperature's right around the 90s. Real sunny and a real clear sky. Of course, last summer, excuse me, I mean last year, I believe I spent Easter up at Great Lakes, if I can recall. I hope this background noise isn't very bad like I said before there's always noise here on the ship somewhere and just happens to be one right here where I'm making a tape recording at the tape that I made last night the earlier part of this tape probably you could notice an awful lot of noise in the background there well I was causing the noise from outside from the ship but now I've got the hatch closed down and there's only this little winding sign in the background and I don't really think that it should bother the reproduction on the tape recorder too much. We also mentioned about a voice switch on a microphone, which is only actuated when a voice is being transmitted through the microphone. I've seen these before in some magazines that I have back home. They show plans on how to build these, and you can also buy tape recorders with this feature built in. I believe that sound right there is a jet going overhead outside. As I was saying, these little switches that you can build, it's a transistorized relay circuit. You can build this into a tape recorder or build it into an external box on the outside of your tape recorder to use only when there's being voice transmitted through it. I haven't seen any of these sold separately. The only ones I've seen are the ones already built into a tape recorder or the ones that you can build yourself. This would be a pretty handy little gadget if you actually did a lot of this type of tape recording where you only wanted the recorder to run while there was a voice being recorded into it. In Bill's last letter that he wrote me, which I received about three or four days ago, he said he felt there would be a fairly good chance, So I'm almost 100% sure that he would be able to see me in Da Nang when we arrive there this Tuesday, the 16th. All hands stand clear of the forward back while rating 48 radar. And a little interruption right there. I suppose you heard it all. So he feels that he'll have a pretty good chance to see me when we get in there. But of course it all depends just on how long we're going to be there. I understand we're not going to be staying overnight, just there during the day and the afternoon. so we'll see by then just exactly what does happen. I hope David got his little envelope of souvenirs that I sent him. He ought to be pretty well happy about the coins. He can take them to school and show them to his classmates and I'm sure he'd be quite proud of them. Some little souvenir that I figured he would like to have there. As for the patches, if you want to, you can sew them on the back of his khaki jacket that we got him for Christmas. I've got some of those just like that on a jacket that I bought over here, and I've got quite a few patches on them. I've been keeping it for a souvenir. Most likely I'll be buying another tape recorder over here. This time I think I'll buy a rather inexpensive and small recorder, which takes a two, three-inch reel. I can get one pretty cheap, and I feel this is an easy way to send tape recordings to those back home and Bill who have the conventional type recorder with the take-up reels on it. I imagine this will be a well of a way to keep everyone happy and satisfied, and this will be a rather inexpensive investment for me. I can imagine what it's like back home right now with the spring weather starting to come around. It's really nice to hear everyone say that the weather finally turned for the good back there after the winter that you had. But like you said, I'm sure that after summer does get here, you'll all be hoping for a few days when it does cool off and you do have some rain. Over here, like I said before, it's always hot, warm, sticky. just about everything you can associate with the summer back home. On the 11th, I received two letters from you back home. I received one also there from David. One of the two was from him about the thank you note for the chopsticks and, of course, the bad news about the broken arm. And as I read his letter, I kind of figured it wasn't his right arm that was broken because he wouldn't have been able to write the letter, so I came to a quicker conclusion that it must have been his left arm. If you're listening, take good care of that arm and before long, you'll be feeling just normal again after they take that cast off. And try to keep that cast clean, you know. You can't go around having a dirty cast on your arm all the time. Always carry a pen in your pocket so your friends can write their names and autographs on it, okay? Well, since this Tuesday is the 16th of April, it seems to be a pretty important milestone for me in more ways than one. Of course, it'll be three months since we left San Diego and only three more months to go until the 16th of July when we are due back. Also, March 8th month since I've been on active duty and only 16 more to go. So that puts me just about a third of the way through my short career, so to say, in this outfit. And the 16th of last month, March, marked my third year since I enlisted in the reserves while I was still in high school. Of course, I went up another bracket of pay, which increased to about $12 a month, which is really a big deal. but as long as they're willing to give me more money i guess i shouldn't really complain about it of course there were a lot of unhappy guys on the ship last night because as i mentioned earlier in the tape we were expected to be anchored about 9 30 and liberty call would go soon after that well they horsed around as usual and they got anchored about 10 o'clock and they didn't have the liberty boats launched or anything and guys started filing off of the ship between 11 o'clock and 11.15 finally and we decided that it just actually wasn't worth it to go over on the base and have to be back so soon. So like I said, I decided to stay aboard and I guess I have to wait for the next liberty boat in Hong Kong as we get off the line up there in the Gulf of Tonkin. But I must admit that our Liberty in Yokosuka was one of the finest Liberty ports we've had over here and the longest Liberty that we ever will have. But it was a pretty good experience up there, and, of course, as my pictures will testify when you see them, I did quite a lot of sightseeing up there, and of course I do have an awful lot to say about the place. A day or so before I sent my last tape to you, which was about two weeks ago, I had quite a scare, even though I didn't amount to very much. One of my buddies that worked down at the ship's office had told me the night before that one of the officers had went to the ship's office and took out my service record for some reason. I didn't really think too much of it because it's something that they do quite often when they want to check up on a guy. So the next morning, I was up here at my working space, and one of the other fellas came around and told me that this officer wanted to see me immediately. So I proceeded to where he was, and he informed me to put on my undressed blues because we were going over to the base for a moment. Okay, of course, I started to wonder what it was about, but I didn't dare ask him because you just don't do these type of things unless you're actually told. So I went down and got dressed and went off the ship and got in the car with him. He told the driver to take us to the officer of naval intelligence over by the radio communications building here on the base. Well, perhaps I thought that there might be some bad news from home or you can just imagine some of the thoughts that went through my mind when I didn't actually know what was going on. And he didn't have the courtesy to tell me just exactly where we were going or why. Well, after we got there, I soon found out that I was being taken there for questioning concerning the theft of some money from a guy's locker. Well, this is my side of the story in brief. I have been given the combinations of this guy's locker to obtain some... ...to obtain some papers of mine which he had put in his locker. So I got the papers out of his locker and I did not even see the money or I had no knowledge of it being there. so as a result the next morning he finds that his money has gone from his locker and has pointed an accusing finger at me so i was very willing to cooperate with the questioning that i went through over there because anything to help prove that i didn't have anything to do with it i was really glad to go along with so i went over there over there that morning here with the officer and he left me there with this investigator and I answered all kinds of questions and accounted for most of my activities for the preceding three or four days and where I had spent my money and what on this guy was a pretty nice guy he didn't give me any trouble and I went right along with him they took my fingerprint because they were going to check the fingerprints on the wallet which had the money stolen out of it to see if mine were on there and he also typed up a statement for me in my own words and I signed it saying that I had nothing to do with it and accounting for my side of the story he then asked for permission to come back to the ship with me and look through my locker to see if they could find any evidence which would point an accusing finger at me if I didn't have anything to do with it. Of course, I agreed to this and signed a permission paper for him to do so. And he came back to the ship and checked the locker and found nothing that should have been there. And he told the officer who took me over there that He felt that I had nothing to do with it because I had told him everything I knew, and I was very cooperative with him. And the officer also told me that he thought that I was off the hook and I had nothing to worry about. So there's been a theory disclosed to me by this investigator that perhaps the money wasn't actually taken from the guy's locker. He just tried to make up a story so he could get sympathy from his friends in order to borrow some more money because they had intended on making some rather large purchases over here. So I asked the legal officer here on board the ship who sent me over there to the investigator if I could have a statement, a copy of that statement that I made, which my service record needs as well. They've only got one copy, and it's here on board the ship. But he says that I am off the hook and I have nothing to worry about. so I guess it does make a pretty good story a detective story and I know I didn't have anything to do with it so that's somebody else's job to find out just exactly what the story is but I think they've let it all kind of fade away right now because perhaps they didn't find any evidence to really point anyone out as being the one who did it so I feel a little bit better about it now that I've been questioned about it and I've been told that there is really nothing to say that I had anything to do with it but you can just imagine some of the thoughts that went through my mind as we were going over there and such secrecy so to say I had no idea exactly what what it could have been about even though I knew that this money had been ticket from the guy's locker. I thought that perhaps they had already solved the crime and it was all forgotten about. But like I said, it's all over with now. And I'm kind of glad that they did question me so thoroughly. And I have got myself off the hook. So there's No need to worry about anything back there. If anything else happens to come up about it, I'll be sure to let you know. But the way it looks right now, it's going to be all forgot about. And I haven't heard anything else about it. I have cornered that officer a couple of times and asked him just what it was. And he says, well, we feel that it's all over with now and you don't have anything to worry about. So it does actually make me feel a lot better about it. One of the chiefs just walked in to get a chair to take outside on the deck. This is a pretty nice place up here for sunbathing when it's nice and sunny and clear outside. A lot of guys come up here during the noon hour and soak up a little bit of sunshine. Things here on the ship haven't changed too much since I last spoke to you. Of course, every day you run into a few rather disgusting things, which seems like it could only happen here on the Jewett. But I am strongly thinking about putting in for a transfer to another ship when we get back in the States, because they do have an awful lot of nonsense on this ship, mostly because it's rather new and unorganized. And I understand that we will possibly be back in the States for at least another year before coming back over here again. And I'd like to make another cruise over here before I do get out. But I'm going to think an awful lot about it in the next few months before we do get back to the States and really decide whether I would want to get off of this ship and come back over here on another ship. Of course, it could always be worse in some ways. Chief Collins, 740. Chief Collins. It could always be worse in some ways and better in others. But as far as the living conditions... Now, Samson, FPM 3, dial 201. Samson. As far as living conditions here on the ship are, they're really fine. But in the long run, you still have to put up with some of the nonsense that you wouldn't find on a lot of other ships here in the Navy. Don't get me wrong that I'm the only one that's complaining about this because just about everyone here has a certain gripe about the ship, everyone from the officers on down to the lowest enlisted men aboard. And from what I've heard the guys say who have been on other ships, they say that this one is really a bad one in most of the respect in which they treat the enlisted men aboard. I actually wouldn't know because this is the only one that I have been on, but if there's anything better, I'd certainly like to see it. But the old saying about the grass always being greener on the other side of the fence can certainly hold true for anything that might have concerned the way they run things here. You can probably hear some aircraft noise in the background. We're anchored just about 500 yards from an airfield here in Subic Bay. as Airfield has flights come in quite regularly, similar to a busy airport back in the States. And all the flights bring the mail in. They all stop here and then plane from the carriers out on Yankee Station in the Gulf of Tonkin, come in and pick up the mail, take it back to the carriers, and the helicopters take the mail from the carriers and bring it out to us on the ship. So this is a pretty busy place over here, in Subic Bay, one of the more important naval installations here in the western Pacific. Well, it looks as if my tape is about to run out here, so I'll have to sign off here and tell everyone back home I said hi, and I'm getting along just fine, and I'll be eager to receive a return tape from you. I guess I'll say goodbye for now, and everyone take care.

1968-04-14.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG-29) 1968 CRUISE BOOK — PAGES 92-93

After a trip to the U.S. Naval Station, Yokosuka, Japan, where JOUETT and her
crew recovered from the rigors of the first line period, the ship returned to the
Tonkin Gulf in early April. Our second line period involved some changes from the
first--clear skies greeted us, as the annual monsoon had ended--and a second helicop-
ter, the larger SH-3, was added to our SAR Team during daylight hours.

[Photo: SH-3A "Big Mother" helicopter parked on flight deck with dramatic cloud formations in background]

[Photo: SH-3A helicopter (number 72 visible on fuselage) hovering close above Jouett's flight deck, landing gear extended]

[Photo: View from flight deck showing ship's missile launchers and radar equipment with helicopter operations in background]

segments.text: Hello, Mother, Dad, and David and everyone else at home.
Well, right now I'm in Da Nang Harbor and right beside me is Bill.
He came aboard the ship just about an hour and a half ago.
I was pretty surprised to see him.
He said it was about 12 o'clock. It's about quarter to 3 right here.
This is Tuesday, April 16th.
He's been telling me some of his little war stories and some of the games that they've been playing over here.
And they seem to be in pretty good spirits and pretty good shape.
I'm having a mic over to him right now and I didn't say a few words.
Well, it took a pretty long time getting off this ship.
I got in the, or left, uh, left at Hoi An at the, uh, chopper's ship about, uh, 9 o'clock.
And got in here about, uh, quarter to 9, I think it was.
And, uh, you know, we got pretty high there.
I was pretty surprised, I was surprised the choppers fly.
I thought they could go up.
I got in here around 20 after 9 I think it was.
I ran out of the third mast.
I didn't really know where to go.
I asked the guy who was driving the Navy truck to where the deep water pool was.
He said, I'll take you halfway down there.
I said, okay.
I went down there.
I got another ride on down to here.
I got down here and talked to some guys in security.
This is where all the parts, all down here is, down at the pier is a merchant ship.
And this is around the harbor.
And what would I do by getting out there?
And they tell me all this.
And so I end up going back and forth about three times, back up to St. Matthews, back down here,
and cross the river on a ferry a couple of times.
Going back and forth is what they call the White Alps.
It's a naval operations deal down there along the river.
Yeah, that's how it is.
And when I called up down there, they said, yeah, the ship's in,
and it's so many thousand meters out from southeast of the port or something like that,
and I didn't understand what he said, you know.
So I just took full credit, you know, he knew what he was talking about.
And then when I got down there and went up here,
and I was talking to one of the guys who was on the radio watch up at the pier there,
and there was these small boats there running back and forth to the ship.
And he said, yeah, well, I feel about the guys who, you know, who the ship is, and they'll run you out there.
He said, yeah.
So he ran me out here, and he finally got out here.
He said, I'll let the hands of the air on the ground, man.
It's really rocky.
Well, I think I'll stop.
The ship's rocking a little bit, and I think I'll fix the land and everything out here.
And my point of space, he works out.
Well, I don't think he's going to get seasick.
It's pretty calm out here right now.
But the weather right here is really hot.
I'd say it's at least 90 outside.
the air is pretty heavy and still yeah it's really clear out here it's uh the visibility is very far
but it's a lot nicer than the last time that we were in here which was just about a month ago
no that's wait a minute two months ago as a matter of fact it was in february
the 14th that we were here last and that was just about two months ago
um i gotta do up in that good navy towel here we had hamburgers and nice potatoes at that
Of course, he had to wait in line like the rest of us.
I don't suppose that's any new experience for him.
Might be able to hear some helicopters and jets in the background.
There's a lot of air activity going on around here.
There's an awful lot of ships out here in the harbor.
Doug, did you notice a lot of ships tied up in there?
Yeah, there was a bunch of merchant ships out there.
I think that's the reason why we don't tie up in there
is because they've got so many merchant vessels in there
that they don't have room for the Navy ships.
and you think they might be afraid they might get shot at or fired on?
Yeah, I mean, they have snipers in there, you know, and they're like secure hills.
They really can't be secure.
Nobody's really secure over here, you know.
That's right.
This is where we think you're at, we're secure.
That's definitely right.
The ship's supposed to leave here about 530 this afternoon,
and no doubt we'll be able to find a boat to take him back to the pier.
Hey, hey, he said we might have to swim back.
We can't find any other way back there.
I'm sure he wouldn't mind it being the hot, sticky weather that it is right here.
David, you should be getting those packages by right now.
By the time you begin to take them, you should be getting those packages.
They're coming in about three weeks.
Send them to Parkville Post.
and hope you enjoy this camouflage utility.
I know I do over here.
I think it kind of needs to be worn around.
It's a lot different.
You can wear just the pants and not the shirt
because it's too hot.
You can wear pants and boots and that's about it.
And then you can always use them to play around in,
play army, stuff like that there.
Or play Marines if you want to.
And I hope you really enjoy this time.
I know that one deal I sent,
we found in a Buddhist pagoda,
which is a church type deal that they have over here,
a round deal.
It's made out of wood and carved.
And it's got a hole through the middle of it
and it's placed about a quarter of an inch
and you hit it with a ring,
or a dead ring, but you know,
a knocking sound on it.
It sounds very neat.
And today is really hot for me because I've been doing a lot of walking,
which I wasn't used to doing, especially on a hard ground.
We used to walk in the sand up to our knees.
And walking back and forth, I had to carry all my gear and my rifle
and my 7.82 gear and my helmet and my flak jacket,
which is fairly hot in this type of weather.
It's kind of a relief to get on this ship and take it all off, you know,
and just leave it up there where I came on at and pick it up when I leave again.
It's been fairly hot over here.
It's about 20 miles south of here.
