And last night he did quite a bit of showing around the hill there. Nothing came up on the hill, thank God. I imagine if something came up on a hill, we'd really be moving out of there pretty quick. There wasn't really around there to protect us, just the bunkers that we got down in the fighting holes. I guess that's all we do is get down in the fighting holes or go down to the hills where the Army's at. They've got a bunker with walls on it about four feet wide with sandbags. It's pretty nice. and uh usually was the Korean ring's birthday so they took and set up a bunch of goodies for us and uh I think we had about 6 cases of beer between 15 of us which wasn't too bad oh yeah and uh probably using right now and uh they set up toothpaste soap and uh shaving cream so I guess they might have been hitting around about something I don't know but uh Talk about it on the Korean situation over here. They're kind of messed up. They really don't know what the score things are. They're getting quite a few men wiped out by the VC. But we captured 15 the other night. So I guess they're getting credit for some things. Bill handed the microphone back to me. I guess he wants me to say something now. I gave a little rundown of what we're going to be doing in the next few days. Took us two days to get here from Civic Bay. We left Sunday evening about 6 in the evening. And we got here this morning. It's about 8 o'clock. We got anchored about quarter to 9. We're getting away this evening. We're going to go out for some CT boat operations. There's a couple of CT boats. We'll try our tracking and our gunnery systems right on them. Just a little exercise that we go through every time we come over here. And we'll get up on star station tomorrow afternoon sometime where we'll be Running around in circles for about the next 30 days Okay We haven't got any mail since we left Subic Bay There might be a chance we might get some this afternoon if they had any over here for us and if not We'll get it when we get up on station and the helicopters bring it back out to us again like they did before Like I said before we expected to be pretty quiet up there this time just like it was last time And so the weather could be a lot nicer, which means it's going to be a lot warmer and hotter, a lot more sun. But actually, it's a little bit better than the bad weather we did have up there, all the rain, the fog and everything. It's made the day seem even longer and a lot more boring. I would hope that David started to get used to his arm and he found that he can get along all right with it. Yeah, I told him not to have too good of a time out there shaking. I suppose he really lives it up out there. And I know his heart is really broke because he can't play his drum anymore. Day after tomorrow is payday here on this ship. I expect to leave my money on the books. I don't know just yet how much I'm going to be getting. They should have a pay list up sometime this afternoon. I'll leave my money on the books for another three or four weeks and draw a little bit off of spending Hong Kong. But from now on out, I'm going to be saving most of it and not spend any more than I have to over here. I spent just exactly what I wanted to and bought what I wanted to while we were in Yautuska. And I don't think I'm going to be making any more large purchases while I'm over here. I'd like to get as much stuff back home as I can while I'm over here. Bill just told me here this afternoon that the Illinois State Veterans Administration will send anyone that's over here in Vietnam in the combat zone, will send them $100. dollars because he's going to give me the address as soon as he can get it and uh i'll send a letter back to him real quick i'll send a letter back to him real quick and see if i can pick up on that hundred dollars and see what there is about that they're just handing me a nickel here he says this court-martial offense well i imagine so it carries uh any u.s currency on your person over here because like I said in Japan we had to change our green back to this NPC money yeah funny money is what they also call it and over here in Vietnam they change their NPC into coins also but back in Japan we got to use US coins but over here they have paper money to use for the coins so it's really a kind of a complicated deal but it's all for the better of the economy to keep the money from going to the wrong hands. Now Bill just asked me to ask Zeus if he took it out of his jungle boots that we sent home to him there for Christmas. Bill's got a pair of them on right here and needless to say they look like they've been worn quite a bit. Yeah he took some barbed wire scratches on the top of them and we He was here on the ship with some of his M16s and some of his gear that he brought aboard. And we had quite a crowd of sailors around there asking all kinds of questions and everything. Firing questions of Bill right and left. And he was giving us some pretty good answers. I was kind of surprised to see some of the combat gear over here, which we'd probably never seen or even touched. For a ship being all in a situation where they are really security conscious, They didn't know what they were going to do with his gun when he brought it on board. They didn't know whether to take it down to the small arms locker or just what to do with it. They were kind of confused about it because they probably weren't ever faced with a situation before. So he left it there on the quarterback where he came on board with the rest of his stuff. And they gave him an escort badge, and one of my buddies brought him down. I was laying in my rack catching a noon hour sleep, and I was just starting to get up to go up and get some dinner. And he says, that's right. He said, you better get up. Your brother just called down there and wants you to come up and get him. I said, ah, you're lying. I said, he ain't here. He said, yes, he is. He said, you want me to go up and get him? I said, yeah, go on up and get him. Bring him down here. So he went up and got him and brought him down. And I saw old Bill there. And that's the first question I asked him. I said, do you have anything to eat? He says, no, I haven't had anything since 7 o'clock this morning. And so we finally took up through the trial line and had a couple of handlers at the Now we're all ready for the next meal. Well, they said it's about 5.30, just about time. We're getting underway. I got to go up and stand a watch and a .50 caliber machine gun. We've got two .50 caliber machine guns mounted here in case if we get any attacks from any small boats or anything, which is really ridiculous. ridiculous. You just can't believe how they sweat things when this ship pulls in the port. For example, when we were in Subic Bay for one day, the time before we went to Yokosuka, we stopped there for one day. They let somebody come on board the ship without giving them an escort badge or an escort. They came on board the ship, they had a cardboard box all all wrapped up and they took it up to CIC, which is the place where we have all of our radar gear and our radio transmitters and everything. And they placed this box up there and they walked off the ship. Well, one of the crew members on the ship saw the box over there and went over and unwrapped it. And on the inside there was a nice little note all typed up real neat, which said, this is a bomb. Surprise. So it was that somebody was testing our security strength here on the ship and they had a big shakedown about this and now they really put the pressure on when you're in foreign port now checking everybody that comes on board the ship of course the captain is so afraid somebody's going to take his pride and joy away from him which is true of most captains who have a ship under their command but I guess things are just like that in the Navy. Every branch of the service has their own characteristics and things which are noted for, and I guess this is one thing that the Navy is known for, is a captain who's always worrying about the welfare of his ship. When that captain asked me for my rifle, I said something like, the War Hardened Marines say that rifle stays with me wherever I go, I imagine if I say that he probably had a heart attack or something. You know, we really close a lot of rifles, you know, be out in our reach or not knowing where they're at. Especially, you know, over here. Something does happen right here where we're at now. I doubt anything would, but something did happen. We'd have to get to our weapons pretty quick. I should have really said that to him. He'd probably have had a fit. He'd probably have to find a favor or something for it. Something like that. They don't know what to do, actually. Officers on here, when you call their bluff or call their car, they don't know what to say. They have to go out and get their little book of doing and stuff. That's exactly what they're supposed to do next. You should be getting that tape today or tomorrow, since it's on the target reel. So, uh, taking, playing the shoulder slides and everything, and then, uh, taking the short plate, uh, ground and ground points and all that, and the slides also. I tried to just send the slides and stuff on home, because, uh, they were just mostly, uh, down there at the beach. And, uh, a couple, one slide over, he's over there at the 327PX, and, uh, these little good kids running around, shit-shining boots, talking to one guy. One guy, he was in a truck with a sign of a boot that he was going to put in the truck and a little good kid had a sign of a boot and he looked up when I took the picture. Usually when a, you know what's funny is when there's kids out there peddling off nears and Vietnamese flags and there's a little Arvin Bray, you know. I saw these flags, this guy, this Jack, this Paul Blankens, they said over here these flags that they sell here are actually made over here and they take them on and they stomp them in the dirt and turn them up a little bit and say this is a captured North Vietnamese flag. We hadn't seen them yet in the north of the enemy's flag. They were just in the red and yellow. But one day when we were back there at the battalion area, we were up on the bunker floor. We looked over the rice paddies and the river down there. The groups, they took a long piece of bamboo, I think it was about 30-foot long, and it was about four or five inches in diameter down toward the bottom. They put it up there with the South of the enemy's flag on it, on it and next night we got hit you know with a little bit small ground itself you know two or three guys came came up to the perimeter and we shot some uh grenades at them the import team grenade launchers you know the grenade box on the enemy shot couple of men and captain a couple of uh coffins went down the next morning they wouldn't go down there at night you know to check it out because the guy tore he hit it you know because he shot six grenades down there a couple of them was was in the same area and then spread them out a little bit. And he just tore it and hit that guy that was down there. So they went up in the patrol, you know, we got night patrols out there, you know, they went up in the patrol and checked it out. And the next morning went down there. And also during the night, the dogs and stuff run down to the wire there and stuff, and they go up there around where the firing was at, where the grenades landed at and stuff, and they'd go around and sniff around the kind of ground, and they'd take off running. You know, and then we knew there was somebody down there, And then the next morning we went down there to check it out. A couple of lieutenants and captains went in and checked it out. All they found was a couple of utility jackets and some blood down there. What was that? I imagine they would send a couple, you know, four or five guys out there, you know, to check it out. They probably found a scoop that wounded pretty bad. You know, it just didn't seem that they know how to run it. So you could think on their side, you know, we sent patrol down there. might be an ambush but they always have it set up you know we had the uh 250 calibers and an m60 machine gunner and the m14 with the grenades on the grenade launcher on it so if anything happened down there they'd wipe it out real quick you know without no trouble when they didn't so they got away or whoever's down there i'll tell you about that flag they set up there a little ground assault everything that night and uh so whenever they put that flag knowing that there was a VC in the area, because they put up a flag, you know, to show the VC that they were on our side. These groups of the farming down there was on our side and everything. And so they usually stay watching for that flag pretty well. They finally got the tower built back up over there. CBs came down there. On the front? Yeah, the tower building, yeah. CBs came back there about four weeks later. So that's again for us. They cut it off about 25 foot tall now. They did a pretty good job on it. I just sent a tape home to you the other day. You ought to have it by now. It's probably recording on the other side and ready to send it back. So this tape hasn't ran through all the way, but there's really not too much more to say. So I'm going to sign off here, and I'll hand the mic back to Bill and let him say a few more finishing words. And so everybody be good back there, and Dave be a good boy, and stay out of trouble in school, and try to protect that arm. and don't get mad at anybody and hit them with that cast either because they'll probably be wearing one too. And like I said, they would be good, and I suppose you and Mother are both waiting for school to get out. It's on vacation to be here real soon. Even though it feels like summer right over here, you figure it'd be the same way back home, but I know that it's real nice. Yeah, Bill said he's going to have two years of summer over here, and that's right. and sure the spring weather back here is really nice one of the nicest times of the year so I'll say goodbye for now and be writing a letter soon or sending another tape as I get one from you so long everybody be good be careful and tell David do not trade off his utilities I gave him because they're pretty hard to get unless I got a little pair to trade off for them. The Koreans eat up these American utilities. So I guess we eat up their camouflage utilities. Take care of them and don't get them ripped or torn. You can keep from it. And be good and be careful on your bike if you're riding your new bike with your broken arm. And be good and keep up your homework and schoolwork and everything. Be good in school. And make good grades and not have to worry about flunking or anything like that. And everybody take care, and I guess that's about it from ESL Hewitt, anchored in the South Tennessee off the coast of Da Nang on, what's the date? April 16th. April 16th, 1968 at 3 p.m. 3 p.m. 3 p.m. and I hope everybody is in good condition and everything like that there. When I'm walking through the elephant grass, don't worry, I'll keep my ass down. This is a PS there. I was going to give Mike a little, he had to meet Langley School here in case we just happen to get in on land. We're walking down through the city of Da Nang or maybe Saigon if we get the chance to get down there maybe. and I was going to give him a little language here, which I did say some of it back on my last tape, but I forgot a couple of things. One was opened up, which means I do not understand. I'm like a book is talking to you. You speak a little language and then it gets carried away and starts speaking Vietnamese. Then you just tell him to open it up. Then he'll start over again and then you hope that you get it the second time. And then, uh, Dung Lai, which means stop or halt. That's what we use. That's what we told you. We're going on tweets, checking the ID cards, and if there's anybody outside of the perimeter, he's just waving his hands and all that stuff. In case there's a kid sick or something like that, he wants them to come and take care of him. We tell him, uh, Dung Lai means halt, stop, and we call for an interpreter because we can't speak Vietnamese that good. Then, uh, Chaco La Dai, which means young girl, come here. always a popular phrase. Why would you want to say something like that? Well, you know, I was walking through a veil. You've got to check all the ID cards, all the young people. It's good to have a good reason. Yeah. And then a little crane I picked up. There's quite a bit of it. One of them is you have a veil, which means hello, how are you, and friend. It's a friendly greeting. There goes a small boat down in the water. Good place for a boat to be going, really. A couple of guys going in. Maybe I should have caught that boat. It seemed to be going a little faster than what I came out here. Normally, whenever you're trying to get someplace in a hurry, it doesn't go fast enough. And, let's see. If you think anything else, you're going to get a lead. Well, let's see. Dinky Dow, which means you tell us if these little kids come around pestering you, asking you for chop-chop, which is food in that language, chop-chop, or cigarettes. These little six-year-old kids asking for cigarettes. You tell them, uh, you tell them to dinky-dow, which means, uh, crazy little kids. They don't like it, and they kick off. Or you tell them dee-dee, which means, uh, get away from me or bother me. How do you say rice? Rice. Uh, chop-chop. Well, you know, food. Usually, uh, if you see some, uh, rice, When I went through this one tweet one day, I had this little kid tearing up his parents' home and friends' home and living around him. And I wouldn't let you have that stuff because it would be trapped. And he'd open a big vase and it'd be full of rice and go chop, chop. And I'd take my hand in there and say, okay. And then they have little deals that are like up-sized carrots. You take carrot slices and they turn white. They were white, like a gum or some substance of a gum you chew on for quite a while. The reason why I asked you how you say rice is because in Japan, the word for rice is dozo. D-O-S-O, dozo. That's about one of the only words I learned there in Japan. Then another thing over here when we were doing the Hoi An, we pick up bananas, coconuts. And then the last few weeks we've been in there, they've had watermelons and we asked them how much for the watermelon, they know what it is. In English language, they go, a watermelon, $2. So it's a little one-man watermelon. Buko too much, buko means many, too much, a whole lot. Buko too much, buko. And then usually we can even do them down if we got some time to stick around there. But we got something to trade to them for it. They usually pick it up pretty quick. A guy bought a watch in there in one of the jewelry shops in there. Ten bucks for a watch at a date. And secondhand, you know, self-winding or anything like that. Ten bucks just wasn't too bad. But these droops, they take a $10 in our NPC's money and take it down to the black market and get $12. They just merchandise out of $10. Yeah. from our our NPCs uh well the dollar 18 of their uh piastres or keys whatever they're going to call them what money is called piastres yeah and it's uh pretty big deal in these foreign countries so they can get a hold of any money from the military personnel they'll use it for their own purposes and really have some advantage of it well I guess that's about it in the Vietnamese culture and the highlights of Vietnam and how other people act. I guess I'll be signing off now. So we'll give you bye from Bill and bye from Mike.

1968-04-19.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-04-19.text:
April 19, 1968
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother & Dad,

This morning I got your letter of April 12th. The mail helo is now coming in the morning so its good to start off the day with mail from home.

You should have got the tape by now that Bill and I made in Da Nang. We were glad to see one another and I was surprized he was able to make it. You know we have been pretty fortunate to see each other since we went into the service and I guess this is no exception even though we are over 12,000 miles from home.

Just one year ago I graduated from school at Great Lakes. The time has really went fast and it seems like only yesterday.

I can't imagine why Grandma & Grandpa weren't able to play the tape I sent them on their recorder. I don't remember what speed it was on but it should have been compatiable to be used on theirs. It was done on a mono recorder. Let me know what speeds they can use and I'll send the right speed next time.

I won't be able to mail you any recordings until you send me one. I used my last cartridge for the message from Bill to. So I hope to hear from you once again soon.

The routine up here hasn't changed a bit. The weather is still as bad as it use to be. But I do believe it has warmed up a little since our last time up here.

About the records Connie bought back. I think thats all there was. Bill didn't have a case of 45's and I think the ones he did have are with his stuff. From what Bill tells me she has started writing to him again now that the wedding is off.

I found the newspaper clippings interesting. I suppose it was quite a shock back there about Dr. King. The ships in the fleet flew the flag at half-mast for about five days.

On the first of May I will be working with the E.T.'s (electronic technicians) on maintence and troubleshooting. This is something I have always wanted to do and comes as a surprize to me. Actually we have more E.T.'s than we need even though two were discharged our last time in Subic Bay, so I guess it won't hurt anyone for me to be with them for the rest of the time over here.

I am waiting for one more box of slides before I send my slides on to you. I will make a tape to go with them so you'll know whats going on.

If you noticed any static like sound in the tape Bill and I sent it was some interference from one of the radars. Its pretty hard to find an ideal place to record here on the ship. But I think it didn't hurt the tape too much.

Well, thats about all for now. I hope you enjoyed our tape and found it interesting. So long for now.

Your son,

Mike

1968-04-22.label: Stars and Stripes - 160 Missions Pound N. Vietnam
1968-04-22.attribution: Stars and Stripes - 160 Missions Pound N. Vietnam — Ducy Family Archives
1968-04-22.text:
Pacific Stars & Stripes
April 22, 1968

[Handwritten annotation at top: "April 22, Stars + Stripes"]

Record for Year

160 Missions Pound N. Vietnam

SAIGON (AP)—For the second day in a row U.S. warplanes flew a record number of missions over North Vietnam for the year. But all of the strikes Friday were in the Panhandle, within the limits set by President Johnson three weeks ago.

U.S. Air Force, Navy and Marine pilots mounted 160 missions Friday, hitting bridges, roads, trucks and supply points. It was the largest number of raids flown so far this year, exceeding the record 145 set only Thursday.

The pilots said they encountered light ground fire and evaded several surface-to-air missiles fired at them in the [underlined] coastal area between Vinh and Dong Hoi. [/underlined]

[starred] * The weather is rapidly improving over the North with the monsoon ending, so U.S. air strikes are expected to increase unless additional curtailments are ordered by Johnson.

Johnson, in a major move to encourage North Vietnamese President Ho Chi Minh to begin peace talks, declared three weeks ago that U.S. planes would not attack any targets above the 20th Parallel. The action spares the major cities of Hanoi and Haiphong.

Although Friday's 160 missions set a high for 1968, that is well below the all-time record of 209 set last Aug. 19 before the northeastern monsoons swirled in over North Vietnam.

No U.S. planes were reported shot down, but in its weekly release the U.S. command announced that as of Tuesday, 1,070 planes have been downed by enemy gunners — 823 over North Vietnam and 247 in South Vietnam.

Another 1,002 airplanes have been lost in accidents not involving direct enemy action. The command also announced that 643 helicopters have been shot down, nine in North Vietnam and 634 in South Vietnam, and another 920 choppers have been lost in nonhostile actions.

[starred] * U.S. warships, also in line with Johnson's de-escalation move, did not bombard any targets in North Vietnam, according to the U.S. command. The destroyer Robert H. McCard, in a mission that was the farthest north reported, blasted enemy bunkers and trenchlines inside the Demilitarized Zone.

The primary air raid in South Vietnam was carried out by the giant B52 bombers that sailed in over the clouds above A Shau Valley with four strikes Friday night and Saturday morning.

A fifth mission was in the same general vicinity southwest of Hue.

The B52s have now carried out nearly 30 missions involving about 180 of the high-altitude bombers in the past four days against enemy forces in the valley.

A Shau, near the Laotian border and 30 miles west of Hue, has been a North Vietnamese Army stronghold since March, 1966, when guerrillas overran the U.S. Special Forces camp there.

A huge network of roads and trails has been cut through the valley by NVA engineers, making it a key infiltration area for enemy units moving in to attack South Vietnamese cities along the populated coastal areas to the east.

1968-04-25.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-04-25.text:
April 25, 1968
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother, Dad and David,

I just finished a letter to grandma and thought I'd answer your letter of April 18 which I got today before I go to bed.

Things are still the same up here as they were before. The weather is a lot nicer though and we are getting some real sunny days instead of the fog and rain we were so use to.

Here is a clipping I thought might interest you. Actually this is about all I know about the recent move to slow down the bombing. Vinh is an airfield about 24 miles from us. We can usually see the explosions from the air raids there on a clear night.

I hope everyone had a chance to hear the tape from Bill and me and enjoyed it as much as we did in making it.

I am glad to hear you passed the LPN test and now can count on what you'll be doing next fall.

I got another box of slides today. As soon as I get another tape cartridge from you I'll send the slides with an explanation on tape.

I got two papers yesterday dated April 14 + 16. I am willing to read them if they are still willing to send them to me.

Here are some stamps I've saved for you.

The Stars + Stripes have pretty good coverage on the baseball season and it looks like the Cubs and White Sox are having a little trouble starting off on the right foot.

David, I got your note about recieving the souveniers I sent you. It was good to hear from you. You mentioned that you now have a pigeon and a duck. It sounds like you are going to start a zoo. Now all you need is some rabbits and a few more pets. On second thought a duck and a pigeon demand a lot of attention and they should keep you pretty busy. Keep at your schoolwork and be a good boy. Before you know it you'll be out of school for good and wish you were back in. So make the most of it now.

Well thats all there is to say for now. I'll be waiting to hear from you. So long.

Your son,

Mike
1968-04-25.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-05-02.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-05-02.text:
May 2, 1968
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother,

I got your letter of April 25 this morning after receiving your tape and the pictures yesterday. So I'll go ahead and answer your letter now while I have the time.

Yes, grandma devoted some of her last letter to me telling me how she noticed Connie was so lonely now that her wedding was called off. Big deal! The type of person that I know her as I'd say she brought her own "heartbreak" to herself. No doubt she'll find other interests soon enough and you most likely won't be seeing much of her then. Of course grandma never says anything to me about the past and if she ever does I'm telling you she is barking up the wrong tree. Its as simple as this; you were doing what you thought was right. Bill has managed to live through it and he should be growing wiser, the past is over and the best thing to do is forget it and chalk it up as experience.

This afternoon the chaplian came aboard and heard confessions and said Mass. I took time to attend both.

Our gun system is in pretty bad shape. The fire-control radar is down and we are waiting on parts. Two of the three gun mounts are down and also awaiting repair parts. It kind of makes a guy wonder just what we would do if we had to have some defense sometime. But we aren't out here alone and we know long ahead if we are in danger.

Just a short while ago two Migs were shot down by aircraft from the Ranger, one of the carriers out here. We sent our helo out to search for the VC pilots but I don't think they will have any luck. The action took place about 60 miles north of us.

As far as the correspondence course goes, I applied for the test at least six weeks ago and as of yet the test hasn't got here. I'll have to go to the office again and remind them of it. I want to get this course done and out of the way so I can start on another and this delay isn't helping a bit.

I'll be looking forward to getting the package and the books. Its rather hard to say how long it will take to get here but I'd say about two weeks at least, depending on how you send it.

Today the pay scale for the raise which goes into effect July 1 was posted. According to it I'll be getting $251 a month. Breaking that down that means I'll clear $50 a week. Really great! But thats more than I made in any job I had back home. I just hope I can save up as much as I am expecting to in the next 14½ months.

Well I'll close for now and get this in the mail. Bye for now.

Your son, Mike
1968-05-02.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-05-04.label: Jouett Jargon
1968-05-04.text:
JOUETT JARGON
4 MAY 68

MIG 21 SHOT DOWN OVER GULF

    Aboard the USS Ranger, Tonkin Gulf--A U.S. Navy F4 Phantom protecting American ships and planes in the Gulf of Tonkin shot down a MIG 21 Thursday.
    The MIG pilot parachuted into the Gulf, where U.S. ships and helicopters began a search and rescue operation. By nightfall, Navy spokesmen said the Communist pilot had not been rescued, and chances he would be captured dwindled. The United States has not captured a Communist pilot during the Vietnam War. The Phantom pilot, Lt. John E. Ryan, 27, of Beverly, Mass., and his backseat radar man, Lt(jg) James E. Spencer, 26, of San Pablo, Calif., spotted the Communist MIG heading into the Gulf at 57,000 feet. "He may have been waiting to roll in on one of our own planes," Ryan said.
    The U.S. Seventh Fleet keeps picket ships and radar communications planes prowling the Northern Gulf. Ryan's job was to protect them from MIGs. He had never seen one before Thursday. This was the second time Ryan had seen a MIG in five minutes. The first one headed into the Gulf when Ryan and Lt. Cdr. Barlan Hall of Vancouver, Washington, sped in to intercept it. The MIG turned back over northern North Vietnam, and the Navy pilots were forbidden to follow because of the current bombing pause.
    The second time, the MIG kept coming and turned north when Hall and Ryan spotted him. The U.S. pilots sneaked up behind it and Hall snapped off two missiles, which had no effect. The MIG kept flying straight, apparently with the pilot unaware he was being chased. Then Ryan moved the Phantom up to within a mile or so and opened up with an air-to-air missile. "The missile went straight at him. It did not vary at all," Ryan said. Hall watched as the MIG, minus a left wing, spiraled earthward. He saw the pilot's pink parachute blossom and observed the pilot splash into the Gulf, 70 miles offshore and between the mainland and Hainan Island. Running short on fuel, Hall and Ryan left other Phantoms over the pilot to direct the rescue.

[OVER]

    Two days later it was disclosed that the "Mig" reported shot down was actually a USAF drone carrying radar and radio detection gear over North Viet Nam. The Navy pilots mistook it for a Communist Mig and opened fire with a guided missile. The parachute they reported seeing was a parachute which ejected carrying the electronic equipment after the drone had fell to an altitude of 5,000 feet. A drone is a remote controlled aircraft often used for surveillance and target practice. The Jouett launched its SAR helicopter to search for the assumed "pilot" after the "Mig" was reported shot down.

1968-05-07.label: Stars and Stripes - 2 Jets Lost In N. Viet
1968-05-07.attribution: Stars and Stripes - 2 Jets Lost In N. Viet — Ducy Family Archives
1968-05-07.text:
Pacific Stars & Stripes
[Date unknown, May 1968]

[Mike's handwritten annotation at top: "* OUR HELO PICKED THEM UP" and "Navy Stars + Stripes"]

2 Jets Lost in N. Viet

SAIGON (AP) — The U.S. Command announced Monday that two Navy warplanes were downed Sunday in air strikes over the southern half of North Vietnam. Two of the three crewmen aboard the planes were rescued. *

Headquarters said one of the planes, a Navy F4 Phantom, fighter-bomber, was shot down by ground fire near Vinh, a North Vietnamese city about 145 miles north of the Demilitarized Zone. The two-man crew was rescued.

The second plane, an A4 Skyhawk was downed by unknown causes southeast of Vinh. The pilot is listed as missing in action.

There have been indications that the North Vietnamese command is taking advantage of President Johnson's curtailed bombing campaign to move heavy concentrations of antiaircraft guns into the southern panhandle. Pilots have been reporting heavy antiaircraft fire during recent raids in the vicinity of Vinh.

The latest downed planes raise to 830 the number of American warplanes lost in combat over North Vietnam in more than three years of bombing.

In the curtailed air war over North Vietnam, U.S. warplanes flew a total of 106 missions Sunday. Pilots reported destroying or damaging 12 water supply craft, three bridges and one radar site, 16 antiaircraft sites and two surface-to-air missile sites.

The Air Force's F111 fighter-bombers failed to fly any missions against North Vietnam Sunday for the second consecutive day.

There was no official explanation why the Thailand-based planes did not fly. They had resumed strikes only last Friday after they had halted bombing missions because of the loss of a third F111 on the previous day.

1968-05-07.label: Vigilance — Page 31
1968-05-07.attribution: Vigilance, Cruiser-Destroyer Group publication, August 1968 — Ducy Family Archives
1968-05-07.text:
[Photo (top): Ltjg William A. Simmons is carried from the rescue helicopter minutes after landing
aboard the Jouett.]


JOUETT PARTICIPATES IN 2 SARS

Search and Rescue (SAR) is an important part of the Navy's role in Vietnam. The guided missile frigate
USS Jouett (DLG 29) played a vital role in the Navy's SAR effort recently when her crewmen rescued the
crewmembers of two planes shot down by enemy gunfire.

The ship participated in two rescues in 20 hours. In the first, the crew of the plane had to eject near
the Vietnam coast. Moments after the radio distress signal was picked up by the Jouett, she had launched
her rescue helicopter.

While the helicopter flew to the scene, friendly aircraft circled over the men, marking their spot for
the helicopter and keeping off unfriendly gunfire. The helo picked up the first survivor 16 minutes after
leaving the Jouett. Four minutes later the second survivor was rescued.

With both men safely aboard, the helo headed back to the Jouett, where the airmen were given medical
checkups, a tour of the ship and then taken back to their carrier, the USS Enterprise.

A few hours later, the second SAR alert was sounded. Another craft from the Enterprise was downed, this
time inland. Five minutes after the alert was sounded, the Jouett's rescue helo was airborne and flew to
the scene as the downed aviator's wingman circled overhead, marking the spot.

The pilot of the downed plane had extracted himself from his parachute and guided the helo to his
location, on a wooded hillside, by using his survival radio.

One helo crewmember lowered the rescue harness to the downed pilot while the other crewmember manned
the helo's machine gun, to cover the craft against sniper fire. The downed pilot was quickly taken
aboard the helo and transported to the Jouett.

After a checkup in sick bay and a tour of the ship, the pilot was returned to his aircraft carrier.

[Photo (bottom): The Jouett's medical team prepares the rescued aviator for evacuation to the USS
America.]

1968-05-08.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-05-08.text:
May 8, 1968 12:30 am
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother and Dad,

I got your letter of April 29 two days ago on the 6th. I'm making an attempt to type this just to keep in practice so, over look any mistakes I may make.

Here are some clippings I got over here. I thought you may find them interesting to read. This afternoon we rescued two more pilots who were shot down about 1/2 mile off the coast. We launched the helo and in about 30 minutes they were back with the pilots. They were shook up a little but were not injured. We got with in 12 miles of the mainland which is the closest we have ever been up here. It was a real clear day and you could see a lot of the land over there. Things have picked up considerably since our last time up here as you can most likely tell in the newspapers. So, this makes four rescues for us and all of them in this line period.

We are suppose to rendevous with an oiler tomorrow night and recieve 1,000 pounds of mail which will be mostly 3rd and 4th class. There is a chance your package may be there, I hope so.

I haven't yet made any firm decisions on when I'll be taking leave. The first half of August I will be taking the test for second class so that means I will have to be here for that and any leave upon arrival in the states is out of the question for that reason. As far as your coming out here I don't think it is really necessary right now. I think it would be better to wait till Bill got back from overseas, then you could see both of us out here. I don't really know when I will be home next. It may be in the fall or after the first of next year. As far as Christmas goes I can't say. I don't really care for that travelling this distance during those holidays after my experience with making connections last time. At any rate it is a lot easier and cheaper for me to come home than for you to travel out here. So, for right now lets hold off and see when I'll be making my way back home. No doubt both of us will stay here on the west coast for the rest of our time and there will be plenty of time to make it out here later on.

I got word that I will be taking the test for the correspondence course tomorrow morning. Would you believe I applied for it on Feb. 27 and it just got here? I was told that one test for another guy took seven months to get here. It is believed that the test officer failed to mail the application out promptly and this may have been the case in regards to mine. I'll let you know when I get the drastic results!

We will be in Hong Kong in less than two weeks. They have been giving us a lot of stuff about keeping out of trouble there because of the Communist groups there. We'll only be there for five days then on to Subic for about three days and back up here. I am pretty sure I am going to buy one of those super 8 movie cameras in Hong Kong. I would like to take some movies over here and I know you would enjoy seeing them.

I sent off the roll of film with the pictures of Bill and me in Da Nang today. They are slides and I'll mail them to you when I get them back with three other boxes of slides I have taken over here.

I guess that's all the interesting news from over here. So long for now, I'll write again, soon.

Your son,

Mike
1968-05-08.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-05-12.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-05-12.text:
May 12, 1968

[Homemade Mother's Day card. Front has hand-drawn flowers (yellow, pink, blue) with hand-lettered text reading "HAPPY MOTHER'S DAY". Inside has the poem typewritten with hand-drawn flowers showing through from the front.]

Mother,

ON THIS SPECIAL DAY,
HERE ARE A FEW LINES TO SAY,
THAT TO ME YOU MEAN THE MOST
SO TO YOU I OFFER THIS TOAST
THAT IN THE YEARS TO COME,
TO ME YOU'LL ALWAYS BE NUMBER ONE.

Love,

Mike

[Handwritten note at bottom left]: Sorry, I couldn't get a card, so I had to use my imagination.
1968-05-12.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-05-13.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-05-13.text:
May 13, 1968
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother & Dad,

It's Monday evening here and about 7:45. Yesterday I got your letter, just one week to the day after you wrote it. I was glad to see the clipping of Bill and me.

Last night I got your package. We refueled from an oiler and they sent over third and fourth class mail. The Newsweek magazines were interesting reading for us. I guess the rioting in the big cities was really something. The paperbacks should be good reading during some of the hours up here. As for the pens, I can always use them. Thanks for everything.

I got a letter from Bill two days ago which he wrote on April 24. How about that service, 17 days to get here. He described an attack they had there and maybe this was the one you read about in the paper.

There was a destroyer hit up here by gun fire off the mainland. They were south of us and one day last week came up to our area. It wasn't too much and only one guy was injured. Maybe you saw it in the paper too. But that is what happens when they start cruising in too close to the beach.

The other day I got 20 newspapers. I read every one of them believe it or not. Three also came last night, the latest dated April 19.

I bet you are glad that school is almost over with all the trouble they have been giving you. And I thought things like that could only happen to a person in the Navy. I guess civilian life has a few bad breaks too.

Tell David to be expecting a letter from me in a day or so. I'll see if I can talk him into reforming a little.

Yesterday was a nice day and gave us a chance to do some sunbathing during holiday routine. I don't spend much time topside so its necessary to go out and get a little sun on your own.

I am really glad you are enjoying and using the tape we made. Don't wear it out though, because we didn't have a chance to play it back. I hope we didn't slip up on anything when we made it. Everytime you mention it I am so glad we took time to make it.

We got parts in for our radar this afternoon and I helped put them in. Right now we are letting it warm up and will be trying it out in a few minutes.

I hoped I would have got another tape from you by now. You said you would send a blank one in the package but must have forgot. At any rate I'll pick up some cartridges in Hong Kong and send a tape from there.

We have been getting quick news releases on the baseball scores. It looks like the Cardinals are hot again this year, the Cubs aren't too bad either but I wish they could at least play .500 ball. Its early in the season and a lot can happen to change the standings. I hope I can take in a few games at L.A. and would like to spend a weekend in San Francisco when I get back.

Well I had better close here. So long for now.

Your son,

Mike
1968-05-13.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-05-16.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-05-16.text:
16 May, 1968

Dear Mother

Heres $200 more to put in my account. This should bring it to just shy of $700.

I am glad you did take time to say what you did on the tape. No, you didn't make me mad. I expected you would have some reaction and I was glad you told me. If you didn't it would have probably meant you had other ideas.

Well thats all I have to say and I hope you enjoy the tape as much as I enjoyed yours.

Bye for now.

Your son

Mike
1968-05-16.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-05-16.label: Tape 3, Side 1 — Mike Ducy
1968-05-16.attribution: Audio cassette recording, Tape 3, Side 1 — Mike Ducy. Transcribed by OpenAI Whisper. Ducy Family Archives

segments.text: Hello, here I am again. This is Thursday, May 16th, and I received the tape that you made yesterday.
I'll try to fill up this whole slide here, and when I get done, I'll give a little report on all the slides I want to send along with it.
Well, tomorrow's going to be our last day up here on station, and that means there'll be no more free mail or any of the other big privileges that they give you while you're up here.
We'll be back in Subic Sunday.
We'll only be there for about eight hours, and then we'll be on our way to Hong Kong.
We should arrive there.
And we expect to arrive there by Wednesday.
Today was payday, and I had $417 coming.
I got two money orders for $100 apiece.
I'll be sending them out in a letter with this tape this evening.
You should get them in a few days.
Go ahead and put them in a bank with the rest of my money.
the rest of the money, I suppose I'll
spend some of it in Hong Kong. I don't intend to spend
too much there. I just want to buy the movie
camera that I mentioned and
spend a little bit of money on any tours
or any other things that they might
have there for sightseeing.
Said in your tape that we didn't
mention how Bill got off the ship
and back into Da Nang
when he was on board the ship. Well,
now that you mention it, I know we forgot
to tell you, but he took
one of the ship's boats back in.
They had to take another guy back in
that came aboard the ship
to work on some electronics here, I believe.
They had to take him back in,
and Bill went back in with him.
They had some of our own people
to pick up there at the same time.
I sent some slides off
that we took here on the ship
on the 8th,
and I expect we'll get them back
sometime while we're in Hong Kong,
so I'll be sending them out to you right away.
I won't even bother to make a tape on them
unless I have some tapes with me.
I was glad to hear David's nice conversation on the tape.
He did a pretty good job, and I'll be waiting to hear for another one from him the next time we send a tape.
I'll go ahead and get the radio for him.
I kind of get an idea of what he would like, and I'll send just a good one.
And he doesn't have to worry about paying me back real soon,
because I know that he probably doesn't have too much money.
But as soon as I get it, I'll send it on to him.
And about the toggle radio that Dad mentioned, I'll go ahead and pick up one.
The prices over here are just about 50% off of what you'd pay back in the States.
So I'm sure I can get something pretty good for a rather reasonable price.
Just like the movie camera that I'm going to buy, it's a Canon Super 8 and I saw them
advertised in the newspaper that I got from back home.
The files had them for the model that I'm going to buy for $209 when I can buy it for
hundred dollars over here and another model which I might buy as well they had
advertised it was a hundred and fifty nine dollars and you can buy them over
here for seventy dollars and these are real good cameras it's like I said a
Canon it's made by Bell and Howell so you know it's a pretty good one
mentioning one of my last letters what my possible leave intentions were upon
arriving back in San Diego there I mentioned that I'd have to be on board
the ship in August to take a test for second class. Well, there's one little hang-up about this.
If I do pass the test, the earliest test results won't come back till in October,
and that means I'll have 10 months left in the service. Well, if you make second class and they
were going to give it to you, you have to have a year left. So this means I have to extend for
two months, and I don't think this is exactly what I want to do. Although being second class
and have a lot more advantages and better pay,
I still don't think I want to give them any more time than what I have to.
So my real reasons for taking the test is that when I do get off of active duty,
I return to the reserve center, and they will give you second class automatically
because you passed it out here.
So that's the only advantage of it.
I know it's going to be a pretty hard test,
and I'm going to spend a lot of time studying on it between now and August.
but as far as any extension goes it could be any an extension of my active duty from two months
to eight months if I do want to have second class and if I pass the test so I don't think
that sounds too advantageous to me right at this time I read in your last letter the mother wrote
that the Pritchetts were coming back home on the 15th of August.
I haven't heard anything from them lately in regards to a letter or anything,
so I suppose she'll be sending me a letter in the next couple of days
explaining about it and all this.
It comes as a pretty big surprise to me
because I figure that they just go ahead and sit tight
and the other grandma and grandpa would probably be out there during Christmas time.
Of course, it's going to still happen.
and I don't know what the party or whatever they have planned back there in Decatur
where John's mother might be,
but I guess it's all up to them if they want to go back there.
A Catholic chaplain came aboard this morning and said Mass.
He was aboard just about two weeks ago.
I kind of figured they were trying to get us all squared away and be good boys
when we get in another Liberty Port, which would be Hong Kong.
Their little sermons and lectures,
They always try to remind us to stay out of certain types of trouble on Liberty.
And I guess they understand the situation over here.
One chaplain mentioned that many ships, as they pass through Pearl Harbor,
coming over here to Westpac, most of the guys on board tend to get different attitudes
and think that all the rules and regulations change.
You can do things over here that will be all right that you wouldn't be able to do back in the state.
And then when the ship pulls through Pearl Harbor on the way back to the United States,
everybody changes their attitudes and says, yes, we'll be good boys and everything like
this.
This was kind of humorous, but I guess that's really the way it is.
I guess it's a pretty big responsibility for these chaplains over here.
I imagine they have to really get out and make a lot of rounds to all these ships out
here.
Of course, every ship doesn't have a chaplain.
the ships that actually do would be the larger ships like the aircraft carriers and when
they're down there they can fly them out by helo like they do when they come up here.
There's been a lot of word going around the ship how we're going to collect combat pay
in July. Well our last day on the line up here is going to be on June the 29th. Well
So they say that we're possibly going to stay here until in July and do some shore bombardment over here.
And when you do this, you can pick up your extra month tax-free pay and the extra $65 combat pay,
and then we'll fire a few rounds and turn the ship around and steam out of here.
This is a way that they can do it, or also they can stay here for six days in July,
and this will count as a whole month in the combat zone.
So that actually all remains to be seen.
Honestly, I don't believe we're going to be back in San Diego
on the 17th of July as we planned.
I tell you, it can be any time between the 17th of July
and the last day of July
because we've kept a lot of schedules that we have
set for ourselves over here,
but going back to the States is just about a thing.
It all depends on how your other schedules were kept over here.
Like I said, we've been extended for five days there in June from the 23rd to the 28th.
And, of course, this can always happen again.
They can give us another short extension just to make sure that the other ships have had enough time to get over here to relieve us.
So actually our arrival in San Diego really depends on when we leave the station up here
and how many stops we do make back to the United States.
Well, we finally got our fire control radar back in operating order.
It's been down for just about a month, I'd say.
It's been down for quite a time.
And I was in there with the guys pitching and doing a lot of troubleshooting and work
with him. I pointed out two casualties that I found to them and we corrected them and
it seems to be working all right now. Actually, it isn't going to do us much good up here
now because we'll be leaving, but we have some target practice scheduled for Saturday
morning before we arrive in Subic Bay on Sunday to test for the gun mounts and the radar.
It's been a pretty bad time for us up here.
We had two of our three gun mounts have been down and out of operating order and our radar
hasn't been up.
So it's been a pretty useless affair as far as our weapons system goes.
One of the requirements for going up for second class in August was to take a military leadership
test which consisted of 100 questions about Navy customs, rules, regulations,
various questions of this sort. I took this test Tuesday. I breezed right
through it pretty well and I passed it so this is one of the steps you have to
take before being recommended for the test in August. Last night we refueled
again from an oiler. We only took on 30,000 gallons at the station where I was at. It's
my psychology that we're refueling all the time up here. It's not really necessary. We
refueled Sunday also. The big reason for this is they want to keep at least 80% of the load
of fuel on the ship in case the owners would get in trouble and they wouldn't be able to
make it up here. We could still steam around and not have anything to worry about. It's
also a big deal for them to see how many refuelings and replenishments that they can pull off
while they're on the line it looks pretty good on the record books and everything and
you know this is what these captains of these ships are always shooting for they're shooting
for something that looks like they're really doing a great job out here and so that's one
of the big reasons why we have to do all this stuff while we're here i don't remember whether
I mention in my letter or not about this, but I'll go ahead and explain anyway. I can
explain a little bit better than what I said in the letter. One of the guys in our division,
he's a third class F.T. If Mother remembers correctly, I told her about this guy while
I was home on Christmas leave. He's in kind of a poor situation. He's, I actually, just
to be frankly i think he's a pretty bad mental case but uh this here stupid stuff that he pulled
has really proved it just about a week ago he uh popped about 20 tranquilizers and about 40 aspirin
and i'm i'm not kidding you he slept for just about 20 hours straight well they waited until
he got sobered up about a day and a half later and they gave him the word to pack his stay bag
and he was leaving and they threw him out on a helicopter and threw him out of here one afternoon
and we're going to take him back to have him sent back to Subic Bay for some medical observation
well I tell you every one of us guys was glad to see him go because we couldn't stand the sight of
him he was a nervous type guy he was always nibbling at your ear telling you some kind of a
story of his some of his big experiences of life and always crying on your shoulder for sympathy and
we were really glad to get rid of him well we got word the other day from the chief
that he's going to be coming back on board the ship in subic bay so i imagine they've
decided he was still fit for military duty which believe me i don't think he is
I don't know why he pulled a stunt.
He might have got a letter from his girlfriend back home or something
or just wanted to see if he could get some attention
and possibly find a way out of the Navy.
I know he isn't going to change any by the time he comes back,
and I expect that he can just about do anything.
Now, I expect his next trick, if he wants to pull anything,
will probably be to jump off the side of the ship.
I also think that when he wants to try this,
there might be somebody right behind him giving him a push.
because he's just that kind of a guy.
Dad mentioned something about rewiring the house.
Actually, when I came home, possibly for good, I imagine that's what he meant.
I think it would be a pretty good idea.
It shouldn't be very much of a job, and it will set us up pretty good there.
Of course, we keep his eye open for all types of little materials,
like he had mentioned in the tape that he picked up the wire and everything.
I'm sure that we'll be able to pull off a pretty good job.
As far as I'm concerned, I think about a 200-amp 30-circuit panel would be very adequate for any circuits that we would have to pick up and leave us plenty of spares in case we ever had to use them.
I took my USAPI test for electronics last week.
I know I mentioned this in my last letter.
And it was a pretty tough one, I'd say.
I'm kind of sweating while I pass it around.
I really hope I did because I want to take out a couple more courses
and get them completed and in and possibly credit for them.
The deal about this test, it took them two and a half months to get that thing back to me.
And, of course, like I said, it was possibly the officer who was in charge of the administering of the test.
It was possibly his fault.
But the funny thing about it is I went in there to this first class personnelman and I told him about this and I would like to have his test checked on.
Well, two days later he comes up to me and tells me that the test just came in.
Uh-huh.
Well, I think he told this officer that I was inquiring about this test and the officer pulled into his files and found that it was still laying there.
It seems kind of odd that the test would just come in after I had mentioned something to him about it.
Another little stunt that happened about this, I was scheduled to take a test on a Wednesday,
Wednesday morning at 8 o'clock.
I was there in the library all ready to go, take the test, and the officer never showed
up.
He didn't come.
About 8.30, the first class, he put in a phone call to the officer's stateroom and wanted
to know if he was there.
come to find out, oh, he claimed to have had a 103 degree temperature
and he would want me to wait to take it, but
he wanted to know if it would be alright with me, and I said, well, I'd like to go ahead and take it right now
if it's alright with you, and he wanted to know, well, what's the big deal about waiting another day
and I said, well, I've been put off long enough now, I'd like to get it out of the way
and he says, well, we'll see about giving it to you tomorrow morning, so
he was there the next morning and he seemed to be in pretty good spirits and
didn't have any harsh words to say.
So I took the test and
they're expecting the results back in about two weeks
from what they've told me.
That's a perfect example of the runaround that they give you here
in the service and if you want anything you've really got to push for it
and get it yourself
because it's a cinch that they're not going to be looking out for you.
I've got these slides I'm going to send home.
I will mail this tape as free mail and the slides I will probably mail them as first class
so you'll be getting a tape before you get the slides most likely
and don't go out and buy yourself a slide projector I think you've got a little one
there at home that will show one slide individually or possibly Uncle John might
want to bring his slide projector up sometime or you might be able to borrow one from somebody
else you know but don't go out and buy one because just because me and Bill are sending home slides
due to the fact that I have bought a slide projector over here and of course they'll
always be at home to be available to be used I will probably most likely send it on home
when I get back into the state it just all depends on if I do take many more slide pictures while I
in the state so you keep this in mind and there will be a slide projector to
watch these slides with well Saturday afternoon we're scheduled to have a
barbecue here on the ship it's gonna isn't something pretty startling to find

1968-05-16.text: Hello, here I am again. This is Thursday, May 16th, and I received the tape that you made yesterday. I'll try to fill up this whole slide here, and when I get done, I'll give a little report on all the slides I want to send along with it. Well, tomorrow's going to be our last day up here on station, and that means there'll be no more free mail or any of the other big privileges that they give you while you're up here. We'll be back in Subic Sunday. We'll only be there for about eight hours, and then we'll be on our way to Hong Kong. We should arrive there. And we expect to arrive there by Wednesday. Today was payday, and I had $417 coming. I got two money orders for $100 apiece. I'll be sending them out in a letter with this tape this evening. You should get them in a few days. Go ahead and put them in a bank with the rest of my money. the rest of the money, I suppose I'll spend some of it in Hong Kong. I don't intend to spend too much there. I just want to buy the movie camera that I mentioned and spend a little bit of money on any tours or any other things that they might have there for sightseeing. Said in your tape that we didn't mention how Bill got off the ship and back into Da Nang when he was on board the ship. Well, now that you mention it, I know we forgot to tell you, but he took one of the ship's boats back in. They had to take another guy back in that came aboard the ship to work on some electronics here, I believe. They had to take him back in, and Bill went back in with him. They had some of our own people to pick up there at the same time. I sent some slides off that we took here on the ship on the 8th, and I expect we'll get them back sometime while we're in Hong Kong, so I'll be sending them out to you right away. I won't even bother to make a tape on them unless I have some tapes with me. I was glad to hear David's nice conversation on the tape. He did a pretty good job, and I'll be waiting to hear for another one from him the next time we send a tape. I'll go ahead and get the radio for him. I kind of get an idea of what he would like, and I'll send just a good one. And he doesn't have to worry about paying me back real soon, because I know that he probably doesn't have too much money. But as soon as I get it, I'll send it on to him. And about the toggle radio that Dad mentioned, I'll go ahead and pick up one. The prices over here are just about 50% off of what you'd pay back in the States. So I'm sure I can get something pretty good for a rather reasonable price. Just like the movie camera that I'm going to buy, it's a Canon Super 8 and I saw them advertised in the newspaper that I got from back home. The files had them for the model that I'm going to buy for $209 when I can buy it for hundred dollars over here and another model which I might buy as well they had advertised it was a hundred and fifty nine dollars and you can buy them over here for seventy dollars and these are real good cameras it's like I said a Canon it's made by Bell and Howell so you know it's a pretty good one mentioning one of my last letters what my possible leave intentions were upon arriving back in San Diego there I mentioned that I'd have to be on board the ship in August to take a test for second class. Well, there's one little hang-up about this. If I do pass the test, the earliest test results won't come back till in October, and that means I'll have 10 months left in the service. Well, if you make second class and they were going to give it to you, you have to have a year left. So this means I have to extend for two months, and I don't think this is exactly what I want to do. Although being second class and have a lot more advantages and better pay, I still don't think I want to give them any more time than what I have to. So my real reasons for taking the test is that when I do get off of active duty, I return to the reserve center, and they will give you second class automatically because you passed it out here. So that's the only advantage of it. I know it's going to be a pretty hard test, and I'm going to spend a lot of time studying on it between now and August. but as far as any extension goes it could be any an extension of my active duty from two months to eight months if I do want to have second class and if I pass the test so I don't think that sounds too advantageous to me right at this time I read in your last letter the mother wrote that the Pritchetts were coming back home on the 15th of August. I haven't heard anything from them lately in regards to a letter or anything, so I suppose she'll be sending me a letter in the next couple of days explaining about it and all this. It comes as a pretty big surprise to me because I figure that they just go ahead and sit tight and the other grandma and grandpa would probably be out there during Christmas time. Of course, it's going to still happen. and I don't know what the party or whatever they have planned back there in Decatur where John's mother might be, but I guess it's all up to them if they want to go back there. A Catholic chaplain came aboard this morning and said Mass. He was aboard just about two weeks ago. I kind of figured they were trying to get us all squared away and be good boys when we get in another Liberty Port, which would be Hong Kong. Their little sermons and lectures, They always try to remind us to stay out of certain types of trouble on Liberty. And I guess they understand the situation over here. One chaplain mentioned that many ships, as they pass through Pearl Harbor, coming over here to Westpac, most of the guys on board tend to get different attitudes and think that all the rules and regulations change. You can do things over here that will be all right that you wouldn't be able to do back in the state. And then when the ship pulls through Pearl Harbor on the way back to the United States, everybody changes their attitudes and says, yes, we'll be good boys and everything like this. This was kind of humorous, but I guess that's really the way it is. I guess it's a pretty big responsibility for these chaplains over here. I imagine they have to really get out and make a lot of rounds to all these ships out here. Of course, every ship doesn't have a chaplain. the ships that actually do would be the larger ships like the aircraft carriers and when they're down there they can fly them out by helo like they do when they come up here. There's been a lot of word going around the ship how we're going to collect combat pay in July. Well our last day on the line up here is going to be on June the 29th. Well So they say that we're possibly going to stay here until in July and do some shore bombardment over here. And when you do this, you can pick up your extra month tax-free pay and the extra $65 combat pay, and then we'll fire a few rounds and turn the ship around and steam out of here. This is a way that they can do it, or also they can stay here for six days in July, and this will count as a whole month in the combat zone. So that actually all remains to be seen. Honestly, I don't believe we're going to be back in San Diego on the 17th of July as we planned. I tell you, it can be any time between the 17th of July and the last day of July because we've kept a lot of schedules that we have set for ourselves over here, but going back to the States is just about a thing. It all depends on how your other schedules were kept over here. Like I said, we've been extended for five days there in June from the 23rd to the 28th. And, of course, this can always happen again. They can give us another short extension just to make sure that the other ships have had enough time to get over here to relieve us. So actually our arrival in San Diego really depends on when we leave the station up here and how many stops we do make back to the United States. Well, we finally got our fire control radar back in operating order. It's been down for just about a month, I'd say. It's been down for quite a time. And I was in there with the guys pitching and doing a lot of troubleshooting and work with him. I pointed out two casualties that I found to them and we corrected them and it seems to be working all right now. Actually, it isn't going to do us much good up here now because we'll be leaving, but we have some target practice scheduled for Saturday morning before we arrive in Subic Bay on Sunday to test for the gun mounts and the radar. It's been a pretty bad time for us up here. We had two of our three gun mounts have been down and out of operating order and our radar hasn't been up. So it's been a pretty useless affair as far as our weapons system goes. One of the requirements for going up for second class in August was to take a military leadership test which consisted of 100 questions about Navy customs, rules, regulations, various questions of this sort. I took this test Tuesday. I breezed right through it pretty well and I passed it so this is one of the steps you have to take before being recommended for the test in August. Last night we refueled again from an oiler. We only took on 30,000 gallons at the station where I was at. It's my psychology that we're refueling all the time up here. It's not really necessary. We refueled Sunday also. The big reason for this is they want to keep at least 80% of the load of fuel on the ship in case the owners would get in trouble and they wouldn't be able to make it up here. We could still steam around and not have anything to worry about. It's also a big deal for them to see how many refuelings and replenishments that they can pull off while they're on the line it looks pretty good on the record books and everything and you know this is what these captains of these ships are always shooting for they're shooting for something that looks like they're really doing a great job out here and so that's one of the big reasons why we have to do all this stuff while we're here i don't remember whether I mention in my letter or not about this, but I'll go ahead and explain anyway. I can explain a little bit better than what I said in the letter. One of the guys in our division, he's a third class F.T. If Mother remembers correctly, I told her about this guy while I was home on Christmas leave. He's in kind of a poor situation. He's, I actually, just to be frankly i think he's a pretty bad mental case but uh this here stupid stuff that he pulled has really proved it just about a week ago he uh popped about 20 tranquilizers and about 40 aspirin and i'm i'm not kidding you he slept for just about 20 hours straight well they waited until he got sobered up about a day and a half later and they gave him the word to pack his stay bag and he was leaving and they threw him out on a helicopter and threw him out of here one afternoon and we're going to take him back to have him sent back to Subic Bay for some medical observation well I tell you every one of us guys was glad to see him go because we couldn't stand the sight of him he was a nervous type guy he was always nibbling at your ear telling you some kind of a story of his some of his big experiences of life and always crying on your shoulder for sympathy and we were really glad to get rid of him well we got word the other day from the chief that he's going to be coming back on board the ship in subic bay so i imagine they've decided he was still fit for military duty which believe me i don't think he is I don't know why he pulled a stunt. He might have got a letter from his girlfriend back home or something or just wanted to see if he could get some attention and possibly find a way out of the Navy. I know he isn't going to change any by the time he comes back, and I expect that he can just about do anything. Now, I expect his next trick, if he wants to pull anything, will probably be to jump off the side of the ship. I also think that when he wants to try this, there might be somebody right behind him giving him a push. because he's just that kind of a guy. Dad mentioned something about rewiring the house. Actually, when I came home, possibly for good, I imagine that's what he meant. I think it would be a pretty good idea. It shouldn't be very much of a job, and it will set us up pretty good there. Of course, we keep his eye open for all types of little materials, like he had mentioned in the tape that he picked up the wire and everything. I'm sure that we'll be able to pull off a pretty good job. As far as I'm concerned, I think about a 200-amp 30-circuit panel would be very adequate for any circuits that we would have to pick up and leave us plenty of spares in case we ever had to use them. I took my USAPI test for electronics last week. I know I mentioned this in my last letter. And it was a pretty tough one, I'd say. I'm kind of sweating while I pass it around. I really hope I did because I want to take out a couple more courses and get them completed and in and possibly credit for them. The deal about this test, it took them two and a half months to get that thing back to me. And, of course, like I said, it was possibly the officer who was in charge of the administering of the test. It was possibly his fault. But the funny thing about it is I went in there to this first class personnelman and I told him about this and I would like to have his test checked on. Well, two days later he comes up to me and tells me that the test just came in. Uh-huh. Well, I think he told this officer that I was inquiring about this test and the officer pulled into his files and found that it was still laying there. It seems kind of odd that the test would just come in after I had mentioned something to him about it. Another little stunt that happened about this, I was scheduled to take a test on a Wednesday, Wednesday morning at 8 o'clock. I was there in the library all ready to go, take the test, and the officer never showed up. He didn't come. About 8.30, the first class, he put in a phone call to the officer's stateroom and wanted to know if he was there. come to find out, oh, he claimed to have had a 103 degree temperature and he would want me to wait to take it, but he wanted to know if it would be alright with me, and I said, well, I'd like to go ahead and take it right now if it's alright with you, and he wanted to know, well, what's the big deal about waiting another day and I said, well, I've been put off long enough now, I'd like to get it out of the way and he says, well, we'll see about giving it to you tomorrow morning, so he was there the next morning and he seemed to be in pretty good spirits and didn't have any harsh words to say. So I took the test and they're expecting the results back in about two weeks from what they've told me.
