So I would wager to say that in his tour of duty over here, he won't stay in one place the whole time. They'll probably move their unit around or move individuals around to certain places while they're over here. I haven't been keeping up on the international news lately, but from what I've been able to read in the stars and stripes, I hear that Saigon is being terrorized quite a bit. They're having a lot of trouble down there. and uh you also mentioned in your letter that they had about 13 towns here in south vietnam and you didn't know whether uh they had too much trouble there in hoi an or not they all mentioned in one letter to me that i got from him it took such a long time to get here that they had an attack one night but the koreans went up there and fought them off and they didn't have any casualties suffered or anything but just uh 13 towns that were attacked i suppose this is something that they're trying to pull off so when they do go to the peace tables as they have mentioned that they're going to if they have gained any victories they can take these with them and say well we've got this on our side and that and everything else and they might be able to get some of the things that they want. I suppose they mentioned that this 13-town area that they hit was similar to the Tet Offensive that they had over here. This Tet Offensive was, of course, during the holiday season here early in February, and this was when Bill first came over here. At the end of this offensive, we were just winding up, and it was pretty successful for the Viet Cong. and they're just starting to recover from it over here from what I've been able to read. Well, I've read one of your books that you sent in a package that I received a couple of days ago. I don't think you censored them books too well, but anyway, they were pretty good reading, and most of the guys, we usually share our paperback books around, and some of the other guys have read a couple of the others, and I've got another one right now that I'm reading but it was a pretty good reading anyway and it's a lot to occupy some of your spare time while you're standing in a child liner while you're on watch. So thanks again for sending everything that you did in there and about the popular electronics magazine that's in there, I sent a letter to those people a while back and I told them I wanted that subscription sent to me here on board the ship. Well, I guess they got their records filed up somewhere and they're still sending them home. So we'll wait for a couple more months and see what happens. And if they're still sending them home, I'll write another letter to them and try to get the address changed again. I really would appreciate it if after you got one of those, you would go ahead and send it on out to me because it's something I'm pretty well interested in and I find these are good readings from time to time. I think when I get back in the States, I'm going to do a little bit of traveling up and down the West Coast there. there. I'm going to try to take in a few baseball games in Los Angeles and I plan to go to San Francisco for at least one weekend and take a lot of pictures and go to a ball game. I'd like to have some pictures remembered by up there. I don't know whether I'll go back there when I'm discharged or not. It kind of all depends. I imagine I'll get discharged out of San Diego when the time comes. But I know there in California on the west coast there's a lot to see and a lot lot to do and this movie camera I plan to buy I'll be able to go and take a lot of good pictures with it and really see some of the west coast and it'd be a pretty good way to occupy some of my time that I have left to spend there because the word is out that the ship will not make another Westpac cruise over here till next summer so that will possibly be June or July and if this is is the case, I will be discharged from the ship, transferred, I mean. I'll be put on another ship because they usually don't like to bring people over here who are getting out within two or three months. They usually transfer them to another duty station there in the States, and then they wait till their discharge time comes, and they send them on out. So it looks like I'll be back in the States for a while, and I had mentioned before in one of my letters are taped i don't remember which that i would like to get a transfer to another ship when i did get back in the states and i can make another cruise over here well i've done some more thinking about this and i think that just one time over here is actually all i want to spend uh it's nothing but a good place to spend your money that you save up over here actually you do get a lot see a lot of the world and everything but uh prices are so cheap over here on certain things is you want to buy a lot of souvenirs and a lot of necessities that you can use back in civilian life and it's uh not really one of the best ways to save up your money i would not like to get transferred to a ship it's not as convenient and as nice as this one which would probably be my luck so i think i'll just be well enough alone and stay around on this ship because like I did say it's planned to be back in the States for at least another good year before it comes back over and also there are going to be a lot of our people get transferred out of our division and might be a chance we'll be getting some new non-rated men on board so things might shape up to be a pretty good situation while we're back there in San Diego So actually, the old saying, the time will tell, really holds true for the way they do things here in the Navy. You really can't plan ahead. You really can't think about what the next few months or even the next few weeks are going to be. You just kind of have to take one day at a time and just see how things pan out from there. One more little item about sending these radios home that I will buy for you while I'm in Hong Kong. I believe I'll either send these Powell or Sam. Now, when I sent Georgia Maze tape recorder back to her, I sent it by airmail, and it cost $6. I think it weighed about 12 pounds. This is pretty expensive to mail something back. And I believe that you can get the SAM or the PAL mail a lot quicker than what we can when it's sent to us over here from the state. So what I believe I'll do, I'll go ahead and send it to PAL, most likely, and save a little bit of money on the postage. and you should get it within possibly three or four weeks. I really don't know how long it does take to get that stuff back to the United States. So I'll let you know when I do send it, and if I have any brochures or any information on it, I'll go ahead and send it right along with the letter so you can see just exactly what you've got coming. You mentioned something about that radio of mine not staying on. Well, I had that problem with it when I was back home, and looks like I got a little troubleshooting job there to do next time I come home try to get that thing fixed and the other large radio that he told me that I had gave him I've got a pretty good idea what's wrong with it so you just tell him that as soon as I can get this radio bought for him over here and have it sent to him he'll have another radio to enjoy all those good sounds of music that are on there well I see I'm just about ready to run out of tape here so I better close this up So I'll tell everyone goodbye and Dave would be a good boy. He's out of trouble there. And most likely I'll be sending another tape from Hong Kong. So so long to everybody and take care and I'll see you on site too for a little slideshow.

1968-05-19.label: Familygram — Capt. Robert S. Hayes, CO
1968-05-19.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-05-19.text:
FAMILY GRAM

                                                            19 May 1968

Dear Family and Friends,

The skies are clear and the sea calm as JOUETT cuts a deep furrow across the South China Sea. We are heading toward the Philippine Islands after 35 days at sea, and I would like to recount to you some of our experiences during this past period.

Certainly the latest chapter of JOUETT's history has been one of the most exciting, as the men of JOUETT found themselves right in the middle of three dramatic rescues of downed U. S. airmen. The first incident took place just an hour before darkness on a Sunday in late April. The evening meal in JOUETT was suddenly interrupted by the announcement over the ship's broadcast system "SAR ALERT. DOWNED AIRCRAFT BEARING 251 DEGREES, RANGE 38 MILES." The Officer of the Deck, LT. Ted Huckabone, immediately increased speed to 27 knots and turned the ship into the wind. JOUETT'S Search and Rescue helicopter, called "Clementine Two", was airborne in a record three minutes, even while the distressed aircraft was still in the air.

Our Commodore, Captain Emerson, assumed personal control of the rescue operation, and put his "Blue Ribbon" team into action. First he ordered "Clem-Two" in the direction of the falling aircraft and simultaneously directed our companion ship, the USS DENNIS J. BUCKLEY, (DD 808), to proceed at top speed to assist. Over the radio the burning aircraft's wingman reported "Two chutes in the air, falling free". This was good news, and meant the plane crew had safely parachuted from the aircraft. As the rescue forces raced to the scene, additional carrier-based planes appeared overhead to mark the location of the survivors in the water.

"Clem-two", piloted by LTJG Skip Yates, and co-piloted by LTJG Lennie Devries, skimmed over the wavetops at maximum speed and arrived on the scene within fifteen minutes of the initial SAR Alert. On the JOUETT we heard the helo report by radio, "Both men are OK and in their rafts." Less than two minutes later, the downed pilot and his bombardier-navigator had been hoisted into the hovering helicopter. Commodore Emerson, in direct radio communication with Commander Task Force Seven-Seven, reported "The rescue has been completed successfully, both pilots are aboard Clem-two enroute JOUETT."

There was high excitement on JOUETT at this, our first rescue, and many of the crew lined the foc'sle to welcome the return of the helo and her rescued flyers. The survivors of the downed Phantom attack bomber emerged from the helo, looking wet but very happy to be safe aboard JOUETT. Resting after the ordeal, the pilot, LCDR D. E. Hernandez of San Diego, recalled that "The helo was on the scene before I had time to complete my ditch routine. It was terrific," and LTJG D. J. Lortscher of Rylander, Wisconsin, the second survivor, recalled thinking while approaching JOUETT, "It's the smallest flight deck I've ever landed on, but it sure looks great from here." JOUETT's first Search and Rescue Effort was completed in just twenty-nine minutes, from the time of the first alert to the time when the rescue helicopter touched down on JOUETT's deck.

It never rains but it pours. Ten days later JOUETT found herself again at the heart of a rescue effort, resulting in the lightning-quick recovery of the two-man crew of another downed Phantom fighter-bomber. It was Wednesday, 8 May, and again out of Combat Information Center came the announcement, SAR Alert". Again Commodore Emerson put his rescue forces into action. JOUETT could be seen to ring up all available speed and swing into the wind. "Clem-two" was airborne in minutes. Friendly aircraft in the area of the crash reported seeing two good parachutes, and that meant both flyers were out of the aircraft. But they landed in the water not far from the coast of North Vietnam and protective fire had to be laid down on the beaches by the friendly aircraft, in order to protect the downed airmen. Our rescue helicopter was "On Top" within sixteen minutes of leaving JOUETT, and was hoisting the first airman aboard. After a hot meal and a few hours of rest on JOUETT, the flyers were on their way back to their carrier with a special JOUETT touch. Their flight suits were washed and pressed by our ship's laundry, and the flyers were able to wear the same uniform home that they left in.

As if to prove conclusively that it never rains but it pours, JOUETT's third rescue followed just twenty hours after her second. This time the downed aircraft was a "single-seater", an A-4 Skyhawk fighter-bomber with just one pilot aboard. In the most hazardous rescue of the three, JOUETT's helicopter had to fly deep into enemy territory and rescue the downed pilot from dense jungle. But the "Can Do" attitude is found in the helicopters that ride JOUETT, just as much as it is found in JOUETT herself, especially when one of our own is in distress. The pilot was found in short order by a courageous helicopter crew, and when they returned to make JOUETT's two hundred and fortieth helo landing, they had their pilot on board. Commodore Emerson spoke for all when he said of this rescue, "It's truly marvelous to see such prompt response."

During this period on station, the tempo of helicopter operations increased to as many as a dozen launches and landings per day. Our previous period on station saw the 200th safe landing, and as this last period drew to a close, we celebrated the 300th safe landing with a large cake. Some of the other statistics of this cruise show JOUETT to be quite a steamer. As of today, we have spent 109 days at sea and 16 days in port since leaving San Diego.

I have been speaking of the exciting events in the ship's life, but much has happened in the lives of her crewmembers, too. Just prior to coming on station, JOUETT held an Awards and Recognition ceremony for the crew. Commodore Emerson presented JOUETT Outstanding Service Awards to eleven deserving members of the crew. The JOUETT conceived award is an engraved plaque, bearing the ship's seal, and is presented in recognition of sustained superior performance. Even to be eligible, one must have a year of such noteworthy service. The names of the latest recipients of the Outstanding Service Award appear at the end of the Familygram, along with a list of the many crewmembers of JOUETT who were recently advanced in rate. At the awards ceremony, each of these men were called forth and given the rating badge of his new rate. Next day on the JOUETT, many new rating badges could be seen on many proud sleeves.

Some of our wonderful Plankowners, members of the original commissioning crew, have left JOUETT for new duties, and the word "Plankowner Departing" has been heard all too frequently of late. CDR Addams departed JOUETT a few weeks ago to assume command of the guided missile destroyer COCHRANE. As executive officer, he was a tremendous influence in transforming JOUETT from a thing of shipyard iron into a living thing, and the warm sendoff that all hands gave to him showed that they thought well of what he had done. One departing JOUETT man for whom we have special hopes is Missile Fire Control Technician Second Class Boulden Griffith. He has been selected for officer training under the Navy Scientific Education Program, and ahead of him lies four years of college and a commission in the regular Navy.

While we were sad to see some of our crew members go, we were glad to welcome aboard other new faces to the crew. LCDR John A. Walker is our new executive officer. He comes to JOUETT from staff duty with Commander Service Force, U. S. Pacific Fleet, and has his home in Kailua, Hawaii. Another event in the lives of some of our crewmembers was reenlistment. Chief Fire Control Technician Glenn H. Underwood, Chief Machinist's Mate Lynn G. Russell, and Boilerman Technician Second Class Frank Z. Leopard all reenlisted for continued active service in the Navy.

A number of congratulatory messages have come in recently, and I would like to share with you quotations from some of these:

From USS TICONDEROGA:  "Your superb performance this past line period
                       most appreciated by the Tico Tigers. Best air
                       control flight following and target area coverage
                       witnessed to date. Well Done."

From USS BON HOMME
            RICHARD:   "A resounding well done. In addition to your
                       savvy in station keeping, communications and air
                       control, we especially commend you for your
                       comprehension of the problem, common sense, and
                       instant support when needed."

From Rear Admiral COUSINS:  "Outstanding performances were noted with
                            pride and admiration. Please convey my personal
                            'Well Done' to all concerned."

These messages give a pleasant taste to this departure from station, and confirm the feeling in every member of our crew that JOUETT has done her job, and done it well.

I hope to write to you again soon and tell you not what we have done on station, but what we have seen during some well deserved liberty. Until then, my best wishes go to each one of you.


                                ROBERT S. HAYES


[Map of Southeast Asia showing the Gulf of Tonkin, Vietnam, China, Formosa, Philippines, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Burma, Malaysia, Sumatra, and Borneo, with JOUETT's operating area marked in the Gulf of Tonkin and South China Sea]

segments.text: Hello Mother, Dad, and David and everyone else at home.
This is Monday, May 20th, and at this time we are on our way to Hong Kong.
We left Subic Bay last night about 8.15 after being there for about six hours.
Our expected time of arrival in Hong Kong should be about 8.30 tomorrow morning.
and I have Liberty the first day in and they are supposed to give us Liberty approximately 9 o'clock
and we'll be having Liberty at 9 o'clock every day so it sounds like it's going to be a pretty good time while we're there.
Well, yesterday in Subic Bay was the first time I had to get off the ship ever since we left Subic here the last time.
It was about 35 days at sea for us this time, I believe.
I went over to the EM Club and had six tall cold bottles of Michelob, which really tasted
real fine.
As I returned to the ship, I received your letter that you wrote on May the 13th and
your package with the candy, which was mailed on May the 13th.
And then I took six days to get here, which is real good.
And I got the package of paperback books, which you mail on April 30th.
Yesterday I also received a letter from Georgia Mae, and she mentioned that they were going
back on August 16th and had invited me to come along with them if I wanted to take my
leave then and go back home.
Well, I imagine I could make it home at that time, but as far as I'm concerned, it's a little bit too early for me to go home right now.
And I don't particularly think I'd care to spend the three days or four days, whatever it takes, to go in the car on the way back here.
As far as your coming out here, I really would recommend it.
You're not really worried about it this summer.
I would rather have you come out here
if you're going to spend the money
I'd rather have you come out here
when Bill and I are both out here on the west coast
and just kind of leave it up to me
and I'll take my leave when I can
and when I actually want to
like I mentioned in my last letter or tape
I don't remember which
but if I do take any leave
it will either be in the fall
say in September or October
possibly Christmas time I'm not promising anything maybe Christmas time I'm not too sure
or after the first of the year I'm really in no hurry to go home for leave as far as I
the way I feel right now uh maybe when I get back in San Diego see how life in the states is I might
want to go home as soon as possible but the way I'm thinking right now it's uh probably be in the
fall or early in the beginning of the year sometime in January. I hope it
doesn't mess up any of your plans. All I can say is if you want to go somewhere
and have a vacation this summer go ahead and go but don't spend your money to
come out on the west coast unless you really want to because if you're gonna
fly out here you're not gonna have any way to get around. If you come to San
Diego that is and I'd much rather have you your toe off until Bill gets out on
on the coast again.
And that way you can be out there while we're both there.
Grandma mentioned that they wouldn't be coming out to the West Coast for Christmas this year
if George and May came home during August.
I'm getting here in a lot of conflicts with everybody.
I know if Grandma would come out during Christmas,
they'd like to see me out here at Christmas time and everything like this.
So it's just kind of a toss-up.
all I can do is just recommend and suggest what I would do if I were in your situation.
So let's just all sit tight for a while and not really worry about it.
Bill and I will still be stationed here on the West Coast for some time to come,
as I mentioned before, and just kind of let us work it from our end.
And it's a lot cheaper and a lot easier for us to come back home than it is for the family
and rather than everybody to come out here just to see us.
So I'll just leave it that way.
Just let me kind of handle it from my end when you'll be seeing me again
as far as my coming home goes.
And I'm sure everything will work out all right.
If you play this tape back to Grandma, tell her thanks a lot for the candy
that she included in the package that she bought from David from the Boy Scouts.
It was real good.
As a matter of fact, there's still some of that left, believe it or not.
But it's going down pretty quick.
It's real good candy.
Thanks a lot, Grandma.
Mother, I'm glad to hear that you liked the impromptu Mother's Day card that I sent you.
Like I said, I used my imagination and kind of threw something together at the last minute,
but I knew you'd be kind of glad to get it, and I was really glad to hear that you enjoyed it as you did.
On site 2 of this tape, you'll find an explanation for some slides I'll be sending right along with the tape.
the tape you might get the slides and tape at a different time but anyway you know there's some
slides that goes with this tape on these slides it was taken on board the ship while Bill
was in the hang there with us. Last Saturday evening we had a little cookout type picnic
here on the ship we had hamburgers and hot dogs everything that would be associated with a picnic
and it was a pretty good occasion.
Of course, it wasn't anything like being in a park or anything back home or all this,
but the atmosphere wasn't too bad, and I think most of the guys had a pretty good time.
They were planning to eat and everything, and it was a change of pace.
It was a real surprise to us because we've never done anything like that before here on the ship,
and I only hope that they can plan more things like that
in the next two months that we have left over here.
I'll probably be sending another tape
in the next couple of days or so from Hong Kong.
I picked up these tapes there in Subic Bay.
They're only $1.25 apiece.
I picked up four of them and I already decided,
well, since I got my slides back yesterday,
I'm going to go ahead and send on a tape with them.
And I'll probably send you a tape message from Hong Kong,
as I said before,
telling you some of the things we've been doing there
and some of the tours and everything were probably going on
and a little bit what it's like there.
I suppose you've been reading in the newspaper
about the rich Chinese there doing some rioting
and such as they were known for.
This might be a bad time for us to go in there,
and again, it might not.
I don't know. It all depends.
We'll have to find out when we get there tomorrow.
But they've been giving us a lot of words of wisdom
and how to stay out of trouble
and do's and don'ts on liberty while we're there.
but I only hope that most of the guys stay out of trouble and watch their step.
One of the bad things about this,
if any members of a ship get in any trouble there in Hong Kong while on liberty,
the whole ship can be expelled from the harbor and no more liberty there for them.
They have to go back out at sea and make their way to the next port.
I just finished sending billet tape while we were in Subic there yesterday.
I went over and bought a small Sony tape recorder.
It cost $22.
And I'm sure to do the job, but I wanted to send tapes back and forth to him.
And I'll probably make a tape and send it on home to Grandma and Grandpa
in answer to the letter that I received from them yesterday.
In the event I don't finish up this side of the tape with my conversation,
just go ahead and turn it on over on track two,
and there'll be a slide review of all these slides I'm sending.
There'll only be 20 slides, and it shouldn't be a very long explanation.
Well, last Friday on the 17th, we were relieved up on station
about 4 o'clock in the afternoon by one of the other DLGs during the 7th fleet.
That Friday afternoon, our helicopter made a 300-space landing aboard the ship,
and I'm most certainly sure that they're going to try for 500 landings
by the time we make our way back to the States.
That afternoon, some pilots from the Enterprise came by
and put on a little show with their A-4s and F-4 aircraft.
This was more or less a flyby is what they called it. They came by the ship and
then some barrel rolls and tilted their wings and everything. This here was the main
reason because we rescued three of their pilots on two different SAR incidents
up here in the Gulf of Tonkin and it's just a little tribute to the Jewett for the
a great job they say that we've been doing up there.
You said in your letter whenever you hear the Gulf of Tonkin,
you always think of us up there.
Well, we're about the only ones up there.
There's our ship and a destroyer that are on station up there
on Southern Star where we were at.
And there is one other DLG and a destroyer up on Northern Star.
So that makes four ships right there in the Gulf of Tonkin where we're at.
And you have a few other ships that patrol in and out of there,
but we are more or less permanently up there while we're on station.
And you have about three or four aircraft carriers running airstrikes down there on Yankee Station
with their assorted DLGs and destroyers running escort for them.
But most of the business up there in the Gulf of Tonkin is taken care of by just the four ships that I mentioned.
and I'm sure that keeping your eyes open in the papers
and seeing about any donned aircraft or anything up there.
I try to keep you pretty well posted.
I take a pretty good set of notes here.
I put in my log as to just what happens,
and I try to compare them to the stars and stripes newspapers that we get,
just what kind of coverage they're giving things up there.
Of course, they never will mention the names of the ships too much.
They'll just say that such and such a pilot.
There are so many planes were downed and rescued at such and such a day.
They won't give too many details on it,
but next time I come home I can give you a pretty good explanation
on just what happens up there and just how things go.
It's really pretty interesting,
and I hope it takes some pretty good movies the next time on station
to show just what a typical day is up there.
We had general quarters this afternoon for a test firing of our gun mounts.
We got all three gun mounts back up again in the fire control radar.
And just as usual, after we start firing the gun mounts, they break down and something
happens to them.
And I believe all three of the gun mounts are down again now, so the gunner's base is
going to have their work cut out for them to get them back up again.
It's kind of bad for them, especially since we're pulling into the Liberty Fort.
They'll have to possibly spend some of their extra liberty hours trying to get them guns back up again.
But that's what the ship's here for, and without those guns, the whole purpose of the ship is useless as far as the defense purpose goes.
Yesterday morning, Sunday, all of us put on our dress whites and went topside, and they took pictures from our helicopter.
These pictures are supposed to be put in the cruise book.
I didn't mention this before, but the ship is in the process of having a cruise book printed,
which is very similar to a high school yearbook.
It will have pictures of all the crew members in it,
pictures of some of our various operations there on the ship and everything.
I've already ordered one.
I'll be real glad to get it.
We are expected to get them when we arrive back in San Diego or thereafter soon.
I'll send it on home to you and let you look at it.
and when I do come home next time, I'll be able to explain just exactly
some of the goings on here on the ship and have pictures to go along with it
out of the book there.
You mentioned in your letter that you wish you could send me a square of sod
so I wouldn't forget what grass looks like.
Well, I tell you, that sounds like a pretty good idea to me,
but I know I wouldn't survive the long trip over here,

that grass there is it just can't survive it's nothing but just brown stubble like it's uh

1968-05-20.text: Hello Mother, Dad, and David and everyone else at home. This is Monday, May 20th, and at this time we are on our way to Hong Kong. We left Subic Bay last night about 8.15 after being there for about six hours. Our expected time of arrival in Hong Kong should be about 8.30 tomorrow morning. and I have Liberty the first day in and they are supposed to give us Liberty approximately 9 o'clock and we'll be having Liberty at 9 o'clock every day so it sounds like it's going to be a pretty good time while we're there. Well, yesterday in Subic Bay was the first time I had to get off the ship ever since we left Subic here the last time. It was about 35 days at sea for us this time, I believe. I went over to the EM Club and had six tall cold bottles of Michelob, which really tasted real fine. As I returned to the ship, I received your letter that you wrote on May the 13th and your package with the candy, which was mailed on May the 13th. And then I took six days to get here, which is real good. And I got the package of paperback books, which you mail on April 30th. Yesterday I also received a letter from Georgia Mae, and she mentioned that they were going back on August 16th and had invited me to come along with them if I wanted to take my leave then and go back home. Well, I imagine I could make it home at that time, but as far as I'm concerned, it's a little bit too early for me to go home right now. And I don't particularly think I'd care to spend the three days or four days, whatever it takes, to go in the car on the way back here. As far as your coming out here, I really would recommend it. You're not really worried about it this summer. I would rather have you come out here if you're going to spend the money I'd rather have you come out here when Bill and I are both out here on the west coast and just kind of leave it up to me and I'll take my leave when I can and when I actually want to like I mentioned in my last letter or tape I don't remember which but if I do take any leave it will either be in the fall say in September or October possibly Christmas time I'm not promising anything maybe Christmas time I'm not too sure or after the first of the year I'm really in no hurry to go home for leave as far as I the way I feel right now uh maybe when I get back in San Diego see how life in the states is I might want to go home as soon as possible but the way I'm thinking right now it's uh probably be in the fall or early in the beginning of the year sometime in January. I hope it doesn't mess up any of your plans. All I can say is if you want to go somewhere and have a vacation this summer go ahead and go but don't spend your money to come out on the west coast unless you really want to because if you're gonna fly out here you're not gonna have any way to get around. If you come to San Diego that is and I'd much rather have you your toe off until Bill gets out on on the coast again. And that way you can be out there while we're both there. Grandma mentioned that they wouldn't be coming out to the West Coast for Christmas this year if George and May came home during August. I'm getting here in a lot of conflicts with everybody. I know if Grandma would come out during Christmas, they'd like to see me out here at Christmas time and everything like this. So it's just kind of a toss-up. all I can do is just recommend and suggest what I would do if I were in your situation. So let's just all sit tight for a while and not really worry about it. Bill and I will still be stationed here on the West Coast for some time to come, as I mentioned before, and just kind of let us work it from our end. And it's a lot cheaper and a lot easier for us to come back home than it is for the family and rather than everybody to come out here just to see us. So I'll just leave it that way. Just let me kind of handle it from my end when you'll be seeing me again as far as my coming home goes. And I'm sure everything will work out all right. If you play this tape back to Grandma, tell her thanks a lot for the candy that she included in the package that she bought from David from the Boy Scouts. It was real good. As a matter of fact, there's still some of that left, believe it or not. But it's going down pretty quick. It's real good candy. Thanks a lot, Grandma. Mother, I'm glad to hear that you liked the impromptu Mother's Day card that I sent you. Like I said, I used my imagination and kind of threw something together at the last minute, but I knew you'd be kind of glad to get it, and I was really glad to hear that you enjoyed it as you did. On site 2 of this tape, you'll find an explanation for some slides I'll be sending right along with the tape. the tape you might get the slides and tape at a different time but anyway you know there's some slides that goes with this tape on these slides it was taken on board the ship while Bill was in the hang there with us. Last Saturday evening we had a little cookout type picnic here on the ship we had hamburgers and hot dogs everything that would be associated with a picnic and it was a pretty good occasion. Of course, it wasn't anything like being in a park or anything back home or all this, but the atmosphere wasn't too bad, and I think most of the guys had a pretty good time. They were planning to eat and everything, and it was a change of pace. It was a real surprise to us because we've never done anything like that before here on the ship, and I only hope that they can plan more things like that in the next two months that we have left over here. I'll probably be sending another tape in the next couple of days or so from Hong Kong. I picked up these tapes there in Subic Bay. They're only $1.25 apiece. I picked up four of them and I already decided, well, since I got my slides back yesterday, I'm going to go ahead and send on a tape with them. And I'll probably send you a tape message from Hong Kong, as I said before, telling you some of the things we've been doing there and some of the tours and everything were probably going on and a little bit what it's like there. I suppose you've been reading in the newspaper about the rich Chinese there doing some rioting and such as they were known for. This might be a bad time for us to go in there, and again, it might not. I don't know. It all depends. We'll have to find out when we get there tomorrow. But they've been giving us a lot of words of wisdom and how to stay out of trouble and do's and don'ts on liberty while we're there. but I only hope that most of the guys stay out of trouble and watch their step. One of the bad things about this, if any members of a ship get in any trouble there in Hong Kong while on liberty, the whole ship can be expelled from the harbor and no more liberty there for them. They have to go back out at sea and make their way to the next port. I just finished sending billet tape while we were in Subic there yesterday. I went over and bought a small Sony tape recorder. It cost $22. And I'm sure to do the job, but I wanted to send tapes back and forth to him. And I'll probably make a tape and send it on home to Grandma and Grandpa in answer to the letter that I received from them yesterday. In the event I don't finish up this side of the tape with my conversation, just go ahead and turn it on over on track two, and there'll be a slide review of all these slides I'm sending. There'll only be 20 slides, and it shouldn't be a very long explanation. Well, last Friday on the 17th, we were relieved up on station about 4 o'clock in the afternoon by one of the other DLGs during the 7th fleet. That Friday afternoon, our helicopter made a 300-space landing aboard the ship, and I'm most certainly sure that they're going to try for 500 landings by the time we make our way back to the States. That afternoon, some pilots from the Enterprise came by and put on a little show with their A-4s and F-4 aircraft. This was more or less a flyby is what they called it. They came by the ship and then some barrel rolls and tilted their wings and everything. This here was the main reason because we rescued three of their pilots on two different SAR incidents up here in the Gulf of Tonkin and it's just a little tribute to the Jewett for the a great job they say that we've been doing up there. You said in your letter whenever you hear the Gulf of Tonkin, you always think of us up there. Well, we're about the only ones up there. There's our ship and a destroyer that are on station up there on Southern Star where we were at. And there is one other DLG and a destroyer up on Northern Star. So that makes four ships right there in the Gulf of Tonkin where we're at. And you have a few other ships that patrol in and out of there, but we are more or less permanently up there while we're on station. And you have about three or four aircraft carriers running airstrikes down there on Yankee Station with their assorted DLGs and destroyers running escort for them. But most of the business up there in the Gulf of Tonkin is taken care of by just the four ships that I mentioned. and I'm sure that keeping your eyes open in the papers and seeing about any donned aircraft or anything up there. I try to keep you pretty well posted. I take a pretty good set of notes here. I put in my log as to just what happens, and I try to compare them to the stars and stripes newspapers that we get, just what kind of coverage they're giving things up there. Of course, they never will mention the names of the ships too much. They'll just say that such and such a pilot. There are so many planes were downed and rescued at such and such a day. They won't give too many details on it, but next time I come home I can give you a pretty good explanation on just what happens up there and just how things go. It's really pretty interesting, and I hope it takes some pretty good movies the next time on station to show just what a typical day is up there. We had general quarters this afternoon for a test firing of our gun mounts. We got all three gun mounts back up again in the fire control radar. And just as usual, after we start firing the gun mounts, they break down and something happens to them. And I believe all three of the gun mounts are down again now, so the gunner's base is going to have their work cut out for them to get them back up again. It's kind of bad for them, especially since we're pulling into the Liberty Fort. They'll have to possibly spend some of their extra liberty hours trying to get them guns back up again. But that's what the ship's here for, and without those guns, the whole purpose of the ship is useless as far as the defense purpose goes. Yesterday morning, Sunday, all of us put on our dress whites and went topside, and they took pictures from our helicopter. These pictures are supposed to be put in the cruise book. I didn't mention this before, but the ship is in the process of having a cruise book printed, which is very similar to a high school yearbook. It will have pictures of all the crew members in it, pictures of some of our various operations there on the ship and everything. I've already ordered one. I'll be real glad to get it. We are expected to get them when we arrive back in San Diego or thereafter soon. I'll send it on home to you and let you look at it. and when I do come home next time, I'll be able to explain just exactly some of the goings on here on the ship and have pictures to go along with it out of the book there. You mentioned in your letter that you wish you could send me a square of sod so I wouldn't forget what grass looks like. Well, I tell you, that sounds like a pretty good idea to me, but I know I wouldn't survive the long trip over here, but I tell you, there in Subic Bay, it is so hot and dry, and the ground is more or less a clay-like. that grass there is it just can't survive it's nothing but just brown stubble like it's uh it's not even what uh anyone from the midwest really knows what good grass looks like they wouldn't even recognize it but uh doesn't really make any difference as long as you're on land and you got a chance to walk around and you don't see water wherever you look it's good to get on it whether it's grass on it or not i'll tell you that i haven't got any results back on my usafi electronic test yet. I suppose the next few days I'll be applying for a couple more courses and get them in there into their office so they can be processed while I'm waiting for the test results to come back. This is a pretty good deal as far as I'm concerned. It occupies some of my time. I'm really interested in it and it's advantage is that you can't pick up some credits for your knowledge what you do learn in it and uh anytime there's a chance to get credit for something i think it's a worthwhile opportunity for somebody to grab a hold of it and take it up if they can well i'm starting to run out of conversation on this tape and the tape's not going any faster than what i'm talking so uh i'll sign off on this side of the tape due to the lack of things to say because i just sent a tape home a couple of days ago i'm sure my next tape i'll send will be a pretty long explanation of the situation in Hong Kong and what it's like there. So be looking for a tape in the next three or four days, possibly. And I'll sign off on this tape here, and I'll see you again on site, too, for a little slide explanation. So everyone take care back there, and David, stay in there and be a good boy now. And when that summer school starts coming around, make sure you get your homework done every night or every afternoon before you go out and play. do that one thing for me, okay? So long, everyone, back home, and I'll see you over on site, too. Bye. Thank you. Thanks for watching! you you you you you Thank you.

1968-05-24.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1968-05-24.text:
24 May, 68
Hoi An

[Written on stationery with printed map of Vietnam]

Mike,

I got your letter yesterday, boy you squids are finely getting to see some action.

Yea I remember that guy you told me about. He must of really been fucked in the mind.

I'll be sending you some slides and a tape for on there around the 10th of June so be looking for them. — Have you gotten that one tape yet?

Boy we had some more hell here again the other night. There were fire fights all over the place. We were lucky only 5 rounds come up our way. It all lasted about on 1½ hours.

Today I was messing with a blasting cap from a gook dud. I threw it on a fire and started to take off. Well I got hit 23 times with shrapnel in the right arm and chest. I dug it all out and put some shit on it to help heal it up. I guess I wont try that again.

I got a letter from Jim Dick yesterday too. He's up at Phu Bai at an ammo dump. He seems to be doing a lot of skating.

Some ass hole Major was up here today to look over the place. He said we live like pigs and don't even act like Marines. So now we have to hold muster at 0730 every morning, and can't fuck off like we did before. All of us are really pissed off about that 0730 deal.

It got up to 107° the 20th. and it was a hot S.O.B.

Well son going to go for now, be good and don't fall off of your tub. See you later.

"Little Brother"
Bill

"THEY CAN FUCK WITH ME ALL THEY WANT BUT THEY CAN'T STOP THE CLOCK." 276 days left in Nam & 15 months left in the Corps. I AM GETTING SHORT! HAHA.
