segments.text: Hello again, Mother, Dad, and David.
This is Saturday, May 25th, and at the present time, our ship is in Hong Kong Harbor,
and we are anchored out here and expect to leave tomorrow morning about 8 o'clock.
I had duty today, so I stayed on board all day long,
and it was a pretty good thing anyway because it rained on and off most of the day
as it has for the past four days that we've been in port here.
The only day it didn't rain was the first day we got in here, Tuesday the 21st.
It was a fairly nice day then, but since then most of the days have been rather rainy.
I got the letter that you wrote on the 18th last Wednesday, which is on the 22nd.
And I believe my last tape that I sent to you must have been about a week ago.
It was just as we had left Subic Bay, I believe we were on our way up here when I last sent the tape.
So I've got quite a bit to talk about here, about telling some of the things about Hong Kong.
So I should fill up most of this side.
And in case my voice does run off the end of the tape, go ahead and turn it on over on this side too.
Well, first of all, Tuesday when we got in here,
I went over and looked at some of the camera equipment that they had.
And I ended up buying myself a Super 8 movie camera.
This is a Canon with a zoom lens.
and I paid $69 for it.
Now, I saw some that were advertising the paper from back home,
and the same kind that I got would cost about $200 at least.
And so I got a real good camera and a real good buy on it,
and I've already shot 150 feet of movie film here.
I suppose I'll probably buy a movie projector while I'm over here sometime but
I'll just kind of hold off on that for a while the main thing I want to do is just take a lot of
pictures while I have the opportunity and I'm pretty proud of my camera and I know it's uh
going to give me all the good use that I want to get out of it
you can go ahead and tell David that I did buy a transistor radio for him
I got a real good buy on it. It is very similar to the one that I have at home.
That Channelmaster, the six transistor. This one is the same size. It's got the same size
speaker and everything else, and it's practically identical to it. And you'll never believe the
price that I paid for it. It only cost $7. Now, I paid about $20 for mine back home,
And I know it's a good one because I bought it in a good store.
So I'm pretty sure that he'll be glad to hear this.
Now, as far as your table radio goes, I saw some here that I like,
but I was running a little bit short on funds.
And I feel that I can pick up the same kind in Subic Bay for about the same price.
I'm not too sure about this, but I'm going to keep my eyes open.
And I'll still be thinking about getting one for you.
But like I said, I did get caught a little bit short on money at the time when I was going out shopping.
And I'll keep it in mind.
Our ship got in here Tuesday about, I'd say, 8.30 or thereafter.
Liberty call didn't go down until about 10.30 because they had all kinds of business to take care of before they let the troops go on Liberty.
So most of Tuesday was spent just window shopping and looking at some of the various merchant sites that they have over here.
And I went out with some of the other guys.
We had a steak dinner.
And I got back to the ship fairly early that night, about 10 o'clock, I'd say.
Wednesday, I had duty, so I had to stay aboard and stand one watch.
It rained most of that day.
That day they had these Chinese people who specialize in painting the ships out here.
They come into port.
They had them come aboard and paint the ship.
And I'm telling you, there was only about 23 people doing it.
But they had most of the whole ship painted out in one day.
I mean everything.
Everything from the water line all the way to the top of the bridge.
They have been coming back for the past couple of days just doing little touch-up jobs.
But this is one big thing.
most of the ships that come into port area, this is one thing that they get done.
They have the whole ship painted out, and these people,
they take things in exchange for it.
They will take your empty brass casings from your ammunition.
We gave them some of this.
They'll also pick up the leftovers from the mess hall
and any garbage scraps that are left on the plates.
They're right there, and they take it right off your plates when you go to put your plates in to be washed off.
People are right there grabbing off the leftovers that you left on your tray.
I suppose they give them a few more other privileges.
There possibly might be some money involved in it.
I don't know, but they don't ask for too much, and the Navy is real glad to have the ship painted out.
It really doesn't go to too much expense for that.
now Thursday
I went on a tour
here in Hong Kong
of the whole
excuse me
of the whole island
that tour started
at 10 o'clock
and it was over
at 2 o'clock
in the afternoon
it was a fairly short tour
and of course
it rained
while we were on the tour
but I
did manage to get off
some good
pictures with my
movie camera
I
took my Instamatic
to take some slides with
but I didn't take any because along the various stops on the tour,
they have these people who sell slides, these boxes of slides.
They sell you five boxes, which is 100 slides, for, well, various prices.
They're all the same thing, but they try to jewel you on different prices
than anything like this on a slide.
I bought my 100 slides for just about $1.25.
I looked at all of them, and they're all pretty good,
and most of them take in all of the places that we covered on the tour.
And since it was a bad day for taking pictures,
this was a real good way to still have pictures of the stops that you made on the tour.
I'll bring these on home with me, and I'll show them to you sometime
and give you a little explanation of just exactly what some of the things are that are over here.
Well, in the morning there on the tour, I had a little accident happen to me,
a rather freak accident.
it had been raining and we were at this one stop and I was walking down some stairs a flight of
stairs and I slipped and my watch band on my left arm as I had stuck out my arm to break my fall
my watch band had twisted and cut a about a three inch gauge more it was more like a scratch
in my left arm and it tore the skin up kind of bad there but it's a funny thing about it didn't
bleed very much and it wasn't very painful so when we got back on the bus I kind of doctored
it up there with what they had on the bus and I continued on out the rest of the tour
when I got back to the pier where the tour bus let us off I went over to the shore patrol
headquarters and showed it to him and asked him if they could you know do anything for me so they
were real cooperative and they got me a boat and they sent me out to the coast guard ship and the
corpsman out there put three stitches in my arm and gave me a tetanus shot and a
novocaine of course to deaden the pain in my arm while he was stitching it up
so after he got done with that i came on back to the ship and i got back rather early to the ship
about 5 o'clock in the evening, I suppose.
I didn't really feel like going back out,
and it was nasty and rainy and everything,
so I stayed on board for the rest of the night.
It doesn't hurt me or anything,
but it's actually just a big scratch.
The corpsman told me he was going to sew it up
because if he didn't, it would probably leave a bad scar,
and it would take a little while for it to heal.
This way, he figured it should do pretty good.
So I've been going to sick bay every morning,
and they've been taking off the bandage and changing it
and then taking a look at it to see if it was getting infected or anything.
I figured that I'd better get some medical attention for it when it did happen
because it wasn't really that bad.
But I figured that medical attention would be the best thing that I could do
because you never know what kind of disease or germs you're liable to pick up over here.
Well, yesterday was Friday, and I took liberty about 10 o'clock
after getting a haircut here on the ship, which made it mandatory.
I had to have a haircut before I could leave or I wasn't going at all.
So I took liberty about 10 o'clock.
I went over and I got a new watch band for my watch
because it tore the other one up kind of bad, the accident that I had.
And I went down to the Hong Kong Hilton, which is a well-known hotel over here.
And I went up to the top floor, the 25th floor,
and I took some movie shots from up there.
I had a beer there.
Later on, I went out and took some more pictures.
I did some window shopping.
I met a couple of guys that I knew, and we caught a street car,
and we went down to one of the other sections in town here.
We did some more window shopping and browsing through some of the department stores down there.
I bought a few items there.
I came on back and left my merchandise that I picked up at the Fleet Club.
I just went out around town and in and out of a few bars.
And I got on back to the ship about 9 o'clock that night.
It rained yesterday also, and I got caught in a couple of monsoons, so to say,
while I was downtown, but otherwise it was a pretty good day.
The rain over here, they say it doesn't rain over here very often.
They say this is quite an exception.
Well, I'd say every place our ship has went, it's been rainy.
Up in Washington, it had rained up there quite a bit.
Back in San Diego, it rained back there quite a bit.
Pearl Harbor, I can't say that we had rain there,
but it only lasted for about a half hour one day.
It's Subic Bay. It's never rained there.
Up in Yokosuka, we had rain.
And, of course, up here in Hong Kong, we also got rain.
In the Gulf of Tonkin, there for a while, we had rain just about every day.
So it's kind of a bad omen that this ship carries along with it.
It seems to rain wherever we go.
And now this is Saturday.
Of course, as I mentioned before, I didn't do very much today.
I did a four-hour watch this afternoon, and I forgot off watch.
I ate supper and just kind of bummed around here on the ship
and decided I'd go ahead and get this tape out to you,
and it would possibly go out in the mail tomorrow morning before we got underway.
I also bought some dress material over here for you and Grandma.
I'll go ahead and send them on home later on as soon as I have a chance
when I send David's radio home to him.
I don't know whether it's possibly the same kind of print and material that they have back in the United States.
When I went in the department store to buy it, this girl tried to talk me into buying some pure silk for the material.
But as far as I was concerned, it was a little bit more than what I had intended to buy or to spend.
It's cotton dress material, and I only hope that it hasn't been imported from the United States.
There wasn't anything on it that said that it was, so I don't assume it has been.
So I hope you'll like it, and I'll try to get it out to you as soon as I can.
I bought a few stamps for Dad there, about four or five Hong Kong stamps that are commemorative type.
And I'll send them on home in a letter just as soon as I can.
It'll probably be sent out sometime while we're in Subic Bay.
we're supposed to get in there Tuesday and we'll be in there till Friday our
next stop they have told us that we leave Subic will be in Da Nang for
another day like we have stopped there twice before now this hasn't been on the
schedule but they put this in right here at the last minute so I don't expect
I'll be seeing Bill while I go there this time because I haven't had time
enough to notify him and even if I did try to right now would be rather useless
unless he happens to be on the top of a hill somewhere
and he sees a ship coming through the harbor somewhere,
he can make it down to the ship,
but I don't think that's going to be the case.
But I wish I would have had time to notify him about it
so he could have came on out again if he wanted to.
I suppose it's, as it was last time,
it was something to give him a little change of pace
and get away from some of the daily routine that they have to put up with.
Well, this month is almost coming to a close.
I tell you, I haven't seen a month go so fast as this one has.
I know it's almost summertime back there.
I can think about it every day and try to imagine what it's like
because being over here just doesn't make you think it's summer
because you don't associate the certain things with summertime as you do back in the good life in the United States.
And it's really kind of hard to believe that this time of the year has came around already.
Like I said, the time has really been going fast over here.
And I know we've just got about eight more weeks left, and we will be back in the States again.
they put out word the other day that our time for getting into san diego would be on the morning of
the 18th of july i suppose this possibly might vary from day to day they also put out a schedule
that on our way back we stopped in subic bay guam we set course for the equator and the 180th
meridian this is right at the middle of the world i suppose and they put you through an initiation
ceremony down there and it's a part of king neptune's court i saw something about this on
television a long time ago and i didn't quite understand it but i know pretty well what it's
about now and there'll be a lot of guys on the ship going to find out just exactly what they
have to go through it's just a little ceremony and they give you a card and a certificate that
you can carry around.
As we cross the equator on the 180th,
we will come back up, stop at Pearl Harbor.
I don't know how long we're going to be there.
And then we set course for San Diego
and expect to get back in there in the middle of July on the 18th.
One of the places we stopped at on the tour
was at a floating restaurant.
It is out in a bay here in Hong Kong
on the back side of the island, and they served Chinese food there.
The meal that we had was about a six-quart dinner.
They had fried rice, some kind of a pork in a sweet sauce.
They had crab foo-yong.
They had—this was real good that they had.
It was creamed corn with crab meat in it, in a soup.
It was real soupy.
It wasn't creamy like creamed corn is, but it had the flavor of it.
It was rather good.
I can't remember what else we had there.
They put just about everything out there that you could associate with the Chinese food.
It wasn't very bad.
It was included in the cost of the tour.
This tour that we took only cost $5 a piece.
And we got to see quite a bit of the island here.
One of our other stops on the tour was at a place they call Tiger Balm Gardens.
This Tiger Balm is an ointment, a medicine that they use over here.
It's supposed to be a cure-all for everything.
And this man that invented this medicine, he built this garden as a playground for the children over here.
It's kind of like a Disneyland over here to the people.
of people. It doesn't have all the amusement rides or anything. It's just a lot of little
statues and little colorful figures and stuff. They're also carved out so the kids can climb
through them and sit on them. It's just a nice little colorful place.
One of our stops on the tour was to take a tram ride. Tram is a word they use over here for,
I would imagine cable car or train.
That's just about what this was.
They have a real steep hill over here on the island.
At the top of it they have apartment buildings.
This track has two of these trams on it.
One of them goes up and the other one goes down.
The one that's going down pulls the one that's going up.
It's just a law of gravity.
They have them both on the same cable
and so the force of gravity from the one going down
gives it the inertia to pull the one going up, up the top of the hill.
I hope that's not too complicated, but that's the way it works.
And they have an incline on there of 70 degrees,
so that's a pretty steep hill that that thing is going up.
We got up the top there, and it was rather foggy,
but I did get some good pictures.
We could see the harbor out here where the ship was.
I tried to get a pretty good picture of that with my zoom lens
that was a pretty short stop up there we rode the tram up to the top of the
peak and we rode the bus back down and made a few stops on the way down on
they showed us some various sites on this uh peak it's called the victoria peak I believe
It's got quite a few apartment buildings and nice homes and mansions and everything.
This is where all the rich people live at.
Actually, over here, there is no middle class of people.
You're either rich or you're either a poor person.
That's the way it is.
And, of course, they took us through some of the slum districts over here, and it's pretty bad.
I'd say that it's three times as bad as some of the poor people that had to live back in the United States.
They live in these little shacks, just a few pieces of wood thrown together with a canvas over the top of them.
Some of these people live in these sandpans, these little boats out on the water.
They live out there. They die out there. They're born out there.
Just every way you want to look at it.
Most of the kids out here are rather young, and they don't go to school
because their parents don't have enough money to put them through school
because the school is not mandatory over here.
If you've got enough money, you can go to school.
If you don't have enough money, well, it's no big thing.
You don't have to go.
So most of these kids over here, these real young ones,
they go out and they roam the streets.
They beg money and everything.
We had a few of them come out here to the ship.
They get these little sandpans.
They come out here and they dive for coins off the sides of the ship.
you know they say hey sailor me dive for coin you throw coin me dive for it or something like that
and we got a pretty big kick about that uh they came out to the ship there for a few days
and we throw pennies or hong kong dollars which is about the size of a half dollar
it's only worth about 30 cents we throw it off the side of the ship and uh they go down there
and dive for it. They'd bring it back up. They were pretty good at it. I suppose they were
really professionals at it. We pulled a pretty good trick on them though. One time
we went in and got a handful of washers. So they were round, you know, they look like coins.
And we pulled them up and the kids, yeah, me dive for it, me dive for it. So we throw it off the
side to them and they'd go down and get it and they'd come back up and they had a washer and they
shot obscenities to us in Chinese we didn't know what they were talking about
but uh they still were fairly disappointed on the fact that we didn't
have throw any money over to them. A lot of the people over here they make little
novelties little souvenirs and things like that they try to sell them to the
tourists and people that come over here there's quite a few British people here
of course as you know Hong Kong is a British colony and it's bordered by Red
China on the other side so you have quite a few British people living here
it's rather nice to see some of these round-eyed people in the same port that
you stop it kind of reminds you of the people back home you get very tired and
very bored of seeing these foreign looking people over here because you
know that you are not in your homeland and you don't really feel at ease with them.
So it does kind of put you in a better position when you do see some people who are your own
color of skin and they have most of your own features. Also it's not very rare to see a sight
with a young boy possibly four or five years old with his younger brother or
sister strapped on his back he carry him around on the streets out begging for
coins or anything like this it's quite a common sight but there are some real
nice districts over here nice buildings houses and things like that and they do
keep these people out of there but you see some of them around the waterfront
around some of the boats and stuff.
You see some of them out on some of the places that the tourists
and the sightseers hit on these tours that they go on.
And it's really a fairly bad situation.
They are overpopulated over here, not enough houses,
not enough food for them, of course.
Most of them are refugees from Red China,
which is just across the bay from us here.
and they want to get out of China so they come over here and their life isn't much better for
them so I imagine they will continue to live like this for a long time the government over here is
trying to make some improvements for them but it's just a never-ending battle as it always is
in a poverty program I'm sure that the President Johnson's war on poverty that he has back in the
United States isn't accomplishing much more than what the British government is trying
to do over here for these people.
Well, Mother, I hope you got most of your deal with the cafeteria work and the school
unions straightened out by now.
I suppose by the time you get this tape, your days working in the cafeteria will be very,
very few left.
I hope that you haven't run into any trouble or anything else
in trying to keep up the application for the nurses school.
I know David's probably still anxious for school to get out.
I hope he does a good job in summer school, though.
And he realizes, I'm sure, if not he should,
that it's going to be pretty important for him this year
because next year he'll be starting in the sixth grade,
and after he gets out of sixth grade, it's only six more years,
and he will be out of high school.
And he's got six pretty important years coming up.
So he'd better start hitting the books a little bit harder if he has to
and try to get something out of it because it's bad to go to school
and have to struggle through, and the only way you can keep from struggling through
is just to do a little bit more studying than what is absolutely necessary.
I hope he's having a lot of good times there in Boy Scouts,
and I hope that he can go to summer camp.
I bet he was really tired when he got back from that 25-mile bike hike,
but it was probably a pretty good experience for him.
It probably might have taken a little bit of weight off of him.
I shouldn't really talk though because I weighed myself the other day and I weigh 195 pounds
so that means I've put on about 15 or 20 pounds since I left the state I guess that's what the
soft navy life does to you well you know you mentioned in your letter that uh Connie had
called you and said that if you hadn't have wrote to Bill and mentioned that her wedding was called
off she would have never have got any more letters from Bill he wouldn't have started writing to her
again well it's I don't know what she was meaning by this uh not knowing a tone of voice that she
was using when she said it but uh if she's complaining she shouldn't be complaining because
I wait you to say that she's lucky that he did write back to her because I think that she treated
him in some pretty bad ways. And if she is complaining, well, she doesn't have to write
back to him. I don't know what she's trying to prove by saying that. Of course, it's no
interest of yours that she'd say such a thing like that. I suppose that she is the type
a person that doesn't think very much before she says something.
I suppose if most people would exercise their brain before they exercise their mouth,
they'd find that they didn't get themselves in so much trouble.
But I suppose her and Bill will both be real happy now that they've each got tape recorders.
And Grandma also mentioned to me in one letter, this is kind of odd and kind of funny,
but she doesn't get to sing letters from Bill as she used to
because he started writing to Connie.
Well, not too much can be said about that,
but I very seldom hear from Bill.
It's at least once a month or maybe even longer,
but it's no big thing because I know that he's possibly pretty busy where he's at.
I've got plenty of time to write and sit down and send a tape and everything,
but, of course, his situation is different,
and it's no big thing.
Just as long as I know I still have him for a brother,
that's the one big thing that counts.
Well, we've got a pretty busy week ahead of us.
Next week, of course, we'll spend a day and a half or so
of that week being on the way to Subic Bay.
While we're on our way there,
we're going to test fire the gun mounts a few times,
see if they're still holding up.
When we get in there,
We're scheduled to have an inspection of the ship later on in the week,
I believe about Wednesday or Thursday.
Thursday they're supposed to have some kind of an awards ceremony,
which they have about once a month there.
They give the new ratings out for the guys that are getting advanced every month,
plus a few other little items that they have to take care of.
Thursday we're supposed to get a holiday routine,
which will possibly mean early liberty while we are in Subic Bay.
And then Friday we get underway for operations off the coast of Vietnam again.
I know from my letters and my tapes I've been mentioning the Subic Bay and the Philippines quite often.
Well, this is more or less a home port for us while we're over here in Westpac.
We've been in port there more days than where we have any other stop.
and it's where we get most of our shipyard work done
and we pick up most of our spare parts and our supplies.
It's a pretty busy Navy port there.
There aren't very many cities around,
so it's just everything here is owned by the Navy.
There are a few small towns right outside the gate,
but they're pretty well oriented towards the sailor
with all kinds of bars and souvenir shops and everything,
trying to take advantage of them and take your money at the same time.
Here in Hong Kong, we are anchored in the bay, of course, like I mentioned earlier,
and there are not any availabilities for shipyard work to be done here.
You can't even pick up commissary supplies,
or you can't even get spare parts from some other ship in port here at the same time.
We do get mail here. That's about the only thing that we do get.
And actually, this is just nothing but a Liberty Fort and rest and recreation for everybody.

1968-05-25.text: Hello again, Mother, Dad, and David. This is Saturday, May 25th, and at the present time, our ship is in Hong Kong Harbor, and we are anchored out here and expect to leave tomorrow morning about 8 o'clock. I had duty today, so I stayed on board all day long, and it was a pretty good thing anyway because it rained on and off most of the day as it has for the past four days that we've been in port here. The only day it didn't rain was the first day we got in here, Tuesday the 21st. It was a fairly nice day then, but since then most of the days have been rather rainy. I got the letter that you wrote on the 18th last Wednesday, which is on the 22nd. And I believe my last tape that I sent to you must have been about a week ago. It was just as we had left Subic Bay, I believe we were on our way up here when I last sent the tape. So I've got quite a bit to talk about here, about telling some of the things about Hong Kong. So I should fill up most of this side. And in case my voice does run off the end of the tape, go ahead and turn it on over on this side too. Well, first of all, Tuesday when we got in here, I went over and looked at some of the camera equipment that they had. And I ended up buying myself a Super 8 movie camera. This is a Canon with a zoom lens. and I paid $69 for it. Now, I saw some that were advertising the paper from back home, and the same kind that I got would cost about $200 at least. And so I got a real good camera and a real good buy on it, and I've already shot 150 feet of movie film here. I suppose I'll probably buy a movie projector while I'm over here sometime but I'll just kind of hold off on that for a while the main thing I want to do is just take a lot of pictures while I have the opportunity and I'm pretty proud of my camera and I know it's uh going to give me all the good use that I want to get out of it you can go ahead and tell David that I did buy a transistor radio for him I got a real good buy on it. It is very similar to the one that I have at home. That Channelmaster, the six transistor. This one is the same size. It's got the same size speaker and everything else, and it's practically identical to it. And you'll never believe the price that I paid for it. It only cost $7. Now, I paid about $20 for mine back home, And I know it's a good one because I bought it in a good store. So I'm pretty sure that he'll be glad to hear this. Now, as far as your table radio goes, I saw some here that I like, but I was running a little bit short on funds. And I feel that I can pick up the same kind in Subic Bay for about the same price. I'm not too sure about this, but I'm going to keep my eyes open. And I'll still be thinking about getting one for you. But like I said, I did get caught a little bit short on money at the time when I was going out shopping. And I'll keep it in mind. Our ship got in here Tuesday about, I'd say, 8.30 or thereafter. Liberty call didn't go down until about 10.30 because they had all kinds of business to take care of before they let the troops go on Liberty. So most of Tuesday was spent just window shopping and looking at some of the various merchant sites that they have over here. And I went out with some of the other guys. We had a steak dinner. And I got back to the ship fairly early that night, about 10 o'clock, I'd say. Wednesday, I had duty, so I had to stay aboard and stand one watch. It rained most of that day. That day they had these Chinese people who specialize in painting the ships out here. They come into port. They had them come aboard and paint the ship. And I'm telling you, there was only about 23 people doing it. But they had most of the whole ship painted out in one day. I mean everything. Everything from the water line all the way to the top of the bridge. They have been coming back for the past couple of days just doing little touch-up jobs. But this is one big thing. most of the ships that come into port area, this is one thing that they get done. They have the whole ship painted out, and these people, they take things in exchange for it. They will take your empty brass casings from your ammunition. We gave them some of this. They'll also pick up the leftovers from the mess hall and any garbage scraps that are left on the plates. They're right there, and they take it right off your plates when you go to put your plates in to be washed off. People are right there grabbing off the leftovers that you left on your tray. I suppose they give them a few more other privileges. There possibly might be some money involved in it. I don't know, but they don't ask for too much, and the Navy is real glad to have the ship painted out. It really doesn't go to too much expense for that. now Thursday I went on a tour here in Hong Kong of the whole excuse me of the whole island that tour started at 10 o'clock and it was over at 2 o'clock in the afternoon it was a fairly short tour and of course it rained while we were on the tour but I did manage to get off some good pictures with my movie camera I took my Instamatic to take some slides with but I didn't take any because along the various stops on the tour, they have these people who sell slides, these boxes of slides. They sell you five boxes, which is 100 slides, for, well, various prices. They're all the same thing, but they try to jewel you on different prices than anything like this on a slide. I bought my 100 slides for just about $1.25. I looked at all of them, and they're all pretty good, and most of them take in all of the places that we covered on the tour. And since it was a bad day for taking pictures, this was a real good way to still have pictures of the stops that you made on the tour. I'll bring these on home with me, and I'll show them to you sometime and give you a little explanation of just exactly what some of the things are that are over here. Well, in the morning there on the tour, I had a little accident happen to me, a rather freak accident. it had been raining and we were at this one stop and I was walking down some stairs a flight of stairs and I slipped and my watch band on my left arm as I had stuck out my arm to break my fall my watch band had twisted and cut a about a three inch gauge more it was more like a scratch in my left arm and it tore the skin up kind of bad there but it's a funny thing about it didn't bleed very much and it wasn't very painful so when we got back on the bus I kind of doctored it up there with what they had on the bus and I continued on out the rest of the tour when I got back to the pier where the tour bus let us off I went over to the shore patrol headquarters and showed it to him and asked him if they could you know do anything for me so they were real cooperative and they got me a boat and they sent me out to the coast guard ship and the corpsman out there put three stitches in my arm and gave me a tetanus shot and a novocaine of course to deaden the pain in my arm while he was stitching it up so after he got done with that i came on back to the ship and i got back rather early to the ship about 5 o'clock in the evening, I suppose. I didn't really feel like going back out, and it was nasty and rainy and everything, so I stayed on board for the rest of the night. It doesn't hurt me or anything, but it's actually just a big scratch. The corpsman told me he was going to sew it up because if he didn't, it would probably leave a bad scar, and it would take a little while for it to heal. This way, he figured it should do pretty good. So I've been going to sick bay every morning, and they've been taking off the bandage and changing it and then taking a look at it to see if it was getting infected or anything. I figured that I'd better get some medical attention for it when it did happen because it wasn't really that bad. But I figured that medical attention would be the best thing that I could do because you never know what kind of disease or germs you're liable to pick up over here. Well, yesterday was Friday, and I took liberty about 10 o'clock after getting a haircut here on the ship, which made it mandatory. I had to have a haircut before I could leave or I wasn't going at all. So I took liberty about 10 o'clock. I went over and I got a new watch band for my watch because it tore the other one up kind of bad, the accident that I had. And I went down to the Hong Kong Hilton, which is a well-known hotel over here. And I went up to the top floor, the 25th floor, and I took some movie shots from up there. I had a beer there. Later on, I went out and took some more pictures. I did some window shopping. I met a couple of guys that I knew, and we caught a street car, and we went down to one of the other sections in town here. We did some more window shopping and browsing through some of the department stores down there. I bought a few items there. I came on back and left my merchandise that I picked up at the Fleet Club. I just went out around town and in and out of a few bars. And I got on back to the ship about 9 o'clock that night. It rained yesterday also, and I got caught in a couple of monsoons, so to say, while I was downtown, but otherwise it was a pretty good day. The rain over here, they say it doesn't rain over here very often. They say this is quite an exception. Well, I'd say every place our ship has went, it's been rainy. Up in Washington, it had rained up there quite a bit. Back in San Diego, it rained back there quite a bit. Pearl Harbor, I can't say that we had rain there, but it only lasted for about a half hour one day. It's Subic Bay. It's never rained there. Up in Yokosuka, we had rain. And, of course, up here in Hong Kong, we also got rain. In the Gulf of Tonkin, there for a while, we had rain just about every day. So it's kind of a bad omen that this ship carries along with it. It seems to rain wherever we go. And now this is Saturday. Of course, as I mentioned before, I didn't do very much today. I did a four-hour watch this afternoon, and I forgot off watch. I ate supper and just kind of bummed around here on the ship and decided I'd go ahead and get this tape out to you, and it would possibly go out in the mail tomorrow morning before we got underway. I also bought some dress material over here for you and Grandma. I'll go ahead and send them on home later on as soon as I have a chance when I send David's radio home to him. I don't know whether it's possibly the same kind of print and material that they have back in the United States. When I went in the department store to buy it, this girl tried to talk me into buying some pure silk for the material. But as far as I was concerned, it was a little bit more than what I had intended to buy or to spend. It's cotton dress material, and I only hope that it hasn't been imported from the United States. There wasn't anything on it that said that it was, so I don't assume it has been. So I hope you'll like it, and I'll try to get it out to you as soon as I can. I bought a few stamps for Dad there, about four or five Hong Kong stamps that are commemorative type. And I'll send them on home in a letter just as soon as I can. It'll probably be sent out sometime while we're in Subic Bay. we're supposed to get in there Tuesday and we'll be in there till Friday our next stop they have told us that we leave Subic will be in Da Nang for another day like we have stopped there twice before now this hasn't been on the schedule but they put this in right here at the last minute so I don't expect I'll be seeing Bill while I go there this time because I haven't had time enough to notify him and even if I did try to right now would be rather useless unless he happens to be on the top of a hill somewhere and he sees a ship coming through the harbor somewhere, he can make it down to the ship, but I don't think that's going to be the case. But I wish I would have had time to notify him about it so he could have came on out again if he wanted to. I suppose it's, as it was last time, it was something to give him a little change of pace and get away from some of the daily routine that they have to put up with. Well, this month is almost coming to a close. I tell you, I haven't seen a month go so fast as this one has. I know it's almost summertime back there. I can think about it every day and try to imagine what it's like because being over here just doesn't make you think it's summer because you don't associate the certain things with summertime as you do back in the good life in the United States. And it's really kind of hard to believe that this time of the year has came around already. Like I said, the time has really been going fast over here. And I know we've just got about eight more weeks left, and we will be back in the States again. they put out word the other day that our time for getting into san diego would be on the morning of the 18th of july i suppose this possibly might vary from day to day they also put out a schedule that on our way back we stopped in subic bay guam we set course for the equator and the 180th meridian this is right at the middle of the world i suppose and they put you through an initiation ceremony down there and it's a part of king neptune's court i saw something about this on television a long time ago and i didn't quite understand it but i know pretty well what it's about now and there'll be a lot of guys on the ship going to find out just exactly what they have to go through it's just a little ceremony and they give you a card and a certificate that you can carry around. As we cross the equator on the 180th, we will come back up, stop at Pearl Harbor. I don't know how long we're going to be there. And then we set course for San Diego and expect to get back in there in the middle of July on the 18th. One of the places we stopped at on the tour was at a floating restaurant. It is out in a bay here in Hong Kong on the back side of the island, and they served Chinese food there. The meal that we had was about a six-quart dinner. They had fried rice, some kind of a pork in a sweet sauce. They had crab foo-yong. They had—this was real good that they had. It was creamed corn with crab meat in it, in a soup. It was real soupy. It wasn't creamy like creamed corn is, but it had the flavor of it. It was rather good. I can't remember what else we had there. They put just about everything out there that you could associate with the Chinese food. It wasn't very bad. It was included in the cost of the tour. This tour that we took only cost $5 a piece. And we got to see quite a bit of the island here. One of our other stops on the tour was at a place they call Tiger Balm Gardens. This Tiger Balm is an ointment, a medicine that they use over here. It's supposed to be a cure-all for everything. And this man that invented this medicine, he built this garden as a playground for the children over here. It's kind of like a Disneyland over here to the people. of people. It doesn't have all the amusement rides or anything. It's just a lot of little statues and little colorful figures and stuff. They're also carved out so the kids can climb through them and sit on them. It's just a nice little colorful place. One of our stops on the tour was to take a tram ride. Tram is a word they use over here for, I would imagine cable car or train. That's just about what this was. They have a real steep hill over here on the island. At the top of it they have apartment buildings. This track has two of these trams on it. One of them goes up and the other one goes down. The one that's going down pulls the one that's going up. It's just a law of gravity. They have them both on the same cable and so the force of gravity from the one going down gives it the inertia to pull the one going up, up the top of the hill. I hope that's not too complicated, but that's the way it works. And they have an incline on there of 70 degrees, so that's a pretty steep hill that that thing is going up. We got up the top there, and it was rather foggy, but I did get some good pictures. We could see the harbor out here where the ship was. I tried to get a pretty good picture of that with my zoom lens that was a pretty short stop up there we rode the tram up to the top of the peak and we rode the bus back down and made a few stops on the way down on they showed us some various sites on this uh peak it's called the victoria peak I believe It's got quite a few apartment buildings and nice homes and mansions and everything. This is where all the rich people live at. Actually, over here, there is no middle class of people. You're either rich or you're either a poor person. That's the way it is. And, of course, they took us through some of the slum districts over here, and it's pretty bad. I'd say that it's three times as bad as some of the poor people that had to live back in the United States. They live in these little shacks, just a few pieces of wood thrown together with a canvas over the top of them. Some of these people live in these sandpans, these little boats out on the water. They live out there. They die out there. They're born out there. Just every way you want to look at it. Most of the kids out here are rather young, and they don't go to school because their parents don't have enough money to put them through school because the school is not mandatory over here. If you've got enough money, you can go to school. If you don't have enough money, well, it's no big thing. You don't have to go. So most of these kids over here, these real young ones, they go out and they roam the streets. They beg money and everything. We had a few of them come out here to the ship. They get these little sandpans. They come out here and they dive for coins off the sides of the ship. you know they say hey sailor me dive for coin you throw coin me dive for it or something like that and we got a pretty big kick about that uh they came out to the ship there for a few days and we throw pennies or hong kong dollars which is about the size of a half dollar it's only worth about 30 cents we throw it off the side of the ship and uh they go down there and dive for it. They'd bring it back up. They were pretty good at it. I suppose they were really professionals at it. We pulled a pretty good trick on them though. One time we went in and got a handful of washers. So they were round, you know, they look like coins. And we pulled them up and the kids, yeah, me dive for it, me dive for it. So we throw it off the side to them and they'd go down and get it and they'd come back up and they had a washer and they shot obscenities to us in Chinese we didn't know what they were talking about but uh they still were fairly disappointed on the fact that we didn't have throw any money over to them. A lot of the people over here they make little novelties little souvenirs and things like that they try to sell them to the tourists and people that come over here there's quite a few British people here of course as you know Hong Kong is a British colony and it's bordered by Red China on the other side so you have quite a few British people living here it's rather nice to see some of these round-eyed people in the same port that you stop it kind of reminds you of the people back home you get very tired and very bored of seeing these foreign looking people over here because you know that you are not in your homeland and you don't really feel at ease with them. So it does kind of put you in a better position when you do see some people who are your own color of skin and they have most of your own features. Also it's not very rare to see a sight with a young boy possibly four or five years old with his younger brother or sister strapped on his back he carry him around on the streets out begging for coins or anything like this it's quite a common sight but there are some real nice districts over here nice buildings houses and things like that and they do keep these people out of there but you see some of them around the waterfront around some of the boats and stuff. You see some of them out on some of the places that the tourists and the sightseers hit on these tours that they go on. And it's really a fairly bad situation. They are overpopulated over here, not enough houses, not enough food for them, of course. Most of them are refugees from Red China, which is just across the bay from us here. and they want to get out of China so they come over here and their life isn't much better for them so I imagine they will continue to live like this for a long time the government over here is trying to make some improvements for them but it's just a never-ending battle as it always is in a poverty program I'm sure that the President Johnson's war on poverty that he has back in the United States isn't accomplishing much more than what the British government is trying to do over here for these people. Well, Mother, I hope you got most of your deal with the cafeteria work and the school unions straightened out by now. I suppose by the time you get this tape, your days working in the cafeteria will be very, very few left. I hope that you haven't run into any trouble or anything else in trying to keep up the application for the nurses school. I know David's probably still anxious for school to get out. I hope he does a good job in summer school, though. And he realizes, I'm sure, if not he should, that it's going to be pretty important for him this year because next year he'll be starting in the sixth grade, and after he gets out of sixth grade, it's only six more years, and he will be out of high school. And he's got six pretty important years coming up. So he'd better start hitting the books a little bit harder if he has to and try to get something out of it because it's bad to go to school and have to struggle through, and the only way you can keep from struggling through is just to do a little bit more studying than what is absolutely necessary. I hope he's having a lot of good times there in Boy Scouts, and I hope that he can go to summer camp. I bet he was really tired when he got back from that 25-mile bike hike, but it was probably a pretty good experience for him. It probably might have taken a little bit of weight off of him. I shouldn't really talk though because I weighed myself the other day and I weigh 195 pounds so that means I've put on about 15 or 20 pounds since I left the state I guess that's what the soft navy life does to you well you know you mentioned in your letter that uh Connie had called you and said that if you hadn't have wrote to Bill and mentioned that her wedding was called off she would have never have got any more letters from Bill he wouldn't have started writing to her again well it's I don't know what she was meaning by this uh not knowing a tone of voice that she was using when she said it but uh if she's complaining she shouldn't be complaining because I wait you to say that she's lucky that he did write back to her because I think that she treated him in some pretty bad ways. And if she is complaining, well, she doesn't have to write back to him. I don't know what she's trying to prove by saying that. Of course, it's no interest of yours that she'd say such a thing like that. I suppose that she is the type a person that doesn't think very much before she says something. I suppose if most people would exercise their brain before they exercise their mouth, they'd find that they didn't get themselves in so much trouble. But I suppose her and Bill will both be real happy now that they've each got tape recorders. And Grandma also mentioned to me in one letter, this is kind of odd and kind of funny, but she doesn't get to sing letters from Bill as she used to because he started writing to Connie. Well, not too much can be said about that, but I very seldom hear from Bill. It's at least once a month or maybe even longer, but it's no big thing because I know that he's possibly pretty busy where he's at. I've got plenty of time to write and sit down and send a tape and everything, but, of course, his situation is different, and it's no big thing. Just as long as I know I still have him for a brother, that's the one big thing that counts. Well, we've got a pretty busy week ahead of us. Next week, of course, we'll spend a day and a half or so of that week being on the way to Subic Bay. While we're on our way there, we're going to test fire the gun mounts a few times, see if they're still holding up. When we get in there, We're scheduled to have an inspection of the ship later on in the week, I believe about Wednesday or Thursday. Thursday they're supposed to have some kind of an awards ceremony, which they have about once a month there. They give the new ratings out for the guys that are getting advanced every month, plus a few other little items that they have to take care of. Thursday we're supposed to get a holiday routine, which will possibly mean early liberty while we are in Subic Bay. And then Friday we get underway for operations off the coast of Vietnam again. I know from my letters and my tapes I've been mentioning the Subic Bay and the Philippines quite often. Well, this is more or less a home port for us while we're over here in Westpac. We've been in port there more days than where we have any other stop. and it's where we get most of our shipyard work done and we pick up most of our spare parts and our supplies. It's a pretty busy Navy port there. There aren't very many cities around, so it's just everything here is owned by the Navy. There are a few small towns right outside the gate, but they're pretty well oriented towards the sailor with all kinds of bars and souvenir shops and everything, trying to take advantage of them and take your money at the same time. Here in Hong Kong, we are anchored in the bay, of course, like I mentioned earlier, and there are not any availabilities for shipyard work to be done here. You can't even pick up commissary supplies, or you can't even get spare parts from some other ship in port here at the same time. We do get mail here. That's about the only thing that we do get. And actually, this is just nothing but a Liberty Fort and rest and recreation for everybody.

1968-05-28.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-05-28.text:
May 28, 1968
Subic Bay, P.I.
Tues. 1900

Dear Mother + Dad, and David,

Here's a short note to let you know I received your May 23 letter today. I found all of the paper clippings interesting and good reading. I am glad everyone enjoyed the slides and tape. You should have got another set by this time.

We left Hong Kong Sunday and arrived here in Subic Bay Monday evening about 1700. I am staying aboard tonight and thought I'd stay sober for once. Only kidding of course.

Tell David I will mail his radio tomorrow or the next day. I don't know how well it will work to pull in the stations he wants to hear but I am sure it will be okay. Let me know how it works.

Thursday afternoon, Memorial Day, we have early liberty. There is suppose to be a Weapons department party for us. I also plan to see about your radio and go into town and take some movies.

We are moored alongside a tender which is anchored here in the bay. In order to go ashore you have to take a boat. This is a little inconvenient and not as good as being tied up to a pier. We are to leave Friday and head back to the Gulf for our usual operations.

David, I was really impressed by the picture you drew. You pictured it just right and have a good imagination. I have some coins to send you and will mail them in a few days. I think you are wise to hold off in going to camp this year. Wait till you make second or first-class then you can have more fun there.

I got a tape from Bill yesterday. His letters never say much but he sure had a lot to talk about on the tape. I'll send him one back tonight.

I hope I haven't discouraged your vacation plans any. Do what you want to, and I'm sure we all will be happy.

Mother, I'm glad to hear you got things straightened out with the school job. Things usually to turn out okay in the long run if you give them time.

Here are some stamps for Dad. I hope he has a place for them.

Well I must go for now. I'll be looking forward to getting your tape. So long.

Your son,

Mike
1968-05-28.attribution: Letter, Mike Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-05-31.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-05-31.text:
May 31, 1968
Subic Bay

Dear Mother,

Here is $100 more to put in the bank for me.

Yesterday was Memorial Day here and really a hot one. I suppose that you had the usual get together back there. Margaret Whiting was at the club last night and performed for about an hour.

I would like for you to send me two more jars of Fostex and a couple of bottles of M.F.C. I don't really need it but its good for preventive purposes and you can't find it over here.

We will leave here this evening and proceed on our usual route back on station. We are due for a short stop in Da Nang.

Well I have to go and get this in the mail. See you later.

Your son,

Mike

My grandma had a picture of Bill today, and he gave a pretty good description of his latest crazy stunt that he did. And I think I wrote, no, no, I couldn't have wrote because we got a letter from him Thursday. And he wrote in that letter that he and one of those Korean corporals was fooling around with a dead grenade. And they pulled the blasting cap off of it and threw it, and it didn't do anything. so he picked it up, Bill did, and there was a fire there where they was going to cook some chow at, and what did he do but throw that thing in the fire? And he took off to run, but he didn't run fast enough, and he got 23 shrapnel scratches in his chest and arms, and on the tape he gave a little bit better description of how it was done, and that a couple of places were scratched deeper and where the shrapnel pieces went in deeper than the other ones did, and he was able to pull them out. And he admitted that he'd learned his lesson. And I'm wondering, do you think that he'll ever grow up on sons like that? He also mentioned that in the letter and the table that the major had been up there to the camp, and I guess he raised quite a bit of hell. And he told them all that they're like a bunch of pigs, and they didn't even act like Marines. So now the poor boys are having to get up at 7 o'clock instead of 9 or 10 o'clock in the morning. And he finds it a little bit rough since they got used to those later hours, and their radio watches have been changed too. and to coincide with when they get up. So he may have to realize that there is military there, but he can't figure out why that they should have to be so strict on them because they're over there. But in a way, I can see that some pretty bad habits could be formed, and the next thing you know, they don't even know what they're supposed to be doing, I would say. He says they also are going to have rifle inspection once a week, which they haven't had, and that doesn't seem to interest him too much. But I'm glad that they got the tape from him because they haven't been very successful in getting tapes from Bill. and I had to laugh because they played the one side. As soon as they got it, they naturally put it on their recorder and started playing it. And they played the one side and it ran out and so Grapple supposedly turned it over to play the second side and he had the thing all fouled up and they couldn't figure out what he was saying or anything. And so she couldn't imagine what was wrong with it because the first side had played off. Well, she says, I know someplace where I can get it to play. They'll know what they're doing. So she brought it down here. And what had happened was he had rewound it and then played it backwards. I don't know whether I'm explaining it to you right or not, But anyway, he had really fouled it up in his way of doing it. And she was just quite amazed when she started hearing the second sight coming through so clear. And he made a real good taste. And said that I think he made her feel a lot better because he let her know, or let them know, I should say, that he only had 275 days left over there and that that would get him back in the States and give him about five months' lapse and he'd be able to spend some time with Georgia Mae and with you there if you were stationed there in San Diego. Also, he'd made the tape on the 23rd and he said that that marked nine months in the Marines and it doesn't seem like he's been in there that long, no really, but I guess he has because I, as you said, have said too, this month went so fast, or May went so fast, and if the next three months go as fast as these last two months have, I don't know how I'm going to get everything done in the summer that I've got planned to do, but I'm going to try to get as much done as I can next week because there just won't be any way of accomplishing too much every morning while I'm running David, and of course, I can always come back home and get something done in the two hours he's in summer school, but it's kind of all you get out of the mood desk you want to leave and so forth. If I get the painting done, that won't be so bad. I can leave anything else that I started to do. We certainly enjoyed your tape we got from you yesterday. And sorry to hear about your little accident you had, but evidently the Ducey family are kind of accident prone right now I wrote told you about me running under that door knocking my glasses off and and getting a slight black eye out of the deal and of course they was this broken arm bit and the bill with the shrapnel scratches now you with the uh gash in your arm while I'm going to get into wonder and but I hope that and I doubt if it has given you any trouble but I hope you don't have any other problems come up like that. And if I remember right, you are probably going to be, by this time that I'm taking this, you should have probably arrived at the Gulf of Tonkin again. And I read in the paper today, in today's paper, where the carrier America was there and it was sending planes out to try to help what they could do. And all during that tape of bills, he kept commenting that we probably could hear in the background the rockets and airbursts going over, but actually none of the sounds came through. and they was really being hit there because all the way through that tape on both sides he'd make a comment about oh that one was close or that one sure was loud and so forth so they must just have a regular 4th of July up there all the time and I've been wondering just what kind of effect that will have on him and also the rest of those guys with all that airburst and so forth I suppose that in due time that you do get over that and waiting to hear something. But I imagine that there is some rehabilitation that's necessary in a situation like this. I don't know. But being as young as he is, he ought to be able to get over any problems that he might have acquired from that situation over there. At least I hope so. Well, this tape looks like it's just about ready to run off. So I'm going to turn it over and see what else I can think to say on it. And maybe if I can get David in here, why, he'll have a few words to say. Maybe Daddy might have something, too. But I thought that by now I definitely owed you a tape. and I'll so I thought I'd see what I could do about sending me one and I know I owed you a letter or should have wrote but I'll try to do better now that some of this cleaning has gotten started and over with so be sure to turn this over now honey and I'll try to say a few more words on the other side you

1968-06-01.label: Familygram — Capt. Robert S. Hayes, CO
1968-06-01.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-06-01.text:
JOUETT FAMILY GRAM

Dear Family and Friends of JOUETT

My last letter to you told some of the events which have involved JOUETT while "on station" -- that is, at sea, patrolling in Tonkin Gulf. Days "on station" comprise the great majority of our time this cruise, almost 80% of the total. This is a high figure, even compared to other Navy ships who serve in the SEVENTH Fleet. Nevertheless, since that last Familygram, JOUETT has had some time away from "work", and has seen some interesting places. I would now like to tell you about them.

First, as the Gulf of Tonkin was disappearing in our wake, we took the occasion to hold a "Fantail Frolic". The announcement published in the Plan of the Day, stated that during the Fantail Frolic attendees were forbidden to be dressed in a regulation Navy Uniform. Every man had to wear something out of the ordinary, an odd hat, or no hat, or perhaps a pair of bermuda shorts. But in no case could full uniform be worn. The crew responded with enthusiasm, and came to the fantail dressed more for a day at the beach. The weather was beautiful, warm, clear sky and just a slight breeze to ripple the blue water. Berets, straw hats, and swimming suits abounded. Refreshments included hamburgers, hot dogs, baked beans, coleslaw, chilled punch, and a big cake to celebrate the 300th landing that day of JOUETT's own Clementine II helicopter. For entertainment, LT Ted Huckabone warmed up on an accordian and the JOUETTEERS played "country and western". Then came the high point of the Frolic, the announcement of the winning entries in the ship's Flag, Song, and Nickname Contest. As you may know, every ship in the Navy has its unique insignia, representing its history, mission and spirit. Many ships go beyond this and adopt their own flag, song and nickname. JOUETT did just this by staging a contest, and providing ALL Hands a try at designing a JOUETT flag, writing a JOUETT song, and conceiving a JOUETT nickname. As it turned out the choice of nickname was a natural. JOUETT has been known to her own crew as the "Jolly J" for some time, and now it is official. You may see our flag flying from the foretruck in a very short while. And the JOUETT song, as you can see, last page, shows plenty of the spirit that has run through JOUETT ever since her nucleus crew formed.

What does the name Hong Kong conjure up in your mind? International city? Ancient China? Shopping Mecca? Jewel of the Orient? That is what we thought of the name, and that is what we found her to be. Hong Kong is only a stone's throw from Subic Bay--a day and a night of steaming. But it is as great a change as one could find in Southeast Asia. At Subic Bay one finds an American directed Naval Base, busy night and day with the sounds of ships loading and unloading and ship repair. The best, almost only, recreation is an island with beaches and ball parks created by the U. S. Navy. But in Hong Kong one finds a British Crown Colony, where many nations of the world show their flags. Hong Kong is a colony of thousands of strange sights, sounds, and smells, of color and contrast, of fantastic bargains for the shopper, of rickshaw and a walla-walla rides, of smart cosmopolitan night spots, of food delights to satisfy the gourmet. Over four million people are crampacked into this 391 square mile area of rugged hills called Hong Kong. This teaming population, representative of all nationalities, is comprised of a few very rich and hundreds of thousands of very poor living side by side in luxury and poverty.

There were more than fifty ships in the harbor when JOUETT arrived with our crew smartly lined up at quarters. We moored to a huge anchored buoy right in the downtown section of the harbor. With our national flag flying from the flagstaff, we felt like personal representatives of the U. S. A.. When the British Commodore of Hong Kong paid a formal call on the ship, we knew that we were.

The city of Hong Kong is situated on Victoria Island, and the water between island and mainland forms the harbor. Where the city extends over onto the mainland, it is called Kowloon. Behind Kowloon are the New Territories, where the city's water is stored, and much of the city's food is grown. The New Territories reach inland twenty-five miles to a river; beyond that river one can see a fence and an outpost, and there Red China begins. A number of us went up to that vantage point just so that we could state we had seen "Red China".

Hong Kong has as many facets to it as one of the gems for which it is famous. There is the downtown financial center with its skyscrapers and marble banks, as solid as New York or London. The banks of the United States, Britain, Red China and the rest of the world stand shoulder to shoulder, and do a thriving financial business. In this section are also the great hotels and shopping districts, frequented by the millions of tourists who come here each year.

- - - There is the artisan section, where skilled Chinese - - - many of them refugees from Red China, ply their trades. Silks, jade, bamboo, ivory, mahogony are the materials in which the craftsmen express the orient.

When one sets out to see the sights, he finds out that he can tour the island in a day, but that it might take a week to see all of the city. For outside of the city, the attractions are fewer, though no less interesting. Victoria Peak stands above the city and dominates the island. A tramway climbs up the steep side; from the top you can see Hong Kong at your right hand, and at your left, Repulse Bay on the far side of the island. What an impressive sight of the harbor. And there in the middle of all the ships we could see our sleek grey JOUETT. Halfway around the island is Aberdeen. Aberdeen is a floating city, and one can hardly see the water in that cove of the island, for the acres of junks that cover it. Because of the scarcity of land in Hong Kong, families live in houseboats tied one to another. It is said that some of these people have never set foot on land. Here also are famous floating restaurants, where one can choose one's own carp from a glass tank, and see it prepared before him. Carp is one of those Chinese delicacies that rather surprise the American visitor.

The fantastic bargains for the shopper dominate the scene for the tourist in Hong Kong as they dominate no other city of the world. Famed as a "Free Port", Hong Kong is flooded with imported goods from every country, in addition to its own manufactured goods. Shopping was one of the major attractions for JOUETTmen. The items brought on board ran from men's clothing, shoes, jewelry, watches, cameras, teak furniture, carved ivory, tape recorders, hi-fi equipment, transistor radios, rattan ware, perfumes, and linens. Needless to say, almost everyone was "broke buying bargains" by the time we departed.

Unfortunately, JOUETT arrived in Hong Kong during a spell of rainy weather, and there was seldom a time when Victoria Peak was not shrouded with clouds. Our photographers had to be nimble to get good pictures from the top. The crew enjoyed the visit to Hong Kong immensely. But I believe it gave pleasure to the city, too, to have a ship visit her without a single Shore Patrol incident. JOUETT left Hong Kong with an unblemished liberty record still intact. And indeed, before we knew it, we were headed back to Subic and resumption of our previous duties.

One last item to tell you. As you may recall, a few months ago a number of our men received JOUETT Outstanding Service Awards. In Subic Bay, we presented additional Outstanding Service Awards to some very deserving men. Recipients were Chief Fire Controlman Glenn H. UNDERWOOD; Chief Electronics Technician William B. KENDALL; and First Class Radarman Richard F. TANNER.

With the passing of the months it was inevitable that we should have some transfers and some new arrivals in ship's company. We said our farewell to key officers who had been with JOUETT since her precommissioning days: Lieutenant Commander Robert S. MALONE, USN, the Engineering Officer, went on to his new positon as Executive Officer of the USS BUCHANAN (DDG 14). Lieutenant Commander Robert E. LANTSBERGER, SC, USN, the Supply Officer, went on to duty on the staff of Commander Cruiser-Destroyer Force, U. S. Pacific Fleet. Lieutenant Robert J. TERHUNE, USN, Gunnery Officer, was transferred to duty as an Exchange Officer for two years with the Royal Netherlands Navy.

Our newcomers include: Lieutenant Carl JAFFEE, USN as Engineering Officer. He came from a year's duty with the U. S. Navy Support Activities, Danang, South Vietnam. Lieutenant William WITHROW, SC, USN, reported on board from the Puget Sound Nval Shipyard, Bremerton, Washington. He relieved as Supply Officer. Finally, Lieutenant (jg) Lawrence V. FAIRCHILD, USN, came from duty in the Guided Missile Cruiser CANBERRA. He is JOUETT's new Gunnery Officer.

We are back in Tonkin Gulf performing the familiar job of search and rescue and air defense. We like our assignment and derive great satisfaction from doing something necessary and doing it well. With so much fine experience behind us, we truly consider ourselves full fledged members of the Navy Tonkin Gulf "Yacht Club". In comparison with the beginning, it all seems "down hill" from now on.

Please keep the letters coming. The sweetest of all sounds these days is "Mail Call".

Sincerely,

ROBERT S. HAYES
CAPTAIN, U. S. NAVY
COMMANDING OFFICER


"THE FRIGATE 29"
by FN Robert J. McNEIL

1.  The U. S. built a great Ship
      and put some sailors on it;
    To prepare themselves for the future,
      and the readiness of her plans.
    To sail across the ocean,
      where every man took notion;
    Of the pride and all her beauty,
      that was shared by all its hands.

CHORUS:
    The JOUETT is a fine ole Ship,
      the greatest of her kind;
    A D-L-G that will always be,

2.  The Captain has command,
      He pledged his honor to it;
    To fight the best He can,
      with the help of every man.
    We share our pride in JOUETT,
      cause we know that we can do it;
    To fight for the rights of freedom,
      and protection of our land. - - - CHORUS

3.  We search the sky for danger,
      for our pilots better safety;
    To cover them on missions,
      while bombing on the land.
    We're known for quick detection,
      which offers us protection;
    We'll work with other units,
    and unite to take our stand.- - - CHORUS

4.  The pilots never worry,
      when in trouble they may hurry;
    To cross the ocean for us,
      whenever in a bind.
    With Clem 2 and Big Mother,
      to the rescue of another;
    For the pilots called us Loveland,
    it wasn't hard to find.- - - - -CHORUS

5.  We've seen the many beauties,
      of countries while off duty;
    Hawaii, Guam, or Subic,
      and don't forget Japan.
    Hong Kong and maybe others,
      will recognize our colors;
    And the value of the battle,
      that we fight in Vietnam.- - - -CHORUS

As JOUETT'S second line period ended and our third began, the ship had gained
proficiency in search and rescue work, through actual practice. To further comple-
ment the DLG/UH-2 SAR Team, JOUETT'S combat information center maintained close
radio and radar contact with all aircraft flying into North Vietnam. Should one of these
aircraft encounter difficulty, the word was passed from CIC "SAR Alert--SAR Alert";
The CIC watch section was bolstered by the presence of additional officers and en-
listed men who man highly sophisticated electronic search equipment. At the same
time, the helicopter was readied for immediate launch. As the officer of the deck
turned the ship into the wind, pilots and flight crew dashed to the Helo, the ship's
Helo detail manned their stations. Within minutes, the Helo was cleared for take-off
and rose into the air, slowly at first, then rapidly accelerating toward the SAR
location.

[Photo: Rescued aviator and crew members on flight deck near helicopter after SAR mission, aviator being escorted from the aircraft]

[Photo: Landing Signal Director from behind, waving paddles to guide returning helicopter onto flight deck]

Five times, the scene of a successful SAR landing was repeated, and eight Navy
fliers owe their lives and their freedom to JOUETT'S SAR Team. In the pages that
follow, no captions are necessary. The relief, elation and fatigue evident in the faces
of rescued pilots and radar intercept officers speak louder than words in describing
the value of the contribution of the USS JOUETT.
