1968-06-08.label: Tape 5, Side 1 — Mike Ducy
1968-06-08.attribution: Audio cassette recording, Tape 5, Side 1 — Mike Ducy. Transcribed by OpenAI Whisper. Ducy Family Archives

segments.text: Hello, Mother, Dad, and David.
Well, today is June the 7th, and in about five more minutes it'll be June the 8th,
because it's five minutes till midnight here, and I'm preparing to stand the mid-watch,
which will last till 4 o'clock this morning. I've been standing these watches all week. We
We stand the same watch for one week and then we rotate to the next watch section.
That way it doesn't get too boring.
As I was getting ready to say, I received your tape that you sent.
So that all three of you spoke on.
I was real glad to hear from everybody.
I was waiting to hear from you because I was eager to send another tape.
And I expected that today I would receive a tape from you and I did.
So I was pretty glad to hear from everyone.
Well, I guess the first thing I'll talk about is what has really happened right now with
the death of Senator Kennedy.
We found out about this yesterday afternoon about 4 o'clock over here and they started
flying a flag at half-mast and everything.
It's kind of a tragic happening and it kind of makes you wonder if it would be better
to stay over here than to go back to the States because of the things happening like that.
But there's something wrong there somewhere, which I'm sure a lot of people realize, and
it's just too bad that it had to happen twice in the same family.
That's all I'll say about that.
Tuesday we arrived up here on Station after stopping in Da Nang for about four hours on
Monday.
We got up here Tuesday and put in our first full day on station.
And about 1 o'clock in the afternoon, we got right into the swing of things
because there was an A-5 shot down about 13 miles from the ship,
just as it was coming back to the aircraft carrier from a strike over there on the beach.
And it had two pilots aboard.
So we sent out our helicopter to rescue him, and they picked up one out of the water, and they couldn't find the other one.
The ones they did bring back were pretty bad. He had a couple of broken bones, a broken collar bone.
He was in pretty bad shape. They brought him aboard, took him to sick bay, and I saw him on a stretcher as they took him by,
and they was giving him plasma as they was taking him to sick bay.
They kept him here on the ship for just a couple of hours and they put him back in the helicopter and took him over to the aircraft carriers for further treatment.
And later on in the afternoon about 4 o'clock, our sister ship up here picked up some wreckage of the plane and they sent it over to us so we could send it back for investigation purposes.
and among us was the life jacket of the other pilot which was torn up pretty bad
so they know for sure that the other pilot didn't survive
and most of the plane wreckage was in pretty bad shape.
The material that those planes are made out of is something that will shatter pretty easy
and can bend without any difficulty.
It's all aluminum.
and in between the wings it has this honeycomb aluminum stuff like to give it weight and make
make it so it's not so uh flexible it's more or less a filler and uh that stuff here is pretty
easy and can be shattered by shrapnel and everything so we had uh quite a bit of excitement
there. We haven't had any more SAR rescues in the past few days, but I suppose we'll be having some
more because the strikes are pretty heavy over there, and there are some pretty good anti-aircraft
fire from the ground at them planes, and I expect we'll be picking up a couple more pilots while
we're still up here. You mentioned in your tape that you read something about the aircraft carrier
America launching planes over here going in for airstrikes. Well, this is one of the
carriers that's on station over here too with us and I believe this is their first
time to come over here to Westpac on a cruise. It's a fairly new aircraft carrier
and I don't know very much about it. The possibility might be a chance that I
would see it in some port before we go home and if we do I'll take some pictures
and so you know a little bit what it looks like at least.
Most of those aircraft carriers, they all look the same,
and there's no big difference between them.
Speaking of aircraft carriers, the Enterprise, I'm sure you've all heard of it,
is expected to return to the States about the same time we are,
and we got a message the other day that our step is to escort the Enterprise back to the States
and arrive there on July the 18th.
We're not going to make any stops in Australia or any other places.
We're not going to cross the equator like we had planned to do because we're going to go back by the northern route
when we take the Enterprise back.
But of course these plans will probably change like everything else does here in the Navy.
They never do have any definite plans, but this is just what the word is out now.
This is official, and I suppose it could change just as easily as anything else could.
We've only got about 40 days left over here and it's going to be real good to get back
in the state again and see how some decent people live and know that people aren't always
trying to take you for your money and take advantage of you like they do in these sports.
It's too bad it has to be that way but I can't say that I did have a pretty good time over
here and I did see a lot of the Far East over here and I'm pretty satisfied that I know
a little bit more about it than what I did when I came over here.
And I know it's an experience that I won't forget.
I'm glad I've got pictures and souvenirs for memories of various places
and things that I did over here.
I received a letter from Bill the other day,
and he mentioned that he had 270-some days or whatever it is left over here.
I imagine those guys take a pretty good attitude towards that.
It's more of less a joke to them because they're over there for more than a year
whereas I've only been over here for six months by the time I get back to the states but uh
we are getting pretty short on time over here and uh it's just a matter of sticking out these last
few days on station and then we'll turn the ship around and start heading back east again
uh and Bill's letter he also mentioned about getting wounded by the grenade shrapnel and it
sounds just like him it sounds like some of his old pranks of boyhood that he used to pull he
He should have known better, and I'm sure that he did learn a lesson by it.
He did send me a tape that I received from him, which was fairly interesting.
He talked on both sides of it.
And he was interrupted there once by,
they were launching mortar attacks or something on him.
He was always saying, can you hear that in the background?
Can you hear that?
Well, I couldn't hear anything.
I'm sure it was there.
and you said he's mentioned this in your tapes before there's always something here in the
background going off i'd wait to say that this is fairly true and uh i couldn't hear anything
of course he might have been hearing things himself like you said those guys probably uh
have an effect on him from uh all that shell shock or whatever you might refer to it as and
He might have been hearing things himself.
He said in his letter about this major coming up there and calling them pigs and everything.
So I wrote back to him.
I said, well, Phil, how does it feel to be a pig?
And I hope he took this in a joking manner.
If he read it correctly, he would have.
But those guys probably were having more of an R&R situation up there
where they were having more fun than really getting down to business.

That really tears me up that they have to have mustard at 7.30 in the morning and have to get up at 7 o'clock because we get up at 6 o'clock here on the ship every day, including Saturdays and Sundays.
And you don't find yourself laying in the rack at any hours between 8 o'clock in the morning and 4 o'clock in the afternoon, unless it's during your noon hour for one hour.
If you don't have the watch, you can go up there and sleep for an hour.
But you better get out of that wreck when the noon hour is over
when you get back and start doing some work or something.
You're looking busy.
But I know that he probably has the attitude,
and most of those guys do up there, like you mentioned,
that just because they're over here, they should be a little bit more slack.
That's true.
He mentioned in one of his tapes that when he stopped at the Marine Air Base,
the guys around there were all wearing starched utilities and foot shine shoes and real squared
away in their military appearance but he kind of felt like he was out of place because he had his
mustache and they don't allow mustaches there at that base and his utilities were not pressed
or anything like that, and he had dirty shoes.
And I suppose that this Major, whoever he was that came up there,
was trying to keep the morale up a little bit.
I suppose if they could let guys get back on their heels like that
and they start sliding, it would be pretty bad.
So I'd say it was all for their own good.
They probably don't realize this.
Some of them might, and I don't think it would hurt them any
because being in the service, you'll find that they'll do things to you one time
that you don't particularly appreciate, and the next time they'll come around
and it'll all be over with and you will be used to it.
And I'll just sum it up in a couple of words.
He'll get over it. He'll get used to it because there's no other thing that he can do.
Mother, you asked me in my last letter that after looking at the pictures
that I sent home with me and Bill, it looked like we had both grown quite a bit.
Well, I don't know whether I've mentioned this or not, but I weigh 194 pounds,
now. I weighed myself in Hong Kong. And by my calculation, this is just about 20 pounds
more than I weighed when I came on active duty. Bill, I couldn't tell whether he had
grown too much or not, whether he was putting on any weight or anything, because he had
those utilities on, and they seemed to fit him pretty loosely. And I couldn't really
tell, but I know that he does weigh more than I do. And he seemed to me like he could have
grown a little bit of course after not really seeing him I didn't pay too much
attention to his physical features because we had a lot to talk about but
I'd say that he probably has put on a little bit of weight I don't know he
says that they don't have too much to eat that their chow doesn't quite compare to the
good food we have here on the ship so I don't know I don't know whether that's
quite any factor in his growth or not well I got pretty good news back here
today it's not nothing too important but uh i got my results back to my usafi test in the
electronic correspondence course and i got a passing mark in it and i got a certificate
signed by the usafi uh directors and uh it was also signed by the commanding officer the chief
the captain and a couple of papers to be entered in my service record about it and the next day i
went down and tried to do more courses and i should have them within the next three weeks or
and I'll be spending a lot of my time back in the States working on them.
I suppose on nights when I have liberty, I plan to go into San Diego to the public library
and do a little bit of studying on them and get them done.
It'd be kind of a way to get away from the chip and also take liberty and not spend too much money.
I got an application back from the State of Illinois Veterans Commission
for this $100 Vietnam bonus for servicemen who are veterans or who are on duty over here.
And I've filled out my part of it.
I took it up to the chief's office, and they have to fill out some information on there
and notarize it, but I'll be sending it back.
I took it up there about a week ago, and they haven't done anything with it yet.
They seem to resent doing paperwork.
But I'm going to go up in the morning and see if they've got it done,
and if they do, I'm going to send it back out.
Bill also applied for this, and he mentioned in his tape that he didn't sign it or something.
I don't know what he did.
So he had to fill out another one.
I sent it back to him.
He had to fill it out again, and he's going to send his back in.
Dad mentioned on his tape about these Veterans Administration benefits
for guys who go to college or who take an apprenticeship program.
I hope he's not confusing this with the GI Bill.
If not, it sounds like a real good deal because under the GI Bill, you get $130 a month for a college education.
Or if you take an apprenticeship program, you get a certain percentage according to your wage scale that you're getting paid.
And if it's $110 a month or whatever it was that he mentioned, it can be used in addition to the GI Bill.
I would say that it's a pretty good deal.
And if a guy wouldn't take further education, either an apprenticeship or a college,
he'd really be hurting himself because the money's there.
All you have to do is just ask for it.
And I'd like to take advantage of it one way or the other.
I don't really know just exactly how I want to, but I got plenty of time to think that over.
and you can make sure I'm going to make use of the benefits.
You know, here in the Navy, they always say,
well, reenlist, look at all the benefits you get.
Well, my attitude is get out of the Navy.
You've got more benefits out of the Navy than what you have in here.
But there are some guys that fall for that line.
I guess they've got nothing better to do with themselves.
So they kind of like to stay around and take some of the benefits
that the Navy says that they have to offer them.
And they seem to be pretty satisfied with it,
but I don't think that I would be.
Well, I suppose David, I hope that he has got the radio by now that I sent him.
I hope he's pretty happy with it and does what he wants it to.
Like I mentioned in the letter, I didn't have a chance to play it over here
to pick up any United States stations to see how well it works.
So it was fairly inexpensive, and it looked like a good radio.
I'm sure it should do a pretty good job, and I'd like to hear from him,
just exactly how it works.
I want them to be honest with me,
tell me exactly if it picks up the stations it wants to
and how it sounds and everything,
because I'd be pretty interested to find out.
About the table radio that you asked me to buy,
I'm kind of mad at myself
because I couldn't buy the one that I wanted to
when I had the chance to.
It was a Sony table radio with a clock on it.
It was AM and FM in a walnut cabinet.
It measured about 4 inches high.
It was about 12 inches long and about 8 inches deep.
It had a walnut wood grain cabinet and it was really nice.
It only cost $32.
It was transistorized with an AC plug on it to use on house current.
I wish I could have picked it up there in Hong Kong when I had a chance to, but they
didn't have any back in Subic Bay.
I'm going to look again when I get back there.
and we'll do the stop there for possibly one or two days before we go back to the States.
And I'd sure like to get this for you because it's a real nice radio,
but don't let your hopes down.
I want to try to keep in there and try to get it.
I don't think I'm going to get you anything but that one
because I haven't found anything over here that's quite as nice as that
or anything that I myself would particularly want to have.
So there's still a slight chance I might be able to get it for you.
Well, I got the stitches taken out of my arm the other day, I'd say about a week ago, from
the little laceration there that I suffered in Hong Kong.
I suppose my big trouble there was why I slipped and fell down them stairs was because I didn't
have my land legs back again.
You know, how us sailors get after we've been out at sea for such a long time and used to
the motion of the ship and we acquired a different way of walking.
Well, I suppose my difficulty right there was I wasn't used to walking on the land,
and as a result, I suffered a fall, which I don't think that's really why it happened.
I was just not watching what I was doing.
But I got the stitches out now, and it's got a little bit of a scab still left on there.
And where it was cut at, it's still rather red.
I don't know whether it's going to get its color back again or not
or whether it's going to be a little scar there.
but we'll see what it's going to look like here in a couple more weeks.
I'll probably go outside and I'll pick up a little bit of sun on it
and it'll probably take the color again.
It won't have that red and pink color to it if I get some sun on it.
Well, I was glad to hear that you got some new furniture there for the bedroom.
I know it's going to help the appearance quite a bit back here
and a bunk bed that sounds just like old times there.
I'm sure David's pretty happy about it and I know he is pretty anxious to get up there
and sleep in that top bunk.
I'll tell him this, that our bunks, I'm going to refer to them as racks, our racks here
on the ship are three high and I've got a top one.
And I'll tell you, when I come home, I'm not going to crowd him out of that top one.
I'll let him have the top one and I'll sleep in the bottom one because it's just, well
Well as it is right now on the ship it's pretty warm in them top racks because we're over
here where it's a little bit warmer and when the ship is underway it generates more heat
inside the ship because they got the boilers and everything lit off.
But even with the air conditioning you do get a little bit of heat up towards the ceiling
in the ship and it's fairly warm up there.
I can sleep up there without a shirt or without a sheet or a blanket or anything and still
not be exactly comfortable.
But I'm sure it's going to make a lot more room back here in the bedroom and give David
some more room for some of his things.
And I'm sure that they'll last for a long time and you're probably pretty happy that
you did and invest the money and go ahead and get them.
I sent some tapes out here to George, May and Grandma both on the same day.
Actually it's the day before I sent this last tape that you received from me.
I expect some answers from them here pretty soon.
Georgia May hasn't sent me any tapes since I sent her tape recorder,
but I don't know why.
I just got my tape recorder, which would tape on reels,
just a few weeks ago,
and I don't think there's been any excuse why she couldn't have sent some tapes to me.
So I made a first step and sent one to her, and I sent one to Grandma also.
And I hope to hear from them within the next couple of days on a tape.
I got two rolls of movie film back that I took up there in Hong Kong and I've got three
more still out yet.
I should be receiving them, I'd say within the next week or so.
And this buddy of mine that stands watch with me, he's also got a Super 8 movie camera and
he's got some film waiting to be processed and when he gets all his back and when I get
mine back we're going to borrow a projector from one of the guys there on the ship and
We're going to show movies some night on watch,
and we'll get a chance to look at all the good pictures that we took over here and all that.
And I suppose I'll probably go ahead and send mine on home,
or I might keep them out here because when we get back in San Diego,
I'm going to go into one of these pawn shops that they have.
They've got quite a few of them in there.
And I'm going to see if I can buy a Super 8 projector for a pretty good price.
I feel that I could buy one in one of those shops just as cheap as I could possibly buy one over here.
I saw some there before in the state, before we came overseas here.
And with a projector, I feel that you have a chance to look it over a little bit more better than what you would a camera.
And you couldn't go wrong in buying a projector from one of these people, but I wouldn't want to buy a camera from them.
so I'm going to look for a projector when I do get back in the States
and I might keep my movies out here so I can show them to George May and everybody
and if not I'll send them on home to you
and of course you won't be able to look at them either
because you don't have a projector so it won't be doing you much good
but they'll last for a while I'm pretty sure
and I'll be really eager to show them to you when I do come home the next time
I plan to shoot some film depicting some of the activities that go on the ship here during
the daytime.
Some day when I find a pretty clear day I'll get some helicopter operations and some of
the things that happen here on the ship are part of the daily routine.
It'll kind of be a little film story of what happens up here on station every day.
Well, I'm kind of glad I haven't put in for leave upon arrival in the state because
when I do go home the next time I like to have at least 20 days and I'd possibly like
to have 30 days leave.
But the situation is now on the ship that they are going to frown on giving anybody
leave in excess of 15 days when we get back in the state.
And it sounds just like the Jewett trying to mess with the troops on policies like this.
I don't really see why they want to be this way, and nobody else can understand it either,
because we are due back in the States and plan to be in there for quite a long time.
A lot of these guys haven't went on leave for a year at least.
And we're just getting back in the States from six months over here, and I think if
They ought to grant maximum leave and liberty.
But they got something up their sleeve.
They got some plans of their own, I suppose,
where the captain doesn't want to have everybody off running all over the country
because he probably wants to keep as many people on this ship as he can,
even though we're going to stay tight after that Pier 2 back in San Diego for quite a while.
It doesn't sound like being very fair to a lot of people,
but I'm sure most of the guys will be happy to get to go home anyway on leave.
And those of us who aren't going on leave will be getting maximum liberty, I hope,
as far as we know, if the situation is going to be like that.
Maximum liberty there for, I don't know how long it's going to last, to be truthful with you,
but at least we'll get it for a couple of days, maybe two days, maybe two weeks, maybe two months.
I don't know. It all remains to be seen.
but they did say that those who do not take leave now and want leave during Christmas time will get
preference over the other people so uh by Christmas time I'll have about 25 days
and if I decide to take my leave then I suppose I'll get all the 25 days that I have earned
I'll be able to come home for the uh full length time that I want to if not I might hold off for
just a month or so more and then I get the whole 30 days leave but we'll let the days of leave
build up before I really count on what I'm going to do with them it's quite a long ways off and I'd
like to get through most of this summer and the fall and then start planning on what I'm going to
do with my time that I've got built up oh yeah I received a letter the other day from
Naval Reserve Training Center in Decatur, Illinois.
Some of the guys that picked up the mail for us brought it down to me.
He says, oh, it looks like you got a draft notice there.
And I says, no, it's from the Reserve Center.
He says, I can tell you what's in it right now without even opening it up.
I said, it's a letter that's asking me what I've been doing over here.
How about letting them know what I'm up to, what the duty is like,
and everything like that.
So I opened it up, and that's just exactly what it was.
It was from the recruiting officer.
some guy whom I've never heard of before.
He must be somebody new down there.
Congratulating me on my active duty assignment
and hoping that my two years will be very interesting and informative
and wanting to know what the duty was like over here
and what it was like on the ship and what I was up to.
He enclosed a little postcard, postage paid for me
to fill out the information on it and send back to him.
Well, I typed up a letter, a one-page typewritten letter, and sent an envelope back to them,
and also with a picture postcard of the ship so they can post on the bulletin board down there,
and it sort of satisfied him pretty well.
I told him to let me know if anything had been happening back there.
He said that the letter, if I had any questions or anything, any problems or difficulties,
just to let him know, and he'll work them out for me.
So they seem like they're really in there, really trying to satisfy everybody and make them happy.
So they should be getting my letter within three or four days.
And I have it posted down there on the booking board for some of these new recruits coming in there to read.
And they'll look at it like I did when I first came in, reading those letters posted down there and wonder what it's all about.
and they'll find out just like I did and they'll have all their questions answered
and they'll be able to tell everybody else what it's about in a couple of years.
You should have received my short note with the money order right now
and I'll be sending some more money home this next payday.
We get paid Thursday, this being Saturday morning right now.
to get paid Thursday again and I'll be sending another hundred dollars home.
I set a goal for myself when I came over here to have $1,500 in the bank by the time I got back
to the States. Well, due to the fact that I spent a little bit more money over here than what I
planned to, I have cut that goal down to a thousand dollars and I think I should be able
to reach that without any trouble. So I'm going to be sending money home every payday and I've
got nothing else to spend it on over here. I've got no other big things that I want to
spend my money on. I've bought everything that I want, and I expect to have $1,000 or
more in the bank by the time I do get back to the States. You know, when Bill came aboard
the ship here in Da Nang, he paid me the $30 that he owed me, and he gave me this MPC,
which is this military payment certificate which they use over here in some military
areas. They use it throughout Vietnam and we use it up in Japan. Well he gave it to me
to pay me off which I accept it as legal and I figured I could cash this in in Hong Kong
because they think it's about any kind of currency there and I couldn't get rid of it there
but one day here on the ship they were accepting it while we were in hong kong and
they were going to accept it at nine o'clock at the dispersing office well it just so happened
that liberty went at nine o'clock that morning i was scheduled to go on a tour at 10 o'clock
so i had to take liberty and leave the ship at nine o'clock no later in order to be to the tour
on time and I couldn't catch my MPC in and they wouldn't do any favors for me they wouldn't accept
it any later any sooner so I was stuck with it so my other excuse me my only alternative was to send
it back a bill and tell him to buy a money order with it or buy travel checks with it and send it
back to me if he couldn't do that send green back if he could get a hold of him if he couldn't do
that just to hold on to it and pay me back some other time because it's being pretty useless to me
and they do change this from time to time so if i was to keep it for a very long time i probably
wouldn't be able to cash it in anywhere it's useless back in the state actually they call it
funny money it's just uh it's just about what it is it's more that's like play money but it does
have the feeling and texture of American currency. It's made of that fine paper. And he should
have got it by now. I don't know what he's going to do with it. He'll probably go out
and have a big party or something with it, and then he'll pay me back later on. I don't
know. So it's been kind of a runaround with that situation right there.
While this tape is just about to run out on this site, I have a few more words to say.
so I'm going to wind it up on this side of the tape and I'll see you over on side two
there it is
they're hot
okay back again i mentioned there that we stopped sunday in denang where our usually
Excuse me, our usual stop there was pretty much par for the course.
We weren't scheduled to stop in there as far as an advance schedule had been put out
in regards to all of our stops over here.
So I wasn't able to write ahead to Bill and tell him to meet me in there
if he wanted to come up to the ship and see me.
We were there for a pretty short time.
I know it would have been pretty useless for him to make the trip and come up there.
it was a typical day there clear and hot i took the 50 caliber machine gun watch like i always do
when we stop in there i shot a few feet of movie film of the harbor and the area around there
to show you back home and later on the afternoon we got underway and proceeded on up here to come
on stake. It started raining here later in the afternoon just before we left.
I suppose the troops over there on the beach kind of welcomed that quite a bit
because Bill told me that the sand and the sun over there that doesn't do too
much to help the temperatures very much. It gets pretty hot so I suppose they
welcome the rain there if they had that afternoon then Monday morning we passed
through Yankee Station this is where they have the three aircraft carriers
and their various destroyers and their escort ships down there with them I got
a picture one of the aircraft carriers down there I believe it was the
Triconderoga. You probably read about it in the newspaper. We also refueled from an oiler there.
I got some pictures of that also. Most of our refuelings take place at night, and you can't
take pictures at night, of course. But this one took place during a daytime when I had one of my
buddies take the camera up and shoot a few feet of movie film while I was down there on my refueling
station. So we're scheduled to refuel again tonight from the oiler. It's, like I mentioned
before, it's something that they like to do over here, and they seem to want to do it more at
nighttime than what they do during the daytime. So we're also supposed to take on some stores from a
store shift. So it's going to be a pretty full evening of activity starting about eight o'clock
tonight and probably going to carry on up to midnight. But since tomorrow is Sunday,
everybody gets knocked off at 9.30 in the morning, and we have movies in the afternoon
and bingo games and ice cream, and you can lay in your rack or you can go up in sunbaths.
That's if you're not on watch, if you don't have other work to do, if your spaces are
clean and squared away. So it's quite a big deal here. Sunday is here on the Jewett. It's
church services and everything like this. So everybody looks forward to Sunday.
Well, I've kind of run out of words and news and everything for now.
So I'm going to sign off here and wind this up. I'll be waiting to hear from everyone again. Go
ahead and send a tape whenever you want to. I'm always glad to hear everyone's voices. And I know
you've always got a lot to talk about and whenever I receive a tape from you
I'm really eager to answer it and send one right back so I'll be waiting to
hear from you either in a tape or a letter either one and I hope David
starting to enjoy summer vacation already I'm glad that he's gonna have a lot of
fun there and make the most of it we'll probably be spending a lot of days out there at
the pool it's pretty good for him to go out there and soak up some of that sunshine and
just have a pretty good time but really get that book there during summer school and get
the summer school work out of the way and then go ahead and be on your own do what you want to
there for the rest of the day i hope mother i hope you get most of your work you got planned
during the summer taken care of and uh sorry your jobs are concerned dad you mentioned it
I'm going to have three jobs to go to now.
One I'm going to be over with before the summer is through.
It's going to be part of the traveling there,
but I suppose you'll get used to it and it won't be too difficult.
So I'll sign off here and be waiting to hear from everyone back home once again.
So long.
Thanks for watching!

1968-06-08.text: Hello, Mother, Dad, and David. Well, today is June the 7th, and in about five more minutes it'll be June the 8th, because it's five minutes till midnight here, and I'm preparing to stand the mid-watch, which will last till 4 o'clock this morning. I've been standing these watches all week. We We stand the same watch for one week and then we rotate to the next watch section. That way it doesn't get too boring. As I was getting ready to say, I received your tape that you sent. So that all three of you spoke on. I was real glad to hear from everybody. I was waiting to hear from you because I was eager to send another tape. And I expected that today I would receive a tape from you and I did. So I was pretty glad to hear from everyone. Well, I guess the first thing I'll talk about is what has really happened right now with the death of Senator Kennedy. We found out about this yesterday afternoon about 4 o'clock over here and they started flying a flag at half-mast and everything. It's kind of a tragic happening and it kind of makes you wonder if it would be better to stay over here than to go back to the States because of the things happening like that. But there's something wrong there somewhere, which I'm sure a lot of people realize, and it's just too bad that it had to happen twice in the same family. That's all I'll say about that. Tuesday we arrived up here on Station after stopping in Da Nang for about four hours on Monday. We got up here Tuesday and put in our first full day on station. And about 1 o'clock in the afternoon, we got right into the swing of things because there was an A-5 shot down about 13 miles from the ship, just as it was coming back to the aircraft carrier from a strike over there on the beach. And it had two pilots aboard. So we sent out our helicopter to rescue him, and they picked up one out of the water, and they couldn't find the other one. The ones they did bring back were pretty bad. He had a couple of broken bones, a broken collar bone. He was in pretty bad shape. They brought him aboard, took him to sick bay, and I saw him on a stretcher as they took him by, and they was giving him plasma as they was taking him to sick bay. They kept him here on the ship for just a couple of hours and they put him back in the helicopter and took him over to the aircraft carriers for further treatment. And later on in the afternoon about 4 o'clock, our sister ship up here picked up some wreckage of the plane and they sent it over to us so we could send it back for investigation purposes. and among us was the life jacket of the other pilot which was torn up pretty bad so they know for sure that the other pilot didn't survive and most of the plane wreckage was in pretty bad shape. The material that those planes are made out of is something that will shatter pretty easy and can bend without any difficulty. It's all aluminum. and in between the wings it has this honeycomb aluminum stuff like to give it weight and make make it so it's not so uh flexible it's more or less a filler and uh that stuff here is pretty easy and can be shattered by shrapnel and everything so we had uh quite a bit of excitement there. We haven't had any more SAR rescues in the past few days, but I suppose we'll be having some more because the strikes are pretty heavy over there, and there are some pretty good anti-aircraft fire from the ground at them planes, and I expect we'll be picking up a couple more pilots while we're still up here. You mentioned in your tape that you read something about the aircraft carrier America launching planes over here going in for airstrikes. Well, this is one of the carriers that's on station over here too with us and I believe this is their first time to come over here to Westpac on a cruise. It's a fairly new aircraft carrier and I don't know very much about it. The possibility might be a chance that I would see it in some port before we go home and if we do I'll take some pictures and so you know a little bit what it looks like at least. Most of those aircraft carriers, they all look the same, and there's no big difference between them. Speaking of aircraft carriers, the Enterprise, I'm sure you've all heard of it, is expected to return to the States about the same time we are, and we got a message the other day that our step is to escort the Enterprise back to the States and arrive there on July the 18th. We're not going to make any stops in Australia or any other places. We're not going to cross the equator like we had planned to do because we're going to go back by the northern route when we take the Enterprise back. But of course these plans will probably change like everything else does here in the Navy. They never do have any definite plans, but this is just what the word is out now. This is official, and I suppose it could change just as easily as anything else could. We've only got about 40 days left over here and it's going to be real good to get back in the state again and see how some decent people live and know that people aren't always trying to take you for your money and take advantage of you like they do in these sports. It's too bad it has to be that way but I can't say that I did have a pretty good time over here and I did see a lot of the Far East over here and I'm pretty satisfied that I know a little bit more about it than what I did when I came over here. And I know it's an experience that I won't forget. I'm glad I've got pictures and souvenirs for memories of various places and things that I did over here. I received a letter from Bill the other day, and he mentioned that he had 270-some days or whatever it is left over here. I imagine those guys take a pretty good attitude towards that. It's more of less a joke to them because they're over there for more than a year whereas I've only been over here for six months by the time I get back to the states but uh we are getting pretty short on time over here and uh it's just a matter of sticking out these last few days on station and then we'll turn the ship around and start heading back east again uh and Bill's letter he also mentioned about getting wounded by the grenade shrapnel and it sounds just like him it sounds like some of his old pranks of boyhood that he used to pull he He should have known better, and I'm sure that he did learn a lesson by it. He did send me a tape that I received from him, which was fairly interesting. He talked on both sides of it. And he was interrupted there once by, they were launching mortar attacks or something on him. He was always saying, can you hear that in the background? Can you hear that? Well, I couldn't hear anything. I'm sure it was there. and you said he's mentioned this in your tapes before there's always something here in the background going off i'd wait to say that this is fairly true and uh i couldn't hear anything of course he might have been hearing things himself like you said those guys probably uh have an effect on him from uh all that shell shock or whatever you might refer to it as and He might have been hearing things himself. He said in his letter about this major coming up there and calling them pigs and everything. So I wrote back to him. I said, well, Phil, how does it feel to be a pig? And I hope he took this in a joking manner. If he read it correctly, he would have. But those guys probably were having more of an R&R situation up there where they were having more fun than really getting down to business. That really tears me up that they have to have mustard at 7.30 in the morning and have to get up at 7 o'clock because we get up at 6 o'clock here on the ship every day, including Saturdays and Sundays. And you don't find yourself laying in the rack at any hours between 8 o'clock in the morning and 4 o'clock in the afternoon, unless it's during your noon hour for one hour. If you don't have the watch, you can go up there and sleep for an hour. But you better get out of that wreck when the noon hour is over when you get back and start doing some work or something. You're looking busy. But I know that he probably has the attitude, and most of those guys do up there, like you mentioned, that just because they're over here, they should be a little bit more slack. That's true. He mentioned in one of his tapes that when he stopped at the Marine Air Base, the guys around there were all wearing starched utilities and foot shine shoes and real squared away in their military appearance but he kind of felt like he was out of place because he had his mustache and they don't allow mustaches there at that base and his utilities were not pressed or anything like that, and he had dirty shoes. And I suppose that this Major, whoever he was that came up there, was trying to keep the morale up a little bit. I suppose if they could let guys get back on their heels like that and they start sliding, it would be pretty bad. So I'd say it was all for their own good. They probably don't realize this. Some of them might, and I don't think it would hurt them any because being in the service, you'll find that they'll do things to you one time that you don't particularly appreciate, and the next time they'll come around and it'll all be over with and you will be used to it. And I'll just sum it up in a couple of words. He'll get over it. He'll get used to it because there's no other thing that he can do. Mother, you asked me in my last letter that after looking at the pictures that I sent home with me and Bill, it looked like we had both grown quite a bit. Well, I don't know whether I've mentioned this or not, but I weigh 194 pounds, now. I weighed myself in Hong Kong. And by my calculation, this is just about 20 pounds more than I weighed when I came on active duty. Bill, I couldn't tell whether he had grown too much or not, whether he was putting on any weight or anything, because he had those utilities on, and they seemed to fit him pretty loosely. And I couldn't really tell, but I know that he does weigh more than I do. And he seemed to me like he could have grown a little bit of course after not really seeing him I didn't pay too much attention to his physical features because we had a lot to talk about but I'd say that he probably has put on a little bit of weight I don't know he says that they don't have too much to eat that their chow doesn't quite compare to the good food we have here on the ship so I don't know I don't know whether that's quite any factor in his growth or not well I got pretty good news back here today it's not nothing too important but uh i got my results back to my usafi test in the electronic correspondence course and i got a passing mark in it and i got a certificate signed by the usafi uh directors and uh it was also signed by the commanding officer the chief the captain and a couple of papers to be entered in my service record about it and the next day i went down and tried to do more courses and i should have them within the next three weeks or and I'll be spending a lot of my time back in the States working on them. I suppose on nights when I have liberty, I plan to go into San Diego to the public library and do a little bit of studying on them and get them done. It'd be kind of a way to get away from the chip and also take liberty and not spend too much money. I got an application back from the State of Illinois Veterans Commission for this $100 Vietnam bonus for servicemen who are veterans or who are on duty over here. And I've filled out my part of it. I took it up to the chief's office, and they have to fill out some information on there and notarize it, but I'll be sending it back. I took it up there about a week ago, and they haven't done anything with it yet. They seem to resent doing paperwork. But I'm going to go up in the morning and see if they've got it done, and if they do, I'm going to send it back out. Bill also applied for this, and he mentioned in his tape that he didn't sign it or something. I don't know what he did. So he had to fill out another one. I sent it back to him. He had to fill it out again, and he's going to send his back in. Dad mentioned on his tape about these Veterans Administration benefits for guys who go to college or who take an apprenticeship program. I hope he's not confusing this with the GI Bill. If not, it sounds like a real good deal because under the GI Bill, you get $130 a month for a college education. Or if you take an apprenticeship program, you get a certain percentage according to your wage scale that you're getting paid. And if it's $110 a month or whatever it was that he mentioned, it can be used in addition to the GI Bill. I would say that it's a pretty good deal. And if a guy wouldn't take further education, either an apprenticeship or a college, he'd really be hurting himself because the money's there. All you have to do is just ask for it. And I'd like to take advantage of it one way or the other. I don't really know just exactly how I want to, but I got plenty of time to think that over. and you can make sure I'm going to make use of the benefits. You know, here in the Navy, they always say, well, reenlist, look at all the benefits you get. Well, my attitude is get out of the Navy. You've got more benefits out of the Navy than what you have in here. But there are some guys that fall for that line. I guess they've got nothing better to do with themselves. So they kind of like to stay around and take some of the benefits that the Navy says that they have to offer them. And they seem to be pretty satisfied with it, but I don't think that I would be. Well, I suppose David, I hope that he has got the radio by now that I sent him. I hope he's pretty happy with it and does what he wants it to. Like I mentioned in the letter, I didn't have a chance to play it over here to pick up any United States stations to see how well it works. So it was fairly inexpensive, and it looked like a good radio. I'm sure it should do a pretty good job, and I'd like to hear from him, just exactly how it works. I want them to be honest with me, tell me exactly if it picks up the stations it wants to and how it sounds and everything, because I'd be pretty interested to find out. About the table radio that you asked me to buy, I'm kind of mad at myself because I couldn't buy the one that I wanted to when I had the chance to. It was a Sony table radio with a clock on it. It was AM and FM in a walnut cabinet. It measured about 4 inches high. It was about 12 inches long and about 8 inches deep. It had a walnut wood grain cabinet and it was really nice. It only cost $32. It was transistorized with an AC plug on it to use on house current. I wish I could have picked it up there in Hong Kong when I had a chance to, but they didn't have any back in Subic Bay. I'm going to look again when I get back there. and we'll do the stop there for possibly one or two days before we go back to the States. And I'd sure like to get this for you because it's a real nice radio, but don't let your hopes down. I want to try to keep in there and try to get it. I don't think I'm going to get you anything but that one because I haven't found anything over here that's quite as nice as that or anything that I myself would particularly want to have. So there's still a slight chance I might be able to get it for you. Well, I got the stitches taken out of my arm the other day, I'd say about a week ago, from the little laceration there that I suffered in Hong Kong. I suppose my big trouble there was why I slipped and fell down them stairs was because I didn't have my land legs back again. You know, how us sailors get after we've been out at sea for such a long time and used to the motion of the ship and we acquired a different way of walking. Well, I suppose my difficulty right there was I wasn't used to walking on the land, and as a result, I suffered a fall, which I don't think that's really why it happened. I was just not watching what I was doing. But I got the stitches out now, and it's got a little bit of a scab still left on there. And where it was cut at, it's still rather red. I don't know whether it's going to get its color back again or not or whether it's going to be a little scar there. but we'll see what it's going to look like here in a couple more weeks. I'll probably go outside and I'll pick up a little bit of sun on it and it'll probably take the color again. It won't have that red and pink color to it if I get some sun on it. Well, I was glad to hear that you got some new furniture there for the bedroom. I know it's going to help the appearance quite a bit back here and a bunk bed that sounds just like old times there. I'm sure David's pretty happy about it and I know he is pretty anxious to get up there and sleep in that top bunk. I'll tell him this, that our bunks, I'm going to refer to them as racks, our racks here on the ship are three high and I've got a top one. And I'll tell you, when I come home, I'm not going to crowd him out of that top one. I'll let him have the top one and I'll sleep in the bottom one because it's just, well Well as it is right now on the ship it's pretty warm in them top racks because we're over here where it's a little bit warmer and when the ship is underway it generates more heat inside the ship because they got the boilers and everything lit off. But even with the air conditioning you do get a little bit of heat up towards the ceiling in the ship and it's fairly warm up there. I can sleep up there without a shirt or without a sheet or a blanket or anything and still not be exactly comfortable. But I'm sure it's going to make a lot more room back here in the bedroom and give David some more room for some of his things. And I'm sure that they'll last for a long time and you're probably pretty happy that you did and invest the money and go ahead and get them. I sent some tapes out here to George, May and Grandma both on the same day. Actually it's the day before I sent this last tape that you received from me. I expect some answers from them here pretty soon. Georgia May hasn't sent me any tapes since I sent her tape recorder, but I don't know why. I just got my tape recorder, which would tape on reels, just a few weeks ago, and I don't think there's been any excuse why she couldn't have sent some tapes to me. So I made a first step and sent one to her, and I sent one to Grandma also. And I hope to hear from them within the next couple of days on a tape. I got two rolls of movie film back that I took up there in Hong Kong and I've got three more still out yet. I should be receiving them, I'd say within the next week or so. And this buddy of mine that stands watch with me, he's also got a Super 8 movie camera and he's got some film waiting to be processed and when he gets all his back and when I get mine back we're going to borrow a projector from one of the guys there on the ship and We're going to show movies some night on watch, and we'll get a chance to look at all the good pictures that we took over here and all that. And I suppose I'll probably go ahead and send mine on home, or I might keep them out here because when we get back in San Diego, I'm going to go into one of these pawn shops that they have. They've got quite a few of them in there. And I'm going to see if I can buy a Super 8 projector for a pretty good price. I feel that I could buy one in one of those shops just as cheap as I could possibly buy one over here. I saw some there before in the state, before we came overseas here. And with a projector, I feel that you have a chance to look it over a little bit more better than what you would a camera. And you couldn't go wrong in buying a projector from one of these people, but I wouldn't want to buy a camera from them. so I'm going to look for a projector when I do get back in the States and I might keep my movies out here so I can show them to George May and everybody and if not I'll send them on home to you and of course you won't be able to look at them either because you don't have a projector so it won't be doing you much good but they'll last for a while I'm pretty sure and I'll be really eager to show them to you when I do come home the next time I plan to shoot some film depicting some of the activities that go on the ship here during the daytime. Some day when I find a pretty clear day I'll get some helicopter operations and some of the things that happen here on the ship are part of the daily routine. It'll kind of be a little film story of what happens up here on station every day. Well, I'm kind of glad I haven't put in for leave upon arrival in the state because when I do go home the next time I like to have at least 20 days and I'd possibly like to have 30 days leave. But the situation is now on the ship that they are going to frown on giving anybody leave in excess of 15 days when we get back in the state. And it sounds just like the Jewett trying to mess with the troops on policies like this. I don't really see why they want to be this way, and nobody else can understand it either, because we are due back in the States and plan to be in there for quite a long time. A lot of these guys haven't went on leave for a year at least. And we're just getting back in the States from six months over here, and I think if They ought to grant maximum leave and liberty. But they got something up their sleeve. They got some plans of their own, I suppose, where the captain doesn't want to have everybody off running all over the country because he probably wants to keep as many people on this ship as he can, even though we're going to stay tight after that Pier 2 back in San Diego for quite a while. It doesn't sound like being very fair to a lot of people, but I'm sure most of the guys will be happy to get to go home anyway on leave. And those of us who aren't going on leave will be getting maximum liberty, I hope, as far as we know, if the situation is going to be like that. Maximum liberty there for, I don't know how long it's going to last, to be truthful with you, but at least we'll get it for a couple of days, maybe two days, maybe two weeks, maybe two months. I don't know. It all remains to be seen. but they did say that those who do not take leave now and want leave during Christmas time will get preference over the other people so uh by Christmas time I'll have about 25 days and if I decide to take my leave then I suppose I'll get all the 25 days that I have earned I'll be able to come home for the uh full length time that I want to if not I might hold off for just a month or so more and then I get the whole 30 days leave but we'll let the days of leave build up before I really count on what I'm going to do with them it's quite a long ways off and I'd like to get through most of this summer and the fall and then start planning on what I'm going to do with my time that I've got built up oh yeah I received a letter the other day from Naval Reserve Training Center in Decatur, Illinois. Some of the guys that picked up the mail for us brought it down to me. He says, oh, it looks like you got a draft notice there. And I says, no, it's from the Reserve Center. He says, I can tell you what's in it right now without even opening it up. I said, it's a letter that's asking me what I've been doing over here. How about letting them know what I'm up to, what the duty is like, and everything like that. So I opened it up, and that's just exactly what it was. It was from the recruiting officer. some guy whom I've never heard of before. He must be somebody new down there. Congratulating me on my active duty assignment and hoping that my two years will be very interesting and informative and wanting to know what the duty was like over here and what it was like on the ship and what I was up to. He enclosed a little postcard, postage paid for me to fill out the information on it and send back to him. Well, I typed up a letter, a one-page typewritten letter, and sent an envelope back to them, and also with a picture postcard of the ship so they can post on the bulletin board down there, and it sort of satisfied him pretty well. I told him to let me know if anything had been happening back there. He said that the letter, if I had any questions or anything, any problems or difficulties, just to let him know, and he'll work them out for me. So they seem like they're really in there, really trying to satisfy everybody and make them happy. So they should be getting my letter within three or four days. And I have it posted down there on the booking board for some of these new recruits coming in there to read. And they'll look at it like I did when I first came in, reading those letters posted down there and wonder what it's all about. and they'll find out just like I did and they'll have all their questions answered and they'll be able to tell everybody else what it's about in a couple of years. You should have received my short note with the money order right now and I'll be sending some more money home this next payday. We get paid Thursday, this being Saturday morning right now. to get paid Thursday again and I'll be sending another hundred dollars home. I set a goal for myself when I came over here to have $1,500 in the bank by the time I got back to the States. Well, due to the fact that I spent a little bit more money over here than what I planned to, I have cut that goal down to a thousand dollars and I think I should be able to reach that without any trouble. So I'm going to be sending money home every payday and I've got nothing else to spend it on over here. I've got no other big things that I want to spend my money on. I've bought everything that I want, and I expect to have $1,000 or more in the bank by the time I do get back to the States. You know, when Bill came aboard the ship here in Da Nang, he paid me the $30 that he owed me, and he gave me this MPC, which is this military payment certificate which they use over here in some military areas. They use it throughout Vietnam and we use it up in Japan. Well he gave it to me to pay me off which I accept it as legal and I figured I could cash this in in Hong Kong because they think it's about any kind of currency there and I couldn't get rid of it there but one day here on the ship they were accepting it while we were in hong kong and they were going to accept it at nine o'clock at the dispersing office well it just so happened that liberty went at nine o'clock that morning i was scheduled to go on a tour at 10 o'clock so i had to take liberty and leave the ship at nine o'clock no later in order to be to the tour on time and I couldn't catch my MPC in and they wouldn't do any favors for me they wouldn't accept it any later any sooner so I was stuck with it so my other excuse me my only alternative was to send it back a bill and tell him to buy a money order with it or buy travel checks with it and send it back to me if he couldn't do that send green back if he could get a hold of him if he couldn't do that just to hold on to it and pay me back some other time because it's being pretty useless to me and they do change this from time to time so if i was to keep it for a very long time i probably wouldn't be able to cash it in anywhere it's useless back in the state actually they call it funny money it's just uh it's just about what it is it's more that's like play money but it does have the feeling and texture of American currency. It's made of that fine paper. And he should have got it by now. I don't know what he's going to do with it. He'll probably go out and have a big party or something with it, and then he'll pay me back later on. I don't know. So it's been kind of a runaround with that situation right there. While this tape is just about to run out on this site, I have a few more words to say. so I'm going to wind it up on this side of the tape and I'll see you over on side two there it is they're hot okay back again i mentioned there that we stopped sunday in denang where our usually Excuse me, our usual stop there was pretty much par for the course. We weren't scheduled to stop in there as far as an advance schedule had been put out in regards to all of our stops over here. So I wasn't able to write ahead to Bill and tell him to meet me in there if he wanted to come up to the ship and see me. We were there for a pretty short time. I know it would have been pretty useless for him to make the trip and come up there. it was a typical day there clear and hot i took the 50 caliber machine gun watch like i always do when we stop in there i shot a few feet of movie film of the harbor and the area around there to show you back home and later on the afternoon we got underway and proceeded on up here to come on stake. It started raining here later in the afternoon just before we left. I suppose the troops over there on the beach kind of welcomed that quite a bit because Bill told me that the sand and the sun over there that doesn't do too much to help the temperatures very much. It gets pretty hot so I suppose they welcome the rain there if they had that afternoon then Monday morning we passed through Yankee Station this is where they have the three aircraft carriers and their various destroyers and their escort ships down there with them I got a picture one of the aircraft carriers down there I believe it was the Triconderoga. You probably read about it in the newspaper. We also refueled from an oiler there. I got some pictures of that also. Most of our refuelings take place at night, and you can't take pictures at night, of course. But this one took place during a daytime when I had one of my buddies take the camera up and shoot a few feet of movie film while I was down there on my refueling station. So we're scheduled to refuel again tonight from the oiler. It's, like I mentioned before, it's something that they like to do over here, and they seem to want to do it more at nighttime than what they do during the daytime. So we're also supposed to take on some stores from a store shift. So it's going to be a pretty full evening of activity starting about eight o'clock tonight and probably going to carry on up to midnight. But since tomorrow is Sunday, everybody gets knocked off at 9.30 in the morning, and we have movies in the afternoon and bingo games and ice cream, and you can lay in your rack or you can go up in sunbaths. That's if you're not on watch, if you don't have other work to do, if your spaces are clean and squared away. So it's quite a big deal here. Sunday is here on the Jewett. It's church services and everything like this. So everybody looks forward to Sunday. Well, I've kind of run out of words and news and everything for now. So I'm going to sign off here and wind this up. I'll be waiting to hear from everyone again. Go ahead and send a tape whenever you want to. I'm always glad to hear everyone's voices. And I know you've always got a lot to talk about and whenever I receive a tape from you I'm really eager to answer it and send one right back so I'll be waiting to hear from you either in a tape or a letter either one and I hope David starting to enjoy summer vacation already I'm glad that he's gonna have a lot of fun there and make the most of it we'll probably be spending a lot of days out there at the pool it's pretty good for him to go out there and soak up some of that sunshine and just have a pretty good time but really get that book there during summer school and get the summer school work out of the way and then go ahead and be on your own do what you want to there for the rest of the day i hope mother i hope you get most of your work you got planned during the summer taken care of and uh sorry your jobs are concerned dad you mentioned it I'm going to have three jobs to go to now. One I'm going to be over with before the summer is through. It's going to be part of the traveling there, but I suppose you'll get used to it and it won't be too difficult. So I'll sign off here and be waiting to hear from everyone back home once again. So long. Thanks for watching!

1968-06-13.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-06-13.text:
Thursday 9 PM
13 June, 1968

Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother and Dad,

Our past three days up here have been quite active with more than the usual everyday happenings. It all started about 3 AM Tuesday when one of our planes was shot down overland. The search continued into the next morning and one of the helicopters got hit by some small arms fire from some VC troops on the side of a hill. They landed back here and one of it's crew was hit in both legs from the machine gun fire. They gave him some treatment here then sent him off to the carrier for futher aid. They finally gave up the pilot for lost and called off the search. Later in the day one of the helo's on deck couldn't be launched because of engine trouble. We then proceeded to an aircraft carrier to have it lifted off by crane. Well it got dark by the time we got there and it looked like too risky of an operation anyway so they called that off too. Yesterday we set course for Da Nang to have another helo lift it off our deck. We got there about midnight and stayed over night. At 8:00 this morning they brought out a flying crane and lifted it off. We then got underway and are now back here on SAR station. They had some Migs get in pretty close up here this afternoon while we were gone but there hasn't been anything happen yet.

I got your letter of the 4th, today on Tuesday the 11th. As you can tell thats rather slow. We didn't get mail for three days and thats probably why. I decided to wait till today so I could mail these money orders. Today was pay day. Put $130 in the bank and use the $10 for the stuff I had you get me and the postage to mail it. Since you have already sent the box there is a good chance I may get it during our next refueling from an oiler which may be tomorrow because of the trip to Da Nang. We cruised at 29 knots (49 mph) all the way there and back. The only time we do get packages out here is when we refuel from the oilers.

I suppose you have got the tape I sent a few days ago. I hope every one liked it.

Have you started getting the "All Hands" magazines yet? I forgot to ask you many times. I suppose you have though, because I mailed in the supscription about two months ago.

I'm glad to hear David got his cast off and can go swimming now. How's he doing in summer school?

Well thats about all there is from here. I'll be waiting to hear from you again. Bye for now.

Your son,

Mike

1968-06-13.label: Herald Review - Two Brothers from Decatur
1968-06-13.attribution: Herald Review - Two Brothers from Decatur — Ducy Family Archives
1968-06-13.text:
HERALD & REVIEW — "TWO BROTHERS FROM DECATUR"
Newspaper clipping, Decatur Herald & Review (Decatur, Illinois)
Published ~summer 1968 (event date: June 13, 1968)
1 clipping with two photos

========================================================================================
PHOTOS
========================================================================================

[Top photo: Michael F. Ducy in Navy dress blues with white "dixie cup" hat,
wearing glasses. Caption: "Michael F. Ducy"]

[Bottom photo: William Ducy in Marine Corps uniform with garrison cover,
wearing glasses. Caption: "William Ducy"]

[Red editorial stamp/mark across Mike's photo, partially legible]


========================================================================================
ARTICLE TEXT
========================================================================================

TWO BROTHERS from Decatur, P.O. 3.C. Michael F. Ducy, 20, and Pfc. William
Ducy, 18, sons of Mr. and Mrs. Daniel Ducy of 1525 N. Ellen Ave., recently
met in DaNang, South Vietnam.

Michael is serving aboard the destroyer, USS Jovett [sic], which is stationed
in the Gulf of Tonkin. William, with the Marine Corps 7th communications
battalion, flew to DaNang Harbor in a helicopter and visited his brother
eight hours.

Michael, a member of the Naval Reserve, began active duty in August. William
who has been in Vietnam since February, enlisted in August.

Both men attended MacArthur High School.


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

This article describes the June 13, 1968 reunion at Da Nang Harbor when
USS Jouett anchored in Da Nang and Bill flew out by helicopter from the
7th Communications Battalion compound to visit Mike aboard ship. They spent
eight hours together — the only time the two brothers saw each other during
their overlapping Vietnam tours.

Corrections and context:
- The paper misspells Jouett as "Jovett"
- Jouett was a guided missile frigate (DLG), not a destroyer, though the
  terms were sometimes used loosely in civilian press
- Mike's rank: P.O. 3.C. = Petty Officer Third Class (FTG3), age 20
- Bill's rank: Pfc. = Private First Class (USMC), age 18
- Mike "began active duty in August" — reported to Treasure Island Aug 16, 1967
- Bill "has been in Vietnam since February, enlisted in August" — enlisted
  August 1967, arrived Vietnam February 1968
- Both attended MacArthur High School in Decatur, Illinois
- Family address: 1525 N. Ellen Ave., Decatur (matches all other correspondence)

The visit is documented across multiple sources in the collection:
- Mike's June 13, 1968 letter home
- Tape 6 (June 22, 1968) — Mike describes the visit on audio
- Mike's Super 8 film "Da Nang Harbor, Flying Crane" (June 13, 1968)
- Bill's letters to Mike also reference the visit

This newspaper clipping is a key documentary artifact — it's the hometown
paper's coverage of the central narrative event: two brothers from small-town
Illinois meeting in a war zone.

Publication: Decatur Herald & Review (now Herald-Review), Decatur, Illinois.

1968-06-13.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG-29) 1968 CRUISE BOOK — PAGES 120-121

In a highly unique sequence of events, an SH-3 helicopter experienced mechanical
difficulty while on board, and was unable to fly off for needed repairs. Too large to
fit the ship's hangar, the SH-3 was moved forward on the flight deck, while flight
operations continued with the UH-2. JOUETT made a hurried voyage to the port of
DaNang, where a U.S. Army "Sky Crane" helicopter hoisted our disabled "Big Mother"
off the ship. In a matter of a few days, this very helicopter returned to duty, and once
again flew from the deck of JOUETT.

[Photo: U.S. Army CH-54A Sky Crane helicopter lifting the disabled SH-3A "Big Mother" off Jouett's flight deck at Da Nang, the SH-3 suspended by cables beneath the Sky Crane. USS Jouett (hull number 29 visible) seen from port side with mountains and Da Nang harbor in background]

1968-06-13.text:
COMMANDERS BRIEFED ON USS ST PAUL

Vice Admiral W.H. Baumberger, Deputy Commander-in-Chief, U.S. Pacific Fleet and Vice Admiral
W.F. Bringle, Commander, U.S. Seventh Fleet, recently visited the USS Saint Paul for briefings
on current operations.

The heavy cruiser is currently deployed in Vietnamese waters near the Demilitarized Zone. Saint
Paul is the flagship of Rear Admiral S.H. Moore, Commander Cruiser-Destroyer Group, U.S.
Seventh Fleet. She is commanded by Captain Ralph A. Hilson.

[Photo: ARRIVING-(L-R) Vice Admiral W.F. Bringle, Captain Ralph A. Hilson, Vice Admiral Walter H.
Baumberger, arrive on board the USS Saint Paul for briefing.]


TUCKER RATES MUC AWARD

USS Henry W. Tucker (DD 875) was recently awarded the Meritorious Unit Commendation by
Adm. T.F. Moorer, Chief of Naval Operations.

The award was for meritorious service while assigned to the Northern Search and Rescue Unit
of Task Force 77 from September to October 21, 1967.


ARMY RESCUES NAVY; REMOVES 'COPTER

If there was a ten-ton truck in your driveway with a broken axle and your car was in the garage,
could you go to work?

A similar dilemma occurred on the San Diego-based guided missile frigate USS Jouett (DLG 29) in
the Tonkin Gulf that was finally solved with assistance from the Air Force and the Army.

An 11-ton Navy helicopter landed on the Jouett's helo pad. Because of a malfunction that could
not be repaired on the Jouett, the huge 'copter could not take off again. The Jouett's own
helicopter was bottled up in its hangar and Rescue (SAR) station and as long as the disabled
helicopter remained there the Jouett could not perform her primary mission.

In an attempt to get the big "chopper" out of the way, the Commanding Officer, Capt. Robert S.
Hayes jockeyed his ship alongside the aircraft carrier USS Yorktown to see if they could lift the
stalled 'copter with their large crane. No luck. The two ships and the crane just didn't fit
together in the right places. Next, Commander Destroyer Squadron One, Capt. Arthur Emerson, also
on the Jouett, called the Air Force for assistance.

The Air Force responded quickly. They called the Army. The Army dispatched a noisy grasshopper-like
flying machine with a large crane that dropped a hook down to the stalled 'copter and flew away
with it dangling grotesquely like a chicken hawk with a chicken.

It took only a few minutes for the Army helicopter to solve the problem after it arrived. To the
exasperated men on the Jouett who had stewed and schemed for hours to be rid of the thing, it
somehow looked disturbingly simple.

[Photo: UP, UP AND AWAY-Army Sky Crane helo, CH-54A, lifts the incapacitated "Big Mother", SH-3,
helo clear of the decks of the USS Jouett (DLG 29) while she lies at anchor in the harbor at
Danang SVN.]

segments.text: Hi, it's Friday.
It's my third summer school and I really like the radio, what you sent me.
I'll be sending it, put 50 cents in the bank every week until I pay you back.
back. Uh, because a dollar, that'd be kind of hard, because I'd like to have some spending
money, so. That radio that you sent me, it's a pretty good radio, and, uh, I like it real
well. It picks up about everything I want. WLS sounds like WDZ, not a squirrely sounding.
And what, Mommy and me went up to the pride stamp store today and cashed some of her pride stamp books in. And she got a pillow for Daddy and slippers to clip the grass.

fighting three wheels.

you push a lever or something where it's flying.

Then I wouldn't sleep with any covers on.
Then I'd kick my covers off to the side and they'd fall off.
Last night it was cold.
So I had to get down from there and go around looking for all my covers and put them back on.
I took Sammy out to the park, I think it was Tuesday, Tuesday or Wednesday, that was Tuesday.
and I took him he walked out to the water swim around real close to the shore and then when I
get ready to leave he got out of the water and start coming up by the car and looked like he
wanted to come home with me so I caught him and threw him in the water as far as I could
