We've got about six more days left up here in the combat zone and then we head back to Subic Bay for a short stop and make way back to the States. Our time of arrival is still on the 18th of July, and there has been a slight change in our plans from the last time since I talked to you. Our plans were to escort the Enterprise back and not to cross the equator, but as I mentioned, that would probably change, as most things here in the Navy do, and our plans have changed. We are to cross the equator on about the 10th of July. And, of course, you already know the big initiation ceremonies and everything will take place. So it should be quite an experience for most of the guys on the ship because there are about 75, I'll put that between 50 and 75 people on the ship who have crossed the equator before. And the rest of us, which totaled about 350 and never have had the opportunity to do that. The way they do this, if you cross the equator, you are known as a shellback. If you have not crossed the equator, you're known as a pollywog. So that's what I am. I'm a pollywog. And, of course, the shellbacks now are starting to plan what they're going to do and hold little meetings and everything just to get some arrangement on how they're going to hold the ceremonies. Of course, they're outnumbered pretty well, so some of the Paliwags there on the ship have been putting out little signs like King Neptune is dead, Paliwag power, Paliwag rule, and stuff like that. But Navy tradition being what it is, I don't think that just because the shellbacks are outnumbered, they're going to call off the ceremonies because this is a real traditional happening, and no doubt it's going to be carried through all the way. So I'll be sure to have plenty of film in my camera that day and hope to get some pretty good pictures of it. I received your tape of June 14th this afternoon when the mail came in. I was real glad to hear that things are still going along pretty fine back home, and David sounded like he was in pretty good spirits. I hope he does enjoy himself at summer school and summer camp as well. I didn't mean to say enjoy himself at summer school, but I'm sure he'll get a little bit out of it, and I know he'll have a good time out there at Boy Scout camp. Thursday night we refueled from an oiler, and as usual they sent across third-class mail and packages, and I got your care package there the same night. I was glad to get it. It didn't take too long to get here, considering the circumstances. I received a letter from you on the 16th, which you wrote on June the 10th, and I was kind of waiting to hold off the answer, feeling that you would be sending me a tape in a few days and so I held off too loud to you know rather answer this letter our mail on here has been kind of slow it's I don't know why it's been this way this time up here perhaps they haven't got the good facilities to handle it like they had before I don't really know everything if they go through to get mail on here to us but Somewhere along the line it's getting slowed up going back to the States and also coming out here to us. I mentioned we had about six more days left up here in the Gulf and we've got about 27 days left till we arrive back in the States. We've got a status board down here in the gun plotting room and we keep the days counted on that and every day we erase the number and count it down one more. So everybody's pretty well up to date on how many days we've got left over here. And they're starting to make slight preparations for getting back in the States, like cleaning out certain parts of the ship and just making rather small arrangements, one at a time, so we'll be all ready to pull back into San Diego. Thursday morning, they brought the Catholic chaplain aboard, and he said mass and heard confessions. It's, I believe, the second time that he's came aboard since we've been out here on the line. And he was from the Enterprise. He said that he was pretty well impressed by the Jewess and everything that's been going on up here on the ship. And the other day we had three admirals come aboard at one time, and they were very impressed by the way we've been handling ourselves up here. and we're really impressed by the ship. So this put a few points on the captain's side, I suppose. And I suppose they'll have all kinds of write-ups and everything about us back in the San Diego papers and everything when we get back. So it'll be a few souvenirs to cut out of pasting the scrapbook a few years from now. On Wednesday night, about 12 o'clock midnight or thereafter, actually about 12 30 midnight which made it early thursday morning we had a star alert a f4 was down about 10 miles inland and we launched the helicopter and they went in and picked up both of the pilots but i'm like this ship they were injured i believe a little bit and the helicopter did pick up some small arms fire from some ground troops but uh nobody in the helo got hurt this time and they got back safe in the sun and it's the only action that we've actually had up here since i last wrote to you things uh aren't actually quiet up here i was just back on the fantail before i came on watch right now where i'm at now and i could see some uh bombing and uh tracer shells over there on the beach of course we're not really too close i imagine we're about 12 miles or 10 miles off the coast. So we're well out of range of anything over there. But you can see it pretty well during the night. And they're keeping up a steady pace of bombing over there. I don't really think it's doing much good because the war is still going on. And as long as it's still going on, you know that somebody's not doing something right. But it all remains to be seen. there's so many aspects that have to take place before anybody can really claim that they're winning any victory at all. The news weeks that you sent in the package were real good reading. I brought them down here in the gun plowing room and most of the guys look at them and read them. Kind of good to see what's happening back there and see what the politicians are up to, who's taking good care of us servicemen over here and read about all those draft dodgers and everybody else. The news over here is fairly accurate. We listen to the AFVN, which is the Armed Forces Vietnam Network, and they've got pretty good news reports on there. We also receive a little newspaper here on the ship that they print up in the Radio Central, which they receive off of the teletype network. And so we get news possibly one or two days after it comes out, and we get the stars and stripes. But by the time we get the stars and stripes, it's all old news, and we've already read about it or heard about it on the radio over here. So we know pretty well what's going on in the world. And baseball season, I've been keeping pretty well up to date on that, keeping an eye on the baseball scores. I see there that the Cubs aren't doing too bad. They're right around the 500 mark. It seems like the National League, as usual, is pretty tight there. And it's just about open for anyone. Of course, the Cardinals are doing just like they did last year. They're on top, and they just might stay there all the rest of the way through the season. I'm looking forward to when I do get back in San Diego to possibly go up to Los Angeles and take in a few baseball games up there. It's the time of the year when the baseball season is pretty well in full swing, and I'm sure they ought to find a pretty good game up there at this time of the year. I noticed I didn't have my tape recorder turned up too high, so you ought to hear a little increase in volume here. I noticed on your side, too, of the tape there where you were talking at Mother, it was a real week, and I could barely hear it. I couldn't make out hardly anything that you said. I hope you didn't say anything real important. but this is something that you kind of have to watch when you're making a tape recording. Make sure you've got the volume turned up all the way. I hope this background noise isn't too loud. I'm sitting here at the radar console and it puts off a lot of noise because it's got fans in it and all kinds of little gadgets running and everything and it makes a little bit of noise. So I think that my voice is probably drowning it out well enough that you can probably still hear it in the background. Well, I don't know what Bill's been up to. I haven't heard from him in quite a while. Of course, what you've told me in the tape and your letters is mostly news to me because I haven't received any letters from him or anything in a while. He mentioned in his last letter that he was going to send a tape and some slides to me. But it takes an awful long time for his mail to get to me and mine to get to him. But I expect to be hearing from him in a few more days. Well, sorry I had to break off there. We had a target that came up there and it got in about six and a half miles from us. It wasn't confirmed as a friendly target. I don't know what it was. It was some kind of a surface craft, a small boat of some type. So I'll get back to finishing up the rest of this tape now. now. I've got back five rolls of movie film that I've taken over here, three rolls I took up in Hong Kong and the other two I shot in Da Nang and around the ship here. I've got two more out yet and I should be getting them back in about a week or so. I ran out of movie film here on the ship so I've only got the roll left that I have in my camera and I hope to make that last until we stop back in Subic Bay on our way back to the States because I want to get some pictures of some of the stops we'll be making back to the States and our arrival back in San Diego there in July. You mentioned in your tape that the month was almost half over when you wrote, excuse me, when you made the tape and as I make this tape right now, it's being the 22nd of June this month. It's practically over. It's not half over. It's practically over. And by the time you receive this tape, it'll be almost over. These last two months have really gone fast. I don't know where they went to. And the time just has really been flying by. I don't know how it can, but it's been going by pretty quick for me. I mentioned in one of my last letters or on the last tape that I sent that due to the leave situation upon arrival back in San Diego that the duty sections would probably be down to three duty sections. And, of course, when you get down to a small number of duty sections like that, the liberty isn't at its best. But since they have found out just who is going on leave and who is not, they find that not as many people are going on leave as they expected. So it has word out that we will be in fourth section duty. We'll have the same duty and liberty status that we had before we left the state. So this sounds pretty good. I should be able to get in some good three-day weekends there. And I hope this holds true and they don't change their mind like they do so often here. I suppose a lot of the guys are going to hold off for Christmas time but take their leave. Of course, I'd imagine that by the time Christmas season is over with, just about everybody on the ship that wanted to take leave will have taken it and then we'll be back on the ship by then. Of course, everyone's just worrying about getting back to the States now, and we're not looking forward, or nobody knows just exactly how long we will be back in the States, how long we'll stay tied up to the pier. Most of us would be contented to stay tied up there to the pier for another nine or ten months at least. know what the shift schedule is and I don't even believe that the captain knows. We'll probably find out a short time after we do get back in the States after we've been back for a month or so. They'll probably start releasing a little bit of information on what our next operating schedules and such might be. I haven't yet received a tape from Grandma and Grandpa yet nor have I received one from Georgia May I expect if they have sent one it will probably be here in the next couple of days as I said before mail has been real slow over here and we haven't received any mail of past two days so I suppose if they have sent anything it should be on its way and if not I will go ahead and make a couple more tapes and send them on out to them but I sure would like to hear from them Of course, they've probably been tied down and haven't had a chance to do anything. I can understand this. But I still look forward to hearing from everybody back home, and I really enjoy sending these tapes home. And I know that you all are pleased to hear Bill and my voices as well when we do send these tapes home. I applied for two more correspondence courses. I believe I mentioned this once before. I haven't got them yet I imagine they will arrive while we are in Subic Bay which will be there in just about another eight or nine days and they'll probably arrive then I don't have something to work on when I get back in the state I hope to get these done in a pretty quick time and get the test over for them so I can go on and get some more finished. It's something to occupy some of my spare time and I find it rather interesting and enjoyable. So it's a pretty good deal. It's not costing me any more money. It only costs $5 to enroll in it and you can have all the courses you want. You get to keep a textbook and if for nothing else the textbooks the textbooks that they give you are good to have, whether you get any benefits from the course or not, just the idea that you get to keep the textbooks makes it that much worthwhile. I kind of laughed there in your letter when you mentioned about Bill and his little run-in with the captain there in Da Nang while he went in there one day. I suppose that that outfit where they're at up there in Hoi An, they are pretty lax and lenient in some of their ways. doing things and Bill probably thinks a lot of that over there fun games the probably pretty carefree but he still has to be reminded every so often he is in a service and the Marines are as well I suppose they feel it's very necessary to use little ways to remind the troops over there that they are in a serious situation, and they do expect them to put forth their effort and act like they're supposed to. I don't suspect that he really was transferred to Da Nang or wherever he was going to go because of his not having a haircut or not speaking to the officer properly. I do imagine that after a couple more months, possibly he will be transferred somewhere else. It just seems like it's par for the course. I've talked to guys here on the ship who have brothers and relatives over there, and they say that they've only been in one place for about six months, and they transfer him to some other outfit. From what he's told me, they don't seem to be doing too much up there. Of course, I never was able to get too much out of him, just what they do. He didn't relay too much information to me when he came aboard the ship that day, just exactly what they do. Seems like they have the Koreans there doing all the hard work for him, and they just kind of sit back and enjoy themselves. I enjoyed David's conversation on the tape, and he mentioned about taking his duck out to the park. I can just kind of picture that duck trying to get out of the water and follow him up to the car. I remember when he took his first family out there to the park, he was rather reluctant to take it out there, but he did give in, and I suppose he felt just about the same way about this one. I hope that the radio suits him pretty fine. Actually, I'm glad to hear that he said it's working pretty fine, and he's doing what he expected it to. I like his little idea of his savings program that he mentioned. He's going to put 50 cents a week in the bank, so he doesn't have to worry about it too much. It wasn't too much money off of my back to pay for it, and as far as I'm concerned, he doesn't have to worry about it. I wasted money in more ways than one, and I don't consider that a waste of money. So it's nothing to me. When I get back in the States and put on my civilian clothes, I'm afraid I'm going to find that they don't fit me as well as I was wearing them when I left. Of course, I've gained about 20 pounds since I came over here, and I think the big reason why it's not that I've been eating more food than usual because I ate three meals a day before I came over here, but I think the idea of doing a little bit more beer drinking over here than what I did when I was back in the States is a pretty good reason for why I've put on the extra weight. I don't really feel bad, nor do I think that I look bad, but I do notice the extra weight, and I believe I'll take most of it off by the time I do get back to the States or after I do get back there. I'll probably pick up some new clothes while I'm back there in San Diego just to wear around town there and wear on liberty and wear on weekends. So I hope I can keep the waistline down where it should be. And while I'm on the same subject, Mother, you mentioned that the doctor recommended that Dad go on a diet, and you figured you'd go right along with him. And I suppose if you'd twist David's arm a little bit, I suppose he'll go right along with you and he'll be real glad to go on a diet too. I know David would be pretty active this summer at Boy Scout camp and going out to the pool every day and things like this. So he shouldn't have too much of a weight problem in that line. Well, on the 1st of July, the armed forces get a big benefit, one of the many benefits you get while you're here in the service. New pay raise goes into effect. and my pay will jump up $15 a month from $235 a month to $251 a month. And this will be the beginning of the new fiscal year, of course, and we have a big payday scheduled for next Friday. I believe it will be a 16-day payday, and they'll clear all the money off the books and calculate it and see if they made any errors on your pay records or anything and reimburse you for it. So I suppose I'll probably be sending some more money home then. It actually all depends if we stop in Subic Bay or not. I would like to buy a turntable for my high-fly equipment. That's the only item I haven't bought. And if I can get one there in Subic Bay, if we have a chance, I'll probably buy one there. If I do, I don't believe I'll be sending too much money home. But the fact remains to be seen. But of course with the new pay rates for the armed forces, I suppose President Johnson is working on a new tax increase bill. It seems like they're always pulling something like that to give somebody one thing and take away from somebody else to help pay for it. There's more than one way around it and those politicians and government officials, they've got pretty good ways of getting things to work their way. Of course I've heard on the news and read in our little newspapers there that most of these political people who are running for office have started to jump in there and pick up the votes that Bobby Kennedy was most likely to get in these primaries in all these states. And it just seems like no one has forgot actually what's happened yet. And these other candidates for nomination are jumping right in there and trying to pick up the votes. You think it isn't really right for them to do it, but of course they've got to get out and get their votes. It seems like a pretty ruthless way to be a candidate for office, but this is what they have to do. Well, tomorrow's Sunday again, and they're going to slack off on us like they always do on Sunday. They'll give us a holiday routine, and they'll get some of the big benefits of Sunday on here. you spend a little bit more time in our rack if we're not on watch and they'll probably still a movie in the afternoon and have ice cream to go along with it and popcorn yeah that's right we have popcorn here on the chip too they brought a popcorn machine before we left the state and they sell popcorn here every night for 10 cents a bag that's right they sell it they don't they don't give it to you. The idea for selling a popcorn is to make some profit to help pay for the cruise book, which I mentioned that they're going to have ready for us when we get back in the States. So it's a little profit maker for them, and nobody really complains about having to pay for the popcorn because it's a little fringe benefit over here. I did notice the popcorn machine when it came on board the ship that one day. He said, you mean you guys have popcorn? I said, yeah. I said, just like downtown, you go to a movie every night and buy popcorn and Coke. I said, we really got it made. He said, yeah, I guess you do. So, yeah, I kind of had to laugh about that. I'm glad to hear that the dress material arrived safe and sound. I was kind of undecided on what selection of material to pick. I'm not really too much up on what pattern design would look best on who and things like that. So I just decided to get it. And I thought maybe if you wasn't satisfied with yours, you could trade it with grandma. If she wasn't satisfied with hers, she could trade it with you or whatever the situation might be. I was with a couple of other guys when we went in the store there in Hong Kong to buy it and they had a yard goods area there in this department store and they had silk this pure silk and uh this girl that waited on me she uh she's trying to get me to buy some of this silk and I believe it cost about uh let's see I think it was 15 Hong Kong dollars a yard which made it uh about $2.50 a yard in American money. And not being a great connoisseur of dress material, I do know that that is rather expensive. I would like to have got it for you, but I knew this would be just as well, this cotton material, and I only hope it wasn't imported from the United States. It would be kind of an ironic thing. But most of these foreigners over here, they like to get you to spend more money than what you intend to do. And you just kind of have to watch out for them. It's rather funny after you get used to it. You go in some of these shops and these stores and these people, they want you to buy this and they want you to buy that. And I actually get a lot of fun out of turning them down and saying no to them. Because you can't do this back in the United States. Of course, a lot of these merchants, they wouldn't put such a big scene on with you to get you to buy things from them and such. But in the United States, you couldn't be so stern and strict with these people when they try to really put it on you. They get you to buy some of their merchandise. But over here, you can get away with it and you can tell them no. And you can tell them a few other things, too. and there's nothing much they can do about it. I don't imagine it makes for too good foreign relations, but that's too bad. I've got the attitude that everybody over here likes to take advantage of the sailors and the military personnel, and they're out to take all the money from them if they can. Everybody over here seems to have a hand in the sailors' pocket trying to get a little bit of money out of there, and the guys just got to watch out for them. and learn to say no to these people. Well, things up here have been pretty quiet this past week. Just about the everyday routine has been taking place here on the ship. Our radar and our electronic gear here is still up. We haven't had any casualties with it. The gun mounts are still in operating order. So things are going along pretty smooth. Well, I just about reached the end of this side of the tape, and I believe I'm at a loss for words to fill out the other side. So I'll sign off here and tell everyone at home hello and goodbye in the same breath, and I'll be waiting to hear again from everyone and be looking forward to another tape from you. So so long for now.

1968-06-23.label: Tape 7, Side 1 — Mike Ducy
1968-06-23.attribution: Audio cassette recording, Tape 7, Side 1 — Mike Ducy. Transcribed by OpenAI Whisper. Ducy Family Archives

segments.text: Oh, again, everyone, I imagine you're rather surprised to be hearing from me again today
since I just sent a tape to you yesterday and you've probably got it by now.
Oh, it's Sunday, the 23rd of June, and the reason why I'm making this tape is because
I received your letter this afternoon, which was dated the 17th of June, and I decided
I'd go ahead and answer the letter by sending a tape.
I'm getting kind of lazy on my letter writing.
and I figured this would be just a good way to answer your letter.
After you get done with this tape, you can go ahead and tape on over it again
and send me a message back when you have a chance to
because I don't think I'll even come close to filling this full slide of the tape.
Yes, your clipping that you sent me in the letter,
I do know a little bit about what they're talking about there.
This clipping wasn't dated, though,
so I don't really know the time when they were talking about it.
But I didn't hear about the U.S. cruiser Boston being fired on.
I believe I was on watch that night when that happened,
and we got a radio message up here about it.
Then the SWIFT boat that was sank, we also heard about that.
They believe that the Boston was fired on by some VC helicopters, from what I hear.
It wasn't a confirmed message or anything like this.
They had him hear about the Navy F-4 Phantoms that were downed up here by MiGs.
This happens every so often.
What happens is they get these MiGs coming in up here and they send these CAFs, which
is counter air patrol, out after these MiGs from the aircraft carriers.
And these MiGs get them to chase them and they chase them down into a valley or over
a mountain range.
And the troops on the ground open up with some anti-aircraft fire and they knock our
planes out of the air.
so we lose a few million dollars there and a couple of pilots at the same time.
Well, you know, I mentioned yesterday on my tape that I was rather disappointed still
because I hadn't received a tape from Georgia Mae.
Well, unexpectedly, we got mailed this morning, and along with it was a tape from her,
right along with your letter.
So she talked for about a half hour on the tape, and it was rather interesting.
She did a pretty good job on it, and I was real glad to hear from her.
so I just finished up a tape for them,
and I'm going to send it on out to them this afternoon.
I'll be looking forward to seeing the pictures you mentioned
that you're going to take of the dress and the furniture
and David and his duck that he had, Sam.
Sorry to hear that you found a leak there in the roof,
there in the living room.
imagine that it's probably a good idea to go ahead and replace that roofing up
there I know it's been there for a long time so it's gonna save a lot of trouble
rather than having some water damage later on in the fall and the winter when
we start getting some more rain well I'm really glad to hear that grandma is
keeping herself pretty well occupied by the working hours that she's keeping I
I know this will keep her busy and possibly take a little bit off her mind,
and she'll find that she'll enjoy being occupied there.
Georgia may mention that Grandma was going to have the two weeks off,
but they were going to be back during the time they were going to be back in Illinois,
so she'd be able to show them around.
Georgia may mention that she got her driver's license out here in California,
and that came as quite a surprise to me.
Well, it sounds like we've got an entertainer there in the family with the banjo player out of Shakey.
He's taking David over there with him.
I hope he does have a chance to do some more performing.
Like, hey, you never know.
He might grow up to be another Lawrence Welk or somebody like that.
I got a little note there about Larry Feller being classified as a 1-Y.
That kind of struck me kind of funny, even though it could be expected.
I imagine that he's probably trying to find a way to get out of it, of course, like most of these guys do.
They don't want to face reality and face the fact that they've got to serve their time just like the rest of us do.
So I suppose he'll be fighting him off his back for the next couple of years or so until he can really prove his point.
Of course, I sure hate to think of a law enforcement officer having a bad set of legs on him.
It kind of wouldn't make the citizens who pay the taxes sleep kind of bad at night,
knowing he had somebody out protecting him that wasn't really qualified for the job.
But this is what I expected of him.
It sounds just about par for the course.
I forgot to tell David on my tape there yesterday that when he's out there at Boy Scout camp
and while he's sleeping out in the backyard there during the summertime to watch them
crickets and them mosquitoes, don't let them bother him too much.
He's going to have to get used to them.
They're out there to give him a hard time.
And that's one of the big thrills of sleeping outside, seeing if you can withstand all the
tortures of the insects and the creatures out there.
So just put on a lot of insect repellent there, Deuce, and don't let them bother you too much.
Well, I really hate to cut this off, but since I just sent a tape last night, I'm kind of at a loss for words.
So I'll be signing off here and be hoping to hear from everyone back here again real soon.
So so long for now.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.

1968-06-26.label: Stars and Stripes - 2 F4 Pilots Rescued
1968-06-26.attribution: Stars and Stripes - 2 F4 Pilots Rescued — Ducy Family Archives
1968-06-26.text:
Pacific Stars & Stripes
Wednesday, June 26, 1968

After 2 Hairy Hours, F4 Crew Rescued

SAIGON (Special) — The rescue of a downed fighter-bomber crew climaxed two hours of dramatic action aboard the carrier America and in the air over North Vietnam.

It began just 12 minutes after midnight, when the two-man F4 Phantom was downed by enemy fire northwest of Vinh. The crew parachuted to a densely wooded hillside 11 miles inland, just south of the 19th parallel.

Before they hit the ground, the pilot of a second jet gave the distress signal. In less than a minute, radarmen on the missile frigate Jouett had pin-pointed the location of the downed pilots.

The Navy search and rescue commander, Capt. Arthur L. Emerson Jr., aboard the Jouett, alerted other rescue ships and dispatched the guided missile destroyer Preble to launch her rescue helicopter.

Simultaneously, the call went out for the attack aircraft to cover the area where the airmen were downed and to provide an armed escort for the rescue helicopter over enemy territory.

The ill-fated Phantom's wingman, still circling over the downed aircraft, established radio communications with the men, assuring them that the pickup helicopter was on the way.

Under the direction of Radarman 2 O'Alan R. Melton, Sper! cer, Ind., the rescue helicopter and accompanying fighter escorts were guided through the moonless night toward the hillside where the survivors waited.

Back aboard the Jouett, and on the downed Phantom's carrier, the America, the drama of the rescue unfolded to dozens of listeners on the radio network. "He's coming, he's coming. Hang on, baby," one of the jets circling overhead reassured the downed airmen.

After a flight over heavily defended enemy territory, the helicopter arrived at the crash site. Unable to see through the moonless night, the co-pilot, Lt. (j.g.) Leroy Cook, Potomac, Mont., radioed, "We're coming in to get you. Give us a flare!" The accompanying aircraft dropped flares, and soon the hillside was as bright as day.

Even so, the crew members were tangled in the dense undergrowth. Repeatedly, the helicopter attempted to approach them through the thick trees, and after many frustrating attempts set down in a small clearing and turned on a rotating beacon so the flyers could find the aircraft.

The stillness of the night was frequently broken by the sound of small arms fire, as enemy troops closed in on the hill. Tangled in the undergrowth, the pilots could see a sling being dangled by the helicopter, but couldn't reach it.

The helicopter had only enough fuel left for one more rescue attempt. The pilot told the Phantom crew to go to a clearing at the bottom of the hill.

Under the illumination of flares, the two survivors, scattered with mud, flight suits ripped to shreds, darted out of the brush, ran 30 yards across the clearing and dived into the waiting helicopter.

As the aircraft rose from the clearing, it was sprayed with small arms fire. The pilot, Lt. (j.g.) Clyde Lassen, Eaglewood, Fla., radioed the good news. "Both survivors on board, we are coming out." The final obstacle was the heavily defended air route to the sea. An anxious silence gripped the shipboard listeners as they watched their radarscopes.

Then came the report, "feet wet," which meant the helicopter was over the water. The tension ebbed away as the Jouett, which was speeding to meet the helicopter, swung into the wind and turned on all her landing lights to receive the rescue craft.

It was now 2:35 a.m., but the Jouett was bustling with activity. The Phantom crew was immediately given a physical check-up and found to be in excellent condition.

1968-06-29.label: Mike Ducy to Home
1968-06-29.text:
29 June, 1968
Tonkin Gulf

Dear Mother & Dad,

It's about 12:30 AM Saturday morning here and I'm on watch. I received your letter of the 21st day before yesterday on Thursday.

I got my two new courses in the mail the same day and have done three lessons on one already.

Yesterday was pay day. I drew $180 and will probably send some home after we stop in Subic Bay as I want to buy a few last items before we head home.

We get relieved up here at 8:00 AM Sunday then head for Subic Bay. We'll probably arrive there late Monday night and leave again Tuesday afternoon. Then it's a four day trip to Guam where we stop for fuel and mail. As I mentioned before, we cross the equator on the 10th.

Since I made the last tape on the 23rd, there hasn't been anything new happen up here. We had our last refueling here Wednesday night. Of course every day they have MIG tracking alerts several times but they seldom get within 40 miles from us.

We did a little bit of painting the past few days in order to have some of our topside areas looking good for arrival in San Diego. We'll finish up the rest of it next week. It's pretty hot outside during the daytime and that sun just doesn't let up. So as a result we have been taking our time and not doing too much at one time.

I just remembered this will be the last "free" letter I write from over here. Boy, thats too bad! We are starting to lose out on some of the combat zone benefits now that it's time to leave. But we will get the month of July tax free pay and they are talking about combat pay for that month too. But they aren't too sure and may have to deduct it from our regular pay later on if they aren't right.

I hope David is having a good time at scout camp. I'm sure he is enjoying it and it will be a good experience for him.

I'm glad you liked the dress material and have it made already. I'll be eager to see the pictures you took of it.

Well I'm sorry that this is so short but there isn't much more to tell. I'll be looking to hear from you when we stop in Guam. So long for now.

Your son,

Mike

1968-07-01.label: Familygram — Capt. Robert S. Hayes, CO
1968-07-01.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-07-01.text:
JOUETT FAMILY GRAM

1 July 1968

Dear Family and Friends of JOUETT

Standby! We are homeward bound!
The weather is beautiful and the sea is calm as JOUETT proudly slices through the blue depths of the South China Sea. We commenced the 8,787 mile journey back to San Diego, and I would like to tell you of two particular exciting experiences which happened to us during the last thirty days in the Gulf of Tonkin.

The latest pages of JOUETT's history have certainly been charged with suspense and action as JOUETTMEN found themselves in the middle of a dramatic rescue of two U. S. airmen. A few minutes after midnight of the morning of 19 June, the transmission "Give me a flare, give me a flare" crackled in the earphones of Task Force 77 personnel listening to the spine-tingling search and rescue operation taking place on a wooded hill in North Viet Nam. The speaker was a rescue helicopter pilot, LTJG Clyde LASSEN, USN, of Englewood, Florida. He was calling on emergency radio to the survivors of a Navy F-4 Phantom fighter-bomber. The rescue helicopter, eleven miles inland in enemy territory was courageously attempting a quick reaction rescue under the cover of darkness.

It all started when Radarman First Class, Joseph T. WHITTFALL, while on watch in the Combat Information Center of JOUETT, heard the distress call.

The USS AMERICA based aircraft had been hit while on a night mission over North Viet Nam. Both the pilot and the radar intercept officer had successfully ejected. In less than a minute alert radarmen, aboard the JOUETT, flagship of Captain Arthur T. EMERSON, Jr., had pinpointed the location of the downed aviators on a large scale map. Captain EMERSON took the initiative by alerting the rescue ships and putting his "Blue Ribbon" (Destroyer Squadron One insignia) team into action. He directed the USS PREBLE (DLG15), to launch her rescue helicopter for control by JOUETT, nearest ship to the scene. Simultaneously the call went out for attack aircraft to cover the area of the survivors and to provide armed escort for the rescue helicopter when it would fly inland.

The ill-fated Phantom's wingman, still orbiting high overhead, reported to Captain EMERSON on radio that he had established good communications with the survivors on the ground, and that a helicopter pickup was now possible. Under the skillful direction of Radarman First Class Alan R. MELTON, the rescue helicopter and accompanying fixed wing escorts were vectored by radar control through the pitch black night toward the hillside where the survivors were believed to be located.

Back in the CIC of JOUETT, the drama of the rescue, extending more than forty-five minutes, unfolded to dozens of listeners on the radio nets. After a hazardous twenty minutes run-in over heavily defended and heavily populated area, the helo arrived at the location where the survivors should be found. On a moonless night, locating the survivors would be crucial. In a perfectly coordinated operation, the helo co-pilot, LTJG Leroy COOK radioed ahead to the survivors, "we're coming in to get you, give us a flare." At the same time Captain EMERSON directed carrier based aircraft high overhead to drop large area flares. Soon the hillside was as clearly lighted as in day.

Even so, complications resulted from the dense undergrowth in which the survivors were virtually trapped. Repeatedly the helicopter attempted to approach them through the trees, and after many frustrating attempts, even set down in a small clearing and turned on a beacon so that the survivors could see the craft and get on board. The stillness of the black night was frequently punctuated with the sound of small arms fire, as enemy troops closed in from other parts of the hill. The survivors later related the extreme difficulty experienced in extricating themselves from the dense vines and brush of the hillside. At one point they could see the helicopter valiantly dangling a rescue sling close to their heads, but just could not reach it. Time seemed to be running out. The helo had time for just one more attempt before it had to withdraw for refueling.

Suddenly, under the canopy of flare illumination, the two survivors splattered with mud, flight suits ripped to shreds, hurtled out of the brush, ran some 20 yards across the clearing, and dove into the waiting helicopter.

As the olive drab helo rose from the small clearing, it was sprayed with small arms fire. Then LTJG LASSEN radioed the good news: "Both survivors on board, we are coming out." The final obstacle was to traverse the heavily defended air route to the sea.

In the CIC of JOUETT, an anxious silence gripped the listeners as they watched radar scopes for evidence that the brave helo would evade the heavy anti-aircraft fire and reach the safety of the sea. Then came the report, "feet wet", which meant they were out over water. Everyone who heard it felt like cheering. The JOUETT, which had been closing the coast at high speed to reduce the length of the flight, now turned on all her aircraft landing lights, and swung into the wind, to receive the helicopter, and her valiant crew and her two happy survivors.

It was now three o'clock in the morning but JOUETT bustled with activity as though it were mid day. The survivors were given a physical check-up by Dr. Robert N. JONES, MC, USN, Destroyer Squadron One Medical Officer and the officers and members of the crew ate sandwiches and drank coffee, while sharing the fast moving events of the past few hours. Both survivors were found to be in excellent physical condition and soon were telling their story to a crowd of wide-eyed admirers. That same morning at 0900 the two happy survivors were ferried back to their own ship, the carrier AMERICA.

As if the rescue were not exciting enough, on 21 June, JOUETT was paid a great honor and enjoyed a rare privilege when she was visited by three of the most important U. S. Navy Commanders in the Pacific Fleet. This episode of JOUETT history started when eight gongs rang out sharply aboard JOUETT as the word was passed, "Pacific Fleet, arriving." Then the word was passed, "Seventh Fleet, arriving." This was followed by the announcement, "Carrier Division Five, arriving." Shortly thereafter a big SH-3 helicopter landed on the helo deck aft. Admiral John J. HYLAND, USN; Vice Admiral William F. BRINGLE, USN; and Rear Admiral Ralph W. COUSINS, USN, on stepping out of the helo were greeted by Commodore EMERSON and myself.

The three admirals on a surprise visit to JOUETT while conducting operations in the Tonkin Gulf, quickly toured the bridge and CIC area then were briefed on current operations. They also met and congratulated the helicopter crew who had conducted the rescue just related.

Later Admiral HYLAND spoke to the assembled officers and men of JOUETT, commending them on the fine manner in which they were carrying out their job in the Seventh Fleet. He predicted that in years to come they would be happy and proud to know that they had served their nation when it needed them. He noted in particular the success achieved by JOUETT in rescuing downed aviators.

As the admirals bid farewell before lifting off their giant helicopter, the gongs rang out, followed in order by, "Pacific Fleet, departing", "Seventh Fleet, departing", and "Carrier Division Five, departing".

JOUETT men were certainly pleased by this surprise visit and it was a major topic of conversation for the next few days.

This entire month we have been underway except for one night when we anchored in the port of Danang. Everyone has been quite busy with their watch standing and work on board. A common statement has been that "time really flys" because we are so busy and performing such an obviously worthwhile function.

We have had more gains and losses of personnel. Transfered to new duty were CS3 Patrick L. TIERNEY, STG3 Terry R. CURTIS, STG3 Brian K. CAMPBELL, RD3 Joseph W. JOHNSON, SD2 Venancio O. ENCARNACION and ET1 Kenneth W. LUNDEMO. Also transfered to shore at Newport, R. I. was LT Bruce WOOD who has been First Lieutenant and Deck Division Officer since commissioning. LTJG Douglas G. WIDENER has reported on board from sea duty and relieved as First Lieutenant. I had the pleasure of presenting the JOUETT Outstanding Service Award to Yeoman Second Class Rollins David LOW at the time of his transfer.

One last thought! JOUETT will continue to receive mail as we make fuel stops on our way home. Please keep writing.

The magic day we are looking forward to is 18 July when we will be arriving in San Diego. Mark your calendar. More details will follow in the next Familygram.

Robert S. Hayes
ROBERT S. HAYES
CAPT        USN
COMMANDING OFFICER

1968-07-05.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-07-05.text:
USS JOUETT (DLG29)
FPO SAN FRANCISCO 96601

FAMILYGRAM

5 JUL 68

Since departing Tonkin Gulf on 1 July, the JOLLY "J" has been traveling fast on our homeward voyage. First we traversed the now familiar waters of the South China Sea and came to an anchorage in the spacious harbor at Subic Bay in the Philippine Islands. Here we took on fuel, made a few last minute repairs and the crew had a last "shopping spree" at the Navy Exchange (which carries a variety of foreign merchandise).

Underway the same day, we navigated all night through the central Philippine Islands eventually transitting San Bernadino Strait in the morning. Across the almost glassy calm of the blue Philippine Sea, JOUETT left a beautiful wake that seemed to stretch all the way to the horizon. Sunbathing during the noon meal hours became a favorite pastime and the two days of our voyage were fruitful in terms of work accomplished. Now that we are free of the requirement to be close to Battle Stations we are able to devote more time to housekeeping chores. This afternoon we arrived in Apra Harbor, Guam for a fuel stop. The Big "J" has the capacity to steam great distances without taking on fuel, however like a prudent automobile driver, we prefer not to operate too close to an "empty tank". Besides, while our intentions are to arrive home as soon as possible, we can never forget that this versatile frigate, as all units of the fleet, must be ready to respond to various emergencies on short notice.

We plan to be underway for Pearl Harbor before darkness. While fueling at the pier we anticipate that a number of the crew will be able to get ashore for a brief period to shop at the Navy Exchange or see the sights in the vicinity of the harbor.

Now that our course lies East, it is difficult to appreciate that six full months have gone by. I suspect that our wives and sweethearts have found the six months far from the excitement we have experienced and at times intolerably long. But because of our busy schedule, and our daily realization that we were needed, and because of the pressure of constantly changing combat situations, we found the time passing quickly. During this six months JOUETT has been a "steamer" with less than one sixth of the total time in port. Just to quote a few statistics: we will have travelled 50,000 miles, burned over 3,583,086 gallons of fuel oil, and have made 25 replenishments from oilers, stores ships and provisions ships at sea. Our helo deck, under the professional direction of LT Dave HOPKINS has seen 466 helicopters come and go without a single mishap. Five of these helicopters brought back the eight survivors that were rescued from the waters of the Tonkin Gulf and in one case, from North Vietnam itself (the miniature white parachutes painted on the side of the ship represent these rescues). While most of the helo landings were the result of Search and Rescue efforts, almost daily a logistics helo brought mail, urgent repair parts, replacement personnel, and official visitors.

We witnessed a drastic change in the seasonal weather of the South East Asia in the six months we have been here. During the first 35 days on station, Tonkin Gulf was covered with a low overcast and we rarely saw either the sky or the mountains nearby. During the last 28 day period on station, we saw the Gulf in its summer garb, smooth blue seas, clear skies, and unlimited visibility. It was hot and humid, so we appreciated the air conditioning built into our ship's dining and sleeping spaces. During this cruise we did visit some interesting parts of the world that most of the crew had never seen. These included Pearl Harbor, Hawaii; Subic Bay, Philippine Islands; Danang, South Vietnam; Yokosuka, Japan; and Hong Kong, British Crown Colony. Many of these places we visited a second time.

The favorite pastime of JOUETTmen has been photography. I have never seen such a crew of "shutter bugs". A census of cameras would certainly disclose at least one for every man on board. It is not unusual to see a hundred crewmembers appear topside, cameras in hand, whenever the word is passed "Now a flight of aircraft will make a low pass over the ship in two minutes" or "Now there is a famous volcano/good landscape off the port bow".

Of course the main reason JOUETT was assigned to the Seventh Fleet was to assist in the Navy job of defending South Vietnam. We feel proud that we have accomplished our assignment and we are doubly proud that we apparently have done it quite well. A number of the messages have been received on JOUETT's departure complimenting the crew on its outstanding performance.

Yesterday, the 4th of July, we observed this most significant national event with appropriate ceremony and fanfare even this far out at sea. At 1130 we had the reading of the Declaration of Independence over the ship's public address system. This was followed by a 21 gun salute at noon. For those of us who have been directly assisting a young nation maintain its independence, and who were seeing our own nation from the perspective of 8000 miles, I believe this day had greater significance than usual.

In the afternoon we observed holiday routine. At 1600, all hands not on watch assembled on the helo deck for a typical old fashioned cookout. It seems like hot dogs and hamburgers always taste better when cooked in the open air. Our Welfare and Recreation Committee, under LT Bob JAMES, staged a number of contests, ranging from feats of strength and skill to a contest of the best "non-regulation" costumes. In addition our musical groups came forth in their new Hong Kong uniforms and gave us some good country and western music. Commodore EMERSON presented prizes to the winners of the contests. Everyone had as fine a Fourth of July as could be expected away from home.

Now a few words about Homecoming. Since this will be the last mail to leave the ship until 13 July when we anticipate arriving in Pearl Harbor. It is presently planned that the returning ships of Destroyer Squadron One, JOUETT, PREBLE, and HULL, will arrive in San Diego as a unit. Since our Squadron insignia contains a blue ribbon with a big numeral One, we are asking all our friends who are coming to greet the ship at pierside, to conspicuously wear a blue ribbon with a "JOUETT" or "J" pinned to it. Arrival times are subject to change but tentatively we expect to be in sight of Point Loma by 0800 and tie up at the Naval Station between 0900 and 1000. The time of arrival has been selected with you in mind. A time when the traffic is light and you can conveniently arrive. There should be parking reserved in the vicinity of the pier. In order that San Diegans may recognize JOUETT's entry as other than "routine", we plan to display the hull number 29 on our helo flight deck as we enter the harbor at Ballast Point. The number 29, formed of crewmembers in white uniforms, when displayed against the grey background of the ship should be visible from the Cabrillo Monument on Point Loma. After we pass Point Loma the men will fall out of formation "29" and into the normal parade formation for entering port.

The "name of the game" on arrival will be to see how quickly we can commence liberty. As soon as the brows are over, we want to simultaneously permit the crewmembers to get off on liberty and to invite guests to come aboard JOUETT for visiting and refreshments. Refreshments will be available on the helo deck, crews dining hall, chiefs lounge and the wardroom, while a great number of our shipmates will be departing on well deserved leave and liberty, it is necessary for a very few to remain on board with the duty. It is sincerely hoped that as many of you as have the time will come on board for refreshments and to meet the shipmates of your husband or son. We want to make this a very happy occasion with built in flexibility for each man and his guest to do as they would like.

It has been a most successful cruise and I can assure you that your JOUETTmen are returning home in good health and with a great pride in their achievements. We are looking forward with great anticipation to seeing you when the lines go over in San Diego.

Sincerely yours,

Robert S. Hayes
ROBERT S. HAYES
CAPT        USN
COMMANDING OFFICER

1968-07-10.text:
IMPERIUM NEPTUNI REGIS — SUBPOENA
Personalized to DUCY, Michael F., FTG3, USN
Royal Court date: 10 July 1968
1 page, printed form with typed charges

========================================================================================
TEXT
========================================================================================

                    IMPERIUM NEPTUNI REGIS

[Ornate illustration: Neptune/Poseidon with trident, flanked by sea horses
and mythological figures, riding waves]

IN THE HIGHEST COURT OF THE RAGING MAIN.

THE DOMAIN OF IMPERIUM NEPTVNI REGIS
SEND GREETINGS TO:  DUCY, Michael F., FTG3, USN

YOU ARE COMMANDED TO APPEAR BEFORE THE ROYAL COURT ON  10 July 1968

A complaint has been filed with the government of THE DOMAIN OF IMPERIUM NEPTVNI
REGIS, STATE OF THE RAGING MAIN, EQUATORIA, against you:

   WHEREAS:  YOU HAVE CONSPIRED TO ENTER THE ROYAL DOMAIN
             WITHOUT VISA, PASSPORT OR PROPER AUTHORIZATION

   WHEREAS:  YOU HAVE FAILED TO MAINTAIN THE PERSONAL HYGIENIC
             PERFECTION REQUIRED TO ENTER THIS DOMAIN. TO WIT:
             YOU HAVE ALLOWED TO COVER YOUR BODY AND ENTER YOUR
             MIND A CERTAIN AMOUNT OF SLIME THAT IS USUALLY FOUND
             ON POLLYWOGS AND OTHER LOWER SPECIMEN OF THE REALM.

   WHEREAS:  YOU ARE FURTHER CHARGED WITH BROWN BAGGERY, MOPERY,
             DOPEING OFF, CHIT REQUESTING, APPLE POLISHING, SYMPATHY
             SEEKING, GUN DECKING, PROCRASTINATION, GOLD BRICKING,
             LIBERTY HOUNDING AND REVEILLE NEGLECTING.

   WHEREAS:  YOU ARE SPECIFICALLY CHARGED WITH THE HENIOUS CRIMES
             OF: DISTURBING THE PEACE; CAUSED MANY ANXIOUS MOMENTS BY HIS
             FALSE PREDICTIONS OF "NO MAIL TODAY".
             FALSE CLAIM: CLAIMS TO BE A SHELLBACK BUT A SLIMY POLLYWOG
             AND A LOWLY RESERVE.

   WHEREFORE:  THE PEOPLE OF THE DOMAIN OF IMPERIUM NEPTVNI REGIS,
               STATE OF THE RAGING MAIN, EQUATORIA, PRAY THAT THE
               DEFENDENT BE BROUGHT BEFORE THE ROYAL COURT FORTH-
               WITH AND BE TRIED BEFORE THE BENEVOLENT JUDGES PRE-
               SIDING.

Subscribed and sworn to                          NEPTUNUS REX.
before me this ___ day of  July 1968

Royal scribe in and for THE DOMAIN        [Medallion illustration: profile
OF INPERIVM NEPTVNI REGIS.                 of Neptune with crown and trident]
DAVY JONES. ROYAL SCRIBE


========================================================================================
NOTES
========================================================================================

Mike's personalized subpoena for the Equator Crossing ceremony on July 10,
1968. The first three WHEREAS charges are standard boilerplate printed on every
subpoena. The fourth WHEREAS contains typed-in charges specific to Mike:

1. "DISTURBING THE PEACE; CAUSED MANY ANXIOUS MOMENTS BY HIS FALSE PREDICTIONS
   OF 'NO MAIL TODAY'" — Mike apparently had a running habit of predicting no
   mail would arrive, which caused anxiety among the crew who were desperately
   awaiting letters from home. Mail call was one of the most important morale
   events aboard ship during deployment.

2. "FALSE CLAIM: CLAIMS TO BE A SHELLBACK BUT A SLIMY POLLYWOG AND A LOWLY
   RESERVE" — This ribs Mike for two things: falsely claiming shellback status
   (he had never crossed the equator before), and his Naval Reserve status.
   Regular Navy ("USN") sailors sometimes ribbed Reservists ("USNR") — though
   Mike's certificate from FT School correctly shows "U.S. NAVAL RESERVE."

Standard humorous Navy charges explained:
- Brown baggery: acting like a married sailor (bringing lunch in a brown bag)
- Mopery: general aimless behavior
- Gun decking: falsifying records or reports
- Gold bricking: shirking duty
- Chit requesting: excessive requests for special privileges
- Liberty hounding: being overly eager for shore leave
- Reveille neglecting: sleeping through morning call

Mike's rate is correctly listed as FTG3 (Fire Control Technician Gun, Third
Class), USN.

1968-07-10.text:
DAVEY JONES' PLAN OF THE DAY
FIRST WEDNESDAY, 10 JULY 1968
Equator Crossing Ceremony — USS Jouett (DLG-29)
3 pages

========================================================================================

                              NOTES

1. The following message was received last night from His Royal Majesty
Neptunus Rex:

   I have sent Davey Jones, My Royal Scribe, to the good Ship JOUETT tonight
to serve summons on all the landlubbers, pollywogs, sea vermin, and crabs
and eels who have not been initiated into the Supreme Order of the Deep.
The members of my court, in my behalf have brought serious indictments
against those who still have traces of heifer's dust and cow dung on their
feet, as well as those of the big towns who think they are real city slickers.
But, no matter, all will be Shellbacks after the Royal Treatment on the morrow,
at which time those summoned will appear before my Royal Judge and there answer
for offenses committed both aboard and ashore. Remember ye all... Sorrow and
woe will befall those who resist or talk in a light or jesting manner of my
ceremony or of my Queen Amphitrite and her beautiful daughter the Princess!
Farewell, and I will board your fine ship soon, as you proceed into my Royal
Domain.

                                        Signed,

                                        Neptunus Rex

NOTES
========================================================================================

The equator crossing ceremony ("Crossing the Line") is a centuries-old naval
tradition. Sailors who have not previously crossed the equator are "pollywogs"
(or "wogs"); those who have are "shellbacks." The ceremony transforms pollywogs
into shellbacks through a series of humorous ordeals presided over by sailors
playing King Neptune (Neptunus Rex), Queen Amphitrite, Davy Jones (Royal Scribe),
and the Royal Court.

Jouett crossed the equator at the 180th meridian (International Date Line) on
July 10, 1968, homeward bound from WestPac. The "FIRST Wednesday" heading is a
play on the International Date Line — crossing it westbound means living the
same day twice.

Mike's Super 8 film clip "King Neptune's Court — Equator at 180th" captures
this event. He also has 5 slides from the ceremony in Photos/Slides/.

Duty division is MISSILE/FOX — Mike's division had the duty this day.

LCDR John A. Walker Jr. signed as "KING WOG" — the senior uninitiated officer
who leads the pollywogs. Walker received a Navy Commendation Medal at the
October 11, 1968 Awards Ceremony.

Weapons Department (Mike's) assembled at stations 6 and 11 on the forecastle.

The Vietnam Campaign and Service Medal issuance the next day (July 11) marks
the formal recognition of the crew's combat service. All personnel aboard since
February 29, 1968 received both medals.

...Pollywogs were presented to King Neptune, Queen Amphitrite, and the Beautiful
