1968-11-01.label: Naval Station San Diego Welcome Aboard
1968-11-01.attribution: Naval Station San Diego Welcome Aboard — Ducy Family Archives
1968-11-01.text:
NAVAL STATION SAN DIEGO — WELCOME ABOARD PAMPHLET (~November 1968)

Mike Ducy received this pamphlet during separation processing at Naval Station
San Diego in November 1968, after returning from WestPac deployment aboard
USS Jouett (DLG-29). Signed by CAPT A.R. Olsen, Commanding Officer.
Pamphlet revised November 1967 (per base map: 11ND-NSSD-1300/1 REV. 11-67).
17 numbered pages plus base map.

--- COVER ---

[Cover art: Large bold text "WELCOME ABOARD" with Naval Station San Diego
seal/emblem featuring an anchor and "NAVAL STATION SAN DIEGO" around the border]

NAVAL STATION
SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA

--- PAGE 1 ---

WELCOME ABOARD

Welcome to San Diego and the Naval Station.

Our motto, "SEAPOWER SUPPORT", aptly describes the primary mission of the Naval Station which is to provide logistic support to the Operating Forces of the Pacific Fleet. In addition to providing port services and various levels of logistic support to many elements of the Fleet, and to tenant commands located on the Naval Station complex, the Station also provides the principal "receiving station" functions for the Navy in the San Diego area.

No matter how modern our Fleet units, or how well equipped they are to meet their mission of maintaining supremacy of the seas and defending our Country, their capability and effectiveness is dependent upon skilled and adequate manpower. You are that vitally important product which makes our Navy great. For this reason much of our SEAPOWER SUPPORT centers around you and every effort will be made to expedite your transfer to your ultimate duty station where your talents can be put to their maximum use. The Navy, recognizing your importance, has discontinued the use of surface ships to transport personnel to overseas location (who are traveling without dependents) and now utilizes air exclusively as the most rapid and economical means of transportation. Ships schedules, for those units operating in the Eastern Pacific pose a different problem in the rapid movement of personnel and must dictate the length of your stay at the Naval Station. However, you will be promptly transferred upon your ship's arrival in port (if in San Diego), or you will be transferred to an appropriate naval activity outside the San Diego area if your ship is scheduled to arrive in that port.

In addition to the transfer functions mentioned above, our Separations Section is established to assist ships and stations who do not have the capability for separation processing. In this connection every attempt will be made to expedite your processing and speed you on your way to civil life - if that is your choice. I might add, however, that our Separations people are skilled not only in separation processing, but also in reenlistments. The majority of you who have reported for separation have given your Country loyal and faithful service which will not be forgotten. I do, however, urge you to again weigh fully your decision for separation against the desirability of remaining in the Navy. Whatever your decision, please accept my appreciation for having served on the Navy Team and I wish you good health, pleasant living and Godspeed in your future endeavors.

The information contained in this pamphlet is provided for your information and compliance. It contains a digest of basic instructions which will govern your activities and are necessary for the effective operation of the Station and administration of transient personnel. You should read it thoroughly and comply with the regulations and instructions set forth therein. Information not contained in this pamphlet may be obtained from any of the officers or men of the Receipts and Transfer Section, Separations Section, or the Master-at-Arms force, and you are urged not to hesitate in soliciting information from them.

Again, welcome aboard and I hope your stay with us will be enjoyable.

                                        A. R. Olsen
                                        A. R. OLSEN
                                        Captain, U. S. Navy
                                        Commanding Officer

--- PAGE 2 ---

BRIEF HISTORY OF THE NAVAL STATION

The first parcel of property on which the U. S. Naval Station, San Diego is now located was deeded to the U. S. Government by the City of San Diego on 3 September 1919. The property consisted of 21 water acres and 77.2 land acres, the former being mostly marsh lands and tide flats. On 15 February 1921, the Navy acquired the land, buildings and certain machinery from the U. S. Shipping Board, and on 10 June 1921, the USS PRAIRIE proceeded to the vicinity to take over the property preparatory to the receipt of the destroyers which were soon to be placed out of commission. On 23 February 1922, the U. S. Destroyer Base, San Diego was officially established by the Secretary of the Navy in General Order 78. In October 1943, the designation was officially changed to the U. S. Naval Repair Base by which time, through various acquisitions the base had grown to 659 land acres and 262 water acres and the ships, docks, and training facilities were manned by about 28,000 officers and enlisted personnel. On 15 September 1946, the base was re-designated the U. S. Naval Station. By August 1960, through other acquisitions, the property of the Naval Station had grown to 1102.75 land acres and 380.06 water acres.

--- PAGE 3 ---

REGULATIONS

As mentioned previously in the "WELCOME ABOARD" section on page 1 of this pamphlet, you are required to be cognizant of, and to comply with all regulations, instructions, and orders promulgated by the Commanding Officer, Naval Station, San Diego, and by other competent authority. All of the rules and regulations in effect on this Station are available in the Officer of the Day's Office, Building 29. In addition, barracks regulations and a copy of the Plan of the Day are posted on the bulletin board of each dormitory.

DIVISIONS

Transient personnel are assigned to divisions as follows:

Companies      Division      Division Officer
TRN            P-2           Barracks & Training Officer
TO, TC, TF,    P-3           Receipts & Transfer Officer
  TM, TL
TS, TSR, TSP   P-4           Separations Officer
DR, DA, DL,    L-1           Discipline Officer
  DB

A current listing by name, rank, and title of all officers attached to the Naval Station, San Diego is available in the Barracks Petty Officer's Office, Building 57.

MASTER AT ARMS AND BARRACKS PETTY OFFICERS

The Masters at Arms can be identified by their badges which are issued by the Commanding Officer. The Masters at Arms represent the Commanding Officer and have the responsibility of maintaining good order and discipline throughout the Naval Station. The Barracks Petty Officers are responsible for maintaining a high state of cleanliness in the transient spaces, will conduct all musters and assist you as much as possible.

MILITARY COURTESY

Military courtesy is observed at all times on this Station.

CLEANLINESS

You are expected to assist in maintaining cleanliness in the dormitories and other spaces. Deposit all waste paper in the proper receptacles and cigarette butts in ashtrays.

--- PAGE 4 ---

BUNKS

Your bunk must be made up properly in accordance with the picture posted in the dormitories. In view of the large number of transients at this activity, it is imperative that you understand that it is your individual responsibility to do this each day immediately after reveille.

MUSTER

All transient personnel will muster daily at 0745, 1230, and 1630 unless excused by proper authority. Company TSP personnel will muster at 0745 only. Duty section musters at 1600, 1800, and 2100. DO NOT MISS MUSTER. In view of the large number of enlisted personnel in a transient status, and the use of muster to call out immediate outgoing drafts, the offense of missing muster is serious. CPO's will muster with the Barracks CPO in the patio of Building 57. All other transients (E-6 and below) will muster in the patio of Building 57 with their company Barracks Petty Officer. The 1800 and 2100 duty section musters are held in front of the Barracks Petty Officer's Office, Building 57. Morning muster will consist of muster, inspection and physical fitness exercises. You will be inspected daily at morning quarters by your Barracks Petty Officer who has instructions to ensure that transients wear clean, complete uniforms. You will be inspected periodically by the Chief Barracks Petty Officer and by your division officer. All transient personnel are required to have a regulation haircut at all times. Listen carefully at all musters for your instructions and assignment to working parties. It is your responsibility to remain close to Building 57 and the loudspeakers in this area so that you will hear your name when called. If assigned to a working party, keep your supervisor informed of your location so that you may be reached if called.

UNIFORMS

The uniform of the day for pay grades E-6 and below is undress whites or blues, whichever is prescribed in the Plan of the Day. Regulation clothing will be worn. CPO's will wear prescribed complete uniform of the day at all times. Ribbons are required with the liberty uniform. All clothing must be properly stenciled. Stencils may be obtained from the Lucky Bag located in Building 56. Re-claimed clothing must be "DC'd" - if clothing is found in your possession which carries another man's name, SUCH CLOTHING WILL BE CONFISCATED. In addition, attention is directed to the fact that possession of another person's clothing is a violation of the UCMJ and subject to disciplinary action. You are required to be in a clean, complete uniform of the day as prescribed in the Plan of the Day.

--- PAGE 5 ---

CIVILIAN CLOTHING

Company "TO" personnel are allowed to wear civilian clothing on and off the station until their uniforms have been issued. All other transient personnel in pay grades E-6 and below are NOT authorized to wear civilian clothing on board the Station.

SEA BAGS

Do not leave your seabag or other personal effects outside Buildings 56 or 57 while checking in. Keep them in your sight upon reporting until safely checked into the Transient Bag Storage Room. Immediately after reporting to Building 57 for berthing, seabags and other luggage must be checked into the Transient Bag Storage Room topside Building 56. The Bag Storage Room is open from 0630 to 1600 Monday through Friday. If you report on board after the Bag Room has secured, the safekeeping of your seabag and other luggage until 0630 the next morning is your personal responsibility. Under no circumstances should seabags or hand bags be left unattended in dormitories. Seabags, upon being turned in, should be locked. IF FOR ANY REASON YOU REPORT WITHOUT YOUR SEABAG AND ARE ASSIGNED TO COMPANY TC, TF, OR TM, REPORT THIS FACT TO YOUR COMPANY YEOMAN AS SOON AS POSSIBLE.

BAGGAGE

Arrangements for pick-up of baggage shipped to San Diego via commercial carrier can be made at the Bag Storage Room, topside, Building 56. Shipment of prepaid baggage can be made to any address desired. Shipment of COD baggage can be made to addresses in the Continental U. S. only.

SAFEGUARDING PERSONAL PROPERTY

Safeguard your property by keeping your locker locked at all times. Do not leave your personal clothing or other property where it can be stolen (see Section titled "Sea Bags" concerning stowage in Bag Room). Report thieves or suspicious persons immediately to the Master at Arms for investigation. YOU ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR YOUR PERSONAL EFFECTS; if you permit your personal property to be stolen through negligence, the Government will not reimburse you for your loss.

--- PAGE 6 ---

SPECIAL REQUESTS

All special requests must be submitted via your Company Petty Officer and will be submitted twice daily to your division officer for consideration. Requests of an emergency nature will be given special processing.

REQUEST MAST

Preliminary Request Mast is held each working day at 1000 by your Company Petty Officer. Requests that require the Commanding Officer's decision are referred to him via your Division Officer, Department Head, and the Executive Officer.

LIBERTY

A four section watch for personnel in a transient status is maintained on the Naval Station and liberty is granted on a 3 out of 4 basis. It is your responsibility to learn of your watches and assignments to working parties from your Company Petty Officer. It is the policy of this command to assign transients to duties commensurate with their grade. Consistent with this policy, all transients will normally be assigned to some type of work. Regular liberty commences at 1630 and expires on board at 0730. Special liberty is granted only in unusual circumstances. The following limits on liberty travel on liberty are established:

    Overnight liberty..................75 miles
    Weekend or holiday liberty.......200 miles

Requests to exceed the limits above will be submitted on Special Request Form 11ND-GEN-1050/1; indicating address, mileage, and mode of travel in "leave address" space. Example: 23 Alfa St., Los Angeles, Calif., 130 miles, Auto.

LEAVE

While attached to the Naval Station in a transient status, leave cannot be granted except for a bona-fide emergency. Verification is required for emergency leave. The American Red Cross Representative is located in Building 71 and will assist in obtaining necessary verification.

--- PAGE 7 ---

PAY

Company TSP and TM personnel will normally be paid every other Friday (check with your company yeoman for the pay dates). Company TS personnel will receive instructions pertaining to their pay when they first report to their company yeoman. Company TC and TF personnel may be paid by placing their name on the pay list at Window #1, Building 56, provided ten days have elapsed since last paid. All payments are made by check. Company TC and TF personnel may pick up their check after 1330 from their respective company yeoman on the following working day. DO NOT CONTACT THE DISBURSING OFFICE ABOUT PAY OR OTHER DISBURSING MATTERS UNLESS YOU HAVE AN APPROVED REQUEST FORM SIGNED BY YOUR DIVISION OFFICER. Company TO personnel will be paid automatically when their pay record has been opened. Claims will not be processed for transient personnel for dependents' travel already performed or leave rations for leave taken on orders. These items must be processed upon arrival at the ultimate duty station.

PAYMENT OF ADVANCE PAY ON PERMANENT CHANGE OF STATION ORDERS

Upon receipt of permanent change of station orders, provided such change of station is not incident to separation from the service or trial by courts-martial, and subject to the approval of the Commanding Officer, personnel on active duty may be paid an advance of pay not to exceed three months basic pay, less income tax withholdings and the amount of any indebtedness to the Government. Enlisted members are not entitled to an advance of pay if they have less than six months obligated active service remaining from the day the advance would be made.

The purpose of advance pay is to furnish temporary relief from the expenses of providing transportation, temporary storage of household effects, packing and shipping costs, and the procuring of new living quarters for dependents. The amount of each advance of pay will be liquidated within a period of not more than six months starting the first of the month following the month in which the advance was made. An advance of pay not be paid in such an amount which will require the stoppage of insurance and Q allotments.

--- PAGE 8 ---

During the six month period required for liquidation of advance pay, a man's basic pay will be reduced 1/6 if he drew one month's advance, 1/3 if two months' and 1/2 if three months' advance was drawn. Experience has shown that advance pay usually cannot be so budgeted as to avoid a serious reduction in pay, although temporary, will not work a financial hardship on families involved. When such hardship occurs it very often becomes necessary to apply to the Navy Relief or the Red Cross for financial assistance. Such loans must then be repaid, thus prolonging the period of reduced pay. It would, therefore, be most appropriate to draw the minimum of advance pay and none if possible. In order to hold to a minimum the possibility of financial hardship where advance pay is involved, certain limitations on the amount of pay advanced upon transfer from this command due to permanent change of station have been established (see Naval Station, San Diego Manual P5450.4 series).

    a. If the change of stations involves a move from the San Diego area to:

    Location of new     Amount of Advance Pay
    duty station        Married personnel       Other
    (shore station or   or single personnel     single
    ship's home         maintaining homes       personnel
    port)               for dependents
                        in San Diego area

    San Diego area      NONE                    NONE

    West Coast other    1 MONTH                 NONE
    than San Diego

    Middle West         2 MONTHS                NONE

    Overseas or         3 MONTHS                NONE
    East Coast

--- PAGE 9 ---

Personnel desiring an advance of pay (and who meet the above criteria) may request such advance upon notification that a permanent change of station assignment has been received. This request will be made on a special request form and submitted to the Receipts and Transfer Officer via your Company Petty Officer. For further information contact your Company TC or TF yeoman.

SICK BAY

The Naval Dispensary and Dental Clinic are located in Building 74. Emergencies will be seen at any time. Routine sick call is held from 0800 to 0900, and from 1300 to 1400 daily. Keep your Barracks Petty Officer informed whenever you must report for sick call. Company TC personnel will report to the Company TC yeoman to obtain Dental or Health record and intra-station pass prior to reporting to Sick Bay. These passes serve as a receipt for the Health/Dental record. Personnel in Company TF should report to the Transient Health Record Office, Building 74, and obtain their Health/Dental record prior to reporting for sick call.

POSTAL DIRECTORY SERVICE

All incoming mail for transient personnel is handled by the Postal Directory located on the North side of Building 112. Personnel should check at the Postal Directory after reporting aboard to claim any mail which may be held for them. The Postal Directory is open from 0730-1630 Monday through Friday.

Your correct mailing address while in transient status is as follows:

    Name, Rate
    Transient Mail Section
    Naval Station
    San Diego, California 92136

If you have any problems concerning receipt of mail feel free to contact the Postal Directory personnel who will assist in every way possible in locating and/or obtaining your mail.

During your check-out process prior to transfer from this Station, you will be required to complete a Change of Address Card at the Postal Directory. Ensure that you properly complete this card as it is used to forward your mail to you at your given address.

--- PAGE 10 ---

ID CARDS - ID TAGS

Transient personnel are required to have a valid Armed Forces Identification Card and ID tags in their possession. Company TO personnel will be issued an ID card and ID tags as a part of their normal processing. Other transient personnel shall report to the ID Photo Lab, lower deck, Building 56, if their ID card has expired, is mutilated or has been lost, or if ID tags are not in their possession. The ID Photo Lab is open from 0800 to 1530 on regular working days.

DRAFTS

Personnel in transient status in companies TC and TF are subject to placement in an immediate outgoing draft status and may be placed on draft without advance notice. Personnel placed on draft will not be removed from such draft for any reason other than a bonafide emergency. In this respect, ALL PERSONNEL ARE DIRECTED TO HAVE A FULL SEA BAG ON BOARD AT ALL TIMES. Special liberty will not be granted to permit leaving the Station to obtain personal effects prior to departure on draft. The mission of this command is to dispatch transients to their ultimate destination as rapidly as possible; accordingly, retention on board will not normally be authorized except for emergency reasons.

CONDUCT OF PERSONNEL TRAVELING BY PUBLIC CONVEYANCE ON CHANGE OF DUTY ORDERS OR ON LEAVE

You are cautioned to conduct yourself so that there can be no complaint as to your behavior. Any conduct which brings discredit upon the Navy or involves violation of Navy Regulations, will be dealt with in the same manner as if the offenses had been committed on board a naval ship or station. You are informed that conductors of trains, drivers of buses, captains of planes, and masters of steamers are responsible to their employers for the safety and comfort of their passengers and the condition of the equipment in their charge, and that the public carrier representatives have the authority to take such steps as are necessary and legal to restrain disorderly persons traveling on these carriers.

Members of the Naval Service who are disorderly on public carriers can expect no special treatment. If the facts warrant, the offenders may be removed from the train, bus, plane, or steamer by civil authorities, and prompt and appropriate disciplinary action will be taken against such offenders upon their return to naval jurisdiction.

--- PAGE 11 ---

CONCURRENT TRAVEL

Personnel assigned to overseas activities who are traveling concurrently with their dependents should contact the Company TF yeoman as soon as possible after reporting to ensure that all required action incident to the transportation of dependents has been accomplished. Personnel who receive assignment orders to overseas based ships or stations will be called in for interview by the Company TC yeoman concerning concurrent travel.

INFORMATION FOR PERSONNEL PROCEEDING OUTSIDE THE UNITED STATES

All personnel (traveling without dependents) reporting on board for further transfer to activities outside the Continental United States are being transported by air. All bookings are arranged through the District Passenger Transportation Officer, Eleventh Naval District, who coordinates and obtains transportation for a large number of flights from the Twelfth Naval District. Therefore, it is impossible to predict in advance whether commercial, MAC, or a combination of both will be utilized until the call-out draft list is published.

Personnel enroute OUTUS who are furnished commercial air transportation from San Diego to Travis AFB are allowed 2 pieces of baggage and 1 hand carried item. Personnel who are furnished MAC air transportation from Travis AFB to OUTUS are authorized 66 lbs of accompanying baggage unless excess baggage allowance has been authorized. Cost of baggage in excess of authorized allowance will be borne by the traveler.

Personnel furnished commercial air transportation from San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle to ultimate destination OUTUS are allowed 66 lbs of baggage. You must be prepared to bear the cost of baggage in excess of 66 lbs at the following approximate rates per pound:

DESTINATION   COMM    MAC     DESTINATION     COMM    MAC
HAWAII        $ .69   $ .28   PHILIPPINES     $1.74   $ .87
GUAM           1.64    .72    TAIWAN           1.67    .80
JAPAN          1.34    .54    OKINAWA          1.60    .75
ADAK           1.67           KODIAK                   .75
KOREA          1.57    .72

For information, the combined weight of a standard sea bag containing a complete allowance of naval clothing and one small overnight handbag is between 55 and 66 pounds. However, personnel are URGED to weigh their baggage at the time they draw their initial supply of linen on the scale located at the Baggage Room, lower deck, Building 56, and prior to its stowage in the Transient Bag Room, upper deck, Building 56.

--- PAGE 12 ---

If you have over 66 pounds of baggage and are awaiting transportation OUTUS, or have been informed that an assignment has been transferred to transfer you OUTUS, you should call the Household Effects Office, Eleventh Naval District (phone 235-3205) to arrange for shipment of the remainder of your clothing (over 66 pounds). In arranging for this shipment, you will be required to have four (4) copies of your transfer orders. Copies of your orders may be obtained from your company yeoman, Receipts and Transfer Office, lower deck, Building 56.

Personnel desiring transportation to the District Household Effects Office, located at COMELEVEN Headquarters, Building 12, to deliver their excess personal effects for shipment, may request Base taxi service at extension 1101. An approved special request is required to depart the Station during working hours is required.

INFORMATION FOR SHIPMENT OF PERSONAL/HOUSEHOLD EFFECTS

All personnel in pay grade E-4 (with over 4 years service) and above are entitled to shipment of personal/household effects upon permanent change of station, either from sea duty to shore duty, from one shore station to another shore station, or from one sea duty station to another sea duty station. However, on changes of shipboard duty, the ships must have different home ports/home yards or one of the ships must be in the United States and the other ship outside the U. S. in which event you are entitled to shipment of personal effects (sea bag) only to your new ship. Personnel in the above pay grade are also entitled to shipment of personal effects under the following types of orders: (1) Permanent change of duty in connection with the building, fitting out, conversion or activation of vessels and on-board when commissioned; (2) Separation from the Naval Service; (3) Retirement or transfer to the Fleet Reserve; (4) If on temporary duty (at a school) of twenty weeks' duration or over. Personnel in pay grade E-4 (with over 4 years service) and above, on permanent change of station orders, are authorized one regular express shipment by surface transportation of 1,000 pounds or 400 pounds by air which is not to include any furniture. This shipment is solely for the purpose of shipping clothing, bedding and other items of necessity or of special value. The overall limit of weights allowed for various pay grades is listed below.

E-1 through E-4 (Third Class Petty Officer with LESS than 4 years service and non-rated personnel): The only shipment that these personnel are authorized is the shipment of their personal clothing if air travel is directed. (66 POUNDS ONLY IS ALLOWED WITH THE PERSON IN THE AIRCRAFT - SEE SECTION TITLED "INFORMATION FOR PERSONNEL PROCEEDING OUTSIDE THE UNITED STATES"). This shipment is limited to 200 pounds which must be delivered by the man upon application for shipment and thereby permits the individual to ship baggage which cannot be carried in the aircraft.

In arranging for shipment of personal or household effects you will be required to have four (4) copies of your transfer orders for each type of shipment being requested. See your company yeoman for copies of your orders. The Household Effects Office is located at the COMELEVEN Headquarters in Building 12 (near the foot of Broadway, San Diego). You may call the Household Effects Office (phone 235-3205) if you have questions regarding your shipment. It is suggested that you prepare a list of questions that you have prior to visiting the Household Effects Office to ensure that all of your questions are answered. An approved special request is required to depart the Station for this purpose.

--- PAGE 14 ---

SHIPMENT OF AUTOMOBILES OVERSEAS

Personnel who are proceeding overseas for duty and are eligible for automobile shipment may make application at the Naval Supply Center, Household Effects Section, Building 12, 937 No. Harbor Drive, San Diego. Four copies of STO's and proof of ownership or letter authorizing shipment of vehicle overseas is required.

COOPERATION WITH SHORE PATROL

Every member of the Armed Forces is required to give his name, rank or rate, and ship or station, when such information is requested by a member of the Shore Patrol; and such member is required to show his identification card, liberty card, leave papers, and travel orders, upon demand by the Shore Patrol.

HITCHHIKING

Section 21957 of the California Vehicle Code prohibits hitchhiking. In accordance with Naval Station, San Diego Manual P5450.4 series Naval personnel attached to this command are prohibited from hitchhiking (soliciting a ride on or adjacent to a highway other than at a shelter or within a designated pick-up area). Additionally, hitchhiking is unmilitary, dangerous, undignified and inconsistent with standards of conduct and self-reliance expected of military personnel. Hitchhikers constitute a traffic menace on highways and are potential victims of unscrupulous drivers.

PHOTOGRAPHIC EQUIPMENT

While it is permissible to have photographic equipment on the Station, taking pictures within the confines of the Naval Station is PROHIBITED.

--- PAGE 15 ---

VISITS TO MEXICO

Servicemen who visit Mexico are exhorted to conduct themselves in an exemplary manner at all times, bearing in mind the President's "People-to-People" program in which each serviceman shares a significant responsibility. You are required to wear civilian clothing while making unofficial visits to Mexico.

It is recommended that you leave cars on the U. S. side of the border and utilize commercial transportation when proceeding across the border. If you use a taxicab, do not get in until the fare has been PREDETERMINED. MINORS are prohibited from entering bars or buying intoxicants. NO ALCOHOLIC beverages are permitted entry into the State of California. All hands must cooperate with customs officials. Detailed information on visits to Mexico is contained in COMELEVEN Instruction 5710.4 series which is posted on the bulletin board at Window 1, Building 56.

LEGAL ASSISTANCE

Advice is available concerning legal problems at the Legal Assistance Office located in the Eleventh Naval District General Courts-Martial Building, Building 73 on the Naval Station.

TRAFFIC VIOLATIONS

All personnel committing traffic violations of local and state laws are required to settle the same before being transferred. If you are unable to appear because of lack of time, contact the Legal Office for advice concerning how to proceed, and notify your Company yeoman of this action. It is possible for the local authorities to request that service personnel be held in the San Diego area until court action is complete. In cases where the offense is a serious one, personnel who are convicted, can also be processed for administrative discharge.

--- PAGE 16 ---

RELIGIOUS ACTIVITIES

Religious services are conducted regularly for all faiths. The Chaplain is available for consultation in religious matters. Both the Protestant Chaplain and the Catholic Chaplain are located in Building 330. Commencement times of all religious services are announced in the Plan of the Day. You are urged to use all religious facilities.

1968-11-03.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1968-11-03.text:
Nov. 3, 68
Da Nang

Mike,

Well here I am again, in the big "rat hole" Nam.

I can't remember if I told you or not, but I am on patrols for 60 days. I've only been out once at night and tonight will be my 2nd time.

Its not really to bad out there, but it does get kind of scary. you know? The other nite once when we was out the A.R.V.N.'s opened up on us from the other side of the river, we got down for awhile, then up. They fired again and we got down then we moved out and was fired at again but kept going. 3 guys got down and we didn't know it. after we went about 150 ft. we found out they wasn't with us. So we hit our rifle stocks to let them know we were looking for them. The point there I found him in some brush and something moved so he opened up on it then threw a frag. at it, after that the 3 guys started yelling at us. and they were really pissed off at the point. after that happened we come back into the C.A. We was out twice that nite from 7:PM - 11:PM and 2:AM - 5:30 AM. boy

was I tired when we got in.

Jim Dick was out to see me this morning, but I had to leave about ½ hour after he got here. I plan on seeing him again tomorrow on my day off.

Well have the big short timer doing? In 112 more days I'll be on my way home too. and in 25 days I'll be going on R&R to Taipei for 5 fun filled days of booze & pussy!

Well thats about it for now, hope to hear from you soon. Bye for now & take care.

Little Brother
Bill USMC

1968-11-07.attribution: USS Jouett (DLG-29) Familygram, Capt. Robert S. Hayes, Commanding Officer — Ducy Family Archives
1968-11-07.text:
USS JOUETT
FAMILY GRAM

                                                7 November 1968

Dear JOUETT Family and Friends,

Since our return to the United States on 18 July, JOUETT has once again become a familiar sight at the Naval Station, San Diego. The big hull numerals "29" and the distinctive "high-rise" superstructure could be seen at the end of pier two much of the past three months. While many of our crew members took leave and attended various schools ashore, the ship received a modernization of her guided missile system. It is a fact of JOUETT's life that while she is a new ship, she is nevertheless being continually updated: since her completion in the shipyard, she has continued to receive the latest improvements for her weapons and electronics systems.

If you have paid a visit to the ship recently, you may have noticed some changes that have occurred. The Mess Decks area is quickly taking on a "new look". A committee was appointed to present ideas for redecorating this part of the ship, and volunteer manpower is putting their ideas into effect. When the facelifting is complete, there will be a new color scheme, a new tiled deck, and more useable room in this multipurpose space that belongs especially to the crew. Then just outside the barbershop, in one of the ship's main passageways, a large mahogany board has been mounted to display the names of all the recipients of JOUETT's Outstanding Service Award. In previous Familygrams, I have told you of the crewmen who have received the Award, given for a minimum of one year of Outstanding Service aboard JOUETT. There are 40 brass name plates on the board now, and optimistically, there is room left for many more.

The changes in new faces would be even more evident to you in your tour around the ship than the physical changes. Since JOUETT's return to San Diego, six officers and 104 enlisted men of the old crew have departed the ship for new horizons. Eight officers and 68 enlisted men have reported aboard to replace them. That is a turnover of roughly one quarter of the crew. In addition, six officers and twenty-four of our enlisted men have been advanced in rank since JOUETT's return. The twenty-four were advanced because they qualified in all respects for promotion, and successfully passed the Navy's very competitive examination for advancement in rate. The ship is especially proud that three of the twenty-four were selected for advancement to the rate of Chief Petty Officer. They are: Claude GUNNERSEN to Chief Gunner's Mate, Kenneth KLEPPER to Chief Fire Control Technician, and Patrick FEELEY to Chief Sonar Technician.

The proudest new change in the ship's appearance is a small, multicolored pennant that flies from the highest halyard on the ship and the newest (fourth) ribbon on the bulwark of the bridge. They represent the Navy Unit Commendation. In a ceremony on 11 October, Rear Admiral Sheldon H. KINNEY, Commander of Cruiser-Destroyer FLOTILLA Eleven, presented the pennant to the ship after reading the following commendation from the Secretary of the Navy:

For exceptionally meritorious service from 18 February through 29 June 1968 while engaged in operations against enemy aggressor forces in the waters contiguous to hostile coastline of North Vietnam. As a principal unit of TASK FORCE SEVENTY-SEVEN's Search and Rescue forces, USS JOUETT carried out day and night Search and Rescue missions, control of Combat Air Patrol, Strike-Following duties, and Air Defense operations against hostile aircraft. The successful completion of a large percentage of the Search and Rescue missions, involving pilots downed in North Vietnam, reflects the skillful planning and extensive training and preparation accomplished by the ship's personnel in the face of an extremely hostile enemy enviroment. After arrival in the Gulf of Tonkin, JOUETT personnel quickly became noted for the professional manner and exacting thoroughness with which they controlled Combat Air Patrol over North Vietnam and provided Strike-Following services to carrier aircraft interdicting North Vietnamese supply lines. Additionally, JOUETT's aggressive and highly effective techniques in countering enemy aircraft contributed in large measure to the security of Naval ships in the South China Sea. The courage, stamina, professionalism, and dedication displayed by the officers and men of USS JOUETT earned the admiration and gratitude of the pilots and air crewmen of TASK FORCE SEVENTY-SEVEN, and were in keeping with the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. All personnel attached to and serving on board USS JOUETT (DLG 29) during the above designated period, or any part thereof, are hereby authorized to wear the Navy Unit Commendation Ribbon.

At the same ceremony, Admiral KINNEY presented numerous individual awards. I have added a list of the awards and their recipients to the end of this letter.

A few words on the past weeks will bring you up to date on JOUETT's activities. We spent the past two weeks steaming in local operating areas, not far from San Diego, and fulfilled two missions. First, JOUETT was selected as host ship for a Secretary of the Navy Guest Cruise. Three distinguished citizens from the California area rode the ship at the invitation of the Secretary of the Navy in order to learn something of the Navy and the role of seapower as it relates to national security. They had a good chance to talk with JOUETT men about the Navy, and to observe a modern warship in action. As part of her second mission last week, JOUETT fired five Terrier missiles to check out her new missile installation. Both missions were successful. Our guests left us well-informed and well-satisfied with their week at sea.

If you have not visited JOUETT recently - or if you have - we hope you will be able to join us for the Family Cruise on Saturday 23 November. This is our special chance to share the experience of going to sea with you. The days program will include tours of all parts of the ship, views of San Diego harbor while departing and returning to port, buffet lunch, and music by the CRUDESPAC Band. Family and guests of the crew are cordially invited. Dress informally and for warmth. All who make the cruise will receive an honorary crew member card. JOUETT will be in company with four or five other ships of Destroyer Squadron ONE, which will permit some very exciting maneuvers including tactics and hi-line transfers between ships. As the date approaches, detailed information on the family cruise will be promulgated.

For the remainder of this year JOUETT will participate in several short training exercises at sea near San Diego. The object will be in training personnel in their jobs aboard ship and to train the ship in operations with other ships.

From about 9 December until 6 January JOUETT will be pierside at San Diego which will make it possible for all crew members to take leave over some part of the holiday season.

Even though our stateside operations are not as exciting as those in Tonkin Gulf, I trust that occasional familygrams such as this will help to keep you informed of JOUETT's activities. Also for many of our men, the letters from home are still most important.

Sincerely,

ROBERT S. HAYES
CAPTAIN, U.S. NAVY
COMMANDING OFFICER

time aboard Jouett from reporting (Sep 27, 1967) through discharge.

P.C. METTA: The Personnel Officer who signed this document is the
same officer listed as ENS Paul C. Meta on the Oct 11, 1968 Awards
Ceremony program. By November he had been promoted to LTJG.

RESERVE OBLIGATION: Mike remained obligated to the Naval Reserve
until March 17, 1971 — six years from his original enlistment date
of March 18, 1965. This obligation is documented in the 1970
ACDUTRA orders and Oct 27, 1970 mobilization directive.

1968-11-26.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1968-11-26.text:
Nov. 26, 68
Da Nang

Mike,

Well here I am again, sorry for taking so long. But I was going to wait till you got home.

I am still on patrols and doing alright. Yesterday the patrol got hit by 3 V.C., only one guy got hurt by a grenade that was thrown at them by the gooks. I went out that night too, but it was at a later time and in a different area. also there was only 5 of us, I was walking drag man but our radio-man got sick so we couldn't set up any good ambushes. So we brought him in and I took over the radio for the rest of the night. We was delayed going out about 1½ hrs. because we had 2 red alerts in about a 3 hrs. Boy the lifers were sure sweating it.

Oh yea, I had my "shipping over" lecture last week! Man all the things bennies they'll give me after 20 yrs. all I said was "I am not interested." and - also passed my G.E.D. test, now all I've got to do is write Mac. and send them my score. I am really happy about it.

In 4 more days I'll be on R&R, I am really going to live it up for those 5 days.

In about 90 days I'll be on my way home. I guess I could say I'm SHORT!, since I started out with 393 days. and time really has flown for me, last year at this time I was home on leave.

Now tell me how the big town doing? Have you started looking for a job yet?

Well I guess I'll be going for now, take care, and watch yourself with those Decatur girls. ha ha. Bye for now.

"U.S.M.C.                          Little Brother
 NEVER AGAIN"                      Bill
1968-11-26.attribution: Letter, Bill Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-12-08.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1968-12-08.text:
Dec. 8, 68
Da Nang

Mike,

Well I am back from my R&R. and let me tell you I really had a wonderful time. and would like to go back, but I doubt I will. and those girls there really were fine, if you know what I mean.

Yea, I'd sure like to see your new car, it sounds like a mover.

Talking about shot guns, would you take and oil mine down real good for me? Its been a little over a year for it. David should be able to show you some good hunting places.

Yea I am still on patrols, last night we was out in a 7 man-ambush. I was set up in some brush along this trail when I heard some movement comming my way. Well I threw a hand illum, and lite up that area, I spotted something trying to move out, I fired about 10 rounds at it. We then broke the ambush and checked out the area, all we found was a little blood. So I guess he was hit.

Today we had a USO show, and was it bad. They had guts to be on that stage.

Now tell me how big Decatur is doing? I bet its still dead as usual.

Well now only 77 more days left over here in this hell hole! I just hope days go by fast, like the 316 before have done.

Thats about it for now, write when ever you can and good luck in getting a job.

Little Brother
Bill

P.S. 1 more day and I'll be 19 years old. Wow. B.F.D.

SHORT!
1968-12-08.attribution: Letter, Bill Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1968-12-20.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1968-12-20.text:
Dec. 20, 68
Da Nang

Mike,

Well here I am again, and still going strong.

Your job sounds like it might be something good. What are the chances for raises for you. $100.00 a week ain't bad for starting out.

Well in 11 more days I going to be requesting mast for Lance/cpl. I think 13 months in grade is too much, and I could sure use the $20.00 extra.

The action around here has been picking up a little. Last night about 8:30 the ARVN's down at the bottom of our hill caught 2 V.C. in a ville about 50 meters from our C.P. They had a radio listening to a V.C. broadcast. They took them in and their small camp for questioning. Talk about the ways they have to make the V.C. talk. 1st they beat the shit out of them with bamboo sticks, then put them in a small barb-wire pen about 2½ ft in Dim. and about a foot high. While in there the V.C. were being poked with the sticks. Well all in all they spilt the beans about what was happening around the Da Nang area. One thing they said was there is 51 V.C. in our near area. One kid was 16 and the other was 17, at first I felt sorry for them, but they sure wouldn't feel that way for us if they popped us off. So when we took it slow and easy down the trail, in about 50 yds. we found a boobie trap. Luckly they weren't armed yet. The C.O.C. bunker told us to forget our main mission, and to set up an ambush at the edge of this ville. So we set there for 5 hrs., but didn't see anything but a dog, but we cut him a hurr and didn't blow him away.

I've been carrying a 12 ga. shotgun, (which holds 6 rounds) on the day patrols mostly to kill snakes with. I got 3 yesterday while crossing a paddy. I'll start carrying it at nights while walking dogs when they get me some OO buck, now all they've got is #4 buck. I don't like it at night cause the pattern is so big.

Well I've got only 65 more days left over here in the Nam. And have been here for 328 days. I just hope the time keeps flyin by.

I'd best be goin for now, I've got to get up early for the morning patrol. So bye for now, take care and good luck in your job.

Little Brother
Bill

"SHORT"
1968-12-20.attribution: Letter, Bill Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1969-01-06.label: AR Norris to Mike
1969-01-06.text:
6 Jan. 1969

Dear Mike,

    HAPPY NEW YEAR !! Thanks for the letter , we were all glad to hear from you. Glad to hear you got the cruise book alright..What did you think of it? I thought there was going to be more colored pictures. It's good to see you got right in the swing of things getting a job so soon and buying a car && right off.

(Excuse my typing but I never was very good)

    I reported back from leave this morning and it sure was great to get off this boat for awhile. We had a very beautiful Christmas  and New Year's. It sure was nice to be with the family and relatives over the holidays. Meadows had duty New Year's eve ha! ha! Ole was home in ILL. for the holidays and now he's got a touch of the H.K. flu. Underwood ?? what can I say! The jolly J. is still the same. As a matter of fact , we have a material inspection this friday 11 th. So things haven't changed very much , alot of new faces but thats about all.

    Good Luck in that six week school you are suppose to attend in Chicago and in that cruel civilian world.

    Well Mike I'm getting short 355 days to go but I hope to get out before Christmas of next year on a holiday cut. Time will tell. This is short but at least you know we're still alive and floating. So take care!!

    From all of us here , HAPPY NEW YEAR!!

                              Sincerely ,
                              Art

P.S. Here's a letter from the
     Bank of America,
1969-01-06.attribution: Letter, A.R. Norris FTG-3 — Ducy Family Archives

1969-02-06.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1969-02-06.text:
Feb. 6, 69
Da Nang

Mike,

Well here I am again and doing fine. Haven't heard from you for a while.

Now I've got only 13 days left over here in Nam. My flight date for the states is the 20th. of this month. I should be home around the 27th. And when I get home let me tell you we're really going to raise hell in that town.

I got my sea bag packed and ready to mail home, and sold some of my gear to the boots that just got in.

I bought a $53.00 suit case at the P.X. for only $30.50 and its really a dandy. I just can't see carrying that sea bag with me home and mailing it is real cheap.

I am off patrols now and back in the co. area. They've got me mostly on working party's and duty driver.

It turned off cold the past few days. It wasn't really cold, but down in the 60's is cold as for over here, and we froze our ass's off.

Well I'd best be going for now, see you soon and take care.

                           Little Brother
P.S. SHORT                 Bill
1969-02-06.attribution: Letter, Bill Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1969-02-18.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1969-02-18.text:
Feb. 18, 69
Da Nang

Mike,

Well here I am again and short as ever. Only 2 more big days and I'll be out of this fucked-up place for good. I'll be on my big freedom bird the 20th.

I plan on staying out at G.M.'s for about 2 days then head on home. I just hope you'll still be in Decatur at least till I get off of leave.

I've got my boot camp I.D. in here and want you to keep it for me. I told the Co. office that I lost it so I could get a new one with my mustach on it.

your place no. is a real good one and easy to remember.

They sure have been fucking with us short timers here at 7th Comm. I was on bunkers last week & now I'm on assit. duty N.C.O. from 12 midnight to 6:30 AM. But one good thing about it they can't stop the clock. Its now 2:45 AM & about 10 hrs. from now I'll be checking out of this chicken shit Bn. for good.

Well I'd best be going for now, see you soon & take care.

Little Brother
Bill

P.S. NOT SHORT -
NEXT!
1969-02-18.attribution: Letter, Bill Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1969-03-01.label: USS Jouett 1968 Command Operations Report
1969-03-01.attribution: USS Jouett 1968 Command Operations Report — Ducy Family Archives
1969-03-01.text:
CONFIDENTIAL
                    DEPARTMENT OF THE NAVY
                   U. S. S. JOUETT (DLG-29)
                   FPO SAN FRANCISCO 96601
                                                         DLG 29:PAO:
DECLASSIFIED                                             5750-1
                                                         1 MARCH 1969
CONFIDENTIAL (Unclassified upon removal of Enclosure 1).

From:  Commanding Officer, USS JOUETT (DLG-29)
To:    Director of Naval History (OP-09B9)
       Washington Navy Yard
       Washington, D. C. 20390

Subj:  OPNAV REPORT 5750-1 for Calender Year 1968; Submission of.

Ref:   (a) OPNAVINST 5750.12A of 31 October 1968

Encl:  (1) Command History of USS JOUETT (DLG-29) for Calendar Year
           1968.
       (2) Documentary Annexes.

1.  In accordance with Reference (a), Enclosure (1) is herewith submitted.

                                        J. A. WALKER, JR.
                                        By direction


DECLASSIFIED BY: CNO (N09N2)
OPNAVINST 5513.16 SERIES
DATE: 16 March 2006


--- PAGE 2 ---

                                                         DECLASSIFIED
                                                         CONFIDENTIAL

              Command History of USS JOUETT (DLG-29)
                    for Calendar Year 1968


I.  Chronology of Highlights

16 JAN-18 JUL  Deployment to Western Pacific.  During three periods on
               the line as South SAR Station Ship, a total of 98 days
               were spent in Tonkin Gulf Combat Zone.

18 JUL-24 OCT  Restricted availability in San Diego while undergoing
               Standard Missile Installation.  Successfully proved
               out by Navy's first operational Standard Missile firings
               on 24 OCT.

11 OCT         Navy Unit Commendation and 76 individual awards presented
               by Commander Cruiser-Destroyer Flotilla Eleven, in
               ceremony on board, San Diego.

23 NOV         Dependents Cruise.  450 dependents and guests spend a
               day at sea.

27 NOV         Change of Command.  Capt. Robert S. Hayes, USN, relieved
               by Capt. Robert C. Barnhart, Jr., USN, in ceremony on
               board, San Diego.

28 NOV-1 DEC   Underway on two hours notice, Thanksgiving Day, to provide
               Emergency Medical Evacuation of ill crewman on Navy
               minesweeper ACME, 1000 miles from San Diego.  Patient
               safely delivered Balboa Hospital, San Diego, 1 DEC.

4-9 DEC        Participated in Commander First Fleet's Strike Exercise
               4-68 ("Beef Trust").

14-31 DEC      Holiday leave period, in port, San Diego.

31 DEC         Competitive cycle completed.  JOUETT awarded Battle
               Efficiency "E" Award for Destroyer Squadron One, plus all
               departmental "E" awards.


                                                         CONFIDENTIAL
                                                         DECLASSIFIED

                              1                    (ENCLOSURE 1)


--- PAGE 3 ---

                                                         DECLASSIFIED
                                                         CONFIDENTIAL

II.  BASIC NARRATIVE


     JOUETT spent the first two weeks of January completing final

preparations for her first Westpac deployment.  COMDESRON ONE also

completed his administrative Inspection of JOUETT and on 16 January

JOUETT cast off her lines from San Diego and headed West to the Pacific

and South East Asia.  JOUETT stopped at Pearl Harbor on 21 January

for CINCPACFLT briefings and liberty.  She got underway on 25 January

and again in company with USS PREBLE (DLG15) and USS HULL (DD945),

JOUETT continued her journey Westward to Vietnam.  After a brief 10

hour fueling stop in Guam on 3 February, JOUETT pulled into Subic

Bay, P. I., on 7 February for minor maintenance and type training.

Underway on 13 February, JOUETT continued Westward and on 15 February

she anchored in Danang harbor, South Vietnam.  Selected officers and

key enlisted men attended briefings on Monkey Mountain by the Air

Force, and on 16 February JOUETT left Danang and proceeded north to the

Gulf of Tonkin, where she relieved the USS HALSEY (DLG23) as South

SAR (Search and Rescue) Station ship on 18 February.  Equipped with a

UH-2 helicopter, flown and maintained by two officers and eight enlisted

men, JOUETT remained on SSAR station until 23 March.  JOUETT, with the

SAR Commander, COMDESRON ONE embarked, participated in twelve SAR's

during this first line period.

     JOUETT was relieved as SSAR station ship on 23 March by HALSEY,

and after a 12 hour layover in Subic Bay for fuel on 24 March, JOUETT

set her course north to Yokosuka Japan.  She arrived in Yokosuka on

28 March for a ten day visit.  During this brief pause, JOUETTmen

conducted a People-to-People community relations project, reconditioning

two churches, a parsonage and various church grounds during three days

of work.

                              2                    (ENCLOSURE 1)


--- PAGE 4 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CONT)

     JOUETT left Yokosuka on 7 April and returned to Subic Bay for
five days, the 11th through the 15th, for supplies and type training.

     Underway on 15 April JOUETT again visited Danang, South Vietnam,
for briefings, but was clear of Danang harbor on the night of 16 April
and relieved HALSEY as SSAR station ship on 17 April.

     The historic Presidential "bombing pause" took place while JOUETT
was in Yokosuka and upon returning to SSAR station JOUETT found that
the majority of the Air Force and Navy strikes were being conducted in
the Vinh area which is adjacent to the SSAR station. Consequently,
JOUETT was considerably more active not only as SAR ship but also
as Strike Support Ship (SSS). While on station, during this, her
second line period, from 17 April to 17 May, the DESRON ONE/JOUETT
Team was personally responsible for the rescue of 5 downed aviators:

     A. LCDR D. E. HERNANDEZ and LTJG D. J. LORTSCHER, F-4 Phantom,
from the USS RANGER (CVA61) on 28 April.

     B. LCDR Ejnar S. CHRISTENSEN and LTJG Worth A. KRAMER, F-4 Phantom,
from the USS ENTERPRISE (CVA(N)65) on 7 May.

     C. LT Dennis A. Lawrence, A-7 Skyhawk, from the USS ENTERPRISE
(CVA(N)65) on 8 May.

     JOUETT, as Strike Support Ship, assisted the strike pilots from
the Yankee station carriers by providing navigational data, target
data and warnings of enemy activity. A very effective rapport was
established between the strike pilots and JOUETT's strike followers
which was further cemented by continual exchange visits.

     On 17 May, JOUETT was again relieved by HALSEY as SSAR station
ship and again she proceeded to Subic Bay to off-load her UH-2 helicopter
and detachment. In and out of Subic Bay on the same day, 18 May,


--- PAGE 5 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CONT)

JOUETT steamed across the South China Sea to Hong Kong BCC where she
visited from 21 to 25 May. Returning to Subic for four days, 28 May
to 31 May, to load her helicopter, helo detachment and various other
supplies, JOUETT once more headed west to Danang. She anchored in
Danang harbor on the morning of 1 June, and after routine briefings,
left that same night.

     JOUETT relieved HALSEY as SSAR station ship on 3 June and remained
on station until 30 June. During her third line period the COMDESRON
ONE/JOUETT Team rescued three more downed aviators.

     A. LTJG COLLINS, F-4 Phantom radar operator, from the USS AMERICA
(CVA66) on 4 June.

     B. LCDR John HOLTZCLAW and LCDR John BURNS, F-4 Phantom, from
the USS AMERICA (CVA66) on 19 June.

     JOUETT also was extremely busy with Strike Support Ship functions,
continuously assisting the strike aircraft in their missions.

     During this last line period JOUETT conducted seven MIG/CAP
controlled intercepts and on 26 June, Richard TANNER, RD1, one of
JOUETT's many expert AIC's (Air Intercept Controller) executed an
intercept that resulted in the destruction of one MIG-21.

     Due to increased MIG activity in the Vinh area, which was detri-
mental to the Navy bombing strikes, JOUETT was given a special assign-
ment as AAW Picket ship just off the coast at 19N/106E, during the
latter two weeks of June. On 17 June JOUETT fired a two missile salvo
of Terrier HTR missiles at a flight of two MIG-21 aircraft and again on
22 June JOUETT fired two more salvoes of two and one Terrier HTR missiles
at a flight of three MIG-21 aircraft. However, JOUETT did not hit any
of the enemy aircraft due to extreme range and evasive tactics on the


--- PAGE 6 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CONT)

part of the enemy.

     CINC[P]AC[F]LT, [F]OR[W]ARD[FLT], and [ADM]RAL[IV] F[A]V[L] (CTF 77) visited
JOUETT on 20 June for briefings. [ADM]RAL[FLT] spoke to the assembled
men on JOUETT briefly, expressing appreciation for the fine job they
were doing on station.

     JOUETT was relieved for the third and final time as SSAR station
ship on 30 June by the USS [B]ARN[E] ([D]LG30), she then returned to Subic
Bay, arriving on 2 July, where she off-loaded her helicopter detachment
and on-loaded supplies and fuel. JOUETT left Subic Bay that same day
and turned her bow westward for San Diego. She stopped briefly (six
hours) at Guam for fuel on 5 July and then continued her homeward
journey, a detour to the equator at the 180th meridian on 9 July
provided JOUETT with an opportunity to initiate many new Golden Shellbacks
and on 13 July she arrived in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.

     JOUETT refueled and left Pearl that same day and arrived in her
home port of San Diego, California on 18 July.

     Upon her return to the United States on 18 July, JOUETT entered
a period of Restricted Availability at Pier Two, Naval Station, San
Diego. While many of the crew took leave or attended various schools
ashore, the ship received the Standard Missile installation, a package
of over 30 ORDALTs modernized the ship's Mark 76 Mod 4 Guided Missile
Fire Control System and adapted it to employ the Standard Missile.
The majority of the changes affected the AN/SPG-55B Missile Fire Control
Radars and the Mark 119 Mod 4 Computers.

     Since the ship had the capability to fire only three different
types of Terrier Missile, the Conventional BT Terrier Missile capability
was sacrificed to make room for the Standard Missile. Thus the ship


--- PAGE 7 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CONT)

was left with the nuclear, beam-riding Terrier (BTN), the homing retrofit
Terrier (HTR), and the Standard Missile. The new Standard Missile
is very similar to the HTR Terrier Missile, and shares the same range
capabilities and flight characteristics. It incorporates certain
design improvements over the HTR, and is expected to have greater
reliability and lower cost.

     The Standard Missile Installation was temporarily suspended from
19-22 August, when the ship got underway to participate in Southeast
Asia Interface Tests.

     Upon return to San Diego on 22 August, the Standard Missile
Installation was proved out 22-24 October, when JOUETT fired a total
of five missiles on the Pacific Missile Range. Of two Standard Missiles
expended, one was a success and one was undetermined; two HTR missiles
expended were both successes; one BT (N) Exercise missile was a failure.

     Riding the ship during the week of the Missile Firings (21-25
October), were three guests of the Secretary of the Navy. JOUETT's
objectives in hosting these prominent civilian personnel from the
California area were threefold:

     (1) To acquaint them with the Navy and the role of sea power
     as it relates to national security.

     (2) To promote an understanding of the Navy, its relations with
     other services, overall capabilities, striking power and flexibility,
     and the sophisticated level of modern weaponry.

     (3) To focus attention on the importance of people in the Navy,
     their competence and high degree of responsibility and level
     of training.

The guests were Mr. Frank H. THOMAS of San Diego; Honorable George

                              6          (ENCLOSURE 1)

                                                        DECLASSIFIED
                                                        -CONFIDENTIAL-


--- PAGE 8 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CONT)

                                                        DECLASSIFIED

CRAWFORD, Municipal Court, San Diego Judicial District, San Diego;
and Mr. Edmund W. BAKER of West Covina, California. During their
week at sea, the guests toured the ship, observed gun and missile
firings, and had the opportunity to talk at length with both officers
and crew.

     One other noteworthy event occurred during the Standard Missile
Installation period. In a ceremony held on board on 11 October,
Rear Admiral Sheldon H. KINNEY, Commander of Cruiser-Destroyer Flotilla
Eleven, presented the Navy Unit Commendation Pennant to the ship after
reading the following commendation from the Secretary of the Navy:

     THE SECRETARY OF THE NAVY TAKES PLEASURE IN COM-
     MENDING USS JOUETT (DLG-29) FOR SERVICE AS SET
     FORTH IN THE FOLLOWING CITATION:

          FOR EXCEPTIONALLY MERITORIOUS SERVICE FROM
          18 FEBRUARY THROUGH 29 JUNE 1968 WHILE ENGAGED
          IN OPERATIONS AGAINST ENEMY AGGRESSOR FORCES IN
          THE WATERS CONTIGUOUS TO HOSTILE COASTLINE OF
          NORTH VIETNAM. AS A PRINCIPAL UNIT OF TASK FORCE
          SEVENTY-SEVEN'S SEARCH AND RESCUE FORCES, USS JOUETT
          CARRIED OUT DAY AND NIGHT SEARCH AND RESCUE MISSIONS,
          CONTROL OF COMBAT AIR PATROL, STRIKE-FOLLOWING
          DUTIES, AND AIR DEFENSE OPERATIONS AGAINST HOSTILE
          AIRCRAFT. THE SUCCESSFUL COMPLETION OF A LARGE
          PERCENTAGE OF THE SEARCH AND RESCUE MISSIONS,
          INVOLVING PILOTS DOWNED IN NORTH VIETNAM, REFLECTS
          THE SKILLFUL PLANNING AND EXTENSIVE TRAINING AND
          PREPARATION ACCOMPLISHED BY THE SHIP'S PERSONNEL
          IN THE FACE OF AN EXTREMELY HOSTILE ENEMY ENVIRON-
          MENT. AFTER ARRIVAL IN THE GULF OF TONKIN, JOUETT
          PERSONNEL QUICKLY BECAME NOTED FOR THE PROFESSIONAL
          MANNER AND EXACTING THOROUGHNESS WITH WHICH THEY
          CONTROLLED COMBAT AIR PATROL OVER NORTH VIETNAM
          AND PROVIDED STRIKE-FOLLOWING SERVICES TO CARRIER
          AIRCRAFT INTERDICTING NORTH VIETNAMESE SUPPLY LINES.
          ADDITIONALLY, JOUETT'S AGGRESSIVE AND HIGHLY EFFEC-
          TIVE TECHNIQUES IN COUNTERING ENEMY AIRCRAFT CON-
          TRIBUTED IN LARGE MEASURE TO THE TO THE SECURITY OF
          NAVAL SHIPS IN THE SOUTH CHINA SEA. THE COURAGE,
          STAMINA, PROFESSIONALISM, AND DEDICATION DISPLAYED
          BY THE OFFICERS AND MEN OF USS JOUETT EARNED THE
          ADMIRATION AND GRATITUDE OF THE PILOTS AND AIR
          CREWMEN OF TASK FORCE SEVENTY-SEVEN, AND WERE IN
          KEEPING WITH THE HIGHEST TRADITIONS OF THE UNITED STATES

                              7          (ENCLOSURE 1)

                                                        DECLASSIFIED
                                                        -CONFIDENTIAL-


--- PAGE 9 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CONT)

     Personnel stability was high in the first half of 1968, with little
turnover in assigned personnel during deployment. However, upon JOUETT'S
return to the United States in July, a rapid turnover commenced which
amounted to roughly one quarter of the crew by November. Six officers
and 104 enlisted men were detached during this period; eight officers
and enlisted men reported aboard as replacements. The turnover in
personnel culminated with the arrival of the perspective Commanding
Officer, Capt. Robert C. BARNHART, Jr., USN. Captain BARNHART came
to JOUETT from a tour of duty in the office of the Chief of Naval
Operations. Prior to that he was Commanding Officer of the USS TURNER
JOY (DD951). He was awarded the Bronze Star with Combat Distinguishing
Device for meritorious service in an engagement with North Vietnamese
motor torpedo boats which attacked the TURNER JOY in the Gulf of Tonkin
on 4 August 1964.

     On 27 November, at 1000, in a ceremony held on board, Captain
Robert S. HAYES, USN, was relieved by Captain BARNHART as Commanding
Officer. From JOUETT Captain HAYES proceeded to Washington, D. C.,
for duty as a Program Analyst in the office of the Secretary of the
Navy.

     The day after the change of command was Thanksgiving, but in the
ship's history it will be remembered as the day of the "ACME Rescue
Mission". Aboard the USS ACME (MSO508), a small Navy Minesweeper in

                              9          (ENCLOSURE 1)

                                                        DECLASSIFIED
                                                        CONFIDENTIAL


--- PAGE 11 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CON'T)

transit from Pearl Harbor to Long Beach, and 1000 miles out from San
Diego, a crewman was stricken with a severe abdominal attack. JOUETT
was chosen by Commander First Fleet to steam to the rescue and provide
medical evacuation. Crewmen were recalled to the ship by radio and tele-
vision bulletins. By 1330, two and half hours after notification,
JOUETT was underway. One half of the crew was aboard, with supplements
borrowed from the duty sections of other guided-missile ships: HALSEY,
PREBLE, DALE, and WILSON. As JOUETT cleared Point Loma, a rescue helicop-
ter from HC-5, Naval Air Station, Imperial Beach, landed on her flight
deck. Pilot and Officer-in-Charge of the helicopter detachment was
LT. John PASSIGLIA. An emergency medical team from Balboa Naval Hos-
pital was on board, ready to perform surgery if needed.

     On the ACME, Hospitalman First Class Walter W. HORTMAN, the stricken
crewmember, and the only medical specialist available on the small ship,
diagnosed his own condition as an apparent perforation of the stomach.

     JOUETT proceeded west at 27 knots. When range to the ACME had
closed to 135 miles, at 1530 on 29 November, the rescue helicopter was
launched. An hour later, the helicopter sighted the minesweeper in the
approaching darkness. HORTMAN was evacuated and returned to JOUETT
without mishap. The surgeons determined that emergency surgery was
not necessary. When JOUETT returned to San Diego late on the night
of 30 November, HORTMAN was transferred to Balboa Naval Hospital. There
he made a successful recovery without the need for emergency surgery.

     Because of the unscheduled ACME MEDEVAC, and the resultant underway
time over Thanksgiving, JOUETT was exempted from participation in the
first days of COMFIRSTFLT's Strikex 4-68. Getting underway on 4 Dec
vice 2 Dec, JOUETT participated in the remainder of "Beef Trust" training

                              10         (ENCLOSURE 1)

                                                        DECLASSIFIED
                                                        CONFIDENTIAL


--- PAGE 12 ---

II. BASIC NARRATIVE (CON'T)

exercise. She returned to San Diego on 9 Dec. On 14 Dec, JOUETT
commenced a holiday leave period which continued through 6 January 1969.

     Upon completion of her first competitive cycle since commissioning,
JOUETT was awarded the Battle Efficiency "E" Award for Destroyer Squadron
One. In addition, JOUETT won departmental "E" Awards for excellence in
Engineering, Operations, and Weapons. The Weapons Department awards
included "E's" for Gunnery and Missiles, and the "A" Award for ASW.
Having the Terrier/Asroc dual launcher system, JOUETT believes she is the
first ship in the Navy to wear both the "A" and the "E" (for missiles)
Awards on the same launcher system.

1969-04-15.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1969-04-15.text:
April 15, 69

Mike,

Well here I am, boy does this place really suck. About the only thing to do around here is drink or take off for the weekend and go about 350 miles to have a good time.

That wasn't to bad on the car, just if it runs better and doesn't leak oil I can get a real good watch for you for $30.29 and a ball from 16.50 - $22.00 shoes are $0.25 and bag is $5.25.

If you could get your hand sized at one of the lanes I think it would fit you better. I've been doing alot of bowling this past week, the highest I've gotten was 194.

Well payday come for us tomorrow, I hope to get about $60.00.

I've been buying alot of record alb's. They're only $2.90 for the $4.70 reg.

That tax refund wasn't much, I'll cash it tomorrow with my other check.

I've got duty this weekend so I won't be leaving this place until next week.

I got in a welding class about 6 miles from base. It cost me $16.00 for 11 weeks, which I go 2 nights a week for 3 hrs. each night. Plus I got 2 books, one on arc welding and the other on blue print reading for welding. I sure hope to do good in it.

Boy I'm glad that I'm getting that cut, they've been getting guys that have more time than me to go to get on a ship for 3½ mo. to Greece and other places. They've got 5 from my section.

Well I guess thats about all the news for now, so take care. Oh, yea could you look up Linda's address and send it to me?

See you soon.

                           Little Brother
P.S. Last but                Bill
not least I've
been running 3
miles a day to get
in shape and lose some
weight.
1969-04-15.attribution: Letter, Bill Ducy — Ducy Family Archives

1969-04-27.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1969-04-27.text:
4/27/69

Mike,

I got your letter last Wednesday with the check in it. I picked up your watch that day. I also got a twist-o-flex of band for it. It was a $6.00 band for only $3.00.

I guess you know by now that I'm getting out the 1st of June, but it'll really be on the 2nd since the 1st is on a Monday. But anyway I'm getting out. 35 days to go!

I sent off a letter to that co. in Mon about my sunglasses the 24th, its really pissed me off not getting them yet.

We've been having really good weather this past week. I layed out in the sun for about 2 hrs. today and got a little red.

Me and a buddy of mine went down to the local skeet range to shoot. Boy those throwers they've got really send those clay pig. out fast. The guy that runs the place said they leave the trap going 65 MPH. and I believe it. It only cost $1.70 for the shells & birds. Which ain't to bad.

Also last night I went bowling and got a 252 score on one game. and the total of 3 games was 557. I was really happy with that 252.

Well I'd best be going for now, its almost 10:00 PM and lights go out then. So take care.

SHORT                          Little Brother
                               Bill

1969-05-20.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1969-05-20.text:
20 MAY 69

Mike,

Well here I am again.
I've started checking out of the USMC. Boy I can hardly waite til I get out.

Here is the list of records that I've got. Most of them are $2.90 and a couple $3.40, cause they've a poster in them.

Well hows your new job doing? I hope fine.

I've only got 3 more welding classes left, then I'll be set for some good money.

Hey could you ask Jackie to check on Linda and find out why she haint written yet?

I've been going up to Maryland the past 2 weekends with a buddy, and have really been having some fun. He's got a 3,000.00 basement turned into a party room like. And we really get drunk.

Well thats about all thats new, see you in 2 weeks.

Little Brother
Bill

1969-10-18.label: Bill Ducy to Mike
1969-10-18.text:
Oct. 18, 69
Da Nang

Mike,

Well here Iam again, I got your letter about 3 days ago. Now Ive finely got time to write back.

How do you like this typewritter? Well Ibought it off a guy for $45. Its not a bad deal, its a Royal.

Guess what, Jim Dick was down to see me, hes now in Da Nang for duty about ½ mile from me at an ammo dump. We plan on meeting at the 327 PX Sun. for a few beers and some sea stories.

Its been raining like a son-of a-bitch the past 6 days. everything is wet and fucked up.

I got wiped out of my mind last night, boy that beer can really fuck you up fast if you havent had any for awhile. If you know what I mean.

I guess you are getting short, I just hope I can get that 6mo. cut when I leve here in Feb.

Yes, I can get thoes Jap. recorders at the PX, but they sell fast, but if Iam lucky I can get ahold of one. Iam getting some real good tapes off a buddy of mine in a few days. Ill send them home so they dont get fucked-up or swiped.

When am I going to make L/cpl? Well Id like to know to. Ive got areal good chance Nov. because they are going by time in grade instead of all that other bull-shit.

Well Id best be goin for now, take care and dont fuck all that pussy!!!!! 128 more days left over here.

Little Brother
Bill
Bill

PS. U.S.M.C.=
U.nesserry
S.hit &
M.assive
C.onfusion

NOTES
========================================================================================

Mike's mobilization directive was updated from NRTC Decatur to NRTC
Springfield, Illinois. This directive tells Mike where to report if the
Naval Reserve were mobilized (M-Day = Mobilization Day). It supersedes the
earlier directive (filed as 19670801 - Directive to Report For Active Duty)
which had assigned him to NRTC Decatur with onward assignment to Naval
Station San Francisco.

The cognizant type commander changed to CRUDESLANT (Cruiser-Destroyer Force,
U.S. Atlantic Fleet) — this is notable since Jouett was a Pacific Fleet
ship under CRUDESPAC. Mike's reserve unit assignment may have shifted to
an Atlantic Fleet command structure.

LCDR B.R. Ness was the Commanding Officer at NRTC Springfield.

This was likely Mike's last mobilization directive before his reserve
obligation ended on March 17, 1971 (six years from his original enlistment
date of March 18, 1965).
